<meta>This page transitions from the blank protective flyleaf to the formal title page of Johannes Kepler’s seminal 1619 work. This is the first printed page of the volume, presenting the full scope of Kepler’s ambitious synthesis of geometry, music, and astronomy.</meta>

### Johannes Kepler’s
# THE HARMONY
## OF THE WORLD

### FIVE BOOKS, OF WHICH:

The First is **GEOMETRICAL**, On the Origin and demonstrations of the Regular Figures <note>The "Regular Figures" refer to the Platonic solids—geometric shapes like the cube or tetrahedron where every face is the same regular polygon.</note>, which constitute Harmonic Proportions.
The Second is **ARCHITECTURAL**, or from **FIGURED GEOMETRY**, On the Congruence of Regular Figures in a plane or a solid:
The Third is properly **HARMONIC**, On the Origin of Harmonic Proportions from Figures; and on the Nature and Differences of things pertaining to song, against the Ancients <note>Kepler refers here to his critiques of ancient Greek music theorists like Aristoxenus and Pythagoras.</note>:
The Fourth is **METAPHYSICAL**, **PSYCHOLOGICAL**, and **ASTROLOGICAL**, On the mental Essence of Harmonies and their types in the World; especially on the Harmony of rays descending from the celestial bodies to the Earth, and its effect on Nature or the <term>sublunary</term> <note>Sublunary: Literally "under the moon." In the science of Kepler's time, this referred to the Earthly realm, which was thought to be subject to change, unlike the "unchanging" heavens.</note> and Human Soul:
The Fifth is **ASTRONOMICAL** and **METAPHYSICAL**, On the most perfect Harmonies of the celestial motions, and the origin of <term>Eccentricities</term> <note>Eccentricity: A measure of how much an orbit deviates from a perfect circle. Kepler's discovery that orbits are ellipses is central to this book.</note> from Harmonic proportions.
The Appendix contains a comparison of this Work with Book III of the *Harmonics* of the famous Claudius Ptolemy, and with the Harmonic speculations of Robert de Fluctibus, called <note>original: "Flud"</note> Fludd, an Oxford Physician, inserted into his work on the <term>Macrocosm and Microcosm</term> <note>The Macrocosm and Microcosm: A traditional theory that the structure of the human being (the little world) mirrors the structure of the universe (the great world).</note>.

*NOW ADDED, DUE TO THE KINSHIP OF THE SUBJECT*
*matter, is a book by the same Author published 23 years ago at Tübingen, titled* The Forerunner,
*or* The Cosmographic Mystery, *on the causes of the Number of the Heavens, the Proportion*
*of their motions, and their Periods, from the five*
*Regular Solids.*

->With the Privilege of His <term>Sacred Imperial Majesty</term> <note>This refers to the Holy Roman Emperor, Rudolph II or Matthias, who granted Kepler legal protection against unauthorized reprinting.</note> for 15 years.<-

## At Linz in Austria,

->At the expense of **GODFREY TAMPACH**, Bookseller of Frankfurt.<-
->Printed by **JOHANNES PLANCK**.<-

### IN THE YEAR 1619.

<meta>This page begins the formal dedication of the work to King James I of England. It follows the blank verso of the title page. The catchword "uem" at the bottom right indicates the first syllable of the first word on the following page ("suauissimam").</meta>

# TO THE
## Most Serene and Most Powerful
### Prince and Lord
# LORD JAMES,
## Of Great Britain, France, and Ire-
## land King, Defender of the Faith,
## etc.

->*My Most Merciful Lord.*<-

**W**HY I should send these books of Harmony <note>original: "Harmonices." Kepler uses the Greek genitive form for his title, *Harmonices Mundi*.</note> to be published among men, sent away across the sea from the court of the most August Emperor <note>Referring to the Holy Roman Emperor, Matthias, whom Kepler served as Imperial Mathematician.</note>, my Lord, from his hereditary Austrian Kingdoms and Provinces, and finally from Germany itself, and why I should present them to your most serene sight, O Illustrious King: I had reasons partly present, and partly of old.

First, I did not think this foreign to my duty; so that because I earn the Emperor’s stipends in the Mathematical field <term>Mathematicâ</term> <note>Kepler's official title was *Mathematicus Imperialis*.</note>, I might demonstrate even to foreigners how much providence the Prince of the Christian Commonwealth <note>A reference to the Holy Roman Empire.</note> maintains for the most divine studies: so that it might be understood, from the undisturbed course of the ornaments of Peace through these provinces, that the sinister rumor of internal war <note>This refers to the beginning of the Thirty Years' War (1618–1648), which was just starting to devastate Central Europe as Kepler published this work.</note> will, along with the reality of it, no doubt soon be extinguished: and that this somewhat harsher Dissonance, as in a Pathos-filled Melody, is even now about to [break forth] into its [most sweet harmony...] <note>The sentence continues onto the next page.</note>

<summary>This page contains the opening of Johannes Kepler's dedication of "The Harmony of the World" to King James I of England, framing the scientific work as a product of imperial peace despite the gathering clouds of the Thirty Years' War.</summary>
<keywords>Dedication, King James I, Holy Roman Emperor, Harmony, Thirty Years' War, Mathematics, Peace</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Kepler’s formal dedication to King James I of England. It picks up mid-sentence from the previous page, where Kepler was describing the peaceful reign of the Emperor and the resolution of political discord into harmony.</meta>

<lang>English</lang>
<sig>D3</sig>

# D E D I C A T I O N .

[to be] a most sweet closing <note>original: "suauissimam Clausulam." This completes the sentence begun on the previous page.</note>. Indeed, whom could I judge a more worthy estimator of Imperial Goodness than a great King? Whom could I have chosen as a more fitting Patron for a work on the Harmony of the Heavens—redolent of Pythagoras and Plato—than that King who has testified to his study of Platonic wisdom in his own writings <note>original: "domesticis monumentis." This refers to King James I’s published literary and philosophical works.</note>, which we even hold in public for the veneration of his subjects? [A King] who, while still a boy, judged the Astronomy of Tycho Brahe <note>Tycho Brahe (1546–1601), the Danish astronomer whose meticulous data Kepler used to derive his laws of planetary motion. James I had visited Tycho at his observatory, Uraniborg, in 1590.</note>, upon which this work rests, to be worthy of the ornaments of his own genius? [A King] who, finally, having become a man and holding the rudders of his kingdom, noted the vanity of Astrology with public censure? Which vanity, truly, is most clearly exposed in Book IV of this work, where the true foundations of the effects of the stars are uncovered: so that it can be a doubt to no one that you will be the most intelligent judge of this whole Work and all its parts.

But a greater cause for this dedication comes to me from long ago. When first, a little less than <unclear>twenty</unclear> <note>The source text has a burn mark partially obscuring "paulò" (a little), but the context refers to the roughly twenty years since Kepler's first major work, the *Mysterium Cosmographicum*.</note> years ago, I conceived the material of this work in my mind and named its title—the specific motions of the Planets not yet being known, in which, however, an instinct of Nature dictated that Harmonies were present—even then I destined the patronage of the work to Your Majesty, if it should ever succeed and be completed; and this, as if it were my vow, I testified once and again to your Ambassadors at the Imperial court. 

The reasons for thinking of this patronage of my *Harmonies* were supplied to me by that manifold Dissonance in human affairs, manifest indeed, so that it cannot but offend; yet fused together from concordant and articulate intervals, the nature of which is such that it soothes the hearing in the midst of discord with the promise of a following sweet concord, and sustains it with that same expectation. For truly, it was a persuasion worthy of a Christian man that there is a God who moderates every Melody of human life; it is a patience worthy of the greatness of God not to be offended by the length of dissonances, nor to cast away hope; reflecting that [it is] not God...

<summary>Kepler argues that King James I is the ideal patron for his work because of the King's intellectual background in Platonic philosophy and his past support for Tycho Brahe. He also explains that he has planned this dedication for twenty years, seeing the "harmonies" of his work as a divine remedy for the "dissonance" of human conflict.</summary>

<keywords>Johannes Kepler, Harmonice Mundi, King James I, Tycho Brahe, Pythagoras, Plato, astrology, planetary motion, dissonance, harmony, Christian providence</keywords>

--- Page 15 ---
<meta>This page continues Kepler’s dedication to King James I. Having previously praised the King’s intellectual pursuits and his rejection of superstitious astrology, Kepler now connects the King’s political achievement—the unification of England and Scotland—to the cosmic principles of harmony that form the subject of this book.</meta>

->D E D I C A T I O N .<-

# D E D I C A T I O N .

providence acts slowly, but the span of our individual lives flies away swiftly. I was taught, indeed, by sacred oracles <note>original: "sacris oraculis." A reference to the Bible or divine revelation.</note>, that all things are destined by God for certain and beneficial uses: even these dissonant things, to illuminate and commend the sweetness of Harmony. Why my desires should command me to expect some beginning of restored harmony especially from your *Davidic Harp* <note>original: "Harpe Dauidicâ." This refers to King James's reputation as a scholar-king and poet, likening him to the biblical King David, a musician and unifier.</note>, *Illustrious King*, is not for this place to explain at length, lest I seem to disregard the warnings of the prudent. Yet, no one may forbid me to touch upon this part of the glory of your deeds, long ago confessed by the whole world: that having acquired the kingdom of *England* by inheritance and the consent of the people, you shortly gave to it the name of *Great Britain*, shared with the *Kingdom of Scotland*. From both provinces you tempered one *Kingdom and Harmony* (for what else is a kingdom, but *Harmony*?); you most happily removed the hereditary discord of the most hostile Nations; you utterly extinguished the memory of frequent and most bloody slaughters, by which, as if by certain marks, the series of centuries was punctuated. 

This domestic work of yours seemed to me to contain a sign (among other weightier matters) that was not untrustworthy: that even abroad, as a *King* among *Kings*, and a *Defender of the Faith* among the faithful of *Christ*, you would perform some greater, more excellent, and even more lasting work. This indeed I pursued both with my silent prayers and with a public omen in my *book on the new star* <note>original: "libro de stellâ nouâ." Referring to Kepler's 1606 work *De Stella Nova*, which discussed the supernova of 1604 and was also dedicated to James I.</note>, which burned like a *Carbuncle* <note>original: "Carbunculus." A reference to a glowing gemstone; Kepler mentions this was a well-known Scottish verse or heraldic reference associated with the King’s ascent.</note>. Therefore, as if what I hoped for and prophesied were already accomplished, I proposed all the more firmly to attune my own *Worldly Harmonies* <note>original: "Mundanas Harmonias." The title of the present work, *Harmonice Mundi*.</note> to such a praiseworthy *Harmonizer* <note>original: "Harmoştę." From the Greek *harmostes*, meaning a regulator or governor who brings order.</note>.

<margin>
<unclear>sidone</unclear>
</margin>

I would wish here that public *Dissonance*, of *voices* clamoring in *three ways* <note>original: "Vocum trifariam." Likely a reference to the three main religious/political factions of the era: Catholics, Lutherans, and Calvinists.</note>, were a little milder to me, so that I might be heard publicly according to the sentiment of my soul: in which matter, what outcome might have seemed to breathe upon my prayers? what wounds of the head, which...

->D E D I C A T I O N .<-

# D E D I C A T I O N .

...by all <term>Harmonies</term> attempted, and by which Physician: and how I even depicted this Physician in vivid colors long ago in my book on the <term>New Star</term> <note>original: "stella noua." Kepler refers to the supernova of 1604, which he described in his 1606 treatise. He often used astronomical events to reflect on earthly politics.</note>? But what reward will there be for the effort if, while striving for Harmony with my private noise, I do not overcome the public clamor because of the weakness of my lungs <note>original: "imbecillitate laterum." A common Latin idiom for physical stamina or the strength of one’s voice.</note>, and instead increase the annoyances of discordant sound in my own ears? It must indeed be confessed—alas!—that the cross-cut wound <note>original: "vulnus decussatum." Kepler is likely referring to the religious and political divisions of Europe, shaped like a cross.</note>—or if we prefer a more sacred and auspicious word, the *cruciform* wound—is still swollen with many lips; and since none of them are closing, the medicine has so far been ineffective and mocked on all sides. This is because the Physician, in order to deceive a delirious patient into taking the medicine, 
<margin><unclear>and none ...</unclear></margin>
adds many things at once, and many things that seem to deviate greatly from sound reason. I am revived, however, by this very thought: that the supreme Healer <note>original: "Curator." Kepler identifies God as the ultimate doctor of a broken world.</note> of our wounds is certain of His art, and applies nothing in vain. Therefore, He who has already begun the cure, who has already prepared and shown to the world these healing remedies <note>original: "consolidantia," referring to medicines that close wounds.</note>; meanwhile, through public calamities, He uses corrosive agents <note>original: "erodentibus," substances used to eat away dead flesh.</note> until—the putrid and wild flesh of extinguished charity being consumed—some sensation of pain reaches the depth of the living flesh. He will undoubtedly also use soothing treatments very soon to reduce the swellings, so that there may finally be a place for those healing remedies; and at last, this long-lasting **Dissonance** (to return to the proposed example) may end in pure and lasting **Harmony**. In this hope, even against hope, I am confirmed not only by the success of my Harmonic speculations—as one whose success far exceeds his boldness in searching—but also by this fact: that among other things necessary for the perfection of the Work, which for so many years have remained in their original place, I have seen Your **Royal Majesty**, to whom I had destined the patronage of this work before it began, safe and flourishing until now. Nor shall I cease to strive with devoted prayers to God, the author of Peace and Concord, that...

<summary>Kepler employs an extended medical metaphor to describe the religious wars of Europe as a "cruciform wound" that God, the supreme Healer, is currently treating with "corrosive" calamities to prepare for a final, harmonious healing. He expresses hope that King James I will remain a stable patron to see this cosmic and political harmony realized.</summary>

<keywords>Thirty Years' War, King James I, divine providence, medical metaphor, Harmony, New Star, religious peace, patronage</keywords>

--- Page 17 ---
<meta>This page concludes Johannes Kepler's dedication to King James I of England. It follows a sentence where Kepler expresses hope that God, the supreme Healer, will protect the King and his realm. The text transitions from theological reflection to a formal request for royal patronage and a signature identifying Kepler's official titles in Linz.</meta>

# D E D I C A T I O N .

...may [God] protect both your life and Royal Majesty in safety, until that desired outcome.
In the meantime, I humbly ask Your <gloss>Royal</gloss> Majesty, with reverence, to look upon this work on <term>Harmonies</term> <note>original: "Harmonices." Kepler's landmark work "Harmonices Mundi" (The Harmony of the World) explores the mathematical and musical relationships in geometry, music, and astronomy.</note>—dedicated to your Name—with a serene countenance, and to interpret this sign of my most devoted affection toward You as fair and good; and indeed, may you delight your Royal mind with the contemplation of the works of God, as much as the necessary duties of the Kingdom will allow; and by the examples of <term>Concord</term> <note>original: "Concordiæ." Here meaning harmony or agreement, particularly the mathematical order Kepler found in the heavens.</note> shining forth from the visible works of God, may you strengthen and stir up within yourself a zeal for Concord and for Peace, both Ecclesiastical and Political; and finally, may you deign to favor me and my studies with your most merciful Royal patronage. Given at <term>Linz</term> <note>original: "Lentiis Noricis." Linz was the capital of Upper Austria, located in the ancient Roman province of Noricum.</note> on the banks of the Danube, on the <term>Ides of February</term> <note>February 13th.</note>, in the year of the Western era 1619.

->*To Your Most Serene Royal Majesty*<-

->*Venerating with all submission,*<-

<header>ON THE HARMONY OF THE FIGURES: Preface.</header>

# ON THE HARMONY OF THE FIGURES:
## Preface.

<margin>Proclus on the intellectual essence of geometric things.</margin>
**S**ince we must seek the causes of harmonic proportions from the divisions of a circle into a certain number of equal parts—divisions which are performed geometrically and scientifically (that is, from demonstrable regular plane figures)—I have deemed it necessary to point out at the start that the conceptual <note>original: "mentales," referring to distinctions existing in the mind or as abstract categories</note> differences of geometric things are today, so far as appears from published books, entirely ignored. Thus, one encounters no one, even among the ancients, who indicated that they had exactly understood these specific differences of geometric things, except for Euclid and his commentator Proclus. To be sure, the distribution of problems into Plane, Solid, and Linear by Pappus of Alexandria and the ancients whom he follows is suitable enough for explaining the mental habits arising around each part of the geometric subject; yet that distribution is both brief in its wording and applied to practice, making no mention of theory. And truly, unless we occupy ourselves with our whole mind in the theory of this matter, we shall never be able to attain the harmonic ratios. Proclus Diadochus, in his four books published on the first book of Euclid, acted expressly as a theoretical philosopher regarding the mathematical subject. If only he had also left us his commentaries on the tenth book of Euclid! <note>Euclid’s Book X is notoriously difficult and deals with irrational magnitudes; Kepler considers this essential for distinguishing which proportions are "harmonic."</note> He would have freed our geometers from a neglected ignorance and would have entirely relieved my labor in explaining these differences of geometric things. For it is easily apparent from his very introduction that those distinctions between "Mental Beings" were sufficiently known to him, since he established the same principles for the whole of mathematical essence which also run through all Beings and beget all things from themselves: namely, the **Limit** and the **Infinite** (or the Bound and the Unbound), recognizing the **Limit** or the circumscription as the *Form* and the **Infinite** as the *Matter* of geometric things.

For Shape and Proportion are the proper characteristics of Quantities; shape of individual things, proportion of things joined together. Shape is perfected by boundaries; for a straight line is bounded by points, a plane surface by lines, and a body by surfaces; it is by these that it is circumscribed and shaped. Therefore, those things which are finite, circumscribed, and shaped can also be grasped by the mind; but infinite and indeterminate things, insofar as they are such, can be narrowed by no boundaries of demonstration and compared to no knowledge that relies on definitions. Furthermore, shapes exist in the **Archetype** <note>In Kepler's philosophy, the "Archetype" is the supreme internal blueprint in the mind of God used to create the universe.</note> before they exist in the Work, and in the divine mind before they exist in creatures—different indeed in the manner of their subject, but the same in the form of their essence. Therefore, for quantities, "Shaping" becomes a kind of Mental Essence, or intellection: their essential difference. This is much more clear from proportions. For since a shape is perfected by several boundaries, it happens that because of this plurality, the shaping makes use of proportions. Truly, what a proportion could be without the action of the mind can in no way be understood. And so, even on this account—that he gives boundaries to quantities as an essential principle—he posits that shaped quantities have an intellectual essence. But there is no need for argument; let the whole book of Proclus be read, and it will be sufficiently apparent that the intellectual differences of geometric things were rightly known to him. Even if he does not place this affirmation separately on its own in the open and conspicuous view so as to remind even the half-asleep reader; for his speech flows like a full riverbed, strewn on all sides with the most abundant maxims of the more recondite Platonic philosophy, among which is this singular argument of this book.

<summary>Kepler argues that musical harmonies are rooted in geometric shapes, lamenting that modern mathematicians have forgotten the "mental" or "theoretical" essence of geometry understood by ancients like Proclus. He asserts that geometry and proportion are not just physical observations but exist as divine "Archetypes" in the mind of God.</summary>

# ON DEMONSTRATION. BOOK I.

<margin>Petrus Ramus’s <note>Petrus Ramus (1515–1572) was a famous French humanist and reformer of logic who often criticized traditional academic authorities like Aristotle and Euclid for being impractical.</note> unfair and ignorant criticism of Euclid.</margin>
But in our current age, no one has yet found the time to penetrate such deep mysteries. Proclus's book was read by Petrus Ramus, but as far as the core of philosophy is concerned, it was despised and cast aside along with the tenth book of Euclid. Ramus, who had written both a commentary on Euclid and what seemed like a defense of him, was rejected and ordered to fall silent; truly, the anger of this hostile Critic was turned against Euclid as if he were a criminal. The tenth book of Euclid was condemned by a harsh sentence, to the effect that it should not be read—even though, if read and understood, it could reveal the mysteries of philosophy. Read, I pray, the words of Ramus, than which he never produced anything more unworthy of himself: *Mathematical Lectures, book 21. The subject matter, he says, proposed in the tenth book, is handed down in such a way that I have never discovered a similar obscurity in human literature or arts. I call it an obscurity not for the purpose of understanding what Euclid teaches (for that alone which is present and before one's eyes might be clear even to the unlearned and illiterate), but for the purpose of looking deeply within and exploring what the intended end and use of the work is, and what the genera, species, and differences of the subjects are; for I have never read or heard of anything so confused or tangled. Indeed, it seems as if Pythagorean superstition has been led into this cave, etc.* But by Hercules, Ramus, if you hadn't believed this book was too easy to understand, you would never have slandered it with such "obscurity." Great labor is needed, stillness is needed, care is needed, and a special attention of the mind, until you grasp the intention of the writer. When a noble mind has struggled toward that goal, then at last, seeing itself moving in the light of truth, it is drenched and exultant with incredible pleasure; and from that "watchtower," as it were, it perceives the whole World and all the differences of its parts with the greatest exactness. But as for you, who here act as the patron of ignorance and of the common crowd of men who hunt for profit from everything—divine or human—I say to you: let those things be *prodigious sophisms*; let Euclid be to you *a man who intemperately wasted his leisure*; let those *sharp points of his have no place in Geometry*; let it be your business to pluck at what you do not understand. As for me, who investigates the causes of things, no paths have opened to them except through the tenth book of Euclid.

<margin>Lazarus Schonerus <note>Lazarus Schoner (1543–1607) was a German mathematician and follower of Ramus.</note>.</margin>
Lazarus Schoner, following Ramus in his own *Geometry*, confessed that he could see absolutely no use for the five Regular Solids <note term="Regular Solids">The five Platonic solids: the tetrahedron, cube, octahedron, dodecahedron, and icosahedron. These are the only shapes where every face is an identical regular polygon.</note> in the World, until he read through my little book, which I titled *The Secret of the Universe* <note>original: "Mysterium Cosmographicum," Kepler’s 1596 work arguing that the distances between planets are determined by the five Platonic solids.</note>; in that book, I prove that the number and intervals of the Planets are taken from the five Regular Solids. See how the teacher Ramus harmed his student Schoner. First, Ramus, having read Aristotle—who had refuted the Pythagorean philosophy concerning the properties of the Elements being derived from the five solids—immediately conceived a contempt for the whole of Pythagorean Philosophy. Then, since he knew Proclus had belonged to the Pythagorean sect, he did not believe him when he affirmed what was most true: namely, that the ultimate goal of Euclid’s work, to which absolutely all propositions of all the books refer (except those leading to the Perfect Number), is the five regular solids. From this arose in Ramus the most confident persuasion that the five solids were to be removed from the goal of Euclid's *Elements*.

Once the goal of the work was taken away, as if the design of a building were removed, there remained in Euclid a shapeless heap of propositions, which Ramus attacks as if it were some ghost throughout all twenty-eight books of his *Lectures*, [with] great [things to be] said—

<summary>Kepler defends Euclid's Book X against the criticisms of Petrus Ramus, arguing that these difficult geometric theories are the key to understanding the structure of the universe and the five regular solids.</summary>

<header>ON THE HARMONY OF FIGURES.</header>

# ON THE HARMONY OF FIGURES.

<margin>Lazarus Schöner’s <note>Lazarus Schöner (1543–1607) was a German mathematician and follower of Ramus.</note> opinion on the five solid figures.</margin>
...with harshness of speech, great recklessness, and in a manner most unworthy of such a man. Following this persuasion of Ramus, look, Schöner himself also believed that the regular bodies <note>The five Platonic solids: the tetrahedron, cube, octahedron, dodecahedron, and icosahedron.</note> are of no use; and not only this, but he also neglected or despised Proclus, following the judgment of Ramus. From Proclus, he could have learned the use of the five bodies both in Euclid’s *Elements* and in the fabric of the world. Indeed, the student was more fortunate than the Master, because Schöner joyfully accepted the use of the bodies revealed by me in the *Fabric of the World* <note>Kepler refers here to his first major work, the *Mysterium Cosmographicum* (1596), where he proposed that the distances between the planets were determined by the five Platonic solids.</note>, which Ramus had rejected when it was emphasized by Proclus. For what does it matter if the Pythagoreans attributed these figures to the elements, and not, as I do, to the Spheres of the World? Ramus should have striven to remove this error of theirs regarding the true subject of the figures, as I have done; he should not have abolished this entire Philosophy with a single tyrannical word. What if the Pythagoreans taught this same thing as I do, but wove their opinion in veils of words? Does not the Copernican form of the World exist in Aristotle himself, though wrongly refuted by him under other names—while they called the Sun "Fire" and the Moon the "Counter-Earth"? <note>Kepler suggests that ancient Pythagorean concepts like the "Central Fire" were actually hidden references to a sun-centered (heliocentric) universe like that of Copernicus.</note>

<margin>The mystical interpretation of the Pythagoreans concerning the five figures.</margin>
For if the arrangement of the spheres was the same among the Pythagoreans as among Copernicus; if the five Bodies were known, and the necessity of their fivefold number; if they all constantly taught that the five bodies are the Archetypes of the parts of the World; how much is left for us but to believe that their opinion, read as a riddle by Aristotle, was refuted according to the literal sense of the words rather than their true meaning? While Aristotle reads "Earth," to which they gave the Cube, they perhaps meant Saturn, whose Sphere is moved away from Jupiter by the interposition of a Cube. Indeed, the common people ascribe rest to the Earth, but Saturn has been allotted the slowest motion, closest to rest; for this reason, even among the Hebrews, it obtained its name from "Rest" <note>The Hebrew name for Saturn is *Shabbatai*, derived from the root *sh-b-t*, meaning to rest or cease, as in "Sabbath."</note>. Likewise, Aristotle reads that the Octahedron was given to Air, when they perhaps meant Mercury, whose sphere is enclosed by an Octahedron; and Mercury is no less swift (being indeed the swiftest of all) than mobile Air is considered to be. By the word "Fire," perhaps Mars was suggested—which elsewhere is also named *Pyroeis* <note>original: "Pyroeis," from the Greek for "fiery."</note> from fire—and to it the Tetrahedron was given, perhaps because its sphere is enclosed by this figure. And under the veil of "Water," to which the Icosahedron was attributed, the star of Venus could be hidden (as its course is contained by the Icosahedron), because the humors <note>In ancient medicine and astrology, humors were bodily fluids associated with planetary influences; Venus was linked to moisture.</note> are subject to Venus, and she herself is said to have risen from the foam of the Sea, hence the name <term>Aphrodite</term> <note>The Greek name for Venus, derived from *aphros*, meaning "foam."</note>. Finally, the word "World" could have signified the Earth; and the Dodecahedron ascribed to the World, because the Earth’s course is contained by this figure, divided into twelve parts of longitude <note>Referring to the twelve signs of the Zodiac.</note>, just as that figure is contained by twelve planes in its whole circuit. Therefore, the fact that the five figures were distributed in this way in the Mysteries of the Pythagoreans—not among the Elements as Aristotle believed, but among the Planets themselves—is most strongly confirmed by Proclus, who handed down this purpose of Geometry: that it teaches how the heaven received suitable figures for its specific parts.

Nor is there yet an end to the damage that Ramus has done us; look at Snell, the most skillful of modern Geometers, clearly supporting Ramus in his preface to the Problems of Ludolph van Ceulen <note>Ludolph van Ceulen (1540–1610) was a Dutch mathematician famous for calculating pi to 35 decimal places.</note>. First he says, <margin>Willebrord Snell’s <note>Willebrord Snell (1580–1626) was a Dutch mathematician and astronomer.</note> opinion on Binomials:</margin> *that the division of ineffables into thirteen species is useless for practice.* I concede this, if he recognizes no use except in common life, and if no con-

...what the use of physical contemplations is for life. But why does he <note>Willebrord Snell (1580–1626), a Dutch mathematician mentioned earlier in the text.</note> not follow Proclus, whom he cites, who acknowledges some greater good of Geometry than the arts necessary for life? If he had, then indeed the use of the tenth book would have appeared in assessing the types of figures. Snellius cites geometric authors who do not use Euclid’s tenth book. Truly, all those authors treat either linear problems or solid ones, and concern themselves with figures or quantities of such a kind that do not have their end within themselves, but clearly tend toward other uses, nor would they even be sought out without those uses. 

But regular figures are sought for their own sake as **Archetypes** <term>Archetypes: original models or patterns on which the structure of the world is based.</term>; they have their perfection in themselves and are among the subjects of plane problems, notwithstanding the fact that a solid is also enclosed by plane faces; similarly, the matter of the tenth book belongs chiefly to planes. Why then should things of a different kind be cited? Or why is merchandise estimated as cheap because Codrus <note>A character from Roman satire representing a poor man; here, a metaphor for someone concerned only with basic survival.</note> does not buy it to feed his belly, but Cleopatra buys it to adorn her ears? *Is such a torment fixed only for geniuses?* <note>Kepler likely refers to the "crux" or "cross" as a metaphor for a difficult intellectual puzzle.</note> Indeed, it is for those who vex the *Ineffable* <term>Ineffable: Kepler refers to irrational numbers (like the square root of 2) which cannot be expressed as a simple ratio of whole numbers, making them "unspeakable" in classical Greek mathematics.</term> with numbers—that is, by trying to speak them out. 

But I treat these types of figures not with numbers, not through Algebra, but by the reasoning of the Mind; truly because I have no need of them for calculating market accounts, but for explaining the causes of things. He <note>Referring to Snellius or Ramus.</note> thinks those subtleties should be separated from the **Systematic Instruction** <note>original: "Στοιχειώσει" (Stoicheiosei), referring to the foundational arrangement of Euclid's Elements.</note> and hidden away in libraries. He acts entirely as a faithful disciple of Ramus, and his effort is not misplaced: Ramus took the form away from the Euclidean building and pulled down the summit—the five bodies <note>The five Platonic solids.</note>; with these removed, the whole structure was dissolved, the walls stand cracked, and the arches threaten to ruin. Snellius therefore even takes away the cement <note>Here, Euclid's tenth book, which provides the logical proofs for irrational magnitudes needed to construct the Platonic solids.</note>, since it has no use except for the solidity of the house joined together under the five figures. 

O happy understanding of the disciple, how skillfully he learned to understand Euclid from Ramus! That is, they think they are called **Elements** <note>original: "Στοιχεῖα" (Stoicheia)</note> because there is found in Euclid an all-encompassing abundance of propositions, problems, and theorems for every kind of quantity and the arts concerned with them; whereas the book is called **Elements** <note>original: "Στοιχειώσις" (Stoicheiosis)</note> from its form, because the following proposition always relies on the preceding one, all the way to the last of the last book (and partly of the ninth), which cannot do without any of the prior ones. They turn the Architect into a forest-keeper or a timber-merchant, thinking that Euclid wrote his book for the sake of serving all others, while he himself alone would have no house of his own. But enough of these matters in this place; I must return to the main point of the discourse.

<margin>The occasion for this Book I.</margin>
For when I saw that the true and genuine differences of geometrical things—from which I must derive the causes of Harmonic Proportions—are generally completely ignored; and that Euclid, who had handed them down with great care, was being driven out, oppressed by the quibbles of Ramus, and because of the disruptive noise of those behaving wantonly, he was heard by no one, or else was telling the mysteries of Philosophy to the deaf; and that Proclus <note>Proclus (412–485 AD), a Neoplatonist philosopher whose commentary on Euclid was vital to Kepler’s thought.</note>, who could have opened the mind of Euclid, unearthed hidden things, and made difficult concepts easy to grasp, was also held in ridicule, and had not continued his commentaries as far as the tenth book; I saw that I absolutely had to do this: first, to transcribe from Euclid's tenth book those things which especially served my present purpose; and to bring to light the sequence of matters in that book, with certain divisions interspersed.

<header>ON THE HARMONY OF FIGURES</header>

...I might bring forth and indicate the reasons why certain parts of the divisions were omitted by <term>Euclid: the ancient Greek "Father of Geometry" whose "Elements" remains the foundation of the field</term>; then, finally, the figures themselves had to be addressed. In cases where they were demonstrated most clearly by <term>Euclid</term>, I was satisfied with a simple citation of the propositions. However, many things that were demonstrated by <term>Euclid</term> in another way were repeated here for my proposed goal—namely, for the comparison of knowable and unknowable <note>In this context, "knowable" (scibilium) refers to figures that can be constructed using only a compass and straightedge, which Kepler links to the "knowable" proportions of the divine mind.</note> figures—or things that were separate had to be joined, or the order had to be changed. I have organized the series of Definitions, Propositions, and Theorems with continuous numbering, as I did in my <term>Dioptrics: Kepler's 1611 work on the theory of lenses and optics</term>, for the convenience of citations. Even in the <term>lemmas: a "helping theorem" used as a stepping stone to a larger proof</term> themselves, I was not overly precise, nor was I too worried about specific vocabulary, being more intent on the things themselves; for I am no longer acting as a Geometer in the realm of Philosophy, but as a Philosopher in this part of Geometry. And I truly wish I could have discussed these geometric matters even more popularly, provided it were also more clear and tangible. But I hope that fair-minded readers will think well of my effort in both respects: both that I hand down these Geometrics in a popular style, and that I could not entirely overcome the obscurity of the material through my diligence. To those readers, I give this final piece of advice: if they are entirely unskilled in Mathematical matters, they should skip over my narrations and read only the propositions, from XXX until the end; and, having placed faith in the propositions themselves without the demonstration, let them proceed to the other books, especially to the last; lest, terrified by the difficulty of the Geometric arguments, they deprive themselves of the most delightful fruit of Harmonic contemplation. Now, with God's help, let us approach the matter.

# On the Demonstrations of
### Regular Figures.

## I. Definition.

**A** plane figure is called regular which has all sides and all angles, facing outward, equal to one another.

<margin>
As here in **QPRO**, the sides **QP, PR, RO, OQ** are equal, and the angles **QPR, PRO, ROQ, OQP** are equal.
</margin>

## II. Definition.

**O**f these figures, some are primary and radical, which do not exceed their own boundaries, and to which the given definition properly applies. Some are "augmented," which, as it were, exceed their own sides; this happens by continuing the non-adjacent sides of some radical figure until they meet. These are called <term>Stars: Kepler was the first to mathematically define and name these "star polygons," such as the pentagram</term>,

<meta>catchword: Ut bis (meaning: "As twice")</meta>

<summary>Kepler explains his philosophical approach to geometry, prioritizing the "knowable" nature of shapes over rigid academic style, before defining regular polygons and introducing the concept of star polygons.</summary>
<keywords>Euclid, Dioptrics, regular figures, star polygons, knowable vs unknowable, harmonic contemplation, geometry, definitions</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Johannes Kepler’s geometric foundations in Book I. Having previously discussed his philosophical approach and the legacy of Euclid, he now moves into formal definitions and propositions concerning regular polygons, star polygons, and the criteria for their construction and inscription within circles.</meta>

<header>ON DEMONSTRATION. BOOK I.</header>

*Just as here A B C D E is a perfect pentagon <note>original: "quinquangulum"</note>, and is a primary figure, not requiring any other perfect figure from which it might be produced by the extension of its sides.*

*But F G H I K is a five-pointed star <note>original: "stella quinquangula"</note>, and an enlarged figure, formed by extending pairs of non-adjacent sides—for example, AB and DC—until they meet at point L.*

## III. Definition.

**S**emi-regular figures are those which, while having varying angles, have four equal sides, such as the Rhombi <note>A rhombus is a diamond shape where all sides are equal, but the angles are not 90 degrees.</note> NMPO and GEKD.

## IV. Proposition.

**A**ll Regular figures can, with all their angles at once, rest upon <note>In modern geometry, we say the figure is "inscribed" in the circle.</note> the same circle.

*For by Proposition 21 of the Third Book of <term>Euclid: the ancient Greek mathematician whose "Elements" defined the rules of geometry</term>, all equal angles can be inscribed in the same segments of a circle, and likewise in equal segments of the same circle. However, all angles of a Regular figure are equal; therefore, all the angles of a single figure can be inscribed in equal segments of a single circle. But it is also necessary that they all be actually inscribed once one is inscribed. For all sides are equal; therefore the segments of the circle which are cut off by the two sides of a single angle are also equal, according to Proposition 24 of the Third Book of <term>Euclid</term>. Thus, both the angle and the endpoints of the sides coincide simultaneously on the same circle. Moreover, the endpoints of the sides are themselves the angles. It would be otherwise if, despite the angles being equal, the sides were not equal: for then the necessity of inscribing all the points would be dissolved.*

## V. Definition.

To **D**escribe a Figure is to determine by a geometric act the proportion of the lines subtending the angles <note>lines that connect the corners of the shape through its interior</note> to the "legs" or sides of the angle; from these determined proportions, to construct the elementary triangles of the figure; and from these joined triangles, to complete the figure itself.

*For given the proportion of DA to AE and ED, the triangles DAE, DAC, and CAB are formed: from which the figure is composed.*

<meta>catchword: VI. Of</meta>

<summary>Kepler defines regular pentagons versus star polygons and proves that any regular polygon can be perfectly inscribed within a circle. He also establishes his method for "describing" a figure by breaking it down into its constituent elementary triangles.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Kepler’s geometric foundations from Book I. Following the previous page’s discussion on the properties of regular and semi-regular polygons, Kepler now transitions into the formal definitions of what it means to "inscribe" a figure and, crucially, what it means to "know" a geometric quantity in a mathematical sense.</meta>

<header>ON THE HARMONY OF FIGURES.</header>

## VI. Definition.

1 **T** o **inscribe** a Figure in a circle is to determine, by a <term>geometric act: a construction performed using only a straightedge and compass</term>, the proportion of the side of the figure to the diameter of the circle in which it is to be inscribed; once this proportion is established, the proposed figure is easily drawn within the circle.

*As in the case where LD is given as the radius <note>original: "semidiameter"</note>, or its double as the diameter; if we know what must be done with it to grant the side DE its proper length, we can afterwards easily complete the figure by repeating that length DE around the circumference.*

## VII. Definition.

5 **T** o **know** in geometric matters is to measure by a known measure; in this business of inscribing figures in a circle, that known measure is the diameter of the circle.

## VIII. Definition.

5 A thing is said to be **knowable** <note>original: "Scibile"</note> which is either immediately measurable by the diameter itself (if it is a line) or by its square (if it is a surface); or that which is formed at the very least from such quantities by a certain and geometric reasoning, which, however long the series of steps may be, ultimately depends upon the Diameter or its square. In Greek, this is called *gnōrimon* <note>original: "γνώριμον," meaning "known" or "familar" to the mind</note>.

## IX. Definition.

**A** **demonstration** is the deduction of a quantity—whether it is to be described or known—from the Diameter, through possible intermediate steps. In Greek, this is called a *porisma* <note>original: "Πόρισμα," usually referring to a corollary or a geometric deduction</note>.

*Thus, a demonstration commonly produces either a description or knowledge. A Description indeed offers the bare quantity, but knowledge further professes the quality or the certain quantity. Moreover, a certain line can be geometrically determined—in Greek, taktē <note>original: "τακτή," meaning ordered or fixed</note>—which nevertheless may not yet be "known" by an act of the mind as to what kind of line it is. Conversely, some quality of one or more lines may be known, which nevertheless does not yet determine or necessitate them: namely, if that quality is common to many other things that differ in quantity. Furthermore, the description of certain lines is easy, while the knowledge of them is most difficult. Finally, many things can be described by some kind of geometric act, yet by their own nature they cannot be "known," according to how we defined "knowable" above.*

<summary>Kepler defines the geometric concepts of "inscribing," "knowing," and "demonstration," establishing the diameter of a circle as the fundamental unit of measure for all geometric knowledge. He distinguishes between the simple act of drawing a figure (description) and the deeper mathematical understanding of its properties (knowledge).</summary>

<meta>This page continues Johannes Kepler’s definitions in Book I of *The Harmony of the World*. Having defined what it means for a figure to be "knowable" (Definition VIII) and what a "demonstration" is (Definition IX), Kepler now distinguishes between "proper" and "improper" demonstrations and begins to categorize the various degrees of geometric knowledge based on how a figure relates to the diameter of a circle.</meta>

<header>ON DEMONSTRATION. BOOK I.</header>

## X. Definition.

**P**roper demonstration is when the number of angles of a Figure (or of one related to it by a double or half number of sides) is the <term>middle term: a logical link in a syllogism that connects the starting premise to the conclusion</term> for determining the proportion which the side has to the Diameter.
*For every regular figure is either a triangle itself, or is resolved into triangles by drawing diagonals. Since every such triangle has three angles equal to two right angles, in a Triangle <note>original: "Trigonico"</note> the angle is a third part; in the smallest angle of the elementary Square <note>original: "Tetragonici"</note>, a fourth part; in the Pentagon, a fifth part; in the Heptagon, a seventh part, etc., of two right angles <note>Kepler is referring to the central angle or the angle governing the construction; for a triangle, 1/3 of 180° is 60°, which defines its shape</note>. And from this quantity of the angle, the demonstration of each figure begins.*

## XI. Definition.

**I**mproper demonstration is when the proportion of the side to the diameter cannot be determined Geometrically from the number of angles applied directly, unless the side of another figure is employed that does not have a double or half number of sides.

## XII. Definition.

**T**here are different degrees of knowledge <note>original: "scientiae"</note>: some remote, others near. The first and nearest degree is when I know and am able to demonstrate that some line is equal to the diameter, or a plane (though formed differently) is equal to the square of the diameter.
*Here the known measure measures the knowable perfectly, that is to say, by itself and in one single act.*

## XIII. Definition.

**T**he second degree is when, the diameter having been divided into a certain number of equal parts (or its square similarly divided), the proposed line or plane is equal to such a part or parts. Such a line is called in Greek *rhētē mēkei* <note>original: "ρητὴ μήκει"</note>, **Expressible in length**. A plane of this kind is simply called *rhēton* <note>original: "ρητὸν"</note>, **Expressible** <note>In modern geometry, these are often called "rational" quantities, meaning they can be expressed as a ratio of whole numbers</note>. For number is the language of Geometers.
*We arrive at this degree of knowledge either through description and inscription, or also by relationship with some other quantity which was reached through those means. Therefore, this quality does not determine just one single quantity; for it is not enough for determination to know that something is compared in this or that way for the sake of commensuration; one must also know this: in what way, that is, by what number it is Expressible.*

## XIV. Definition.

**T**he third degree is this: when a line is **Inexpressible** <note>original: "Ineffabilis"</note> in length, but its square is **Expressible** <note>original: "Effabile"</note> and belongs to the second degree. It is called <term>expressible in power: ῥητὴ δυνάμει</term> <note>original: "Effabilis potentiâ"</note>.

## XV. Definition.

<margin>What "Irrational" means to Latin Geometers.</margin>
<margin>Surd Numbers.</margin>
**A**ll the degrees that follow are called <term>Ineffable: Ἄλογοι</term> <note>original: "Ineffabiles"; literally "without speech" or "without ratio"</note>. Latin translators have rendered this as **Irrational**, at the great risk of ambiguity and absurdity. Let us bury this use of the word, for there are many lines which, although they are "Inexpressible," are nonetheless governed by the best of reasons <note>Kepler is making a pun: just because a number is "irrational" in math doesn't mean it lacks "reason" or geometric logic</note>. Arithmeticians, using a similar metaphor, call them **Surd** numbers—that is, they speak no more than a deaf person <note>Latin: "surdus"</note> hears. However, under this name they include both quantities expressible only in power and those that are truly inexpressible. 

Therefore, the fourth degree in order, but the first of the Ineffables, is when neither the line nor its square are Expressible; yet the square can be transformed into a rectangle whose sides are Expressible at least in power. This line is called the <term>MESE: middle</term>, because it is the mean proportional between two lines that are expressible only in power and commensurable with each other: for instance, if one is Expressible in length and the other only in power; or if both are Expressible only in power, yet their powers are not to each other as a square number to a square number.

Such a line is not known or measured by the length of certain equal parts of the diameter, nor is its square measured by the square of the diameter. Furthermore, neither of the two lines between which the **MESE** is the mean proportional are measured by the diameter simultaneously; but the squares of those lines are, at last, measured by the square of the diameter.

The square of a **MESE** is itself called a <term>MESON: middle area</term>, whether it remains in a square form or is transformed into a rectangle. This is the second kind of Plane after the Expressible plane. By these two planes—the Expressible and the Meson—the following species are distinguished from one another.

## XVI. Definition.

**W**e now transition to other singular lines by the coupling of two lines, which themselves introduce new degrees of knowledge. For let either the diameter, or something commensurable with the diameter at least in power (and thus Expressible), or even some "Middle" <note>Mese</note> line, be cut. Let it be cut, I say, into two unequal parts; or let any two parts be compared from the sections of two such lines, whether they are composed of the parts themselves, or composed of their powers (either increased or diminished). I say two parts that are generally unequal: these will either be commensurable with each other in length, or indeed incommensurable in length but commensurable in power. Here, although the individual parts have clearly departed from commensuration, some of them, when joined—either by their squares being combined into one sum, or by a rectangle formed between them—still constitute planes which have hitherto been...

->ON THE DEMONSTRATION. BOOK I.<-

...fully explained, do so no less than those that are commensurable with one another. However, since there are many ways to pair two such completely incommensurable lines—one being lower-ranking <note>Kepler uses the word "ignobilior," implying a hierarchy of geometric "nobility" based on how easily a shape or line can be known or constructed</note> than another—we cannot assign all such pairs to a single degree.

## XVII. Definition.

**L**et the fifth degree of knowledge be when two lines are neither both **Expressible** <note>original: "Effabiles"</note> nor both **Medial** <note>original: "Mesæ"</note>, and are furthermore completely incommensurable with each other, yet together they produce "Expressible" results for both the sum of their squares and their shared Rectangle. This is no less than what is produced by two lines that are Expressible in length (according to Euclid, Book 10, Proposition 20), or even two lines expressible only in power, yet still commensurable in length with each other (according to the same source). For example, the side of a square of 2 <note>the square root of 2</note> and the side of a square of 8 <note>the square root of 8</note> are in a double ratio to each other, because their squares (2 and 8) are in a quadruple ratio. They are, therefore, Inexpressible in length, yet commensurable with each other. Their squares, 2 and 8, joined together make 10, an Expressible plane. And when multiplied by each other (which is to form a Rectangle), they produce the rectangle 4, which is also expressible. I maintain that this same result is produced by two lines that are neither Expressible nor Medial, and are furthermore completely incommensurable; therefore, they are not to be referred to the second or third degree of knowledge like those earlier examples, but to the Fifth.

Note, therefore, that in this degree we measure neither the lines themselves, nor the squares of each individually, but we measure both their shared Rectangle and the sum of their squares joined together; so that whatever one square lacks in being expressible is exactly compensated for by the other square joined to it.

## XVIII. Definition.

**T**he sixth and lower-ranking degree of knowledge is when two joined lines, which are neither expressible nor Medial, and are also incommensurable with each other, produce at least one result that is Expressible, while the other is Medial <note>original: "Meson"</note>. This is twofold: either the sum of the squares is expressible and the Rectangle is Medial; or the sum is Medial and the Rectangle is expressible.

*In the first effect, they are similar to two Expressible lines that are commensurable only in power. For both in power—that is, their Expressible squares—also produce an Expressible sum; but the Rectangle is Medial, according to Euclid, Book 10, Proposition 22.*

*In the second effect, they are similar to two Medial lines commensurable only in power, which are related to each other like two Expressible lines, between which the first of the two Medials is a mean proportional; according to Euclid, Book 10, Propositions 26 and 28. For because they are commensurable in power, when added in power they produce a sum commensurable with its parts. But the parts are Medial, and whatever is commensurable with a Medial is itself Medial, according to Euclid, Book 10, Proposition 24.*

<page-num>12</page-num>
<header>ON THE HARMONY OF FIGURES:</header>

Here we measure the <term>Rectangle</term> <note>In geometry, "measuring a rectangle" refers to finding its area by multiplying two lines</note> of two lines by the plane square of the diameter, but not also the sum of the squares: for we find for it only two lines forming a <term>Rectangle</term> equal to it, whose squares we may measure by the square of the diameter.

## XIX. Definition.

**T**he seventh degree of knowledge, even lower-ranking than the previous ones, is when neither of the two results produced by two incommensurable lines is expressible—neither the sum of their squares nor their shared <term>Rectangle</term>—yet both are still **Medial** <term>Meson</term> <note>A "medial" area is the square root of a rational area, essentially an irrational value that still maintains a geometric relationship to the original square</note>.

*These are similar in their effect: two Medials commensurable only in power, where one is to the other as one of those lines—between which a **Medial** <term>MESE</term> is truly a mean proportional—is to a third line, which is also commensurable only in power, according to Euclid’s Book 10, Proposition 29.*

*<term>Euclid</term> teaches how to find these three pairs, distinguished by two types of Planes, primarily because they contribute to the composition and construction of the species that follow.*

## XX. Definition.

**T**herefore, the Eighth Degree of knowledge is derived from the preceding intermediate steps. It again concerns individual lines, but those which are constituted either by the composition of two "names" (that is, two lines joined from the preceding pairs) or by the subtraction of one from another (called **Fitting Together** <term>Epharmozusæ</term> <note>original Greek: ἐφαρμόζουσα. In geometry, this refers to lines that are applied to or coincide with others, often used in Euclid’s construction of "Apotomes" or subtractions</note>), thereby creating a new species. Thus, in these cases, we know or measure not the whole lines, nor the squares of the whole lines, nor the two "names" of each individually, but rather their joined squares and their shared <term>Rectangle</term>, as in the preceding degrees 18 and 19. And although we could count as many degrees of knowledge as there will be species (of which the earlier is always "nobler" or more perfect than the later), nevertheless, because every composition or subtraction refers back to its own degree, and no diversity is created by the act of composition or subtraction itself—since all relate equally to their pairs of Names or Elements—we shall therefore establish only one degree for them; but let us recognize that its species are distinguished by their "nobility" <note>Kepler uses "nobility" to describe how close a geometric figure is to the "ideal" of rational, expressible numbers</note>.

## XXI. Proposition.

**I**t must be understood, however, that from two lines that are commensurable with each other in length, nothing arises that ought to be taken into account here: whether they were **Expressible** <term>Effabiles</term>, **Medial** <term>Mesæ</term>, or of a lower rank.

*For if they are commensurable in length, the whole composed of them will also be commensurable with its parts. But that which is commensurable with an Expressible line is itself Expressible.*

*...through the definitions before Euclid's Book 10, Proposition 20. Those lines commensurable to a <term>Medial</term> <note>original: "Mese"</note> are themselves Medials, according to Proposition 24 of the same book. And any line commensurable to one of the following <term>Irrationals</term> <note>original: "Ineffabilibus," literally "unspeakable" things</note> after the Medials belongs to the same species as that line, according to Propositions 66, 67, 68, 69, 70, 103, 104, 105, 106, and 107. And this is also the case with other more remote species not mentioned by Euclid, which constitute more remote degrees. Even if it were not so with those, it would not concern us here. For they either fall back into one of the species we have already established from the incommensurables—and thus do not increase the count—or they create lower-ranking <note>original: "ignobiliores," literally "less noble"</note> species of their own or of another genus; and so they do not belong in this place, where we are constructing degrees that are closest in nobility to those already mentioned.*

## XXII. Definition.

**H**aving passed over those lines which are commensurable in length, let us proceed to those which are commensurable only in <term>power</term> <note>Lines "commensurable in power" are those whose squares have a rational ratio to each other, even if the lines themselves do not</note>. If two such <term>Rational</term> <note>original: "Effabiles"</note> lines are added together, a **BINOMIAL** is formed; if one is subtracted from the other, the remainder is an **APOTOME**. There are six subordinate species of each, according to **Propositions 48 and 85 of the tenth book.**

If, however, two such <term>Medial</term> <note>original: "Mesæ"</note> lines are combined, forming either a <term>Rational Rectangle</term> or a <term>Medial Rectangle</term>: they become **BIMEDIALS** by addition, and **APOTOMES OF MEDIALS** by subtraction—the former being named "first" and the latter "second."

In this case, one cannot join a <term>Rational</term> line with a <term>Medial</term> line; for two such lines are simply incommensurable, a category that must be dealt with in the following section.

## XXIII. Proposition.

**T**here remain, therefore, lines that are plainly incommensurable with one another. Among these, certain pairs cannot provide the required effects; such are two Medials, or one Medial combined with one Rational.

*The former fail because of the low rank of the pair, and the latter because of their clashing Natures. See Euclid’s Book 10, Propositions 71, 108, and 109.* Therefore, no species of composition can be derived from these; only the lower-ranking lines remain for us, once the Rationals and Medials have been excluded.

## XXIV. Proposition.

**F**rom the first pair of such plainly incommensurable lines—namely those which, in the seventeenth proposition, were found to be knowable in the fifth degree—there is born again, by addition or subtraction, a <term>Rational</term> <note>original: "Effabilis"</note> result; and these are necessarily the **BINOMIAL** and the **APOTOME**, see Euclid’s Book 10, Propositions 112, 113, and 114. For instance, if both the sum of the squares of the Binomial and Apotome and their shared <term>Rectangle</term> are Rational, it is necessary that each <term>term</term> <note>original: "Nomina," the two parts of the binomial line</note> of the one be commensurable with the corresponding terms of the other, which does not happen in all BINOMIALS and APOTOMES.

*That two such lines, performing the two required effects, are necessarily made...*

<sig>XXVI</sig>

The **Binomial** and the **Apotome** <note>In Euclidean geometry, a Binomial is a line formed by adding two rational lines that are only commensurable in power; an Apotome is formed by subtracting one from the other.</note> are demonstrated in the same way that Proposition 33 of the tenth book [of Euclid] is demonstrated, provided that instead of lines "rational in power only" <note>original: "ῥηταῖς δυνάμει μόνον"</note>, lines "rational in length" <note>original: "ῥηταὶ μήκει"</note> are used; and where the word "medial" <note>original: "μέσον"</note> occurs, "rational" <note>original: "ῥητὸν"</note> should be placed: and finally, let the Definition of the Binomial and Apotome be compared.

That a **Rational** <note>original: "Effabilis," meaning a value that can be expressed or "spoken"</note> result is produced again from the addition <note>original: "compositione"</note> and subtraction <note>original: "abstractione"</note> of a Binomial and an Apotome—which perform the two required effects—is clear as follows. For since the sum of the squares is Rational, and the rectangle <note>The product of the two parts of the line</note> is Rational; therefore, for those parts joined into one, the square will consist of the square of each part and two common rectangles (that is, from two Rational parts). Therefore, the whole square will also be Rational; and thus the line composed of them, which is the <term>side</term> <note>The square root</note> of that square, is also rational. Let the Binomial be *lm* and its square *ko*; let the Apotome be *lt* and its square *tk*. Let *tk* and *ko* joined together be Rational, and let the Rectangle from *tl* and *lm* be Rational; then two such rectangles, *km* and *kx*, complete the square of the whole composed line *tm*, which square is *to*.

Regarding subtraction, it is proven in this manner. For if the line composed of *tl* and *ml*—that is, *tm*—is rational, then its half *tp* will also be Rational, acting as the Major Term <note>original: "Nomen," the first part of a binomial</note>, while *pl* is the Minor Term, and the other half is *pm*. Subtract from it *ms* equal to *tl* itself; the remainder *ps* will also be Rational, and the whole line *ls* will be double *ps*. But *ps* is the remainder after the subtraction of the Apotome *ms* from the Binomial *lm*. Therefore, the remainder becomes Rational.

## XXV. Definition.

**I** Therefore, from the second pair of the sixth degree **preceding in No. XVIII**, involving lines clearly incommensurable to one another, where the sum of their squares is Rational but their Rectangle is **Medial** <note>A "Medial" line is the side of a square equal to a rectangle contained by two rational lines commensurable only in power</note>; from their addition is born the **MAJOR** <note>original: "MIZON"</note>; from their subtraction, the **MINOR** <note>original: "ELASSON"</note>.
From the third pair, where the sum of the squares is Medial and the Rectangle is Rational, the line born from addition is named **POWERFUL OVER RATIONAL AND MEDIAL**; that from subtraction is named **MAKING WITH A RATIONAL A MEDIAL WHOLE.**
Finally, from the fourth pair of the seventh degree, **preceding in No. XIX**, where both effects [the sum of squares and the rectangle] become Medial; by addition it becomes **POWERFUL OVER TWO MEDIALS**, and by subtraction **MAKING WITH A MEDIAL A MEDIAL WHOLE.**

And behold the Origin of the twelve Euclidean species [of irrational lines], and the causes of their number. For Euclid did not think he should proceed further to more remote species—those which produce either the sum of squares, or the common Rectangle, or both, beyond the Rational and Medial categories—into "less noble" <note>original: "ignobiliores"</note> species.

## XXVI. Definition and Comparison.

Those things could have sufficed for us even for establishing the degrees of Demonstrations by which the sides of figures, necessary for us for **Harmonics**, are distinguished: were it not for the fact that other properties were added to those already listed; or rather, were it not for the fact that the properties listed so far were preceded by other, more noble ones, with which the degrees of scientific Demonstrations are enriched.

We have come to composition [addition] and abstraction [subtraction]; where we took lines to be added or subtracted loosely, with no necessity of a certain quantity imposed upon them. But if we now tighten the laws, by imposing a certain proportion on pairs—not indeed given such that those joined made one of the twelve species [of irrational lines]; but pairs given otherwise, specifically to one given straight line and its larger part to be found, such that the smaller part is to the larger as the larger is to the whole composed of both; or conversely, the Larger to the smaller, as the smaller is to the residue: that which remains when the subtraction of the two is made will not always result in a more remote degree, but as the case arises, we will fall back into one of the already explained species. Having made this return, we will compare the established line, which is by itself of the eighth degree, with lines of the fourth degree.

For just as in the fourth degree (Definition XV), two straight lines by their joint action formed a plane, from which, when reduced to a square, a line was born, called the <term>Mese</term> <note>original: "Meſe," the Greek term for the middle proportional in a geometric series.</note>: so now two straight lines, the Whole and one part, form the other part itself by subtracting, or two parts form the whole by adding. In the former case, the forming lines were commensurable with each other only in power; here, commensurability being dismissed, there succeeds an identity of proportion between the whole and the parts. In the former case, there was a similarity of proportion between the smaller and the line to be produced, and between the line to be produced and the larger; here also there is a similarity of proportion between the two lines to be produced, and between one of them and the proposed whole, in subtraction: but in composition, between one of those to be produced and the proposed [whole], and between the proposed and the other line to be produced. In the former case, therefore, given two lines, a Rectangle was given equal to the square of the line to be produced, and thus the plane came before the line; here on the contrary, once the two lines to be produced are formed, there finally follows equality between the Rectangle of the extremes and the square of the Mean, through Proposition 17 of the sixth book and Proposition 11 of the second book of <term>Euclid</term> <note>Euclid's 'Elements' is the foundational textbook of geometry; Book II, Proposition 11 describes the construction of the "extreme and mean ratio," now known as the Golden Ratio.</note>.

In the former case, the forming lines had squares commensurable with the square of the proposed straight line; here <term>Euclid</term> teaches, in Proposition 30 of the Sixth book, to take a square commensurable with the square of the proposed line—namely, five-and-a-half-fold <note>original: "ſeſquintuplum." In the geometric construction of the Golden Ratio, one uses a square that is 5/4 (one and a quarter) the size of the square of the original line's half; Kepler's term here refers to the specific ratio involved in this Euclidean construction.</note> of it—and from the side of this square to take away half of the proposed line, so that the part to be established in the proposed line remains. Once this part is taken from the proposed line, the other required part was left (or, when added to the whole, the third required part was also made). For all these reasons, these parts seem to be assigned to the fourth degree.

But at this point, the line is rendered more noble than the <term>Mese</term> itself, whatever position that proportion occupies; because the <term>Mese</term> depends on the proposed Expressible line by a longer chain composed of four links: but the parts of this...

# On the Harmony of Figures

<page-num>16</page-num>

They rely on their own proportion, which they have immediately to the proposed **Expressible** <note>original: *Effabilem*. In classical geometry, an "expressible" or "rational" line is one that can be measured or whose square is commensurable with a given standard.</note> line itself. And so it happens that there can be many **Medials** <note>original: *Mesôn*. A "medial" line is the side of a square equal to a rectangle contained by two rational lines commensurable only in power.</note>, all distant from the **Expressible** by the same degree; but the larger part in this proportion of the **Expressible** line itself becomes only one, and altogether for each line after the **Expressible**, it is one unique line. By this name, its demonstration is equated in a certain way to the first degree.

When, therefore, a proposed straight line is ordered to be the whole, and two such parts of it are sought, then this is called by Geometers the <term>section according to Extremes and Mean</term> <note>Now commonly known as the Golden Ratio.</note>. This name certainly implies that while an ordinary section of a whole into two parts does not otherwise look at a proportion—or if one part is compared to the whole in the same proportion as the smaller part is to the larger, then four terms are created (two extremes and two means)—here, on the contrary, only three terms are created: the whole and the smaller part are the two extremes, while the larger part is the single mean term.

It is also called, for the same reason, a proportional section. Modern writers call both the section and its proportion <term>Divine</term> <note>original: *Divinam*</note>, because of its wonderful nature and manifold privileges; the chief of which is that if the larger part is always added to the whole, the compound is again similarly cut; and that which was the larger part now becomes the smaller; and that which was the whole now becomes the larger part of the compound, according to Proposition 5 of the Thirteenth Book of Euclid.

## XXVII. Proposition.

Since, however, such a section has a place in all lines—in an <term>Expressible length</term>, in that which is <term>Expressible only in power</term>, in the <term>Medial</term> <note>original: *Mese*</note>, in the twelve remaining species already reviewed, and in all others—we have need in the present work for only two of its species, which coincide with the species explained thus far, according to the two lines to be cut. For it is either **Expressible** in length, or it is a <term>Greater</term> <note>original: *Mizon*. A specific type of irrational line defined by Euclid.</note> line. But if the line proposed for cutting is **Expressible** in length, the larger part of the section becomes an <term>Apotome of the fourth species</term> <note>A technical term for a line formed by subtracting one rational line from another, where the square of the whole is greater than the square of the subtracted part by the square of a line commensurable with the whole.</note>; and there corresponds to it a <term>Binomial</term> of the same fourth species, having names in common with it. But beware of being confused: that line is called the "larger part" in relation to the proposed line; but here the same is called an <term>Apotome</term>, not in relation to the proposed line, but qualitatively. If you ask what it is an apotome of, the answer is that it is the apotome of something which is commensurable only in power to the proposed line—specifically, one that can do [is the square root of] five-fourths of the proposed line.

*Let GA be the line proposed for cutting, and let it be Expressible in length. Let a right angle GAM be formed, and let AM be half of GA. Having joined the points G and M, with M as the center and the distance GM, let a semicircle PGX be drawn, and let AM be continued to the points P and X on its circumference. Let a square PO be formed upon PA. Therefore, the line GA is cut proportionally at point O. This AO, then, is the larger part of the proportionally cut GA; but the same AO (or its equal AP) is an Apotome, not of GA itself, but of MP or MG.*
