# ON DEMONSTRATION. BOOK I.

<margin>
It is very common among theologians that what involves a contradiction is impossible; and that God's knowledge does not extend to such impossible things, especially since these formal reasons of geometric matters are nothing other than the very Essence of God. For whatever is in God from eternity, that is one individual divine essence. It would therefore be, in a way, to know Himself to be other than He is, if He were to know those things which are incommunicable as if they were communicable. And what flattery this would be, for the sake of the unlearned who will not read this book, to defraud all others!
</margin>
...in the eternal simplicity: because by its own nature it is among the unknowable things. And yet there are some scientific properties of this non-Entity, as conditional Entities. For IF there WERE a **heptagon** <note>a regular seven-sided polygon</note> inscribed in a circle, the ratio of its sides would have such properties. Let it suffice to have given this warning.

<margin>
Albrecht Dürer's definition of the side of the heptagon.
</margin>
There are also other false propositions by geometers concerning the sides of figures of this kind, which even a more skillful **mechanics** <note>practical or applied geometry used by craftsmen</note> would refute; though they are thrust upon the youth for the sake of mechanics. For example, when the side $AC$ of a heptagon is set by **Albrecht Dürer** <note>The famous German Renaissance artist, who published a manual on geometry for craftsmen in 1525</note> as equal to the half-side of a triangle $AB$ in the same circle. Truly, this is too short, as even mechanics itself teaches. However, lest a too-crude manual experiment should deceive anyone, he will be able to detect the falsehood by this reasoning alone before setting his hands to work. The side of a triangle is proven to be **expressible in power** <note>original: "Effabile potentiâ." This means the square of the side's length is a rational number.</note> from the number of its angles; and therefore its half is also so. The side of a heptagon is NOT **expressible in power**, by the very fact that it is a heptagon; and because seven are neither six, nor five, nor three. For prime numbers produce <term>species</term> <note>fundamental geometric types or categories</note>; and species are incommensurable among themselves, nor is one the same as another.

<margin>
Of others.
</margin>
Concerning the **paralogisms** <note>logical fallacies or errors in reasoning</note> of **Carlo Mariano of Cremona** and **François de Foix-Candalle** <note>1512–1594; a French bishop and mathematician known for his work on Euclid</note> regarding the heptagon, see **Christopher Clavius**, *Practical Geometry*, Book VIII, proposition 30, and in the commentaries on Euclid’s Book IV, proposition 16.

This arena of study also stirred up the most illustrious **Lord Marquis of Malaspina**, Ambassador of the Serene Duke of Parma to the Imperial Court in the year 1614. With a most ingenious diagram, he surpassed all the descriptions of everyone else, believing that the chord subtending three-fourteenths of a circle was equal to five-quarters of the radius, and thus expressible in length. The apparatus of his demonstration was of such skill that even **Euclid** himself might not have noticed that something unproven had been assumed.

# Proposition XLVI.

The division of any arc of a circle into three, five, seven, etc. equal parts, and into any ratio which is not a continuous doubling of those previously demonstrated, is not within a **Geometric possibility** of the sort that generates scientific knowledge.

*Dividing an arc into two, four, eight, and so on—specifically by continuous doubling—is certainly Geometric, and has been used until now. <term>Trisection</term> <note>dividing into three</note> happens to occur for the whole Circle through the Triangle; and for the Semicircle, as in the Hexagon; and for the fourth part, as in the Dodecagon; and for the fifth part, as in the Pentadecagon; and for an arc of 135 Degrees, as in the Octagon; and for an arc of 108 degrees, as in the Decagon. Similarly, division into five happens to occur for the whole circle through the Pentagon; and for the semicircle, as in the Decagon; and for the third part of the circle, as in the Pentadecagon; and for an arc of 150 degrees, as in the Dodecagon. The same is true for the halves, quarters, and other parts of these arcs in the proportion of continuous sub-doubling. But this does not happen because of any inherent quality of Trisection or <term>Quinisection</term> <note>dividing into five</note>, but by accident, and because of other properties of figures discussed thus far.*

*But that indiscriminate trisection, or division into any other proposed ratio that is not continuously doubled, is impossible, is clear from a comparison with possible bisection. In bisection, the medium for the arc and the angle it measures to be bisected is a straight line subtended to the arc <note>a chord</note>, which can be Geometrically divided into two equal parts; since the equality of these parts is followed by the equality of the parts of any arc, whether small or large, with respect to the whole circle. It is from this same source that in a Triangle, one may argue from the equality of the sides to the equality of the opposite angles. But this "medium" <note>the chord</note> fails us in the other divisions. For even if a straight line subtended to an arc can be divided into any number of parts, and that Geometrically, it does not follow that any proportion of the parts of the chord (beyond the proportion of equality) results in the same proportion of the parts of the arc. Just as in a Triangle, it is not permitted to argue from any proportion of the sides (except for equality) to the same proportion of the opposite angles. For if a chord subtended to an arc is divided, for example, into three equal parts: if the dividing lines are perpendicular to the chord, the middle part of the arc will be smaller than the sides; but if the dividing lines originate from the center of the arc, the middle part of the arc will be larger than the sides. Therefore, between the [infinite] distance...*

# ON PROOFS BOOK I.

*...finite, and the center of the circle is the point from which two cutting lines, drawn out, would divide both the <term>chord</term> <note>original: "subtensam"</note> and its arc into three equal parts. That point, however, is always farther removed from the arc of the circle as the arc to be trisected becomes smaller, yet not in a constant proportion. Since the arcs of a circle can be diminished toward infinity, the distance of this point will also run out toward infinity. Truly, of the infinite, or of infinite variety, there is no scientific knowledge. And this difficulty holds for <term>Trisection</term> <note>dividing into three parts</note>, which is even simpler and closer to equality. A much greater difficulty arises in the following divisions of any arc—for example, into 5, 7, 9, 11, and so on, equal parts. In those cases, it is no longer even possible for there to be a single point from which a straight line could be drawn that divides the chord into the commanded equal parts and also divides the arc into the same equal parts.*

<margin>The nature of Bürgi's method for dividing an arc into several equal parts.</margin>
*Whatever aids we can bring to general division, derived from the number that names the division, must necessarily be general and common to the chords of any arc, whether large (which differs greatly from its chord) or small (which differs little). Yet, to leave the proportion of the parts of a chord to the parts of its arc vague is not to determine it scientifically. And let this be said especially concerning the <term>Bürgian Analytics</term> <note>The methods of Jost Bürgi (1552–1632), a Swiss clockmaker and mathematician who developed early algebraic and logarithmic techniques</note> regarding Trisection or <term>Quinisection</term> <note>dividing into five parts</note>, etc., which we treated extensively in the preceding Proposition. Although everything said there also applies here, some things said there are more specific to this place, and they become clearer and more remarkable in the division of arcs than in the division of the whole circle. For, to omit those common criticisms—that the starting principle is begged by commanding us to do exactly what we were asking how to do; that the properties of continuous quantity are not scientifically produced through discrete quantities or Numbers; that whatever number is elicited for the side determining the commanded part of the arc, it can teach nothing other than that the result is either greater or less than what is required—and just as raw and undigested matter relates to something formed, or as an indeterminate and undefined quantity relates to a figure, so too does that Analytic method relate to Geometric determinations. That method is especially excellent and noble in this semi-mechanical <term>Cossic</term> <note>From "Cosa" (the thing), an early term for algebra</note> art, but it is degenerate and cast down in scientific Geometry. Because every chord smaller than the diameter is associated with two unequal arcs of the circle, one smaller than a semicircle and the other larger; therefore, the chord of an aliquot part of the smaller arc is smaller, and the chord of an equal part of the larger is larger. This Bürgian Analytic prescribes something general not only for these two unequal arcs, but also for many other chords of the circle, which is useful for expressing all of them very closely in numbers. For example, in trisection, the law is this: If an arc is given (let it be 48 degrees) and its chord, and that arc is to be divided into three parts, each of 16 degrees; that is, the chord of this part must be found, or its proportion to the chord of the whole 48 degrees. Then I am ordered to make it so that as the chord of the whole is to the sought chord of the part, so is this part to a second proportional, and the second to a third proportional. Now I am ordered to triple the chord of the part and take away from it the third proportional; what remains is said to equal the chord of the whole. That is: from the given chord, let the third part be multiplied cubically, as a fraction; let the resulting number be added to the whole. Having been increased thus, the third part is a little smaller than the sought chord. For if this itself, multiplied cubically, is added again to the whole, the third part thus increased comes closer to the truth; and this continues on into infinity. By this process, one arrives gradually near the chord of 16 Degrees.*

## ON THE HARMONY OF FIGURES:

But if you set $n$ as a larger number to be cubed, and roughly as much as the compass indicates is owed to the third part of the remainder of the circle—after 48 degrees are removed, namely 312 degrees, of which a third is 104—then you will also complete the <term>chord</term> <note>original: "subtensam"; the straight line connecting the two ends of an arc</note> of arc 104, and its complement 256, in this manner. Nor is this all; but if you also add a full circle of 360 degrees to 48 and 312, you will find another chord for the thirds of those sums (namely 408 and 672, which are 136 and 224) through the same <term>Cossic Name</term> <note>original: "Nomen Cofficum"; 'Cossic' refers to early algebra, from the Italian 'cosa' meaning 'the thing' (the unknown variable). Kepler uses this to describe algebraic solutions.</note>. And in general, for as many units as remain in the sectioning number after two are removed, that many times one may add a whole circle, or the arc proposed to be cut, so that the chords of the new arcs may be tracked down by the same cossic name. From this, the vast difference appears between these cossic names and the <term>scientific degrees</term> <note>Kepler distinguishes between 'cossic' (algebraic/numerical) results and 'scientific' ones, which he believes must be based on the inherent, constructible properties of geometry.</note> which I explained in the preceding sections.

Can a more noble art not be found, by which the divisions of arcs of every kind might be achieved? I answer that if all the chords of the arcs to be divided are considered under a common notion, and if we possess only those aids which are common to all sought-after chords—such as any number of continued proportionals in the sought ratio—then no one can devise anything more noble; such a person merely repeats what has already been done and, in their confusion, posits a contradiction in terms. For from common principles, nothing specific to any individual case can be concluded.

But if we begin a discussion on the specific differences of the lines that are <term>subtended</term> by the arcs to be divided, the state of the question changes. In place of a "universal" division of an arc, we substitute the division of the whole circle by a **Regular figure**, which provides its own specific property to the proposed chord. We have already treated these Regular figures above and will do so more fully in what follows. Indeed, in this very question, we were seeking a means by which we might describe some of those figures. Since such a means ought by nature to be prior to the thing itself that is to be produced through it, we would surely be begging the question if we sought aid from the Regular figures to facilitate our "Means."

<margin>The universal arc divisions of Pappus and Clavius.</margin>
But here some adversary might object to me: that **Pappus of Alexandria**, in the fourth book of his *Mathematical Collections*, Proposition 31, provides the trisection of an angle by means of a **Hyperbola**; and in Proposition 35, the division of an angle in any given ratio by means of the **Quadratrix** and the **Spiral** <note>original: "Helicen"</note>. And **Clavius**, in Book 13, Proposition 25 of his *Practical Geometry*, performs the same by the **Conchoid of Nicomedes**.

Yet the discoveries of those authors establish no possibility for a "Universal Scientific Geometric Division." To make this clear, I will first explain the mechanisms of Pappus regarding trisection; then, I will bring to light the difference between those and scientific descriptions.

<margin>Pappus's trisection of an angle.</margin>
First, Pappus himself, in the preamble before Proposition 31, divides problems (which he calls *Geometretica* in a general sense, whereas "Geometric" has a specific meaning for us) into **Plane**, **Solid**, and **Linear**. He admits that the trisection of an angle cannot be achieved through **Plane** means (which, in my specific sense, are the "scientific geometric" degrees I have explained). For this reason, he rebukes the ancient Geometers for their ill-considered efforts, as they toiled here in vain.

He himself, therefore, achieves his trisection through **Solids** <note>In classical geometry, 'Solid' problems required the use of conic sections like the hyperbola or parabola, rather than just a straightedge and compass.</note>, but achieves universal division through "figured lines" <note>Linear problems required complex curves like the spiral, which were considered less 'pure' than circles and lines.</note>.

<header>ON THE DEMONSTRATION, BOOK 1.</header>
<sig>f 2</sig>
<meta>catchword: For (Nam)</meta>

# ON THE DEMONSTRATION, BOOK 1.

*The method of **Trisection** <note>The division of an angle into three equal parts—a classic problem that cannot be solved using only a straightedge and compass.</note> is as follows. Once the angle to be trisected is proposed, a perpendicular line is dropped from a point on one leg to the other leg, which is understood to determine the length of the legs. With the other leg made shorter, and with lines drawn parallel to the perpendicular—one from the first point and another from the proposed angle so that their meeting forms an angle—one then causes the surface of a **Cone** (a solid figure) to pass through the point where the perpendicular was dropped. Next, he inclines the Cone so applied, or makes it "nod," until its surface marks out a section on the plane called a **Hyperbola** <note>original: "Hyperbolen"; a type of smooth curve formed by the intersection of a double cone by a plane.</note>, which has those drawn parallels as its own **Asymptotes** <note>original: "Asymptotôn"; lines that a curve approaches ever more closely but never actually touches.</note>. Then, from that point where the perpendicular was dropped, using an interval that is double the first leg, he describes an arc on the plane, cutting the line of the Conic section. Finally, having connected the center of the arc with this common intersection, he draws a line parallel to it from the proposed angle. When this is done, he demonstrates that a third part has been cut away from the angle.*

*Pappus <note>Pappus of Alexandria (c. 290–350 AD), one of the last great Greek mathematicians of antiquity.</note> indeed makes this a **solid problem** <note>In traditional geometry, "solid" problems required conic sections (like the hyperbola) rather than just "plane" tools (ruler and compass).</note> in this way, by the use of a Cone, a solid figure. But insofar as a Conic section called a Hyperbola can be drawn on a plane even without a Cone—between given Asymptotes forming a right angle and through a given point between them—this same problem seems also to be classified among **Linear problems** <note>original: "Linearia"; problems involving more complex curves like spirals or quadratrices.</note>. For such a line is produced by geometric motion and a continuous change of intervals; that is, it is represented by as many points as you wish, in an indeterminate number. This is no less true than for the **Quadratrix** and the **Helix** <note>Two types of complex curves used by ancient mathematicians to square the circle or trisect angles.</note>, the lines by which he performs the Trisection and the All-variant section in Proposition 35. Such is Pappus's device.*

*What then shall we say? Is it not true that between given Asymptotes, through a given point, only one single Hyperbola is written, whether that happens by the "nodding" of a Cone or by the continuation of infinite points? Is there not only one single section of a circle with a Hyperbola from one side? Is there not one single and certain inclination of the line connecting the points of the Hyperbola to the diameter of the figure?*

*Indeed, I confess that all these things are necessary and certain, provided that the Hyperbola has already been drawn. For even earlier, in the analytic trisection of **Bürgi** <note>Joost Bürgi (1552–1632), a Swiss clockmaker and mathematician who developed a precursor to logarithms and worked with Kepler.</note>, there was a certain and necessary length or proportion of the **chord** <note>original: "subtensa"; the straight line connecting the ends of an arc.</note> of the established third part relative to the chord of the whole arc. But because we are not asking what the thing is once it is already done, but rather **how** the thing which is not yet done is finally to be done—so that it may exist—we therefore have nothing more from the **Solid** and **Linear** problems of the ancients regarding the required science of lines than we previously had from the **Analytic** doctrine of the moderns. To be sure, there is only one single line of a Hyperbola that can be drawn between placed Asymptotes through a proposed point in their plane. But before it is drawn, I am ordered to tilt a Cone over the point of application for a while, until the curve exists and is drawn. Or, without a Cone, I am ordered to change the lines which delineate the Hyperbola through continuous points for a while, until the Hyperbola is sufficiently prolonged. And those parts which fall in between the points already made, I am ordered to imagine as made. I am ordered on both sides to pass through that which exists by the **potential** of infinite division by means of a single **act** or motion; so that by this transition, that which lies hidden in that potential infinity might be reached, yet without the light of **perfect science**, such as the problems called **Plane** by the ancients possess.*

*Postulates of this kind are frequently used by the Frenchman **François Viète** <note>A founder of modern algebra who also worked on geometric constructions.</note> and the contemporary **Belgian geometers** <note>Likely referring to Adriaan van Roomen or Simon Stevin, who were known for solving complex geometric problems through numerical or mechanical methods.</note> in their solutions to those problems which are not solvable by their own nature, except **inartificially** <note>original: "inartificialiter"; meaning through mechanical, numerical, or trial-and-error methods rather than pure geometric logic.</note>—either through numbers or through geometric motions governed by a certain infinity of changes.*

*For when everything has been made ready that is thought to serve in making the mind certain: we shall hold the determination of that which is sought, whether it be greater or smaller than the truth, and always getting closer; as we said before regarding the Analytic trisection.* <note>Kepler refers to the "Analytic" or algebraic method of approximating a solution, which can get closer and closer to a value even if it cannot reach it exactly through geometry.</note>

<margin>There is no scientific transition from Planes to solids</margin>
*What I say is true regarding this solid problem of Trisection, as the very word "solid" warns us. For unless the proportion of the solids is given as it exists between two cubic numbers: we will not be able to measure the proposed solid by another known solid to inform the mind. This is because two mean proportionals* <note>Finding "two mean proportionals" is the geometric equivalent of finding a cube root, a problem that cannot be solved with only a straightedge and compass.</note> *cannot be established exactly in a plane. Although they can exist in cubes, there is no passage from planes to those cubes of any kind without the two means themselves; it is as if the bridge has been washed away.*

<margin>It is impossible to find two mean proportionals scientifically.</margin>
*And as for finding the two mean proportionals, others teach it through Geometric motion* <note>mechanical methods involving moving parts or sliding rulers</note>, *commanding what is unattainable regarding the certainty of an adequate Geometric act. Pappus himself also teaches it through Conic sections, to be expedited by the benefit of two proportionals, since even a Cone is a type of solid. Thus, the principle is always begged; and the bridge lies on the opposite bank.*

## Proposition XLVII.

**F**igures with an odd number of sides greater than 5 (except for the Fifteen-sided figure <note>original: "Pentekædecagono"; a 15-sided polygon is constructible because it combines the constructions of a triangle and a pentagon.</note>), along with the chords of several of their parts, and indeed their entire Classes, are all of the same status as the Heptagon <note>original: "Heptagonus"; a 7-sided polygon.</note> and the other figures with a Prime number of sides.

*For if the number of sides is odd and not one of the Primes: it is either the smallest multiple of two odd Primes; or the square of some Prime; or a multiple of one Prime and the square of another Prime; or a multiple of multiples or squares, either separately or joined.*

*But if these figures were describable, inscribable, and knowable; then they would either have a proper demonstration from their angles, or an improper one from a comparison with the figures with which they share properties. But they do not have a proper one, because they do not have a Prime number of sides from which a demonstration could be formed. They do not have an improper one—neither the first type, for example, the Twenty-one-sided figure* <note>original: "Unetvigintangulum"; a 21-gon.</note>, *because the figures sharing properties with them (either both or one of them, such as the Heptagon here, following the Triangle and Pentagon from which the Fifteen-sided figure is made) have no proper demonstration, according to the preceding Proposition 45; nor the second type, for example, the Nine-sided figure* <note>original: "Nonangulum"; a nonagon.</note>, *because a section of some arc (say, a third part) into as many equal parts as the whole circle received is not possible, according to the preceding Proposition 46; nor the third or fourth types, because the earlier figures sharing properties with them are unprovable.*

<margin>The side of the Nonagon is not knowable</margin>
Concerning the Nine-sided figure <note>original: "Enneagono"; another term for nonagon.</note>, whose number 9 is the square of the first odd Prime among Primes (namely, three), Geometers have struggled until now, with many striving to demonstrate even the side of this figure. However, they were all in vain, and they would never have attacked this problem if they had paid attention to the distinction between the knowable and the unknowable.

<margin>Campanus on the Nonagon</margin>
Campanus <note>Campanus of Novara (c. 1220–1296), a mathematician famous for his commentary on Euclid.</note> wanted to demonstrate the Nonagon through the Trisection of an angle, which was shown to be unknowable in the preceding Proposition 46. Even if it is necessarily trisected by the method of Pappus and Clavius <note>Christopher Clavius (1538–1612), a Jesuit astronomer and mathematician.</note>—granted, that is, the use of Geometric motion—what is that to the plane figures we are dealing with here? For solids are needed to act as assistants for the trisection...

...lines, the Hyperbola, the Quadratrix, the Spiral, or the Conchoid? <note>These are "mechanical" curves that Kepler distinguishes from "geometrical" ones (circles and straight lines) because they cannot be drawn with a simple compass and straightedge.</note> Even Campanus <note>Campanus of Novara, a 13th-century mathematician famous for his commentary on Euclid.</note> himself, while attempting the trisection of an angle, did not notice that he was assuming the third part of the angle was already a certainty, when that was the very thing to be sought. There is a passage in my own copy at the end of Euclid's work on page 586, pertaining to the end of Book IV.

Giordano Bruno of Nola <note>A famous Italian philosopher and mathematician. Kepler often disagreed with his geometric "proofs."</note> in the opposite sides $BC$ and $EF$ of a hexagon $ABCD EF$, extended on both sides, draws perpendiculars $GH$ and $IK$, touching the circle at $AD$. Then, having drawn the diagonal $IH$ of the resulting parallelogram, he thought the circle was cut such that between the points of contact $AD$ and the points of intersection $M$ and $N$, there exist ninth parts of the circle, $AN$ and $DM$. Yet it is demonstrated from the diagram that since the square of that semi-diagonal $LH$ is "expressible in power" <term>effabilis potentiâ <gloss>A term from Euclid meaning a line whose square is a rational number relative to another square.</gloss></term>—namely, 7 sixteenths of the square of the diameter—for angle $ABH$ is 60 degrees; therefore $BH$ is half of $AB$, or $AL$; and its "power" <note>In this context, "power" refers to the area of the square built upon the line segment.</note> therefore, is one quarter of the power of $AL$;

<margin>Giordano Bruno's Nonagon.</margin>

Therefore the power of $AH$ is three-quarters <note>original: "dodrans"</note> of the power of $AL$. But the power of $LH$ equals the powers of $LA$ and $AH$ combined. Consequently, the sine of 40 degrees—which is half the chord of two-ninths of the circle—would have to be "expressible in power," specifically the square root of three twenty-eighths of the square of the diameter. For by dropping the perpendicular $AO$ from $A$ onto $LH$, as the power of $LH$ (7 sixteenths) is to the power of $HA$ (3 sixteenths), so the power of $LA$ (4 sixteenths) is to the power of $AO$, which is 12 sevenths of one sixteenth—that is, three twenty-eighths. Thus this chord of the nonagonal angle would be "nobler" than certain premises, and commensurable with them; even though it has an odd number of sides—specifically, a number [9] produced by the first prime [3] squared—having nothing in common with the **Square** <term>Tetragon</term> and **Triangle** <term>Trigon</term> through the bisection of arcs, which are the figures to which this degree of "nobility" <note>Kepler uses "nobility" to describe figures that can be perfectly constructed and known by the human mind.</note> properly belongs.

### XLVIII. Corollary.

**I**t follows, therefore, that the boundaries of Conception, Science, Determination, Description, and Demonstration consist within the first Orders of figures: so that there are no more than four classes of knowable figures. Three have their own proper demonstrations, in which the heads of the families are: in the first, the **Square** <term>Tetragonus</term>, following the diameter of the circle, whose character is the number 2; in the second, the **Triangle** <term>Trigonus</term>, whose character is 3; in the third, the **Pentagon** <term>Pentagonus</term>, with character 5. There is also one class of "improper" demonstrations, whose number is a multiple of two of these, 3 and 5: namely 15. For the first figure of that class is the **Pentadecagon** <term>Pentekædecagonus</term>.

### XLIX. Proposition.

**S**ince, however, bisection (which the first proper class uses) is common to both the second and third classes, it is clear that the first class exists by one law, and the remaining two by another; so that the first has a familiarity with both of the others, while those two [are set] against each other in their configurations...

<meta>catchword: distin- (distinguished)</meta>

<summary>Kepler refutes Giordano Bruno's attempt to construct a nine-sided figure (nonagon), proving mathematically that such a construction is "unknowable" through geometry. He then categorizes all constructible polygons into four distinct classes based on the numbers 2, 3, 5, and their product 15.</summary>

distinguished, so much so that of those which have their own proofs, there are in a certain way only two Classes.

*For the Square and Octagon immediately attach themselves, as if in their entirety, to the Triangular sect; because the sixth and twelfth parts of a circle joined together make a fourth part <note>1/6 + 1/12 = 3/12 = 1/4 (the square)</note>, and the twelfth and twenty-fourth parts, when combined, make an Eighth part <note>1/12 + 1/24 = 3/24 = 1/8 (the octagon)</note>. And the Square accommodates itself in a certain way to the Pentagonal sect; because a fifth part of the circle, with a twentieth added, constitutes a fourth part <note>1/5 + 1/20 = 5/20 = 1/4</note>. The cause is that the Numbers 3 and 5 can be divided into numbers of a continuous double proportion: for the parts of 3 are 1 and 2; the parts of 5 are 1 and 4 <note>Kepler is noting that 3 = 2^0 + 2^1 and 5 = 2^0 + 2^2, linking them to the binary divisions used in geometry and music</note>. But such a communion does not exist between the classes of Three and Five. For although a sixth part of the circle, added to a thirtieth, constitutes a fifth: yet the thirtieth is of the Fifteen-sided class <term>Pentekadecagonic <gloss>From the Greek 'pentekaideka' (fifteen) and 'gonia' (angle).</gloss></term>, which does not have its own independent proof. In the same way, the tenth of a circle, added to the fifteenth (behold the mixture of the fourth class) makes a sixth. Because of this duality of Classes, the characteristic numbers are, in the first 1 and 2, and in the second 20, or its half, 10. These things, therefore, are to be recalled below in Book III and assigned to the distinction of the genres of song.*

## 50. Comparison of Figures
### or the divisions of the circle.

**T**he diameter holds the first rank; for it is expressible <term>effabilis <gloss>In Euclidean geometry, a line whose length can be expressed as a rational number relative to a given unit.</gloss></term> in length. Second is the side of the Hexagon, which is equal to the semi-diameter <note>The radius</note>, and is thus expressible in length. In the third place stand the Square and Triangle, because they have sides that are expressible only in power <note>Their lengths are irrational (like the square root of 2 or 3), but their squares are rational numbers</note>. The fourth rank is held by the sides of the Dodecagon (12-sided), the Decagon (10-sided), and their associated star-polygons; for they are among those inexpressible in power, being Compounds of the first species—namely, Binomials and Apotomes <note>Euclidean terms for specific types of irrational numbers formed by adding or subtracting two terms</note>; specifically, those of the Dodecagon are of the First species, and those of the Decagon are of the Fourth. In the fifth place follow the sides of the Pentagon and its star, as well as the sides of the Octagon and its star; for they are from the fourth species of compounds, called the Greater <term>Mizon <gloss>Greek for 'Greater'.</gloss></term> and the Lesser <term>Elasson <gloss>Greek for 'Lesser'.</gloss></term>.

Lest any good quality noted in the Decagon should prejudice the Pentagon; or lest the same species of the Octagonal side should equal its own figure to the Pentagon or Decagon, a new virtue approaches the Pentagon at its very origin: namely, that through this Sect, which shares in the Number Ten, the Divine Proportion <note>The Golden Ratio (approx. 1.618), which Kepler famously championed as a fundamental principle of nature.</note> reigns everywhere. This proportion is immediately present in the sides of the Pentagon and its star; but it does not belong to the Decagon and its star except by the mediation of the side of the Hexagon; and to the Octagon, it clearly does not belong at all.

Beyond these properties of the sides, there is yet another assessment of nobility: that figures are distinguished by the fitness and perfection of the area which the figure encloses. Here, after the diameter (which has no area, and which alone cuts the area of the circle into two equal parts, as Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the ancient astronomer whose 'Harmonics' Kepler sought to update.</note> reminds us, no less than it cuts the circumference), the Square and the Dodecagon hold the chief place, as they have an expressible area. The Square has an especially high prerogative because its area is the same as the square of its side—indeed, the very species of area is "square." Thus it encloses half of the square of the diameter. The Dodecagon stands after these first principles, enclosing three-quarters <term>dodrantem <gloss>A Roman unit for three-fourths.</gloss></term> of the square of the diameter. In the next place follow the Triangle, the Hexagon, and the Octagon, whose areas are of the Medial species <note>A term from Euclid for a specific type of irrational area.</note>. The areas of the Pentagon and Decagon as yet have no names or designations in our logic.

->END of Book I.<-

Now, he transitions from individual shapes to how they interact—specifically, how they fit together to fill a plane, a concept he calls "congruence." # BY JOHANNES KEPLER
# THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD

## BOOK II.

### On the Congruence of Harmonic Figures.

---

### Prologue.

**I** have thus far explained the mental <gloss>intellectual/noetic <note>original: "νοεράν" (noeran)</note></gloss> essence of the individual regular figures. What follows is their property when joined together, and as it were, their effect within geometry, which is congruence or incompatibility. For "demonstrability" <note>The ability to prove a figure's properties geometrically.</note> and "congruence" are not of the same breadth; while the former belongs to individual figures and extends into infinity through the continuous doubling of the sides of a single figure, the latter is restricted by certain laws where multiple figures are called into one association. Because of the growth of the angles, congruence hinders itself and quickly comes to an end. 

And although there is a choice of degrees in knowledge and demonstration, and those figures we have explained differ greatly in nobility from those we have dismissed without a name; nevertheless, congruence does not walk perfectly in step even with this nobility of demonstration. Therefore, one is not the cause of the other, but both depend on the same common cause (which is the fitness of the angles of the figure), yet each according to its own laws. 

How truly necessary this part of our speculation is for us can be seen from the very purpose of the whole work. Since we have undertaken to explain the origin of Harmony and its most excellent effects in the whole world, how could we say nothing about the congruence of figures, which are the headwaters of harmonic proportions? For the Latin words *to fit together* and *congruence* <note>original: "Congruere & Congruentia"</note> mean the same as the Greek *to fit/tune* and *harmony* <note>original: "ἁρμόττειν & ἁρμονία" (harmottein & harmonia)</note>. 

Furthermore, this effect of figures within geometry—and within that part of architecture <term>Archetypal Architecture <note>The study of the fundamental geometric blueprints God used to design the universe.</note></term> that deals with archetypes—becomes a kind of image and prelude to those effects outside geometry and outside the concepts of the mind, in natural and celestial things themselves. For this property of congruence, which results in some structure and physical embodiment, is such that it even invites the speculative mind to do something externally—to create and to give it a body. And so, lying hidden from eternity in the most blessed divine mind, through the orders of Ideas—as the supreme good, which is communicative of itself—it could not be contained within its own abstraction...

# On the Congruence of Regular Figures
## I. DEFINITION.

**C**ongruence <term>Congruence: Kepler's term for "tiling" or "tessellation"—the way shapes fit together without gaps.</term> is of one kind in the plane, and of another in the solid. In a Plane, Congruence occurs when the individual angles of several figures meet at a single point in such a way that no gap is left.

## II. DEFINITION.

**T**his is called **perfect**, when all the angles of each meeting figure come together in the same way <gloss>species</gloss>, so that all such junctions are similar to one another, and the order of the junctions can be continued to infinity.

## III. DEFINITION.

**M**ost perfect, when the figures meeting in the plane are also of the same kind <gloss>species</gloss>. <note>This refers to tilings using only one type of regular polygon, such as all squares or all hexagons.</note>

## IV. DEFINITION.

**I**mperfect, when a larger figure is indeed surrounded on all sides by similar junctions, yet a continuation to infinity is not possible; or, if it is possible, it is not without a mixture of different types of junctions. A lower degree of imperfect congruence occurs when a larger figure is not suited to meet with a similar type at all its angles.

## V. DEFINITION.

**S**olid congruence exists, and a solid figure <note>meaning a polyhedron</note> is formed, when the individual angles of several plane figures constitute a solid angle; when the regular or semi-regular figures are fitted together, no gap remains between the sides of the figures which meet each other on the opposite part of the solid figure, which cannot be closed by a figure of one of the types employed, or at least by a Regular one.

*Note that there is another kind of congruence—not of plane figures to form a solid figure, but of the solid figures themselves with one another, to fill a solid space around a single point. These types of bodily figures are only...*

## VI. DEFINITION.

**T**he most perfect solid Congruence <term>Congruence: In this 3D context, this refers to "space-filling" or "honeycombing"—how shapes pack together without leaving gaps.</term> and solid figure is when even the Planes <note>Kepler uses "Planes" to refer to the faces of the 3-dimensional solid.</note> are all congruent figures of the same type.

## VII. DEFINITION.

**T**his is either entirely regular, when the Planes are regular; and it has all its angles on the same spherical surface, and similar to one another.

## VIII. DEFINITION.

**O**r it is semi-regular, when the Planes are semi-regular (see book I, definition III) and it has solid angles distinguished and dissimilar in their number of lines; yet of no more than two kinds; nor arranged on more than two spherical surfaces described from a single center; and it has as many angles of each kind as one of the Regular figures possesses.

*It is no objection that this solid Congruence is called "most perfect": for the imperfection that exists in its planes should not be attributed to the solid formation, but is incidental to it. However, this semi-regular form is called "most perfect" only in an equivocal sense.*

## IX. DEFINITION.

**P**erfect congruence of a lower degree is when the Planes are regular, and all angles are on the same spherical surface and are similar to one another; but the Planes are nevertheless of different species <gloss>types</gloss>, though there are as many of each individual kind as there are in one of the most perfect figures—that is, no fewer than 4, since a solid figure is bounded by a minimum of 4 Planes.

## X. DEFINITION.

**A**n imperfect congruence or figure is when, the other conditions remaining the same, the larger figure is found no more than once or twice.

<margin>A. B. on page 53 and following.</margin>*For in that case the figure becomes more similar to a part than to the whole, and here more similar to a plane than a solid; since every solid is bounded by at least 4 surfaces. As in the following copper-plate prints at letters A and B, where the larger figure is a Heptagon. These two classes, with the number of sides of their larger figure, extend to infinity; starting from the Triangle on both sides—which in class A is among the most perfect regular congruences—then passing through the quadrangle; and then in class B, we arrive again at one most perfect regular congruence. All the others are imperfect.*

# ON THE HARMONY OF FIGURES:

## XI. DEFINITION.

**A** figure is **Semi-solid** if it does not satisfy all the parts of the fifth definition; <note>referring to a previous definition regarding the perfect filling of space without gaps.</note> as when, after fitting plane figures together, the congruence does not return completely into itself, but leaves gaps; otherwise, it maintains the rules prescribed in Definitions VI and VII.

## XII. DEFINITION.

**P**lane Figures are **congruent** when they either enclose a solid figure or fill a plane without any gap, the figures themselves being Regular or semi-regular.

## XIII. DEFINITION.

**T**hose Regular plane figures inscribed in a circle (provided they are inscribable) are called **Incongruous** if they form neither a solid figure inscribable in a sphere—either by themselves or with others of their own or another class—except an imperfect one; nor do they cover a plane, whether by themselves, with Star-polygons <term>Star-polygons: Kepler's "Stellis," referring to self-intersecting regular polygons like the pentagram.</term> of their own class, or with figures and stars of another class all around.

<margin>A. B.</margin>
*Note here that the heptagon <note>original: "septangulum"—a seven-sided polygon.</note> and such are excluded, despite the fact that two parallel heptagons, joined by either seven regular squares or fourteen regular triangles, completely enclose a solid; this is because only two heptagons meet, resulting in a figure that is disc-like and similar to a plane, but by no means globe-like or spherical. See the letters A and B in the figure on folio 53 and following. Thus the fifteen-sided figure <note>original: "Quindecangulum."</note> is also excluded, despite the fact that it fills a place in a plane at certain angles with related figures; it is excluded because it does not do this at all its angles all the way around.*

## XIV. PROPOSITION.

**N**o fewer than three plane angles meet in a congruent plane.
*For around any point of meeting, the sum of angles is equal to four Right angles <note>In modern terms, 360 degrees.</note>: but the angle of no regular figure is equal to the sum of two Right angles <note>180 degrees, which would be a straight line, not a polygon angle.</note>; therefore, two angles, no matter how large, are still less than four right angles: therefore, two do not fill the plane surface, according to Definition I.*

## XV. PROPOSITION.

**N**o fewer than three plane angles meet or rise up to form a solid angle.
*For two would meet not only at their edges but with their entire surfaces, and would enclose nothing of a solid body: which is contrary to the definition of a solid angle in Euclid.*

## XVI. PROPOSITION.

**T**he sum of angles meeting in a plane is always 4 right angles, and never greater; the sum of those meeting in a solid is less than this sum.
*For in a plane, no more than 4 right angles can surround a single point: therefore, when the sum equals 4 right angles, no gap is left, and by Definition I, the congruence is then in a plane. If the angles cover a plane, they do not rise up into solidity. And conversely, if the angles fitted together in a plane leave a gap—that is, whenever they are less than 4 right angles—then*

Five planes indeed meet at a point if one <term>Hexagonal</term><note>A six-sided figure.</note> shape is joined to four <term>Triangular</term><note>Three-sided figures.</note> ones; since the hexagon equals two triangles <note>Kepler is likely referring to the angle measurement here: a hexagon’s angle is 120°, and two triangles contribute 60° + 60° = 120°.</note>, the form is like that at letter L.

<margin>2. M. N. O.</margin>
Alternatively, if two <term>Quadrangular</term><note>Four-sided figures or squares.</note> shapes are joined to three triangular ones; because they equal three other triangular shapes. This is a form such as in M, or as in N, which is continuously uniform; or finally, as in O, which is of a non-uniform continuation.

But if you took two triangular and three quadrangular shapes, they would already exceed four right angles; much more so if two larger angles were brought to two triangular ones.

<margin>3. P. R.</margin>
Indeed, four shapes of two species meet if two Hexagonal shapes are joined to two Triangular ones. The form is like that in P, or as in R.

Otherwise, however you couple sets of four: you will always produce either more or less than four right angles; and therefore you will not pave a flat space.

If we join three shapes, then, being careful that there are no more than two species; first, they cannot be two Triangular, nor two Quadrangular, for they would not exceed two right angles, and there would be left over for the third a space that no single shape can fill.

<margin>4. S.</margin>
But with one Triangular shape placed among three, two <term>Dodecagonal</term><note>Twelve-sided figures.</note> shapes fit together: and the continuation is possible; nor are other meeting-points mixed in. Let the form of this plane be seen at letter S.

<margin>5. V.</margin>
And with one Quadrangular shape assumed among three, two <term>Octagonal</term><note>Eight-sided figures.</note> shapes fit together, and this form is also continuable: let it be seen at letter V.

<margin>X. T.</margin>
Refer here the Octagonal star, on the basis that its hollow angle equals a Quadrangular angle: thus the octagon is divisible into a star and eight quadrangular triangles, two of which make a square. And so three Quadrangular shapes and two rays of two stars fill the space: a mixed form, as at letter X: or also mixed in another way, as at letter T.

<margin>6. Z.</margin>
Leaving behind now the joining of three shapes using the Triangular and Quadrangular, if we come to the <term>Pentagonal</term><note>Five-sided figures.</note>, two of them can be taken, because joined they exceed 2 right angles: and one <term>Decagonal</term><note>Ten-sided figure.</note> shape fits into the remaining space: for a Decagon is crowned by ten Pentagons: but this form is not purely continued. See the diagram at letter Z on the inner side.

<margin>Z.</margin>
Refer here, therefore, the Pentagonal star, when there are three Pentagonal shapes and one ray of a star; because the hollow angle of the star also takes one pentagonal angle, no less than the gap of three Pentagons takes the ray of the star. See the same letter Z on the outer side.

<margin>Aa.</margin>
Although not even in this way does the continuation succeed unto infinity; for the rule of this sect is unsociable, which, having admitted a few of its own, immediately fortifies itself. Behold these two forms also in another way, at letter Aa.

But if you wish to continue it at all, certain "monsters" <note>Kepler uses the term "monstra" (monsters/prodigies) to describe irregular or distorted polygons that must be used to fill the gaps when regular ones don't fit perfectly.</note> must be adopted: two Decagons joined together, with two sides worn away in each; a series of five-angled structures is made even in infinite continuation, such that in the first and narrowest five-angled series there are five Decagons, with no intermediate monster: In the second, looser series, linear rows of Decagons are mediated by single couplings of two Decagons joined together; In the third, the places of the individual angles...

<summary>Kepler calculates which combinations of different regular polygons (like triangles with hexagons, or squares with octagons) can perfectly meet at a vertex to tile a flat plane. He also introduces "star" versions of these tilings and notes that pentagonal tilings are "unsociable," requiring irregular "monstrous" shapes to continue infinitely.</summary>

Each pair of two <term>decagons</term><note>A ten-sided polygon.</note> joined together occupies a space, with a single decagon standing between them. In the fourth arrangement, whole decagons again stand at the corners, while two decagons, arranged at equal intervals, mediate the two corners. In the fifth arrangement, stars stand with each of their outermost rays in each corner; however, two whole decagons fill the lines, and in the middle, there are two joinings of decagons. And so, following this, every single five-angled form brings something new. The structure is most laborious and most ingenious, and should be viewed at the same letter Aa.
<margin>Aa.</margin>

To this you may also refer the <term>decangular star</term><note>A ten-pointed star polygon.</note>, into whose hollow angle the angle of a <term>pentagon</term><note>A five-sided polygon.</note> fits; and conversely, two <term>tridecile</term><note>original: "Trideciles". In Kepler's geometry, this refers to an angle of 108 degrees, which is the interior angle of a regular pentagon.</note> rays agree with two pentagonal ones and fill the space completely. This form accepts unequal pentagons; and although it can be continued, it nevertheless admits gaping, empty decagons into the middle. The form is to be seen at letter Bb.
<margin>Bb.</margin>

A single pentagon cannot be taken into a grouping of three planes <note>Meaning three shapes meeting at a single vertex.</note>, for its angle is six-fifths of one right angle, according to Proposition 34 of Book I <note>A right angle is 90 degrees; 6/5 of 90 is 108 degrees, the interior angle of a pentagon.</note>; therefore, 14-fifths would be left for the remaining two angles, or 7-fifths for each; no figure has such an angle <note>7/5 of a right angle is 126 degrees. No regular polygon has an interior angle of 126 degrees.</note>. Nor can two <term>hexagons</term><note>Six-sided polygons.</note> be taken: for the remainder is also a hexagonal angle and it becomes the form reported above, whereas here we are seeking structures from two species, not from figures of a single species. Through the following many-sided figures, whose angle is larger than a hexagonal one, once two angles are subtracted from four right angles <note>360 degrees.</note>, less is left for the remainder than a hexagonal angle has; but if one is subtracted, less is left for the remaining two than two hexagonal angles have. But regarding those figures which have fewer and smaller angles than a hexagon, we have already dealt with which and how many they can be when three of them pave a flat surface.

### XX. PROPOSITION.

**From the plane angles of three species, a flat space is congruently filled in four ways.**

In this case, three or more <term>trigonal</term><note>Triangular (3-sided).</note> angles are not permitted; for three triangular angles make two right angles; less is left than the sum of the smallest angles after them, namely the <term>tetragonal</term><note>Square (4-sided).</note> and pentagonal ones. Because of this, two tetragonal angles or larger ones should not be associated with two triangular ones, because not enough space would be left for the angle of a figure of the third species.

<margin>i.</margin>
Therefore, if there are two triangular angles and one square one, a <term>dodecagonal</term><note>Twelve-sided.</note> one will be associated with them; however, the form is not continued: see letters Cc, Dd, and Ee for three forms, all pertaining to the first case.
<margin>Cc. Dd. <unclear>Mercury symbol</unclear></margin>

The <term>dodecagonal star</term> should also be referred to here, as above. For four triangular angles, one square angle, and one ray of the star will fill the place. See forms Ff, Gg, and Hh.
<margin>Ff. Gg. Hh.</margin>

If one pentagonal angle is joined to two triangular ones, the remainder will be incongruent, 32-fifteenths <note>Kepler is calculating using fractions of a right angle. Two triangles (60°+60°) and one pentagon (108°) leave 132° remaining to reach 360°.</note>, for no angle has 16-fifteenths. But if one hexagonal angle is added to two triangular ones, the remainder will also be hexagonal, and the form will be one of those mentioned above. Therefore, there cannot be pairs of triangles here anymore.

Consequently, if there is one triangular angle, three square angles will not be added to it, for too much is produced; nor is enough space left for the angle of a third species.

Let two square angles be added to one triangular angle; in the remainder reaching four right angles
<margin>ii.</margin>

<margin>li. Kk.</margin> The <term>hexagon</term><note>A six-sided polygon.</note> will fit; it is a double form, continuable with the figures at Letters Ii, but at Kk it is not continuable without mixing. *And this is the second case.*

A single <term>trigon</term><note>A triangle.</note> does not join with two <term>pentagons</note>, for there remains a gap of 14 fifteenths of one right angle <note>Kepler calculates angles in fractions of a right angle (90°). A triangle (60°) plus two pentagons (108°+108°) equals 276°. The remaining gap to reach 360° is 84°, which is indeed 14/15 of 90°.</note>, which is foreign to regular figures. Nor does it join with one pentagon; for again there remains 32 fifteenths, since no regular figure has an angle of 16 fifteenths <note>96°</note>. Nor does it join with one hexagon; for they make two right angles <note>60° + 120° = 180°</note>, whereas no single angle of a polygon can be that large; but half of this would be the quantity of a <term>tetragon</term><note>A square.</note>, which has already been discussed. Nor does it join with a single <term>heptagon</term><note>A seven-sided polygon.</note>, <term>octagon</term><note>An eight-sided polygon.</note>, or <term>enneagon</term><note>A nine-sided polygon.</note>; for there would remain for the angle of the third species of figure either 40 twenty-firsts, or 11 sixths, or 16 ninths, none of which are found in any regular figure.

Therefore, a single trigon combined with a single <term>decagon</term><note>A ten-sided polygon.</note> leaves a gap of 26 fifteenths, which is the size of the angle of a <term>pentedecagon</term><note>original: "Pentekadecagonicus"; a fifteen-sided polygon.</note>. This is indeed a congruence, but at least an incomplete one. For the pentedecagon is odd-sided; therefore, by Proposition 17, different species of junctions are mixed at the angles of the same figure. A decagon, having an even number of sides, could be surrounded by alternating trigons and pentedecagons, but immediately two such pentedecagons would run into each other and obstruct themselves.

Furthermore, a trigon cannot be joined with an <term>hendecagon</term><note>An eleven-sided polygon.</note>, for there would be left 56 thirty-thirds, an angle which no regular figure possesses.

Finally, a trigon with a <term>dodecagon</term><note>A twelve-sided polygon.</note> leaves a dodecagonal gap, a form which has already been mentioned.

If the trigon were joined to larger figures, the gap would become smaller, and we have already dealt with the smaller figures. And so we have finished with the trigon, as far as admitting it among three species.

When more than one angle of a <term>tetragon</term><note>A square.</note> is taken away from four right angles <note>360°</note>, they do not leave enough space for two angles of two other species, since those joined together would be larger than two right angles.

<margin>3.</margin> A single tetragon, joined to a single pentagon, leaves a gap for an <term>icosagon</term><note>A twenty-sided polygon.</note>. Thus the icosagon is associated at all angles and fits legitimately; but this order is not continued toward the outside. *It is, therefore, an imperfect congruence.* Behold the <margin>Ll.</margin> figure at letter Ll. This is the third case.

<margin>4.</margin> A tetragon joined to a hexagon leaves a gap for a dodecagon. <margin>Mm.</margin> Behold the figure at letter Mm: This is the fourth and final case.

To this you may refer the <term>dodecagonal star</term>, which twelve trigons fill: so that here four angles meet to fill the <term>fullness</term><note>original: "soliditatem". In this planar context, it refers to the complete filling of the 360° around a point.</note>, namely two trigons, a <margin>Nn</margin> tetragon, a hexagon, and the ray of the star. Behold the figure at letter Nn.

A tetragon added to a heptagon leaves a gap of 11 sevenths, an angle which no regular figure has. Added to an octagon, it leaves an octagonal gap: a form discussed above. Thus we have finished with the tetragon.

A pentagon with a hexagon leaves a gap of 22 fifteenths; with a heptagon, 48 thirty-fifths; with an octagon, 13 tenths, since no regular figure has an angle that size. And now the gap begins to be smaller than the angle of an octagon, which is 15 tenths. But we have already completed those that have smaller angles. Thus we have finished with the pentagon.

A triple hexagon fills a flat space <note>120° x 3 = 360°</note>; therefore, it cannot be mixed with two figures larger than itself. And so the mixing of three figures is concluded.

## XXI. PROPOSITION.

**F**our or more species of plane figures do not fit together at individual angles to fill a <term>solid space</term><note>A "solid space" here refers to a 3D corner or vertex where multiple faces meet.</note>.
*For the four smallest possible angles are these: the <term>Trigon</term><note>Triangle (60°)</note>, the <term>Tetragon</term><note>Square (90°)</note>, the <term>Pentagon</term><note>108°</note>, and the <term>Hexagon</term><note>120°</note>. But the first and last of these combined equal two right angles <note>60° + 120° = 180°</note>, the second is a right angle <note>90°</note>, and the third exceeds a right angle by one-fifth part of a right angle <note>108° is 1 and 1/5 of 90°</note>. Thus, joined together, they are greater than four right angles <note>60 + 90 + 108 + 120 = 378°, which is more than the 360° required to lie flat, let alone form a 3D corner</note>. Therefore, by Proposition XVI, they do not fit. It follows even more strongly that four right angles will be exceeded by any combination of larger angles.*

## XXII. AXIOM.

**W**hen two plane angles are not together greater than a third, they do not form a <term>solid angle</term><note>A 3D vertex</note> with it.

## XXIII. PROPOSITION

**T**wo plane angles of an <term>odd-sided figure</term><note>Such as a triangle or pentagon</note>, meeting with one of another species, do not form any regular solid.
*For by Proposition XVIII, the solid angles become <term>non-uniform</term><note>Literally "difformes" or "of different shapes," meaning the vertex wouldn't look the same from all sides</note>, which is contrary to the definitions from V to X.*

## XXIV. PROPOSITION.

**T**hree plane angles, from three distinct species of figures, one being odd-sided, meeting together, do not complete a perfect solid figure.
*For again, by Proposition XVII, the solids become <term>diverse in form</term>, which is against the definitions.*

## XXV. PROPOSITION.

**T**he most perfect and regular congruences of plane figures for forming a solid figure are five.
*This is a <term>scholion</term><note>An explanatory note or commentary</note> on the last part of the last book of Euclid. For by Proposition XV of this book, we begin with three angles [at a vertex], and by Proposition XVI we stop at six <term>Trigons</term>, four <term>Tetragons</term>, and three <term>Hexagons</term>, because by Proposition XVII, these equal 4 right angles <note>360°</note>.*
<margin>Number 2 of the following figure.</margin>
*Therefore, three <term>Trigons</term>, fitting together at individual angles, make less than 4—that is, they produce two right plane angles <note>3 * 60° = 180°, or 2 right angles</note>; thus, when three triangles are joined, the gap is filled by a fourth <term>Trigon</term>. From this comes the **Tetrahedron**, or Pyramid.*
<margin>Oo. and Number 5 on the following leaf.</margin>
*Four <term>Trigons</term>, fitting at individual angles, produce 8 thirds <note>Kepler measures in units of 30°, so 60° = 2/3 of a right angle. 4 * 2 = 8 thirds of a right angle, or 240°</note>, which is less than 12 thirds, or 4 right angles <note>360°</note>: and by joining the sides of the triangles, a Pyramid with a gaping quadrilateral base is formed: to which another such Pyramid fits from the opposite side with a similar gap, to close the figure on all sides. From this comes the **Octahedron**.*
<margin>Pp. and number 4 on the following leaf.</margin>
*Five <term>Trigons</term>, fitting at individual angles, produce 10 thirds <note>300°</note>, which is less than 12 thirds: and by fitting ten and ten sides to a common angle, a Pyramid with a five-sided base is formed. For the angles at the base to also become <term>five-planed</term><note>Having five faces meeting at each vertex</note>, it is necessary that for every two planes in that base, three other plane angles meet, and thus fifteen others must fit those ten, and as many be extended on the other side: which sum of thirty planes belongs to ten <term>Trigons</term>; from which in the middle a belt or <term>co-</term>* <note>The text cuts off mid-word "columna" or "corona" describing the middle section of an icosahedron.</note>

<summary>Kepler proves that only five regular solids (the Platonic solids) can exist by calculating the sum of angles at a vertex. He demonstrates why combinations of four or more types of shapes, or certain irregular combinations, cannot form a perfectly symmetrical 3D object.</summary>

*Three square angles are three right angles, which is less than four flat right angles <note>3 × 90° = 270°, which is less than the 360° of a flat surface</note>. *Three pentagonal angles are 18-fifths of one flat right angle <note>Each angle of a regular pentagon is 108°. Three of them equal 324°. If one pentagon is surrounded at its base by five others in this manner, the figure gapes upward with five flat pentagonal angles and has five projecting flat pentagonal angles. Therefore, another figure of the same kind must be built facing it; and the five projecting flat angles of either one will fit into the five remaining gaps of the other, and vice versa. From this is born the* **Dodecahedron** <note>A 12-sided solid made of pentagons</note>. *Thus, we have finished with those solids made purely of pentagons, and likewise with all figures that can be joined from a single species; for three hexagonal angles, by Proposition XVI, do not rise to form a solid <note>Three 120° angles of a hexagon equal 360°, making a flat surface rather than a corner</note>.*

<margin>The Cosmic Figures.</margin>
*These are those five bodies which the* **Pythagoreans** *and* **Plato**, *and* **Proclus** *the commentator on Euclid, were accustomed to call the* **Cosmic Figures** <note>original: "figuras mundanas"</note>. *As for how they were applied to the bodies of the world, I said in the preamble to Book I that it remains uncertain. Indeed, there is a common persuasion, derived from* **Aristotle**, *that those philosophers looked toward the five simple* **Bodies of the World** *according to the five-fold number of these figures: namely, to the four* **Elements**—**Fire, Air, Water, and Earth**—*and to the so-called* **Fifth Essence**, *or* **Celestial Matter**; *comparing the properties of the figures with the characteristics of those simple bodies. <note>This figure illustrates a complex **pentagonal tiling**. A <term>tiling</term> (or tessellation) is a way of covering a flat surface with geometric shapes so that there are no gaps or overlaps. In Figure Y, Kepler demonstrates how five-sided pentagons and five-pointed stars can be woven together into a cohesive, though non-repeating, pattern.</note>

<note>Figure Z shows a variation of the **star pattern**. These diagrams are significant because regular pentagons cannot tile a flat surface perfectly on their own; they require the addition of other shapes, like these stars, to fill the gaps. Kepler was deeply interested in these "imperfect" but harmonious arrangements.</note>

->Aa<-

<note>Figure Aa displays a pattern composed of the **rhombus** (a diamond shape). Kepler explicitly credited these designs to the artist **Albrecht Dürer**, who published them in his 1525 manual on geometry titled *A Course in the Art of Measurement* <note>original: *Underweysung der Messung*</note>. By including these engravings, Kepler connects the world of practical Renaissance art and drafting to his own mathematical theories on the fundamental harmonies of the universe.</note>

# CONGRUENCE, BOOK II.

<margin>5. The Octahedron as a symbol of Air</margin>
...a quadrilateral <note>original: "quadrilaterum"</note> dividing the body of the figure into two equal parts, just as a great circle divides a globe suspended from two poles: this is a certain image of mobility, as air is the most mobile of the elements, both in the speed and the variety of its directions. <note>original: "plagarum"</note>

<margin>3. The Tetrahedron as a symbol of Fire</margin>
<margin>4. The Icosahedron as a symbol of Water</margin>
In the <term>Tetrahedron</term> <note>A solid with four triangular faces; the simplest of the Platonic solids.</note>, the fewness of its planes seems to signify the dryness of fire, since the definition of dry things is that they are contained within their own boundaries. In the <term>Icosahedron</term> <note>A solid with twenty triangular faces.</note>, conversely, the multitude of planes seems to signify the moisture of water, since moisture is defined as being contained by the boundaries of other things. Indeed, a small number of planes indicates things that are one's own, while a large number indicates things that are adopted or foreign. Furthermore, the plane triangle is proper to the Tetrahedron because the entire Tetrahedral figure is a solid triangle; but that same triangle is not proper to the Icosahedron, but rather borrowed, because the solidity of the Icosahedron is more similar to Pentagons than to Triangles. Again, in the sharpness of the Tetrahedron rising from a single base, the penetrating and dividing power of Fire seems to be shadowed forth. In the blunt and five-lined angle of the Icosahedron, we see the power of filling up liquids, which is the power of moistening. In the smallness and thinness of the Tetrahedron, we see the nature of fire; in the globe-like mass of the Icosahedron, the nature of water, possessing a shape like that of a drop. In the Tetrahedron there is the most surface area and the least body; in the Icosahedron the bodily mass is much greater than the surface. Just as in Fire the form excels, in Water the matter excels.

<margin>2. The Dodecahedron as a symbol of the Heavens</margin>
The <term>Dodecahedron</term> <note>A solid with twelve pentagonal faces.</note> is truly left for the celestial body, having the same number of planes as there are signs in the celestial Zodiac; and it is demonstrated to be the most capacious of the remaining figures, just as the heavens contain all things.

This analogy, although plausible—not indeed to *Aristotle* (who, since he denied that the World was created, could not acknowledge an <term>Archetypal</term> <note>Referring to the "Archetype," or the original divine blueprint used by God to design the universe.</note> power in quantitative figures, since no power to create anything physical resides in them without an Architect)—but to me, and to all Christians, who hold by faith that the World, when it did not exist before, was created by God in weight, measure, and number, according to Ideas co-eternal with Himself. Although, I say, this analogy is plausible in general, yet when shaped into specific details, it is held by no absolute necessity. It suffers from objections, not only because of the discrepancy of certain properties within the same analogy, but also because of the greater suitability of the Dodecahedron and Icosahedron with Fire; and finally, because there is much greater dispute regarding the number of the Elements and the stillness of the Earth than there is regarding the number of these figures.

If the *Pythagoreans* stopped here, I do not blame *Ramus* <note>Petrus Ramus (1515–1572), a French humanist and logician known for his critiques of Aristotle.</note> or *Aristotle* for rejecting this analogy after it was torn apart in debates. But twenty-four years ago, I investigated these five bodies in the fabric of the world in a far different way. I said in the preamble of Book I that it seemed consistent to me that this was also the doctrine of the ancients, but hidden according to the custom of their sect. For <term>Copernican Astronomy</term> <note>The heliocentric model, placing the Sun at the center of the solar system.</note>—or that of the ancient *Aristarchus of Samos, the Pythagorean*—possesses such an arrangement of the moving World that there are in it six Orbs or paths, drawn around the body of the sun, which is immobile in the center. These are separated by large and unequal intervals: *Saturn* is the outermost, then *Jupiter*, then *Mars*, then *Earth with the Moon*, then *Venus*, and finally *Mercury* the innermost. Since the proper and essential characteristic of these five figures is their inscription into a spherical surface with their angles, and their circumscription around a spherical surface with the centers of their planes, a certain interval between two orbs is fixed for each figure. Nothing could seem more plausible than that those six celestial orbs...

inter- <note>Catchword for the next page, beginning the word "intervals" or "interposed."</note>

<summary>Kepler explains the symbolic relationship between the Platonic solids and the four elements, plus the heavens, while arguing that these shapes form the mathematical blueprint for the spacing of the planets in the Copernican system.</summary>

# ON THE HARMONY OF FIGURES:

<margin>Look back at the diagram in Book V, chapter III.</margin>

...the five intervals were taken by the Creator from the five figures; in this order: the cube is conceived by the mind between the Orbs of Saturn and Jupiter, the <term>Tetrahedron</term> <note>A four-faced pyramid made of triangles.</note> between Jupiter and Mars, the <term>Dodecahedron</term> <note>A twelve-faced solid made of pentagons.</note> between Mars and Earth, the <term>Icosahedron</term> <note>A twenty-faced solid made of triangles.</note> between Earth and Venus, and the <term>Octahedron</term> <note>An eight-faced solid made of triangles.</note> between Venus and Mercury.

This distribution can be explored through numbers; it brings with it a necessity and does not anxiously seek out the number of bodies, but occupies what has been found. Finally, it is so constructed that for these twenty-two years, not only has it found no opponent, but it has even drawn over the disciples of the reckless master <term>Ramus</term> <note>Petrus Ramus (1515–1572), a famous philosopher who critiqued traditional Aristotelian logic and Euclidean geometry.</note> and of the <term>Euclid-scourger</term> <note>original: "Euclideomaſtigis"; a derogatory term for those who attacked the validity of Euclidean geometry.</note>; and today it draws so many over that mathematicians have long been demanding a second edition. But to deal with this matter in more detail is not the purpose of this second book; the reader will find more below in book five, and also some in Book IV of the *Epitome of Astronomy*, where the genuine metaphysical origin of these five solid figures is explained: for that origin through angles is not the true origin, but follows as something posterior in nature.

## PROPOSITION XXVI.

**T**wo other congruences of twelve planar Pentagonal stars can be added to the most perfect regular congruences, as well as two semi-solid ones: the octangular and decangular stars.

<margin>
See also below in Book V, chapter I, and in the copperplate engravings previously mentioned.
</margin>

For pentagonal shapes enclose solid figures with spikes on all sides: one of which is made of twelve five-lined angles, the other of twenty three-lined angles. The former stands on three angles, the latter on five at once; the former is more beautifully raised upon an angle; the latter sits more upright, leaning on five. In these, although a regular plane does not appear on the outside, but instead the Isosceles Triangle of the pentagonals, nevertheless five of this kind always coincide in one and the same plane, surrounding a pentagon hidden beneath the solidity like its own heart. Together with it, they form the said pentagonal star, or in the German idiom, the <term>Drudenfuss</term> <note>original: "pedem Trutta"; literally "trout's foot." A folk name for the pentagram, used as a protective symbol against spirits.</note>, which <term>Theophrastus Paracelsus</term> <note>The famous Swiss physician and alchemist (1493–1541).</note> called the <term>sign of health</term>. The idea of the body is in a way the same as that of its plane; for just as in this—namely, in the five-angled star—the sides of two triangles always meet in one straight line, which in its lower part becomes the base for one exterior triangle, but a side for the innermost pentagon: so in the solid, the individual isosceles triangles of the five solid angles always meet in one plane, of which five triangles (or the innermost marrow and heart of the star, the pentagon) becomes the base in one of a standing solid angle, or in the other, of the five underlying solids. Moreover, the kinship of these figures is so great—one with the Dodecahedron, the other with the Icosahedron—that these latter, especially the Dodecahedron, seem in a way truncated and mutilated if compared with those spiked ones.

However, the octangular and decangular stars, by the sides of their rays (which always coincide in one straight line in the first and fourth, skipping two), meet two by two and form, in the former case, a certain cube; in the latter, a certain dodecahedron. These figures are not angular but "eared" <note>original: "auriculatas"; likely referring to the way the points protrude like ears from a central mass.</note> because, when two plane angles are joined together, a gap must necessarily occur which cannot be closed. Therefore, according to Proposition XI, it is only a semi-solid congruence.

These solid ones are called the most perfect congruences, and these others semi-solid, because the sixth definition of this book applies to them regarding solidity; while the definition of a perfect figure (which is the second in book I) applies to the planes themselves—that is, they are secondarily perfect. Nor do we speak absurdly of a "most perfect semi-solid," because we are indicating that something is being begun; to which not the 9th or 10th, but the 6th definition would apply if it could be perfected.
