# PROPOSITION XXVII.

**S**emi-regular figures—specifically flat <term>Rhombi</term> <note>A four-sided figure with equal sides but where the angles are not necessarily right angles; a diamond shape.</note>—also fit together perfectly to form solid shapes, and they do so in only two ways.

<margin>Vu, and here is a smaller figure.</margin>
For from *twelve flat Rhombi* of a certain proportion of their diagonals, a *Solid Rhombus* is formed. This is the shape of a *honeybee’s cell*, specifically regarding its six sides and its solid triangular base. For when six rhombi are joined such that obtuse angles meet obtuse and acute meet acute, they create three obtuse-angled gaps and three pairs of acute angles projecting at the top, and the same number at the bottom. Therefore, the three projections of the three rhombi on each side, joined at their obtuse angles, fit into the gaps, and their own gaps receive the projections of the others.

<margin>Concerning this also see above on page 49, in Definition V.</margin>
<margin>Xx, and here is a larger figure.</margin>
In the same way, *thirty flat Rhombi*, using a different proportion of diagonals, create a *Triacontahedral Solid Rhombus* <note>A thirty-sided solid made entirely of identical rhombi.</note>. For five rhombi joined at their acute angles form two solid peaks standing on opposite sides; where they are joined at their obtuse angles, they leave gaps. Other obtuse angles of five and five more rhombi fill these gaps. Finally, around the middle of these two "shells," a <term>Zone</term> <note>A belt or band of faces wrapping around the middle of the solid.</note> composed of ten rhombi circles around, joining the two shells together.

That there are no more perfect <term>congruences</term> <note>The way geometric shapes fit together without gaps.</note> of rhombi is proven as follows. There are always two acute and two obtuse plane angles in a rhombus; one acute and one obtuse angle together always equal two right angles. No more than three obtuse angles can meet, or they would exceed the limit of four right angles <note>A total of 360 degrees, which would make the surface flat or impossible to close into a solid.</note>. If you were to join only three acute angles, you would create a *Rhombic Hexahedron*—much like a Cube—but with only two sharp solid corners placed very far apart; the other solid angles in the middle of the body would not be equidistant. Therefore, they do not follow the laws of Definition VIII, which does not allow for only two angles to exist on the same sphere. Furthermore, of the six obtuse solid angles, each would be enclosed by two obtuse plane angles and one acute; such irregularity is again against the definitions. Therefore, it is not enough for only three acute planes to meet. But neither can six acute angles (of six rhombi) meet. For if each angle were two-thirds of a right angle <note>60 degrees.</note>, the obtuse angles would be double that size, namely four-thirds <note>120 degrees.</note>. Thus, three obtuse angles or six acute angles would both form exactly four right angles <note>360 degrees.</note>; they would not form a solid corner, but would instead spread out into a continuous flat surface, as seen in figure *G*.
<margin>G. page.</margin>
However, if the acute angles are made smaller, the obtuse angles will become larger, and three of them will exceed four right angles. Therefore, there are only two most perfect rhombic congruences: one in which four acute rhombic angles meet at a solid point, and another in which five meet. To these, the Cube is added as the source of all rhombi, because its face has four equal sides, just like a rhombus.

# PROPOSITION XXVIII.

**T**here are thirteen species of perfect solid congruences of a lower degree; from these, the thirteen <term>Archimedean Solids</term> <note>Semi-regular solids where the faces are regular polygons of two or more types, but all corners are identical.</note> arise.

<sig>b 2</sig>
<meta>Catchword: With</meta>
<margin>XIII. Archimedean</margin>

<summary>Kepler describes how rhombi can form two specific solids—the rhombic dodecahedron (likened to a bee's cell) and the rhombic triacontahedron—and provides a geometric proof for why only these two exist. He then introduces the thirteen Archimedean solids as the next class of geometric figures.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Kepler’s systematic exploration of semi-regular solids (now known as Archimedean and snub solids). He is moving from figures made of rhombi to those composed of a mixture of regular polygons, such as triangles, squares, and pentagons.</meta>

<page-num>62</page-num>
<header>ON THE HARMONY OF FIGURES:</header>

Since diverse figures are mixed in this degree, by Proposition XXI, the figures of either two or three species will be mixed. If two, then among them there are either <term>Triangles</term> <note>original: *Trigoni*</note> or there are not.

<margin>oo</margin>
Therefore, from *Triangles* and <term>Squares</term> <note>original: *Tetragoni*</note> three solids are created which indeed satisfy Definition IX. For that definition rejects these three forms in which a <term>solid angle</term> <note>A vertex where three or more faces meet.</note> is closed by one *Square* plane angle together with either two or three *Triangular* plane angles; or with two *Squares* and one *Triangle*. This is because in the first case there is only one *Square*, and it becomes half of an *Octahedron*, and the solid angles are of different shapes; in the second case there are only two *Squares*, and in the third only two *Triangles*. According to Proposition X, these are examples of imperfect congruence.

<margin>I. The Snub Cube.</margin>
There remain, therefore, these ways in which the planes close a solid angle: First, four *Triangles* and one *Square*. For these are less than four right angles <note>The sum of the angles meeting at a point must be less than 360 degrees (four right angles) to form a convex peak.</note>. Thus, six *Squares* and *thirty-two* (that is, 20 and 12) *Triangles* fit together, and a *thirty-eight-sided* <note>original: *Triacontaoctohedrica*</note> figure is made, which I call the **Snub Cube** <note>original: *Cubum simum*</note>. This is depicted in the following diagram as Number 12.

For *five* *Triangular* planes and one *Square* exceed four right angles, whereas to close a solid they must be less than four right angles, by Proposition XVI. Likewise four *Triangles* and two *Squares*. Indeed, three *Triangles* and two *Squares* make exactly four right angles <note>This would result in a flat tiling, not a 3D shape.</note>.

<margin>II. The Cuboctahedron.</margin>
Second, two *Triangles* and two *Squares* are less than four right angles. Here, therefore, eight *Triangles* and six *Squares* fit together to form one *fourteen-sided solid* <note>original: *Tessareskaidecaëdron*</note>, which I call the **Cuboctahedron**. It is depicted here as number 8. However, two *Triangles* with three *Squares* exceed 4 right angles.

<margin>III. The Rhombicuboctahedron.</margin>
Third, one *Triangle* and three *Squares* are less than 4 right angles. Here, therefore, eight Triangles and eighteen (that is, 12 and 6) quadrangles fit together into one *twenty-six-sided solid* <note>original: *Icosihexaëdron*</note>, which I call the cut **Rhombic Cuboctahedron**, or **Rhombicuboctahedron**. It is depicted here as number 10.

In these three, then, there are *Squares* next to *Triangles*; it follows that we should also associate *Pentagons* with them separately.

<margin>IV. The Snub Dodecahedron.</margin>
*Five* *Triangular* planes do not stand next to one *Pentagon*, because they could not even stand next to a *Square*, which is smaller than it. Therefore, four *Triangles* with one *Pentagon* make less than 4 right angles, and eighty (that is, 20 and 60) *Triangles* fit together with twelve *Pentagons* to form a **ninety-two-sided solid** <note>original: *Ennenëcontakadyhedron*</note>, which I call the **Snub Dodecahedron** <note>original: *Dodecaëdron simum*</note>. It is pictured here as number 13. And in this order of "snub" figures, the *Icosahedron* could be the third, which is like a *Snub Tetrahedron*.

<summary>Kepler identifies and names several Archimedean and snub solids, including the snub cube, cuboctahedron, and snub dodecahedron, by calculating which combinations of polygons can meet at a vertex to form a 3D shape.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Kepler’s systematic proof regarding which combinations of regular polygons can meet at a single vertex to form a semi-regular (Archimedean) solid. ## CONGRUENCE BOOK II. 63

<margin>Pp.</margin>
*If you associate three <term>triangular planes</term> <note>original: *planos Trigonicos*; equilateral triangles</note> with one pentagonal one, the result is as above: only two pentagons would be included in the solid. If you associate two triangular planes with one pentagonal one, only a single pentagon comes into the solid. In the former case, a "zone" or middle column is formed; in the latter, a pyramid—both being parts of an <term>Icosahedron</term> <note>A 20-sided regular solid made of triangles.</note>. Nor are the solid angles here of the same species, because one vertex is surrounded by five triangles, as in the Icosahedron. Thus, we are finished with the case of a single pentagon.*

<margin>V. Icosidodecahedron.</margin>
*But three triangles with two pentagons produce more than <term>four right angles</term> <note>In Euclidean geometry, the sum of the plane angles meeting at a vertex must be less than 360 degrees (four right angles) to form a convex peak. If they equal or exceed 360°, the surface remains flat or cannot close.</note>. Therefore, we are finished with the possibility of admitting three triangles into a partnership with pentagons.*

*Two triangles with two pentagons produce less than four right angles. Therefore, twenty triangles and twelve pentagons fit together into one <term>thirty-two-sided solid</term> <note>original: *Triacontakaëdyhedron*</note>, which I call the **Icosidodecahedron**. It is depicted here as Number 9. Since we have already rejected two triangles with one pentagon, we are now finished with the case of two triangles.*

*One triangle with three pentagons produces more than four right angles. However, with two pentagons, by Proposition XXIII, it produces nothing regular, because the pentagon is an odd-sided figure <note>Kepler argues that if you have an odd-sided polygon like a pentagon, the polygons surrounding it must alternate in a way that is impossible if you only have one triangle at the vertex.</note>. Thus, we are finished with pentagons in partnership with triangles.*

*Four triangles with one <term>hexagon</term> <note>original: *Hexagonico*</note>, and two triangles with two hexagons, fill the plane exactly <note>i.e., they sum to 360 degrees and would form a flat tiling rather than a 3D corner.</note>. But three triangles with two hexagons are greater than four right angles. With one hexagon, only two hexagons are received into the figure; therefore, three triangles are rejected. Two triangles are equal to one hexagon <note>in terms of the angle sum</note>, which is why they were rejected by Proposition XXII. It remains for one triangle to be joined with two hexagons. Thus, four triangles and four hexagons fit together into one <term>octahedron</term> <note>Kepler refers to the total number of faces; this is actually the truncated tetrahedron.</note>, which I call the **Truncated Tetrahedron**. <margin>VI. No mention of three triangles either, for the reasons often cited. Two triangles with two planes of any figure larger than a hexagon exceed four right angles; therefore, no further mention should be made of two triangles with two planes of a larger figure; nor of two triangles with one plane of a larger figure, because the latter is rejected by Proposition XXII. There remains to be examined the case where one triangle is joined with two planes of a figure larger than a hexagon. A hexagon with two others fills a flat surface; with larger ones, it exceeds four right angles. Therefore, this is the end of combinations made from two species of planes.

But if planes of three species can meet at one solid angle: first, two plane angles—one of a square and the other of a pentagon—exceed <term>two right angles</term> <note>180 degrees</note>. Those larger than these exceed it much more. Three angles of three triangles equal two right angles; therefore, three <term>triangular planes</term> cannot be admitted, lest the total sum exceed four right angles.

Two triangles with one square and one pentagon (or a hexagon or any larger shape in its place) are rejected by Proposition 23, because a triangle, being an odd-sided figure, would have to be surrounded by a square and a pentagon, or a hexagon, etc. <note>Kepler’s rule requires that the faces surrounding an odd-sided polygon must alternate or match in a way that allows the solid to close symmetrically.</note>

*If a <term>dodecagon</term> <note>twelve-sided shape</note> takes the place of the decagon in this partnership, four right angles are filled exactly, and no solid is formed; likewise, if an octagon takes the place of the hexagon, and any shape larger than an octagon is the third, four right angles are exceeded. No less is this true if the square is absent and three larger even-sided figures of different types are joined. Therefore, the entire <term>Archimedean family</term> <note>the semi-regular solids first described by Archimedes</note> stands within thirteen types, which was to be demonstrated.*

### XXIX. COROLLARY.

Fitting figures are twelve in total: eight **Radical** or Primary ones, and four **Augmented** or Starred ones.

| | |
|---|---|
| 1. **Triangle** | 7. **Dodecagon** |
| 2. **Square** | 8. **Icosagon** <note>twenty-sided shape</note> |
| 3. **Pentagon** | 9. **Pentagonal Star** |
| 4. **Hexagon** | 10. **Octagonal Star** |
| 5. **Octagon** | 11. **Decagonal Star** |
| 6. **Decagon** | 12. **Dodecagonal Star** |

*The degrees of <term>congruence</term> <note>how well they fit together</note> are distinct. In the **first degree** are the Triangle and Square, because they fit together both in solids and in a flat plane, whether with their own kind or joined with others.*

*In the **second degree** stand the Pentagon and its star. For they fit with their own kind in a solid, and they assist each other in a plane; but the Pentagon is superior because it also fits with several other shapes in both planes and solids.*

*The **third degree** belongs to the Hexagon, because figures of this type fit together in a plane, and with others in both solids and planes.*

*The **fourth degree** is held by the Octagon and Decagon with their stars. For those Radical shapes fit with several others in solids, while the stars fit with their own kind to a certain extent; in a plane, however, all four fit with others, though the octagonal star-section does so more variously and perfectly.*

*The **fifth degree** contains the Dodecagon with its star; because they fit in solids not at all, yet in a plane they fit with others in many ways. Thus, in solids they are hindered by size alone. Because of their usefulness in flat patterns, this class is to be preferred over the fourth degree.*

*The **final degree** is that of the Icosagon, because it fits only in a plane, and only with other shapes, and even with those it fits imperfectly.*

*But if we consider the <term>Plane</term> <note>a flat, two-dimensional surface</note> alone, the order of the figures will be this: 1. <term>Hexagon</term> <note>original: *Hexagonus*; six-sided</note>. 2. <term>Square</term> <note>original: *Tetragonus*</note>. 3. <term>Triangle</term> <note>original: *Trigonus*</note>. 4. <term>Dodecagon</term> <note>twelve-sided</note>. 5. Its star. 6. <term>Octagon</term> <note>eight-sided</note>. 7. Its star. 8. <term>Pentagon</term> <note>five-sided</note>. 9. Its star. 10. <term>Decagon</term> <note>ten-sided</note>. 11. Its star. 12. <term>Icosigon</term> <note>original: *Icosigonus*; twenty-sided</note>.*

*All other figures are <term>incongruent</term> <note>they cannot fit together to perfectly tile a surface</note>, yet the closest to congruence is the <term>Pentadecagon</term> <note>original: *Pentekadecagonus*; fifteen-sided</note>, because it begins to fit with others in the plane: but it is excluded by Proposition 23, in that it cannot be surrounded equally on all sides as the Icosigon can. After that is the figure of 16 sides and similar ones, which clearly do not fit with other regular shapes, as the size of their angles prevents it. But the <term>Heptagon</term> <note>seven-sided</note> and similar shapes are incongruent for a far different reason: because neither their whole angles, nor any aliquot parts of their angles—which are proper to the figures—fit with other regular shapes.*

*Thus, in the three classes of figures that can be proven by themselves, <term>congruence</term> <note>the ability to tile or fit together</note> ends with the Octagon, the Dodecagon, and the Icosigon; in the fourth, "false" class, it does not even begin. These findings have their use in Book IV regarding the selection of <term>Aspects</term> <note>astrological relationships between planets</note>.*

## XXX. COROLLARY.

**F**rom these things, the genuine distinction between <term>demonstration</term> <note>the logical or geometric proof of a shape's properties</note> and <term>congruence</term> of figures for the sake of <term>latitude</term> <note>here, spatial extent or width</note> becomes apparent.

*For: 1. The degrees of proper demonstration extend beyond the Octagon, Decagon, and Dodecagon into figures with doubled sides infinitely; but congruence stops at the Octagon, Icosigon, and Dodecagon. 2. The Pentagon with its star, for the sake of demonstration and knowledge, is less noble than the Dodecagon; but for the sake of congruence in a solid, it is much more noble. 3. The Octagon follows the Pentagon in the former case, but precedes it here. 4. The <term>Hexadecagon</term> <note>original: *Hekkadecagonus*; sixteen-sided</note> held a higher place there than the Icosigon; and yet that is an incongruent figure, while this one is congruent to a certain extent. 5. But in the Pentadecagon, there is a beautiful agreement of both matters, preserving the same analogy: because among demonstrations none occurs that is proper to it, but only accidental; while among congruences none is perfected, but some are at least begun, though not occupying the whole figure. These things are to be noted below in Book III regarding the origin and use of the <term>semitone</term> <note>original: *semitonij*; a musical interval</note>.*

->Book I: Commentary on the First Book of Euclid’s Elements<-

> *Since philosophy encompasses many faculties, and Mathematics many as well; concerning one part of it called Harmonics, and concerning Numbers (believed to be the principles of Harmonics), he writes these things:*

It prepares the efforts of the Mind for Theology. For those things concerning the truth of divine matters which seem difficult to grasp and more sublime to those who are uninitiated, are demonstrated by Mathematical Reasons to be reliable, manifest, and beyond controversy, through certain Images. For they show the evidence of <term>supersubstantial</term> <note>existing beyond or above material substance; metaphysical</note> properties in Numbers: and they make clear in the realm of reasoning what the powers of Intellectual Forms are. Therefore, Plato teaches us many wonders concerning the Nature of the Gods through the species of mathematical things: and Pythagorean Philosophy veils its instruction on divine matters with these, as if with coverings. For the whole of that **SACRED DISCOURSE** <note>original: *SERMO SACER*; likely referring to the *Hieros Logos* attributed to Pythagoras</note> is of this kind, as is <term>Philolaus</term> <note>a Pythagorean philosopher who believed the earth moved around a "central fire"</note> in the *Bacchae*, and the whole Pythagorean method of teaching about God.

Again, it perfects us for Moral philosophy, implanting in our character Order, decency, and harmonic conduct; it also teaches which figures, which melodies, and which movements are fitting for virtue: with which doctrine <term>Athenaeus</term> <note>a Greek rhetorician and grammarian</note> also wishes those to be refined and perfected who are to devote themselves to Moral virtues from their youth. Because it also explains the proportions of Numbers familiar to the virtues—some indeed arithmetic, others Geometric, and others Harmonic; it also shows the Excesses and Defects of Vices, by all of which we are directed toward a <term>moderation</term> <note>original: *mediocritatem*; the Aristotelian "golden mean" or middle path between extremes</note> of Character and toward decency.

# ON THE ORIGIN OF HARMONIC
# PROPORTIONS, AND ON THE
## Nature and differences of things
### pertaining to
### Song.

**H**itherto, following the Nature of things, we have first spoken of Regular Plane Figures; then we passed to their <term>Congruencies</term> <note>the way shapes fit together to fill a space without gaps</note>.
In the following sections, it will be necessary to deviate somewhat from the Natural Method, so that the understanding of the human mind—which not infrequently employs a different path—may be all the more assisted. For the nature of the subject required that we should have explained in the third place those proportions in the abstract which are formed between a circle and a part cut off from it by any side; and what other types of things arise from the composition and division of such proportions. Then, in the fourth place, we would have passed to the works of the world, which either God the Creator himself adjusted to these types of proportions, or which <term>sublunary Nature</term> <note>the earthly realm "below the moon," which Kepler believed was influenced by the geometric "aspects" or angles of the planets</note> practices daily according to the rule of such proportions in the angles of the planetary rays. Finally, we would have added human Music, showing how the human Mind, informing the judgment of hearing, imitates the Creator by a natural instinct in the selection and approval of those same proportions in voices which pleased God in the adjustment of the celestial motions. Because, however, it is difficult to abstract the differences, kinds, and modes of Harmonic Proportions in the mind from musical voices and sounds—since no other words are available to us for explaining the necessary matters than those of Music—we must therefore join the third topic with the fifth and last in this book. We must speak not only of abstract Harmonic Proportions, but also anticipate this human imitation of creation in song. The work of the creation of the heavens, however, because of its sublimity and the difficulty of believing it, must be deferred to the last place, according to that order prescribed in the title of the book. And so much for the order of things to be discussed.

# ON HARMONICS BOOK III.

...the singing of Melodies, not only in Temples and choirs of Musicians, but everywhere even without artistic training, even at crossroads and in the fields.

This antiquity of Song appears from the first book of Genesis. For there must have been great delight from the Song of the human voice (when I say delight, I mean harmonic and harmonious intervals) which already moved Jubal, the eighth from Adam, so that he learned and taught how to imitate the Song of men with brute instruments. Unless I am mistaken, this Jubal is Apollo—with a slight change of letters—who surpassed his brother Jabal—the author of cattle-breeding and who delighted in the rustic pipe (believed by the Greeks to be the God Pan)—with the clear ringing of the newly discovered Lyre, having borrowed the material for the strings from his brother Tubal-cain, who shall be our Vulcan <note>The Roman god of fire and metalworking</note> because of the allusion in the name.

However ancient the form of human Song may be, composed of consonant or harmonious intervals, the causes of those intervals nonetheless remained hidden from men; so much so that before Pythagoras they were not even sought; and having been sought for two thousand years, I shall be the first, unless I am mistaken, to bring them forth most exactly.

Pythagoras is said to be the first who, when passing by a blacksmith’s shop and noticing the sounds of the hammers were harmonically tuned, discovered that the difference in sounds came from the size of the hammers, so that the large ones produced low sounds and the small ones high sounds. Since proportion is properly observed between sizes: having measured the hammers, he easily noticed the proportions by which the harmonic intervals of voices were established, and which were dissonant; which were **Harmonious**, and which **Unharmonious**. For he immediately passed from hammers to the lengths of strings; where the ears indicate more exactly which parts of a string sound in consonance with the whole, and which are dissonant from it.

Certain proportions having been found as <term>the fact of the matter</term> <note>original Greek: *to hoti*—referring to the observation that something exists</note>, it remained that the causes, or <term>the reason why</term> <note>original Greek: *to dioti*—referring to the underlying logical or physical cause</note>, should also be investigated: why these proportions defined harmonious, sweet, and consonant intervals of voices, while other proportions defined dissonant, ear-shunning, and unusual ones. And for two thousand years the opinion was held that the causes must be sought from the properties of the proportions themselves, as they are contained under the terms of discrete quantity, namely of **Numbers**. For the Pythagoreans saw that perfect harmonies are established if strings under equal tension have a proportion between their lengths of double, and triple, and quadruple, among the numbers 1, 2, and 1, 3, and 1, 4. These proportions are called in Arithmetic, **Multiples**. Again, they saw that the consonances of strings were a little more imperfect which make the <term>sesquialtera</term> proportion <note>A ratio of 3:2, where one value is 1.5 times the other</note>, the <term>Hemiholia</term> <note>The Greek term for the 3:2 ratio</note>; and the <term>sesquitertia</term> <note>A ratio of 4:3, where one value is 1.33 times the other</note>, the <term>Epitriton</term> <note>The Greek term for the 4:3 ratio</note>: namely, between the numbers 2, 3 and 3, 4. These two proportions joined together make the double proportion between the numbers 2 and 4, or 1 and 2; but the smaller, between 3 and 4, subtracted from the larger 2 and 3, left the <term>sesquioctava</term> <note>The ratio 9:8, which defines a whole tone in music</note>, between 8 and 9. And they perceived that there was so much in...

...the interval of a Tone <note>The whole tone, such as the distance between C and D</note>, which is the most common in all song. And yet, the number 8 is the cube of 2, and the number 9 is the square of 3. Thus, these numbers were already at hand: 1, 2, 3, 4, 8, and 9. Since unity itself is both its own square and its own cube; and the number two has 4 as its square and 8 as its cube; they also added to the number three—besides its square, 9—its own cube, 27. They did this because they believed one must progress all the way to cubes, for the reason that the entire World and all sounding things consist not of empty surfaces, but of solid bodies <note>In geometry, a "square" represents a 2D surface, while a "cube" represents a 3D solid; Kepler is explaining why the Pythagoreans felt 3D reality required cubic numbers</note>. Finally, from this beginning, such a great opinion of these Numbers grew—because they were the Primes and their squares and cubes—that the Pythagoreans judged that the whole of Philosophy should be composed from them. For Unity represented to them the **Idea**, the **Mind**, and **Form**; because just as unity is indivisible and remains the same whether multiplied as a square or a cube, so too the Ideas were indivisible, universal, and "Always the Same." Therefore, they made unity the symbol of the *Nature of Identity*, while the other numbers were symbols of the *Nature of Alterity* <note>original: "Alteritatis," meaning the state of being "other" or different</note>. The number Two, therefore, signified otherness and **Matter**, because it admits division, just as matter does; and just as two becomes 4 when squared and 8 when cubed—which are numbers distinct from 2—so matter can be unstable and multiform. In another sense, the number Two also signified the **Soul**, because while the Mind is motionless or enjoys uniform (that is, circular) motion, the Soul, by contrast, receives multiple motions from the body, and relates more familiarly to rectilinear motions, which exist in sixfold difference <note>Up/down, forward/backward, left/right</note>. Finally, the number Three noted for them the **Body**, composed of Form and Matter, just as 3 is composed of 1 and 2; and because worldly bodies have as many dimensions as the number Three has units.

<margin>To the Pythagoreans, the Soul is Number and Harmony.</margin>
Nor were Numbers merely symbols of the three principles; rather, the Soul itself was already being composed by them out of these numbers, and all their proportions, and the subdivisions of proportions into <term>sesquialteras</term> <note>the 3:2 ratio, or a perfect fifth</note>, <term>sesquitertias</term> <note>the 4:3 ratio, or a perfect fourth</note>, and <term>sesquioctavas</term> <note>the 9:8 ratio, or a whole tone</note>. Thus the Soul, the bond between Mind and Body, was in its essence nothing but Harmony, and composed out of harmonies. Without a doubt, that consideration led them to this dogma: the fact that the human soul is so greatly delighted by voices which, by their magnitude, form and contain certain harmonic proportions.

## Excursus on the Pythagorean Tetractys.

From the principles explained just before, that <term>Tetractys</term> <note>original: "Tetractys," a triangular figure of four rows of dots (1, 2, 3, 4) totaling ten, which the Pythagoreans considered sacred</note> seems to be derived—the "ever-flowing source of the human Soul" by which the Pythagoreans used to swear. In my opinion, it is thus: because between any two of the three cubes 1, 8, and 27—for example between 1 and 8—there are two mean proportionals: 2 and 4. Therefore, the four numbers 1, 2, 4, 8 (whose sum is 15), or 1, 3, 9, 27 (whose sum is 40), make up that Tetractys. For two cubic numbers have two proportionals between them, just as two plane numbers have one proportional, as is known from geometry.

<summary>Kepler explains the Pythagorean belief that the soul and the physical world are built from the numbers 1, 2, and 3 and their geometric progressions (squares and cubes). He interprets these numbers as symbols for Mind, Matter, and Body, and connects them to the musical ratios that govern human delight in song.</summary>

<page-num>5</page-num>
<header>->ON HARMONICS, BOOK III.<-</header>
A 2

# ON HARMONICS, BOOK III.

Or let that <term>Tetractys</term> <note>The sacred Pythagorean symbol consisting of 10 dots arranged in a triangle of four rows (1, 2, 3, and 4)</note> be 1. 2. 3. 4. Here, 1 is the principle of Numbers; 2 is the first of both Numbers and the Even numbers; 3 is the first of the composite and Odd numbers. When 1 is multiplied by 3, a rectangle of 3 is formed, as if from an odd source; but when 2 is multiplied by itself, a square of 4 is formed, as if from an even source. In the construction of the latter, it is proper for the length and width to be equal, just as in the rectangle of the former they are unequal. Therefore, the sum of 1, 2, 3, and 4 is 10, and the human soul is accustomed to counting to 10. And just as there are four Numbers—the same number, that is, as there were units in the fourth row—so also through them, four species of harmonies exist: between 1 and 2 is the <term>Octave</term> <note>original: "Diapason"</note>, as it is between 2 and 4; and between 1 and 4 is the <term>Double Octave</term> <note>original: "Dis-diapason"</note>, which they considered as one type; between 1 and 3 is the <term>Octave plus a Fifth</term> <note>original: "Diapason Epidiapente"</note>, which they held to be the greatest harmony of the system, and this is the second; the third is between 2 and 3, the <term>Fifth</term> <note>original: "Diapente"</note>; and the fourth is between 3 and 4, the <term>Fourth</term> <note>original: "Diatessaron"</note>. They did not recognize any more harmonies than these.

These are my own thoughts. But on the same Tetractys, Joachim Camerarius <note>A 16th-century German classical scholar</note> wrote slightly differently, and perhaps more correctly, unless he was misled by his extensive reading of ancient authors. In his Greek commentaries on the *Golden Verses of Pythagoras*, he writes: *"First, they uniquely designated the <term>Denary</term> <note>The number ten</note> by the word 'Number.' It was in this sense that Plato said in the Phaedo that the whole half of Numbers is odd. For if two rows of numbers are described alternating from unity to ten, there will be one row of Odds and another of Evens, in this manner:"*
1. 3. 5. 7. 9. (*The sum is 25, an odd number and the square of five.*)
2. 4. 6. 8. 10. (*which is the same number of items as there were odds.*)

*"Or, if unity is omitted as being the principle, and the Denary as being the 'Number' spoken of uniquely, it is thus:"*
2. 4. 6. 8.
3. 5. 7. 9. (*The sum is 24, an even number.*)

This is that *enigma: that Odds are Evens.* For each of 3, 5, 7, and 9 are odd, yet altogether they are four in number, which is even (*And the sum 24 is even.*)

Therefore, the <term>Denary</term>, uniquely called *Number* by the Pythagoreans, has this property: it is collected from unity and its continuous multiples up to four. For it forms an equilateral <term>number triangle</term> <note>A "triangular number" where the dots form an equilateral triangle</note> whose base is Four and whose vertex is unity. From this, the Pythagoreans called every number a <term>Tetractys</term>. Indeed, by doubling the sides of the first Tetractys, another Pythagorean Tetractys is formed: the number 36. This number was most celebrated and useful among them in every way; specifically, it is a <term>numerical Triangle</term> whose base is Eight. Thus, in many demonstrations they used the number 36, especially in Harmonics. For in the arrangements of the shapes of this Number, these numbers are found: 12, 9, 8, 6. With these numbers, they demonstrated that all Harmonic Consonances were encompassed according to the proportions of their intervals. For the number 36 is a **Square**, and its side is 6. It is a **Triangle**, whose side is 8. It is an **Oblong Rectangle**, whose length is 9 and its other length is 12. (*For nine times four and twelve times three both make 36.*) Finally, when these 6, 8, 9, and 12 are cast into one sum, the result is the number 35, called **Harmony** by the Pythagoreans; when unity is added to this, it completes the number 36 again. Furthermore, of the numbers which are collected in natural order from those preceding them (that is, from the triangular numbers 1, 3, 6, 10, 15, 21, 28), 36 is the first (and the only one below 1225) that is a **square**, and it has 6 as its side—the first <term>perfect number</term> <note>A number equal to the sum of its divisors, 1+2+3=6</note>.

and thus it gives birth to the number ten, the mother of all things, as we have said. Moreover, the progression of unity is of this kind: for the World is One. The number Two signifies the first multiplicity contained within it. The number Three signifies the bond and Knot necessary for the fitting together of things: For it is not possible that two things alone should come together into one, apart from a Third.

<header>THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD, BOOK III.</header>

# THE HARMONY OF THE WORLD, BOOK III.

<margin>
The philosophy of numbers of Hermes Trismegistus
</margin>
*The Quaternary [the number 4] is the definer and enumerator of the Elements. For the world is a solid body; and solid bodies always require two middle terms so that they may fit together in a continuous proportion. The sum of these (namely 1, 2, 3, and 4) is the Decad [the number 10], of which we have spoken thus far. For this is the adornment of the universe, the dowry with which its maker endowed it.* Thus far Camerarius <note>Joachim Camerarius (1500–1574) was a German classical scholar who wrote on Pythagorean and ancient philosophy.</note> quotes from the ancients; many things agreeing with these are emphasized by Hermes Trismegistus <note>A legendary Hellenistic figure associated with a body of mystical and philosophical texts known as the Hermetica.</note> (whoever he may have been) to his son Tatius: whose words are these: *The Unity, according to reason, encompasses the Decad, and again the Decad encompasses the Unity.* Next, he composes the concupiscent <note>The desiring or emotional part of the soul.</note> faculty of the Soul from twelve "avengers," or ethical vices, according to the number of the signs of the Zodiac, to which he subjects the Body and this power of the Soul tending toward the body. The Rational faculty of the Soul, however, he himself composes from a <term>Decad</term> <note>original: Denario. The number 10.</note> of Ethical Virtues. So, while the Pythagoreans celebrate the <term>Tetractys</term> <note>original: Tetractyn. A triangular figure of ten points, representing the source of all things.</note> as the fountain of Souls, and Camerarius says there were several Tetractyes—not only that which rises from the base of four to the sum of 10, but also another special one, which from the base of the <term>Ogdoad</term> <note>original: Ogdoadis. The number 8.</note> to the peak gathers the sum of 36—Tatius here also hints at the same from the doctrine of his father Hermes, when he says there was a time when he himself was still in the Ogdoad, or the number Eight. The Father, however, refers the Son to the *Pimander* <note>The "Poimandres," a central text of the Hermetic corpus where a divine mind reveals the secrets of the universe.</note>, singing of the <term>Octonary</term> <note>original: Octonario. A group of eight.</note>; in which surely occurs the Octonary of the Soul's ethical habits, seven indeed corresponding to the seven planets, as it appears, beginning from the Moon; the eighth truly more divine and quieter, corresponding, I think, to the idea of the sphere of the fixed stars. Everything is also conducted through Harmonies; there is much emphasis on Silence, much mention of Mind and Truth; there are proposed the Cave, the Depth, the Inner Sanctuary, the Mixing Bowl of Souls, and many other things: so that there can be no doubt that either Pythagoras followed Hermes, or Hermes followed Pythagoras. Added to this is the fact that Hermes hands down a certain Theology and worship of the divine power; often he is a paraphraser of Moses, and often of the Evangelist John <margin>John 3</margin> in his own sense, especially concerning Regeneration; and he impresses certain ceremonies upon his disciple. Meanwhile, authors affirm the same of the Pythagoreans: that a part of them were devoted to Theology and various ceremonies and superstitions; and Proclus the Pythagorean places Theology in the contemplation of Numbers.

->This by way of digression: let us now return to the Pythagorean demonstration of harmonic proportions.<-

<margin>
The Error of the Pythagoreans concerning the Number of Harmonies.
</margin>
The Pythagoreans were so greatly devoted to this form of philosophizing through Numbers that they no longer stood by the judgment of the ears, even though it was by the evidence of the ears that this Philosophy was first reached. Instead, they would define what was fitting or unfitting, what was Consonant or dissonant, from their Numbers alone, doing violence to the natural instinct of hearing. And that Harmonic tyranny stood until Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 AD), the Greco-Roman astronomer and music theorist who sought a middle ground between pure math and sensory experience.</note>; who first, fifteen hundred years ago, asserted the sense of hearing against the Pythagorean Philosophy. He received among the fitting sounds not only the proportions mentioned above and the <term>sesquioctave</term> <note>original: sesquioctavam. The ratio 9:8, which defines a whole tone.</note> for a Tone, but also admitted the <term>sesquiquinone</term> <note>original: sesquiquinonam. The ratio 6:5, which defines a minor third.</note> for a minor Tone, and the sesquiquinde-

## ON PROPORTIONS

<margin>Ptolemy's error regarding the number of Harmonies and Concordances.</margin>
In this way, Ptolemy corrected the Pythagorean speculation about the origin of harmonic proportions as if it were stumbling, yet he did not remove it entirely as if it were false. Although he restored the judgment of the ears to its proper dignity in his words and doctrine, he nevertheless abandoned it again, himself clinging to the contemplation of abstract numbers. For the cause of number and of individual harmonic proportions is not even in this way equal to its effect; instead, it falls short in defining <term>Consonances</term> <note>original: Consonantijs. Intervals that sound stable and pleasant, like a perfect fifth.</note>, and exceeds it in other <term>Concordances</term> <note>original: Concinnis. Intervals that are musically useful or melodic, but not necessarily "perfect" harmonies.</note>. Ptolemy still denies that the Thirds and Sixths, both the minor and major (which are contained in these proportions 4:5, 5:6, 3:5, and 5:8), are consonant—something which all modern musicians with good ears affirm. Conversely, he accepts the proportions 6:7 and 7:8 and others among the musical concordances. Thus, in a melody proceeding from **UT** to **FA**, some middle pitch is established between **RE** and **MI**, in a proportion where 7 is the middle between 6 and 8. For the sake of notation, this becomes **RI**, and now one could sing **UT. RI. FA.** just as one can sing **UT. RE. MI. FA.** This is most abhorrent to the ears and singing practice of all men; however much the strings might be tuned this way, since they are inanimate, they do not offer their own judgment but follow the hand of an unskilled theorist, offering no resistance.

<margin>His error in taking a non-cause for a cause.</margin>
Furthermore, even if that cause sought from abstract numbers and this effect (the Consonances) were perfectly equal in scope, it might not seem absurd to view it as an archetypal cause. It would testify that the Father of things, the Eternal Mind, contemplating those numbers, took from them the Idea for the intervals of voices—and to ensure they pleased human souls, He provided for it through the conformation of those souls. However, the matter would still not be entirely clear: why these numbers 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, etc., contribute to musical intervals, while 7, 11, 13, and the like do not? Numbers as numbers do not show the cause of this from within themselves. For that cause regarding the <term>Ternary</term> <note>original: Ternario. The number three.</note> of principles, and the family of squares and cubes derived from it, is no cause at all, since the number five is excluded from it—yet five will not allow its right of citizenship to be snatched away from the origin of musical intervals.

Nor does it satisfy the theorist to know that the numbers 1, 2, 3 are symbols of the Principles of which natural things consist. For an interval is not a natural thing, but a <term>Geometrical</term> one. Unless, therefore, these numbers count something else more closely related to intervals, the philosopher will be unable to place any faith in this cause, but will suspect it as a non-cause.

For these reasons, I have decided for twenty years now that I must labor on this: to make this part of Mathematics and Physics more illustrious by discovering such causes which, on the one hand, [agree] with the judgment of the ear...

Kepler argues that the true cause of harmony must be found in geometry, not just arithmetic.</summary>

...[so that] they might satisfy [the requirements] in establishing the Number of Consonances and other Concordant intervals, and not run beyond what the ears can bear. On the other hand, they established a clear and open distinction between the Numbers that form Musical intervals and those alien to this business—those which finally, with respect both to the Archetype and to the Mind (which uses the archetype to shape things according to it), have a kinship with intervals, and therefore shine with the clearest likelihood. 

For since the boundaries of Consonant intervals are <term>continuous quantities</term> <note>In Kepler’s philosophy, "continuous quantity" refers to geometry (lines and shapes), whereas "discrete quantity" refers to arithmetic (individual numbers). He argues that music is fundamentally geometric.</note>; the causes that separate them from Dissonances must also be sought from the family of continuous quantities, not from abstract Numbers, as a discrete quantity. And since it is the Mind that has so formed human Souls that they are delighted by this interval (which is the genuine definition of consonant and dissonant), the differences of one from the other, and the causes by which these intervals become harmonic, must also have a mental and intellectual essence. Specifically, this: that the boundaries of consonant intervals are properly <term>knowable</term> <note>original: scibiles. For Kepler, a "knowable" ratio is one derived from a regular polygon that can be constructed using only a compass and straightedge. If a shape cannot be drawn this way, its corresponding musical interval is "unknowable" or dissonant.</note>; while those of dissonant intervals are either improperly knowable or unknowable. For if they are knowable, they can then enter the Mind and be adopted to form the archetype; but if they are unknowable (in the sense explained in Book I), they remained outside the Mind of the eternal Creator and in no way converged toward the Archetype. 

But more on these things once we have delivered this doctrine through its own chapters, which let us begin with God’s help. We shall speak everywhere of Song—that is, of harmonic intervals not as abstract concepts, but as they are concrete in sound. Yet we shall everywhere understand, with ears trained by the mind, those intervals abstracted from sounds, because they produce their grace not only in sounds and human Song, but also in other things lacking sound, as we shall hear in the fourth and fifth books <note>Kepler is foreshadowing his later arguments that these same harmonic ratios govern astrology (Book IV) and the movement of the planets (Book V).</note>.

# CHAPTER I.
## On the causes of consonances.

### DEFINITION.

Since the ancients used these terms—<term>monophonic</term> <note>original: Μονόφωνον; a single sound or voice.</note>, <term>antiphonic</term> <note>original: Αντίφωνον; sounds that respond to one another, like voices in different registers.</note>, <term>homophonic</term> <note>original: Ομόφωνον; sounding the same.</note>, <term>diaphonic</term> <note>original: Διάφωνον; sounding apart or distinct.</note>, <term>symphonic</term> <note>original: Σύμφωνον; sounding together in agreement, or consonant.</note>, and <term>asymphonic</term> <note>original: Ασύμφωνον; not sounding together, or dissonant</note>—for us, **Dissonant** will mean the same as <term>asymphonic</term>, and **Consonant** the same as <term>symphonic</term>. There are different types of Consonance: the **Identical**, which we shall use in place of <term>homophonic</term>; and the **non-Identical**, which we use for <term>diaphonic</term>. Of the Identical, there will be two species: the **unison**, and the **Identical by opposition** <note>Kepler refers here to the octave (2:1 ratio), where the notes are different in pitch but perceived by the mind as the same "kind" of note.</note>.

### DEFINITION.

In Geometry, the terms **Part** and **Parts** differ. For a "Part" is said to be that of which the Whole is a <term>multiple proportion</term> according to a certain measure—for instance, double, triple, or quadruple. However, they are called "Parts" when not only a single Whole, but some multitude of Wholes is a multiple of them. For example, one-seventh is called a **Part**, because the whole circle is seven times this part; but three-sevenths are called not a **Part** but **Parts**, because the sum of three circles is seven times this arc.

Here, however, we shall not use this distinction. Instead, we shall call both of the aforementioned portions a **Part**; that is, every portion of a length that is **expressible** <note>original: effabilis. In Kepler’s geometry, an "expressible" or "utterable" length is one that can be precisely defined or constructed using a straightedge and compass.</note> will be called a **Part** by us, with this restriction: that it be no larger than a semicircle.

The **Remainder** <note>original: Residuum</note> shall be called that which remains when an expressible portion is taken away from the Whole, and which is not less than a semicircle.

*The distinction of the Remainder from the Part is extremely necessary, because it is possible for a Part to be consonant while its Remainder is dissonant, as we shall see.*

### DEFINITION.

**String** <note>original: Chorda</note> is used here not for a line segment subtending an arc of a circle, as in Geometry, but for any length that is suited to producing a sound. And because sound is drawn out through motion, in the abstract, "string" is to be understood as the length of any motion whatsoever, or any other length, even if only conceived in the mind.

# AXIOM I.

The diameter of a circle, and the sides of the **Radical figures** <note>Kepler refers to the primary polygons, such as the triangle, square, and pentagon, which he analyzed in Book I as the building blocks of geometry.</note> explained in Book I—those which possess their own unique demonstration—determine a part of the circle that is consonant with the whole circle.

*How a circle might be stretched so that it emits a sound, and how it must be attached to a hollow body so that resonance exists—whether from one point, so that the whole sounds, or from two, so that the parts sound—would be a long matter to explain here. Nevertheless, it was necessary to begin in this way, because we are not only dealing with song (which is harmony made concrete in sounds), but must also understand the interval as an abstract concept apart from sounds. As far as song is concerned, it is enough that a string stretched in a straight line can be divided in the same way that it would be divided if it were curved into a circle, by the side of an inscribable figure.*

## Corollary.

*Consonances are infinite, because the number of demonstrable figures is infinite. However, it is not yet time to speak of the selection of "concordances" <note>Kepler distinguishes between a "consonance" (any mathematically valid interval) and a "concordance" (an interval that is actually pleasing to the human ear).</note>, which does not present itself much further on. Here, the Pythagoreans <note>Followers of Pythagoras, who believed that the universe and music were governed by whole numbers rather than geometry.</note> sought the limits of the magnitude of consonant intervals within their numbers, as if numbers were the causes; yet it is the human sense of hearing alone that sets those limits, for hearing is not of infinite power. Therefore, that narrowing of the number of concordances is merely accidental to the abstract harmonic intervals, rather than being the cause. Indeed, even modern musicians exceed the Pythagorean limits—to say nothing of the celestial harmonies.*

# AXIOM II.

By whatever degree the demonstration of a side is removed from the first; by that same degree does the consonance of the part of the circle (cut off by that side) with the whole circle recede from the most perfect consonance of the unison. Or, whatever the rank of the figure is among the other figures (of which it is a side), that same rank belongs to that consonance among the others.

*This axiom will be employed further down to make a selection of concordances for the sake of sweetness.*

# AXIOM III.

The sides of Regular Figures and Star Polygons that are indemonstrable <note>In this context, "indemonstrable" means a figure that cannot be constructed using only a compass and an unmarked straightedge.</note> determine a part of the circle that is dissonant from the whole circle. This is also true for the side of a figure that is indeed demonstrable, but not through itself, nor by its own unique demonstration. Or, for a lack of its own demonstration, look back to the lack of "congruence" <note>original: congruentia; refers to how shapes fit together to fill a space, discussed in Book II.</note> in Book II. In both ways, the **Quindecangle** <note>A fifteen-sided polygon.</note> is excluded.

# ->AXIOM IV.<-

**Figures which have related proofs for their sides also produce related Harmonies.**

*Through this axiom, the origin and cause of Harmonic Proportions from the remainder <note>original: "ex superfluo" — literally "from the surplus." This refers to the arc of a circle left over after a side of a polygon is inscribed.</note> will be proven.*

# ->AXIOM V.<-

Strings or arcs of a circle, of equal tension, having between them (by reason of their length) the same proportion as exists between a Part or Remainder of a circle and the Whole circle, also possess the same Consonance or dissonance, even if that [relationship] is contained between different limits or sounds.

*In an abstract sense, it should be understood that a circle, together with its part, constitutes certain Harmonic proportions; wherever these are found in other terms—whether in sounds or in silent motions <note>Kepler is preparing the reader for his later argument that the planets themselves create "silent" harmonies through their varying orbital speeds.</note>—they are always harmonic.*

*This Axiom is added, however, because not all Harmonic Proportions arise immediately from the circle itself from the very first division by a Regular figure, but some arise as descendants from those prior to them, up to a certain limit: as we shall see in the propositions.*

*The use of this Axiom is in Propositions VII and VIII.*

...a third, being consonant with one of them, will also be consonant with the other; but if it is dissonant from one, it will also be dissonant from the other, regardless of any different types of consonances or dissonances.

*Note that the "Species of <term>Identical-sounding</term>" <note>original: "Identisoni" — Kepler’s term for notes that sound like the same pitch, specifically unisons or octaves.</note> is placed in the subject, and the "Category of Consonance" in the predicate, so that we may understand two things: First, it does not follow that just because two voices are consonant in any way at all, a third must also be consonant with both, or dissonant from both. This is false regarding the general category, but true for the specific type of identical-sounding notes. Second, it does not follow that if a third note is consonant with one of the identical-sounding notes by a certain specific interval, it will be consonant with the other by that same interval. This is not always true, as I will show by an example, even if it is a bit ahead of schedule. Let there be two voices making an <term>Octave</term> <note>original: "diapason"</note> G and g; let there be a third voice, d. That voice d makes a <term>Fifth</term> <note>original: "diapente"</note> with the lower G; therefore, it also sounds consonant with the upper g, yet not by a Fifth, but by a <term>Fourth</term> <note>original: "diatessaron"</note>.*

*The chief use of this axiom is in Proposition IV.*

# AXIOM VII.

## When two strings or voices produce identical sounds, a third voice that is <term>identical-sounding</term> with one of them will also be identically consonant with the other.

*What could not be stated generally in the previous axiom is now true specifically regarding the identity of sounds.*
*This is used in Proposition III.*

<margin>The Metaphysical Cause of Harmonies.</margin>
**Regarding these Axioms, then, especially the first five, the contemplation is sublime, Platonic, and analogous to the Christian Faith, looking toward Metaphysics and the doctrine of the Soul. Geometry—the part of which relevant here was covered in the first two books—is co-eternal with God and shining forth in the Divine Mind. It supplied God with the patterns (as was said in the preamble to this book) for the adornment of the World, so that it might become the Best and Most Beautiful, and finally most similar to its Creator. Indeed, there are as many images of God the Creator as there are Spirits, Souls, and Minds appointed over their respective bodies to govern, move, increase, preserve, and even propagate them.**

Since, therefore, they [Souls] have embraced a certain pattern of Creation in their duties, they also observe the same laws of work as the Creator, taken from geometry. They rejoice in the same proportions which God used, wherever they find them—whether by pure contemplation, or through the intervention of the senses in things subject to the senses, or even without any reasoning of the Mind, through a hidden and innate instinct. This is true whether God himself expressed these proportions invariably in bodies and motions, or whether, by a certain geometric necessity of infinitely divisible matter and of motions through the quantity of matter, these harmonic proportions occurred at their own times among the infinite non-harmonic proportions, and thus exist not in BEING but in BECOMING. Not only do Minds rejoice...

<page-num>14</page-num>
->## ON PROPORTIONS<-

Images of God [act] by these proportions; but they also use them as laws to fulfill their duties and proportions, expressing them in the movements of their bodies as far as is permitted. Two clear examples will be presented in the following books: one of the Creator God himself, who distributed the motions of the heavens according to harmonic proportions; the other of that Soul which we usually call **sublunary Nature** <note>original: "Naturam sublunarem" — In the Aristotelian worldview, the "sublunary" sphere is the Earth and its atmosphere, everything below the moon, subject to change and decay.</note>, which stirs up <term>Meteors</term> <note>In the 17th century, "meteors" referred to any atmospheric phenomena, including rain, wind, and lightning, not just falling stars.</note> according to the prescription of proportions which occur in the **Radiation of the Stars**. Let the third and proper example for this book be the **human Soul**, and even to some extent that of cattle. For these, having perceived the harmonic proportions of voices, rejoice in them; they are saddened by those that are not harmonic. From these affections of the Soul, the former are called **Consonances**, and the latter **Dissonances**. If another harmonic proportion is added—that of long and short voices and sounds for the sake of time—then they move their bodies in dances and their tongues in speech according to those same laws. To this, the craftsmen of hammers accommodate their strokes, and soldiers their pace; all things live while Harmonies endure, and grow sluggish when they are disturbed.

Whether these and similar things are a matter of Design or Instinct—that is, the work of the Mind—or whether it happens by the necessity of the Nature of the Elements and Matter, so that no temperament comfortable to the senses can exist unless it consists of the harmonic proportions of figures; this has been variously disputed by philosophers. All of them ask: from where does that sweetness arise, which glides into the ears from the proportion of voices, and by which sweetness we define Consonances? Those who incline toward the Matter and Motion of the Elements bring forward this example, which is indeed quite wonderful in itself:

<margin>A wonderful experiment involving strings.</margin>
When a string is struck, it draws another string (which was not struck) into sound along with it, if the second string has been stretched harmoniously with it; but if it is stretched dissonantly, the string is left unmoved. Since this cannot happen by the service of any Mind—because the sound that caused this has no Mind or intellect—it follows that we must say it happens through a "tempering of motions." For the sound of a string has a highness or lowness from the speed or slowness of the vibration by which the whole free length of the string vibrates. These differences in sound do not reside primarily and immediately in the length or shortness itself, but secondarily; because, naturally, as the length is decreased, the slowness of the vibration decreases and the speed increases. Hence it is that while the free length of the string remains the same, the tension itself sharpens the sound; because by leaving the string less slack, it also decreases the space through which it can be vibrated in a reciprocal motion.

Therefore, when two strings have the same tension, so that they can return a unison, then the sound of one—that is, the **immaterial form** <note>original: "species immateriata" — A technical term meaning the "form" or "image" of a physical action (like sound or light) that travels through a medium.</note> of the body of the string, established in vibration—having glided from its own string, strikes the other string. It is as if someone were to let out a shout toward a <term>Chelys</term> <note>original: "Chelyn" — A Greek term for a lyre or lute, originally made from a tortoise shell.</note> or another hollow object; by that shout he strikes that hollow and makes all its strings resonate. That "form of vibration" strikes the other string with the same rhythm of speed by which it also moves, because it is equally tense; so that individual strokes (into which the vibration is understood to be divided) fall upon individual [parts]...

...of the other struck string constantly coincide with the <term>little intervals of rest</term> <note>original: "cessiunculas" — Kepler uses this to describe the momentary pauses at the extreme ends of a string's vibration before it changes direction.</note>; thus it happens that the string moved most of all is the one tuned to a **unison** with the first. But that string is also moved which is of double or half the speed, because two strokes of vibration are completed within one interval of rest of the string, and thus every third stroke from the first always coincides with the end of the interval of rest. Finally, even that string moves a little which is of a **sesquialtera** <note>original: "sesquialteræ" — The ratio of 3:2, which in music produces the interval of a Perfect Fifth.</note> speed, because three little strokes occur within two of its intervals of rest. But now those strokes and these intervals begin to run into each other more frequently and hinder one another; while two of its strokes stray from the end of this interval of rest, only one coincides correctly. By this collision, the motion of the other strings is stopped, just as if someone had placed a finger on a vibrating string. This seems to me to be the cause of this wonderful experiment; to whoever is more successful in the investigation of the mind than I, I shall give the prize.

<margin>What is the cause of pleasure from harmonies?</margin>
What then? If the speed of one string is powerful enough to move another proportioned string which, to the sight, remains untouched: will not these same speeds of two strings relative to each other be powerful enough to produce a sweet tickling of the hearing, for the reason that it is moved in a somewhat uniform way by both strings, and two strokes from two sounds or vibrations fall upon the same moment? Not at all, I say; this matter is not settled so easily. I wonder that **Porphyry**, the commentator on the *Harmonics* of **Ptolemy** <note>Porphyry (c. 234–c. 305 AD) wrote a significant commentary on the musical theories of Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century astronomer and music theorist.</note>, could be satisfied with such a thing regarding the cause of this matter, since he was a philosopher of the deepest investigation. Unless it is likely that he was restrained by the difficulty of seeking the cause, so that he did not penetrate as far as he wished; and he thought it better to put something forward rather than remain entirely silent, which they say is shameful for a Philosopher. For what, I ask, is the proportion of a tickling of the hearing—a bodily thing—to that incredible pleasure which we perceive most deeply within the soul from harmonic **Consonances**? Is it not true that if there is any pleasure from a tickling, the primary place for that pleasure belongs to the limb that sustains the tickling?

<margin>What is sensation?</margin>
For thus I thought sensation ought to be defined in my *Dioptrics* <note>original: "Dioptricis" — Kepler's 1611 work on the theory of lenses and the mechanism of vision.</note>: that it is finally an absolute sensation, producing pleasure or pain, when the "image" of the organ destined for sensation (as it is affected by an external thing) comes inward to the tribunal of the common sense by the passage of the spirits. Now indeed, in the hearing of consonant voices or sounds, what parts of the pleasure, I ask, remain in the ears? Do we not sometimes feel pain in our ears while we gape at this hearing, and place a hand against excessively loud clangs? Nevertheless, we continue to perceive the consonances, and our heart leaps within us. Add to this that this reasoning deduced from motion is strongest in a **unison**; yet sweetness is not at its peak in a unison, but in other Consonances and their composition.

<margin>The cause of the sweetness of Harmonies must be sought from the approval of the Mind.</margin>
Many things could be brought forward to destroy this proposed reasoning of sweetness from Consonances, which I omit to write down too meticulously for the present. I emphasize this one thing, which has already been touched upon by me above and can stand in place of all: that the Works and Motions of bodies, which emulate harmonic proportions, stand on the side of the parts of the Soul and Mind, assigning to them the cause of why Consonances delight. Nor does the authority of the ancients...

<page-num>16</page-num>
<header>ON PROPORTIONS</header>
<meta>catchword: PROPO-</meta>

Of the Ancients; who, defining the Soul now as Motion, now as Harmony, did not speak so much absurdly as they were foolishly understood: since in difficult matters, mystical senses usually lie hidden, concealed beneath the husks of words. Indeed, the philosophy of **Timaeus of Locris** <note>Timaeus of Locris was a Pythagorean philosopher; Kepler refers here to the "Timaeus" dialogue by Plato, which describes the soul's construction through mathematical ratios.</note>, regarding how the soul is composed of **Harmonic** proportions—which was mentioned in the preamble—was refuted by **Aristotle** according to the literal sense of the words. However, I would not dare to affirm that nothing lies hidden in those pages beyond what the words sound like. Indeed, I think no one will deny that this author holds at least this much, which I am asserting here: that it is the **Mind** and the human **Soul** by whose judgment or instinct the sense of hearing distinguishes pleasant (that is, consonant) proportions from unpleasant and dissonant ones. For he who considers this diligently will find that **Proportions** are <term>Beings of Reason</term> <note>original: "Rationis Entia" — Concepts that exist in the mind's understanding rather than as physical objects in the world.</note>, perceptible by reason alone, not by sense; and to distinguish the proportions as the form from the proportioned thing as the matter is the work of the **Mind**.

<margin>From the scientific demonstration of figures.</margin>
Since, however, we have explained two properties of the Regular Figures—the **scientific demonstration of the sides** in each, and the **congruence** <note>original: "Congruentiam" — Here meaning the ability of geometric shapes to fit together perfectly to fill a space or tile a surface.</note> of the wholes joined together—both are not of exactly the same breadth. Regarding **demonstration**, our **axioms** sound most powerfully, because this is more familiar to the proportions of motions, from which sounds also arise.

For **congruence** is in the figures as they are wholes; but the motions (to which harmonic proportions happen) extend the sides of the figure from which they are derived into a straight line (since almost all are considered as rectilinear), and thus they ruin and destroy their own figure, like <note>Kepler alludes to the ancient natural history myth that young vipers eat their way out of their mother's womb, killing her.</note> snakes their Mother. The figure, insofar as it is congruent, divides the whole circle into parts: harmonic proportions extend the divided circle into a straight line, and they erase the act of division made by the figure. Thus, consonances with demonstrable figures run out into infinity; but congruent figures are finished by the number twelve. Finally, any figure makes a single division of the circle; but the parts established in the circle always make two consonances with the Whole.

<margin>And congruence.</margin>
But even if the account of the scientific demonstration of the sides will be more important in this third book than the **congruence** of the whole figures, this latter must not be neglected due to its great kinship in this place. For first, the **Latin** meaning of the word, **Congruence**, if you examine everything, sounds the same as the **Greek** word **Harmony**, which we will deal with in this book: except that usage has distinguished these words slightly based on their subject matter. Secondly, the **congruence** of figures provides some **congruence** to the motions (which we discuss in this and the fifth book). Thirdly, although we do not look so much at the whole figure as at one of its sides, and whatever part that side cuts off is **consonant**; yet at the same time, this is also true: that we do not consider so much how great a part of the circle is intercepted, but rather by what kind of figure it was made—whether demonstrable and congruent, or the opposite. For every figure, from its angles (from which it obtained **congruence** in Book II), also obtained demonstration in Book I. Therefore, the respect for the **congruence** of figures must not be taken away from Harmonies.

Having previously discussed how the mind perceives ratios, he now seeks to prove why the ratio of 1:2 (the octave) is the most perfect harmony based on the geometry of the circle.</meta>

<page-num>17</page-num>
<header>ON HARMONICS, BOOK III.</header>

# PROPOSITION I.

### The Harmony of the Half with the Whole, following the unison, is the only one in the first rank that is simple, perfect, and Identical—specifically, arising from the Opposite.

*For that which is shaped <note>Kepler uses "shaped" or "figured" to refer to polygons like triangles or squares inscribed in a circle.</note> is composed of different parts; therefore, it is neither simple nor Identical. For a Figure has an area, parts related to it, and angles differing by position. However, that which is not shaped—which lacks width in its area, and remains a single, pure straight line in both its parts and its angles, and is equal to the proposed Measure—is, for these very reasons, both simple and the same as the Measure; that is, it is identical. The former types are the Regular Figures inscribed in a circle; the latter type is the Diameter of the circle.*

*1. For all the sides of Figures deflect equally from the center; the Diameter is drawn through the center itself.* 

*2. A Measure <note>Here, the "measure" refers to the compass setting or the line used to divide the circle.</note> that divides the circle from one point using the side of a figure, when it has proceeded to do this several times, finally returns to the first point at the other end of the side; the Diameter, however, passing through the center itself, returns to the starting point immediately at the very first repetition.*

*3. The remaining Figures have both the length of their sides and the surface of the area which they surround; the diameter, surrounding or enclosing no part of the plane, coincides entirely with itself upon the second turn of repeated movements.*

*4. The other Figures that divide a circle create many parts; the Diameter creates the smallest number of all parts, namely only two: for it is impossible to divide a whole into fewer than two parts.*

*5. Since the Diameter is that measure to which the sides of figures must be compared for the sake of understanding and demonstration; the sides of the remaining figures are described with more labor, and are brought into the state of scientific knowledge through a degree of imperfect demonstration: but the diameter of the circle is described by the simplest law, by a path through the center from one point of the circle to the opposite point, and it equals itself and is the Measure of its very self.*

*6. Also, the sides of Figures in a single division of the circle—or in the casting off of a Part—create unequal portions, making the Part smaller than the Remainder; the diameter leaves the Part cast off equal to the Remainder. This proportion of equality is pure, simple, and perfect; because parts that are equal to one another are the Same <term>Identical</term> <note>original: "Idem" — In Kepler's harmonic theory, "identity" refers to the Octave (1:2), where the two notes are perceived as the same pitch at different registers.</note> for the purpose of measurement.*

*7. Finally, the other figures divide the circumference of the circle into several equal parts, but they divide the area of the circle into unequal parts, because one area—the area of the figure—is left in the middle, larger than any of the segments; the diameter divides not only the circumference but also the area into two equal halves at the same time.*

*But according to Axiom II: the nature of the side or line that divides the circle harmoniously passes into the harmony itself. Therefore, the Harmony of the part which the diameter cuts from the circle—that is, of the semicircle with the whole circle—is simple, perfect, and Identical. And by Axiom V, all other lengths that are related to each other as the Whole circle is to its half likewise create the same Identical, perfect, and simple harmony. And in Numbers (not purely abstract and counting numbers, but lengths that have been numbered), the Double Proportion <note>original: "Proportio dupla" — the ratio of 1:2.</note>, such as between 1 and 2, as well as between their equal multiples, produces the Identical Harmony.*

*Note here, that just as the diameter, through all its simplicities and perfections, is nevertheless not so simple as a point; but remains a line, with two circu-*
