### CHAPTER V. 
First. Second. Third. Fourth. Fifth. 6. 7. 8.
->First. Second. Third. Fourth.<-

<margin>What the Octave or Diapason is.</margin>
It follows, therefore, that the last note in the counting of the sequence is the eighth in number. And from this, the interval obtained the name of the "Octave." The Greeks, looking to its identity-like consonance, call it <term>Diapason</term> <note>original: "Διαπασῶν"; literally "through all," referring to the full range of notes.</note>, as it is also written in Latin letters; it is as if, once all the differently sounding notes are used up, the singer's voice returns to itself in the eighth sound. From there, a new beginning and a new series of <term>concinnous</term> <note>fit-together or melodic intervals</note> notes arises, similar in every way to the first: see Proposition I.

->The Fifth. &emsp; The Fourth &emsp; The System of the Octave<-
---
<note>Musical notation on a five-line staff showing sequences of notes labeled as the Fifth, the Fourth, and the complete Octave scale.</note>
---

In vain do people philosophize here about the Number—specifically, why does the eighth voice consume all others and return to the same? The true answer must be given by "begging the question" <note>An argument where the conclusion is assumed in the premise; Kepler suggests the answer is self-evident in nature.</note>: namely, because nature has made it so that the interval of the double proportion <note>The 2:1 ratio.</note>, which according to Chapter I is <term>identity-sounding</term> <note>original: "Identisonum"; notes that sound the same but at different pitches, like a high and low C.</note>, is divided into seven concinnous intervals, which are defined by eight sounds, as has been proven in this chapter. <margin>What is a System?</margin> They themselves think this happens because the number 8 is the first Cube and the first <term>Tessera</term> <note>a die or square/solid shape</note>. But what does the sectioning of a string have to do with solid shapes? And why does the twenty-seventh voice (which is the second cube) not also return to the same sound?

For this reason, the name <term>System</term> <note>a structured collection of notes</note> properly and primarily belongs to the interval of the double proportion, divided by its seven concinnous steps, described by its eight voices or strings, and expressed on instruments: concerning which, see Chapter IX below.

<margin>The Double Octave.</margin>
In those intervals that exceed the Octave (or Diapason), among the multiples of the Octave, the double Octave is usually called the <term>Disdiapason</term> in Greek <note>original: "Δὶς διὰ πασῶν"</note>; the triple is the <term>Trisdiapason</term>, and so on. In other cases, the Octave (or its multiple) is expressed and the excess is added, in this manner: "The Fifth above the Octave," or "The Octave above the Fifth," or <term>Diapaponepidiapente</term> <note>original: "Διά πέντε ἐπὶ διὰ πασῶν"; a compound term for an octave plus a fifth, i.e., a twelfth.</note>. Sometimes we also proceed by number, calling them the Ninth, Tenth, Twelfth, etc.

This reading of consonant intervals into concinnous ones is natural. This quantity and the number of concinnous elements (not greater than three) does not rest solely on the ears being accustomed to it; rather, the sense of hearing has this by natural instinct. Nor can any other intervals, or any other number of them, be taken as concinnous into which any of the consonances may be divided. For if you wished, for example, to add the <term>Diesis</term> <note>A very small interval, roughly a quarter-tone.</note>, first of all, that is a secondary product of the dissonant concinnous intervals; secondly, even if you most wanted to add it because it is a product of consonances, you could not do it alone. For it would drag with it the <term>Limma</term> or <term>Minor Semitone</term>, which arises only from dissonances. But it is agreeable for the hearing to distinguish that which comes from consonances; and while admitting the former during singing and among the secondary intervals, it rejects this other one as illegitimate. Therefore, the Diesis will not be among the principal intervals of the Octave.

### CHAPTER VI.

<summary>Kepler defines the Octave (Diapason) and the "System," arguing that the return to the same sound after eight notes is a natural property of the 2:1 ratio rather than a mystical property of the number eight itself. He also discusses how to name intervals that extend beyond a single octave, such as the Twelfth or the Double Octave.</summary>

# ON HARMONICS BOOK III.
## CHAPTER VI.
### Concerning the types of song: the Hard and the Soft.

The types of figures were discussed in Book I, Proposition XLIX. Since the sections of the string themselves imitate these very figures (according to Axiom II of this book), it follows that because the section of the continuous double proportion <note>The 2:1 ratio, or octave.</note> and the Trigonal <note>original: "Trigonica"; refers to the division of a circle by an equilateral triangle.</note> section (and its continuous double) are among the first figures with expressible sides—namely the Triangle and the Quadrilateral—while the Pentagonal section is made from an inexpressible side <note>The "inexpressible" or "ineffable" side refers to the irrational ratio (the Golden Ratio) involved in pentagonal geometry.</note>; therefore, by Axiom IV, those [rational] sections produce one genus of song, and the [pentagonal] sections produce another. To this latter genus, the bisection <note>The division of the string in half.</note> is also added, not because of the four-sided figure <note>The square.</note>, but solely because of the identical consonance of bisection.

From this, therefore, two Genera of sections are born. One possesses these sections: **The Soft Genus.** <note>Known today as the Minor system.</note>

<header>ON PROPORTIONS</header>

<margin>CHAPTER VI.</margin>
These are the two types of Song celebrated by everyone. The first is indeed called *soft song* <note>Known today as the Minor system or key.</note>, because there are found in it the intervals of the *Third and Sixth* arranged from the lowest note as "soft" <note>meaning minor intervals: the Minor Third (5:6) and Minor Sixth (5:8)</note>. The latter is called *hard song* <note>The Major system.</note>, named after the intervals of the same name arranged in the same place in the octave system <note>meaning major intervals: the Major Third (4:5) and Major Sixth (3:5)</note>. The reasoning for these names was given in the preceding Chapter V.

For just as in that location, the ratio 5:6 <note>Minor Third</note> did not allow for 3:5 <note>Major Sixth</note>, so here the ratio 4:5 <note>Major Third</note> does not allow for 5:8 <note>Minor Sixth</note>. This is because the nature of a melodious song requires that the Third combined with the Sixth must form a perfect Fourth, or *fourth* <note>original: "diatessaron"; the interval of a perfect fourth, ratio 3:4</note>.

From this, the natural "fence" or boundary of each genus appears. For since in soft song the lowest place holds 5:6 and in hard song it holds 4:5, and the difference between them—namely the *diesis* <note>A very small interval with the ratio 24:25</note>—is not among the ordinary harmonious intervals (according to Chapter IV), it follows that the 4:5 (the *major third*) and the 5:6 (the *minor third*) cannot stand together in the same natural series of a song in that lowest position. Instead, if the 4:5 *major third* is adopted, the 5:6 must be exiled from that position for that turn; or if the latter is received, the former is thrust out. In this arrangement, the 4:5 brings with it the 3:5 <note>Major Sixth</note>, and the 5:6 brings with it the 5:8, the *minor sixth*.

Furthermore, God himself expressed this distinction between both types of harmony in the motions of the planets, as we shall hear in Book V.

Regarding those three Genera of the Ancients, which bear the names *Diatonic*, *Chromatic*, and *Enharmonic*, I deliberately refrain from speaking of them here, lest I confuse the reader. You might, however, interpret the *Diatonic* as *Hard Song*, and the *Chromatic* as *Soft Song*; or perhaps the *Diatonic* refers to each individual system, while the *Chromatic* is a mixture of the hard and the soft. The *Enharmonic*, however, has nothing corresponding to it in natural song; in practical *Music*, however, certain things correspond to it to some extent, such as the *vibrations of the human voice*, the *tremolo of Organs*, *mordents on the strings of the lute* <note>original: "pandurae"; a long-necked lute</note>, and similar ornaments.

See what we discuss concerning these Genera below in the Appendix to the text of *Ptolemy* <note>referring to Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century astronomer and music theorist</note>.

---

## CHAPTER VII.
### On the full division of one Octave
### in both types of song, and on the natural 
### order of all harmonious intervals.

Thus, so far, Nature herself has shown that in soft song, the third harmonious interval from the bottom is the *minor tone* (9:10), the fourth is the *major tone* (8:9), and the fifth is the *semitone* (15:16). In hard song, however, the third from the bottom is 15:16, the fourth is 8:9, and the fifth is 9:10.

There remain in both types of *Song* two pairs of thirds, one minor and one major, which have not yet been actually divided by natural string sections into the smallest harmonious elements.

First, let us see into which harmonious intervals those can be divided; then, in what order each should be placed.

Nature teaches us enough if we can divide them into the same elements of which we have seen they consist so far, as nature demonstrates, the *Fourth*... <note>original: "Diatessaron"</note>

<margin>CHAPTER VI.</margin>
...the <term>fourth</term> <note>original: "diatessaron," the interval of a perfect fourth, ratio 3:4</note> consonances; we ought not to use others whose examples nature does not demonstrate. Arithmetic therefore teaches that the ratios 4:5 <note>the Major Third</note> and 5:6 <note>the Minor Third</note> are composed of 8:9, 9:10, and 15:16. Thus 5:6 consists of 8:9 and 15:16. See how these are the same elegant divisions as before.

Unless you arrange the **Major Tone** <note>The ratio 8:9, the larger of the two "whole tones" in just intonation.</note> in the lowest position of each lower Third, it would be impossible to have a single string <note>or "note"</note> that serves both types of song <note>the "Soft" (Minor) and "Hard" (Major) systems</note>. For if in the *soft song* you could not place the major tone in the lowest position, you would necessarily have to place the semitone 15:16 there, because only these two intervals are contained within the undivided interval of 5:6. Conversely, in the *hard song*, the **Minor Tone** <note>The ratio 9:10.</note> would have to be placed in the lowest position, because that undivided consonance—namely the Major Third—does not contain the semitone which would have been placed at the bottom in the soft song. Thus, two strings would be required: one longer string for the soft song to create the semitone with the lowest note, and another to create the major tone for the hard song.

Secondly, it is added that it seems consistent with nature that, wherever we have a free choice of division, the larger intervals should tend toward the **grave** <note>lower-pitched</note> sounds, because the grave sounds themselves are <note>mathematically</note> smaller than the acute sounds <note>Kepler is likely referring to the length of the string: a longer string produces a lower/grave sound, but in terms of "perfection" or frequency ratios, he considers their placement relative to the base.</note>.

By this same primary reasoning, we shall also prove that the upper third, which has remained undivided until now, must be divided so that the **major tone** is in the highest position, lest the seventh string be doubled. For in the soft song the upper interval is 4:5, and in the hard song it is 5:6, according to the natural method delivered for the upper intervals. Therefore, if we were to arrange the perfect tone (the other element of the Third) in the lower position of this upper Third, then the same interval arising from notes of different heights would reach toward notes of different heights, making two notes out of one. These reasons are demonstrative and clearly necessary; they suffice against the authorities of **Ptolemy**, **Zarlino**, and **Galilei** <note>Vincenzo Galilei, father of Galileo Galilei</note>, who place the minor tone in the lowest position of the octave.

Therefore, the eight strings are explained by these numbers, reduced to the same lowest common denominator.

You see expressed in the smallest possible numbers not only the proportions of all eight string lengths, but also those of the four upper and four lower notes in smaller numbers; and especially the proportions of the three upper and three lower notes. Regarding the middle notes of these and their numerical values, I have a disagreement with other authors in this chapter. For position VII in both Genres of song <note>the "Soft" and "Hard" systems</note> is 405. And position II, in both, is 640.

Remember, however, that only the eight principal strings of each Genre are set down in this chapter: concerning the accessory strings, one of which the Hard Song adopts almost at the top position, we shall investigate in the following chapter. For here our aim is to see how the penultimate and second-lowest strings are to be established so they can be the same in both Genres.

And because in the joining of these eight principal strings of both songs, it happens that two of them are doubled on musical instruments: therefore, in the common system, there become ten principal strings for one octave <note>original: "Diapason"</note>. Nevertheless, no more than eight "Places" are recognized (and are so called). See the origin of this term in Chapter IV. **

## CHAPTER VIII.
### On the number and order of the smaller intervals of one octave.

The lowest and highest intervals, as well as the fourth, are by nature <note>i.e., by mathematical necessity</note> made into **Major Tones** <note>the interval with the ratio 8:9</note>. The others are made so by the imitation of nature. From these, again by the imitation of nature—which cuts a **Minor Tone** <note>the interval 9:10</note> into a semitone and a <term>diesis</term> <note>a very small interval, roughly a quarter-tone</note>—semitones of the ratio 15:16 are likewise cut off for the sake of greater variety, especially in the bends or turns of the song, and this occurs in the upper part of the interval. There remain, therefore, in the lower part, <term>Limmata</term> <note>the Pythagorean "leftover" interval</note> or **major dieses** of 128:135, which exceeds the <term>diesis</term> 24:25 by one <term>comma</term> <note>the tiny interval 80:81, the difference between a major and minor tone</note>.

The necessity of this division is especially great in the highest interval, which we made a major tone <term>major tone</term> <note>A major tone is a ratio of 9:8, slightly larger than a minor tone of 10:9.</note> in the preceding chapter. This is because the "hard song" <note>original: *cantus durus*; this refers to the musical system using B-natural, analogous to the modern Major scale.</note> uses either a semitone at the top or a major tone interchangeably as the situation requires, though it uses the semitone more frequently and almost formally. This is because, just as the ordinary seventh note makes an <term>Epitriton</term> <note>original: *Epitriton*; a Greek term for the ratio 4:3, also called a Fourth or *Diatessaron*.</note> or **Fourth** (3 to 4) with the fourth note—specifically the ratio of 405 to 540 mentioned in the previous chapter—so too this "extraordinary" seventh note likes to form a <term>perfect fifth</term> <note>original: *diapente perfectum*; the ratio 3:2.</note> or ratio of 2 to 3 with the third note. This is because the third note is characteristic of the "hard" genus (specifically 576), so that the melody may be made more shrill or clear by this means. Indeed, 2/3 of 576 is 384; which, when compared with the octave (specifically 360), makes the ratio 16 to 15 <note>The ratio 16:15 is a standard "Just" semitone.</note>.

<margin>
CHAPTER VIII.

The <term>Lack of Skill</term> <note>original: *Atechnia*; a Greek-derived term for a lack of formal art or scientific method.</note> of Organists.
</margin>

You see that in two places, two semitones concur below a <term>diesis</term> <note>A diesis is a very small interval, specifically the difference between three major thirds and an octave in just intonation.</note>, which I previously said would happen. The craftsmen of organs seize upon this, and they use two semitones in place of a whole tone whenever they introduce some unusually bold modulation. Even if, by the rules of their craft, they temper all the intervals so that none are left "pure," they do so to raise and soften the imperfection of the others, ensuring the perfect intervals suffer the least possible loss of perfection. By this reasoning, it happens that all whole tones are equal for organists, and the <term>limma</term> <note>A Pythagorean semitone with a ratio of 256:243.</note> is also equal to the semitone. Thus, for them, two semitones make a whole tone through a perfect bisection; and so that this may succeed more easily, not even the diesis retains its true mathematical perfection among them.

# A Quick Division of the Monochord
# for the Lute and its Rejection by the
## Sense of Hearing.

This place demands that I fulfill what I promised above toward the end of the second chapter: namely, that I compare my own findings with the <term>Lute-player's</term> <note>original: *Testudinariam*; from *testudo*, meaning tortoise, the traditional material for a lute's body.</note> division of the Monochord, brought forward (if I am not mistaken) by Vincenzo Galilei <note>An Italian lutenist and father of the astronomer Galileo Galilei; he was a proponent of equal temperament.</note> following the school of Aristoxenus. I shall also consult the ears on this matter, yet in such a way that Reason may speak what the ears themselves would logically say.

For since the <term>Octave</term> <note>original: *Diapason*.</note> consists of seven harmonious intervals (from which it takes the name "Eighth," as said in the previous chapter), and among these intervals there are five whole tones and two semitones; and since any of the tones can be bisected into parts close to a semitone, so that twelve intervals are made as defined in this chapter—represented by the letters G, G#, A, Bb, B, C, C#, D, D#, E, F, F#, G—instrumental musicians have taken this opportunity to establish twelve intervals within one Octave. They do this by a path that is not at all laborious, but entirely easy and ready to hand, as is proper for most mechanical tasks. It is as follows:

They divide the entire length of the lute neck, between the two <term>bridges</term> <note>original: *Ephippia* or *magadia*; the nut at the top of the neck and the bridge on the body which define the vibrating length of the string.</note> upon which the string rests to allow it a free vibration across its full length, into 18 equal parts. They place the first <term>fret</term> <note>original: *ligaturam* or *Tactum*.</note> at the <term>tuning pegs</term> <note>original: *Verticillis*.</note> so that there is 1 part above it and 17 parts below it. Then, having erased the previous division points, they divide these remaining 17 parts anew into 18 parts, and they cut off one part for the second fret just as before. They repeat this twelve times. They claim that with the twelfth cutting, the part of the string remaining is such that there is an Octave resonance between it and the whole string. 

Suppose, then, the length of the string is 100,000 units.
If 18 parts make 100,000, what do 17 make? The result is 94,444.
Again, if 18 parts are worth 94,444, what do 17 make? The result is 89,198.
And if 18 are worth 89,198, what do 17 make? The result is 84,242, and so on.
In this manner, twelve numbers are produced for as many intervals. Placed alongside these are the numbers that the true ratio, demonstrated by me thus far, requires for the quantity of the whole string.

If this ratio were exact, then surely the ratio repeated twelve times would be equal to the double ratio of 1 to 2 <note>The ratio 1:2 defines the octave.</note>. However, good mathematicians know this to be false, since 1:2 and 17:18 are <term>incommensurable</term> <note>They cannot be expressed as a simple ratio of whole numbers to one another in this geometric progression.</note>. <margin>CHAPTER VIII.</margin>

...nevertheless, the mechanical <term>string division</term> <note>original: *sectio chordæ*. The practice of marking where frets should be placed on a musical instrument.</note> satisfies the hearing well enough; this is because the individual numbers closely approach the true values placed alongside them, and because the strings of <term>lutes</term> <note>original: *chelyum*. From the Greek *chelys*, meaning tortoise, referring to the traditional shape of stringed instruments like lutes or lyres.</note> are flexible. Their sounds are also somewhat variable: they are sharper at the start when their motion is still great, having just been released by the finger, and become deeper and more relaxed when the width of the vibration is narrowed into a small space as the string returns to its rest. Furthermore, there is a difference between a lighter or stronger touch, and in a wider or more restrained pluck, according to the skill of the Musician. 

But if you examine the judgment of hearing with the clever investigation of Reason, the disagreement will appear immediately. I prove it thus: the ears certainly recognize the harmony between 100,000 and 50,363, as the Craftsman <note>Referring to Vincenzo Galilei's practical method.</note> affirms; they also recognize it between 100,000 and 50,000, as I affirm. The question is: do the ears notice no difference, and does this harmony possess such a broad latitude? I respond from my harmonic divisions in Chapter II: no. For if they could discern nothing between two <term>consonances</term> <note>Combinations of notes that sound pleasant together.</note>—one of strings 100,000 to 50,000 and another of 100,000 to 50,363—then by the same logic, they would also not discern between the strings 100,000 to 50,000 and 100,000 to 49,637, because the difference between the two sets of consonances is equal in both directions.

But if these parts are not struck against the whole 100,000, but the parts themselves—50,363 on one side and 49,637 on the other—are struck against each other, then it is absolutely necessary for the shorter part to emit a higher sound and the longer part a deeper one. This difference in sound is easily detected by the ears in an examination of <term>unison parts</term> <note>original: *unisonarum partium*. When two strings are intended to sound exactly the same pitch.</note>. It is clear, therefore, that the ears judge the consonance between 50,363 and 100,000 to be the same as that between 49,637 and 100,000 for no other reason than that 50,363 and 49,637 *seem* equal; that is, insofar as neither one differs sensibly from 50,000. Therefore, if the ears respond according to the questions of Reason, they will say that the exact Harmony lies between 100,000 and 50,000—that is, in a ratio of 2 to 1 <note>The mathematical ratio for a perfect octave.</note>. Therefore, it is false that there is an exact Consonance between 100,000 and 50,363.

The same judgment applies to the Harmony between 100,000 and 67,025 <note>A ratio intended to approximate the Perfect Fifth.</note>. For even if the ears do not at first distinguish it from 66,667 (the just length of the truly consonant Part), the remainder of that, 32,975, is not half of 67,025. Therefore, the double of that, 65,950, will sound one way, and 67,025 will sound another, since these strings produce a different sound when compared to each other. The reason the ears do not distinguish them in Harmony is that they approve of the middle number—if the sense is sharpened by reason—namely 66,667, so that its complement is 33,333, which is <gloss>namely</gloss> exactly half of it.

Having now established the sharpness of the sense in judging the Harmony of 2 to 3...

# CHAPTER IX.

->Concerning the Diagram, that is, the modern<-
->notation of strings or voices, by lines and<-
->letters of the Alphabet and<-
->Notes: and concerning the System.<-

<margin>Lines</margin>
The matter is not without dispute; but I follow the necessary reasons. Musicians of our age draw the strings differently in <term>lute diagrams</term> <note>original: *diagrammatib⁹ Testudinariis*. Referring to lute tablature, where lines represent the actual strings of the instrument.</note> than they do in vocal ones. For in the former, the individual lines of the diagram denote individual strings, any of which provide different sounds for different fingerings if they are struck. In vocal printing, not only do individual lines signify individual voices or strings, but the very intervals between two lines signify a string in the middle.

<margin>Strings</margin>
In this way, 4 transverse lines with three intervals denote 7 strings, and 5 lines with 4 intervals denote nine strings. Next, they express the voices of the singing System either by peculiar Notes in their respective places on the diagram (which Notes simultaneously suggest the measure of time), or by the first seven letters of the alphabet, or finally by six syllables: *ut, re, mi, fa, sol, la*; or as the Belgians do today, by these seven: *Bo, ce, di, ga, lo, ma, ni.* <note>The syllables *Bo, ce, di, ga, lo, ma, ni* refer to "Bebization," a 16th-century solmization system intended to provide a unique syllable for each note of the septenary scale.</note>
<margin>Notes.</margin>
<margin>The approach of letters.</margin>

For because there are two kinds of song, <term>hard and soft</term> <note>original: *durum & molle*. These refer to the hexachord systems: *durum* (hard) used B-natural, while *molle* (soft) used B-flat.</note>, starting from one common lowest voice, the difference is this: the third and sixth in "hard" song are one <term>diesis</term> <note>original: *diesi*. Here used as a general term for a small melodic interval or semitone shift.</note> higher than in "soft" song. Therefore, the strings—the third and the sixth—cannot remain stable in both kinds of song; it is necessary to either make them double on instruments and organs (as was done in the numbers at the end of Chapter VII) or to vary them by touch, as I believe was done formerly on the lyre and panpipes. The same must be said concerning the Diagram and the human voice. For since only one diagram is made for the octaves of both kinds rising from the same root, and in it there are only eight places for the eight sounds...

## BOOK III OF THE HARMONICS

indicators; from both types of song, let the ten principal strings be gathered into one octave, <margin>CHAPTER IX.</margin> according to Chapter VII; however, the thirteen universal strings, according to Chapter VIII, result in two sounds, separated by a <term>Diesis</term> <note>A very small musical interval, often considered a "diminished" semitone in Kepler's tuning systems.</note> or a <term>Limma</term> <note>A "remainder" or small semitone found in Pythagorean tuning.</note>, being drawn in the same place on the staff, whether it be on a line or in the space between lines. This is because dieses and limmata are not sung one after another, as are Tones and semitones; for this reason, I also did not wish to call them, as some do, "minor semitones." For this reason, then, certain **Clefs** <note>original: *Notæ*. Here referring specifically to the letter-signs at the start of a staff.</note> had to be placed before the lines and spaces—the images of the strings—by which a "hard" song might be distinguished from a "soft" one <note>The "hard" (durus) and "soft" (mollis) systems roughly correspond to our modern concepts of using B-natural vs. B-flat.</note>, and so that the location of the semitone would be clear, whether it be the ordinary one or the others cut off from the major tones. There is also another more hidden necessity, arising not from the diversity of the Genera, but in any song whatever, from the inequality of the major and minor Tones; so that they may be distinguished against each other in the diagrams. For it is necessary that the syllables *Ut, Re, Mi* <note>The system of solmization (solfège) used by singers to identify notes by their function in a hexachord.</note> be general and applicable to both the major and the minor Tone. Thus, however much these names satisfy those learning to sing and practical organists, they by no means satisfy the theorists. Therefore, by virtue of this office, these letters, when they are prefixed to the Diagrams, are usually called **Clefs** <note>original: *Claves*, meaning "keys." Just as a physical key opens a lock, the clef "unlocks" the staff for the singer.</note>, because without them, the entrance into the diagram is not open to the singer.

Indeed, these same letters are also employed in musical instruments; for they are inscribed on the handles of the plectrums in *Stringed instruments*, or on the *stops* in *wind instruments*. From this inscription, those handles are, by private right, called **Keys** <note>original: *Claves*.</note>, and the order itself, or the System formed from all the handles, is called the **Keyboard** <note>original: *Clavarium*, or *das Clavier*.</note>, and the type of instrument is called the **Clavichord**; because the strings are struck by keys—that is, by handles depressed from the outside—and by plectrums jumping up on the inside.

<margin>Tablatures, or diagrams.</margin>
Furthermore, there are diagrams usually written for Organists, in which, instead of black lines, there are series of letters indicating which Keys ought to be touched: where the letters stand in place of the Notes, which the singing-diagrams used to place upon lines or spaces.

Regarding these letters, some things come to our observation which are quite pleasing. First, not all letters are placed upon their own lines and spaces, but only these: *F, G, C*, whenever the place for one of them is on a line; and *B* also, even when it takes its place in a space.

Next, the letter *C* has a sign far different [from the letter itself], such as is depicted here at the side: <margin>Whence the sign<br> 𝄡 </margin> I think this sign was born from a distortion of the old handwriting of the letter *C*. For because writers used the broad nibs of quills, most Notes were made square-shaped by a shorthand script; a round *C* could not be drawn with those quills. Therefore they made the *C* out of three little lines: one thin one, in place of the hollow, and two thick ones, in place of the horns, with the quill drawn sideways like this: <note>The author describes two thick horizontal bars joined by a thin vertical line on the left.</note>. Now the thin line, as the quill hurried, was for the most part made longer, and stood out on both sides beyond the horns, like this: <note>The vertical line extends past the horizontal bars.</note>. Then, so that the horns might be terminated, they drew little lines parallel to the first, like this: <note>This adds vertical lines to the right of the horizontal bars.</note>. And so at last, out of two such little lines, one was made similar and parallel to the first, and the whole sign became like this: 𝄡. This sign, like the Notes themselves on the lines, is made hollow by the gap of the quill, like this: <note>The C-clef positioned on staff lines.</note>.

Yet it also occurs to me whether this sign might not have been born from the use of the term **Musical Scale** <note>original: *Scala Musica*.</note>, since it presents the figure of a ladder [scala]; as if it were the beginning of the scale.

# ON PROPORTIONS

<margin>CHAPTER IX.</margin>
...of the musical scale, he might have noted where it was placed. Or more truly, was the form of the "scale" [ladder] first made from the letter *C*, and then, from the frequent use of this form, did it begin to be called a "scale," though it was properly a *diagramma* <note>The "diagram" or musical staff.</note>?

<margin>On the letter *f*.</margin>
When, however, there is no place for the letter *C* on a line (because in the past there were mostly only four lines), then there is a place for the letter *F* on one of the lines. This is written in its genuine mark in other higher voices, but in the Bass, it is written as a backward semicircle with two dots next to it <note>The modern Bass clef.</note>. I believe this sign, before it was distorted into its current shape, was originally the Greek lowercase $\gamma$ [gamma]. The two added dots signify a "Digamma" <note>An ancient Greek letter (Ϝ) that looks like a double-stacked Gamma, phonetically similar to 'F'.</note>, because our *F* is the Greeks' double $\Gamma$ [Gamma]. Vincenzo Galilei <note>A famous music theorist and father of the astronomer Galileo.</note> provides evidence that this method of marking the sounds of the system through the letters of the alphabet flowed down from the Greeks, citing very ancient examples of Greek songs. It is also well-known that even the simple Greek $\Gamma$ [Gamma] found a place in our Latin music, as will now be discussed.

<margin>On the letter *g*.</margin>
This *F*, therefore, is the second signed clef. Both are signed near each other where a convenient place for both occurs. The third is *G*, which is expressed in higher voices when there is a place for it on a line. According to ancient custom, it is also signed on the bottom line of the diagram. For the musical scale today begins from the sound $\Gamma$ *ut* <note>The lowest note of the medieval hexachord system.</note>, or *Gammut*, which indicates the lowest *G* pitch; so that the Digamma and Gamma are the same as our *F* and *G*.

<margin>On the letter *b*.</margin>
Furthermore, a *b* is drawn above in the diagram of "soft song" <note>original: *molliscantus*. This refers to the "soft" hexachord which uses B-flat.</note> to distinguish the type of song, whether it falls on a line or in a space. Its presence signifies "soft" song, and its absence signifies "hard" song <note>original: *durum*. The "hard" hexachord using B-natural.</note>. But not only this—the letter *b* is also found on other lines or spaces not assigned to the *b* clef, and by a certain misuse, it is repeated as a sign for the semitone or the syllable *FA*.

<margin>On the letter $\natural$.</margin>
Conversely, when a semitone is extraordinarily established in place of a whole tone, and the syllable *Mi* is used in place of the syllable *Fa*, then the letter $\natural$ or a sign derived from it is placed before the note. For the ancients undoubtedly drew it as <term>$\natural$</term> <note>The "natural" sign, which originally represented a "square" B (B-quadratum).</note>; but in its place we use $\times$ or $\sharp$ [a sharp]. Galilei thinks this sign intends to say the same thing to the reader as the ancient Greek word *diaschisma* <note>literally a "splitting" or "fissure".</note>; for it expresses a fissure clearly enough and indicates to us the "cuttings" of semitones, which we discussed in the preceding Chapter VIII.

In the manuals <note>original: *Manubrijs*. The physical keys or "handles" of the instrument.</note> of Tenor Organs, we do not commit this ambiguity with the letter *b* in an improper place. For first, all the keys of those sounds—which are created by "cutting" semitones away from a whole tone and which increase the total number of notes in an octave system—are both raised (standing out above the principal flat keys) and black in color. Then, on each black key, the letter of the neighboring key is inscribed, but with a "tail" for distinction (except for $\natural$, in whose place a simple *b* is placed on the black key). This tail signifies a higher pitch: *utf, fe, g, ge, b, h, c, ce, d, de*. However, between *f* and *fe*, *g* and *ge*, and *c* and *ce*, there is a <term>limma</term> <note>A small Pythagorean semitone.</note>, and between *b* and $\natural$ there is a <term>diesis</term> <note>A very small interval used in tuning.</note>, even though they use the same letters, just as their two sounds occupy a single place in the diagram—

### Book III on Harmonics

<margin>CHAPTER IX.</margin>
...expressed by letters. But between $d$ and $d_{e}$ <note>Kepler likely refers to a chromatic step, such as D to E-flat</note> there is a semitone; thus these two letters, although they are the same, are not assigned to the same position, but to successive ones. However, a diesis <term>diesis|In this context, a small interval smaller than a semitone, specifically the Pythagorean "leimma"</term> exists between $d_{e}$ and $e$, and these different letters belong in the same position: this diversity must be conceded to ancient custom and softened by use. Finally, between $f$ and $g$, $g$ and $a$, $a$ and $b$, $b$ and $c$, $d$ and $d_{e}$, and $e$ and $f$ there are semitones. Therefore, caution must be exercised here, lest by some analogy from the same writing, we presume anything about the identity of the interval.

This is also particularly surprising, and similarly to be forgiven to ancient custom: that in some clavichords and organs (where octaves are continued), although the same letters are rightly repeated because of the identity of the octave <term>diapason|the interval of an octave</term> resonance, this is not done starting from the first $A$, but from the second $b$. For this is the order of the characters: $C, D, E, F, G, A, b, c, d, e, f, g, a, bb, cc, dd, ee, ff, gg, aa, bbb, ccc, ddd, eee, fff, ggg, aaa,$ etc.

<margin>System.</margin>
Furthermore, what the diagram is on paper, the **System** is on the organ—namely, the series of all strings dividing a single consonant interval. As said in Chapter V, this first of all applies to the interval of the octave <term>diapason|octave</term>, and from that to all larger intervals that any instrument encompasses.

<margin>Ancient names of the strings.</margin>
Even though it is not my purpose to dwell long on the music of the ancients, since it is full of obscurities, I nevertheless did not think I should skip the names by which they designated those eight sounds in the system of one octave; for that naming has a kinship with the letters we have discussed so far.

Ancient writers in the time of Aristotle <note>The famous Greek philosopher, 384–322 BCE</note> numbered the strings thus: *Hypate, Parhypate, Lichanos, Mese, Paramese, Trite, Paranete, Nete*. The sound of the **Hypate** was the lowest, and it seems to have been named so from its position on the instrument when it is held for playing: for it maintains the same position today in the lute <note>original: "chely"</note>, the pandura <note>a long-necked lute</note>, and the cittern <note>original: "cythara"</note>.

And since Aristotle affirms that between the **Hypate** and the **Parhypate** there was a diesis (this is the Platonic semitone <note>original: "Platonicum semitonium"</note>, which, when two major tones were subtracted from the fourth <term>diatessaron|the interval of a perfect fourth</term>, left the ratio $243 : 256$, which he called a Diesis); therefore, the **Hypate** was the same as the one we mark with the letter $A$. The **Parhypate** is the one he marks with the letter $b$. Therefore, the **Lichanos** (so named from the index finger) is $c$. The **Mese** is $d$: and it was called by this name because it was the middle among the seven, at which time there were only seven strings in the psaltery, and the first was struck for the eighth. The **Paramese** has the letter $d_{e}$ or $e$: the older writers omitted this one. The **Trite** is the letter $f$; it was so named because it was the third in order from the high end <note>original: "ab acuto"</note>, just as we call it the sixth from the low $A$ <note>original: "a gravi A"</note>. The **Paranete** is marked with the letter $g$. And the **Nete**, as if it were the last to be touched by the plectrum drawn downward, returns to the letter $a$. This distribution is also confirmed by the fact that the fifth <term>diapente|the interval of a perfect fifth</term> is said to have existed between the **Nete** and the **Mese**.

However, such a system of eight strings could not serve both types of singing unless either the **Parhypate** was shortened by the touch of a finger...

# ON PROPORTIONS

<margin>CHAPTER IX. Which notes were stable for the ancients, and which were mobile?</margin>
...and the *paramese* <note>the 'middle-adjacent' string in the Greek system</note> $de$ so that they might become B-natural or E; or they were tuned by pegs tighter in "hard" song <note>original: *duro*, referring to *cantus durus*, or music using B-naturals</note>, or loosened in "soft" song <note>original: *molli*, referring to *cantus mollis*, or music using B-flats</note>. From this circumstance arose the distinction of notes into **stable** and **mobile**, and the very name *diesis* <term>diesis|a small musical interval, often the difference between a major and minor semitone</term> from the loosening of the mobile strings.

<margin>The Added Note.</margin>
In the composition of several octave systems <term>diapason|the interval of an octave</term>, the method of the ancients was quite intricate; however, it should be observed that they added one note lower than the *Hypate* <note>the lowest note of the standard Greek tetrachord</note> itself, which for this reason was called the *Proslambanomenos* <note>Greek for "the added note"</note>. A trace of this remains in the Musical Scale that our boys learn, which adds below the Latin letter **A** a certain character signifying a lower sound; it marks this note outside the normal order with the Greek letter **Γ** (Gamma): for thus the scale begins, *Gammut*, *Are*, etc. <note>The term "gamut" comes from "Gamma-ut," the lowest note in the medieval hexachord system.</note>

Let it suffice to have touched upon these ancient names of strings in this place. For below, in Chapter XI, all fifteen strings of the composite system will be explained using the ancient terms, but according to later musicians.

Now at last, let us approach our **natural system** of a single octave, and apply to it the letters used in common music.

<margin>The natural system begins from G.</margin>
I establish, therefore, that the lowest note of this natural and demonstrative system is that which the ancients were accustomed to call the *Proslambanomenon* and the musical scale calls *Gammut*; to this, naturally, the letter **G** is to be assigned. The reasons are these: because the notes established through harmonic sections determine such intervals below the octave—when compared with the note of the whole string—as musicians ordinarily establish between **G** and **b**, **natural**, **c**, **d**, **$de$**, and **e**.

Someone might say that these same intervals could be understood between **D** and **F**, **$Fe$**, **G**, **A**, **b**, **natural**; and likewise between **c** and **$de$**, **e**, **f**, **g**, **$ge$**, **a**. Nor do I deny that instrumental musicians use these letters generally, and do not distinguish between the major and minor tones in them. For what would prevent them from transposing a song from **G** to **d**? On their organs, they take the two tones—the Major (8:9) and the Minor (9:10)—which are joined into one interval (4:5) <note>a major third</note>, and then precisely bisect them into two "usual" tones that are equal to each other. Although, in this tempering <note>referring to musical temperament, or the adjustment of intervals to fit keyboard instruments</note>, Galilei <note>Vincenzo Galilei, the music theorist and father of the astronomer Galileo</note> is more accurate. But we are looking here not at the **lack of art** <note>original Greek: *atechnian*</note> of the practitioners, but at the **precision of Nature** <note>original Greek: *akribeian*</note>; therefore, we cannot imitate them. 

And as for the letter **c**, even the musicians themselves would reject the natural system of the octave rising from it, by this argument: For between their own **$ge$** and **a** is a semitone; and this interval is in the fifth place, because **a** is the sixth from **c**. But in the **natural system**, we require a *diesis* before the sixth. Moreover, musicians themselves place the *diesis* only between **b** and **natural**, and between **$de$** and **e**. Therefore, either by the assent of the instrumentalists themselves, or by necessity, our system must rise from either **D** or **G** to express the pure natural system.

Yet the natural system cannot begin from **D** either. For it is their established custom to place the semitone between **d** and **$de$**; however, in my natural system, the **limma** <term>limma|a "leftover" interval in Pythagorean tuning, slightly smaller than a semitone</term> is in the lowest place, which is smaller than a semitone.

---

->Natural system. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Transposition rejected. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Other transposition rejected:<-

<header>ON THE HARMONICS, BOOK III.</header>

## CHAPTER X.

### On Tetrachords and the use of the sylla-
### bles, Ut, re, mi, fa, sol, la.

It was the custom of the ancients to divide the system of the octave <term>diapason|the interval of an octave</term> into two tetrachords <term>tetrachord|a scale of four notes spanning the interval of a perfect fourth</term>, and this was done in different ways according to the various intentions of the musicians. For they were either **conjunct**, called *Synemmena* <note>original: "Synemmena," Greek for "connected"</note>, with one sound established in the middle which produced a perfect fourth <term>diatessaron|the interval of a perfect fourth, a 4:3 ratio</term> both with the lowest note below it and the highest note above it; thus the extreme notes produced a dissonant interval, a seventh <note>original: "Diheptà"</note>, and one whole tone was understood to be added above. For whenever the order required them to strike the octave **a**, they struck the first note **A**, as if producing an identical sound from the opposite side, <note>original: "ἀντίφωνον" (antiphonon)</note> **sounding in opposition**. In this way there were not truly two tetrachords, but rather two intervals of a fourth, forming a single seven-stringed scale <note>original: "Heptachordum"</note>. Or, the tetrachords were **disjunct**, separated by the interval of one major whole tone, called *Diezeugmena* <note>original: "Diezeugmena," Greek for "separated"</note>. This is what the nature of things suggests even in our own division of the system, in which the lower tetrachord has **G. A. ♮. c.** and the upper has **d. e. f. g.**, where a major tone lies between **c.** and **d.** Perhaps even in their physical position these four lowest strings were separated from the four higher ones, specifically by leaving a larger gap between the two boundary strings.

->Conjunct Tetrachords.<- ->Disjunct Tetrachords.<-

---

The reason they thought about the system in terms of the tetrachord was this: they saw that in one harmony of a fourth <note>original: "diatessaron"</note> there are two and a half tones. We also have the major tone, the minor tone, and the semitone in a perfect fourth—all the elements are fitting in a minor concordance <note>Kepler notes that the ratios 4:5 and 5:6 were not even considered concordances/consonances by the ancients</note>. Indeed, the semitone could be in the lowest, middle, or highest position. Therefore, all song seemed to them to be encompassed by three forms of tetrachords:

->Tone. Tone. Semitone.<- ->Tone. Semitone. Tone.<- ->Semitone. Tone. Tone.<-

---

<margin>The semitone is marked with a shorter line for the minor, and a somewhat longer line for the major.</margin>
For me, the forms of tetrachords are multiplied because of the distinction between the minor and major tones; for instead of three, there become six, and in one octave <note>original: "Diapasõ"</note> most of them are doubled. Thus we also have a certain approval from Nature for distinguishing the tetrachords, for the upper is [different] from the lower...

And these are only the forms of the perfect <term>diatessaron|the interval of a perfect fourth</term>; we shall deal with the imperfect ones in Chapter XII.

But if we ignore the difference between the major and minor tone, as the <term>instrument-makers|original: "Organici," referring to builders of keyboard instruments like organs</term> do, then these consecutive disjunct <term>tetrachords|scales of four notes</term> are entirely similar.

| G A B♭ c | & d e f g |
| :--- | :--- |
| G A B♭ c | & d e f g |
| **This at the bottom** | **and this at the top.** |

In both, the <term>semitone|the smallest standard interval in this system</term> is in the same place, either at the top or in the middle; the only difference is that the semitone in the lower <term>tetrachord</term> is one <term>comma|a tiny mathematical difference in pitch, specifically the syntonic comma (81:80)</term> higher than in the upper; which difference is not strongly perceived during singing.

<margin>Transpo-<br>sition.</margin> Therefore, the <term>transposition|moving a melody to a different starting pitch</term> of a song from key to key, common among musicians, is based on this similarity of tetrachords; it is all the more convenient because the instrument-makers have removed the distinction between major and minor tones, and so forth. <note>Kepler is referring to "tempering" the scale, where small mathematical differences are averaged out to allow for easier tuning and transposition.</note>

<margin>Use of the syllables<br>Ut, Re,<br>Mi, fa, Sol,<br>La.</margin> Furthermore, this similarity and threefold variety of <term>tetrachords</term> gave birth in more recent music to those six syllables *ut, re, mi, fa, sol, la:* by which the memory of learners is assisted. But if only a single <term>octave|the interval of an eighth</term> were sung, composed of two similar tetrachords, we could have been content with only four syllables, *ut, re, mi, fa, ut, re, mi, fa,* ignoring the difference between major and minor tones.

But because there are three possible locations for the semitone in a <term>tetrachord</term>; so that these syllables would not be too general, but rather that the semitone would always be denoted by *Mi Fa,* or *Fa Mi:* it was necessary for two other syllables to be added; so that in these [ *Ut, re, mi, fa* ] the semitone would be in the highest place; in these [ *Re, mi, fa, sol* ] the semitone would be in the middle place; and finally in these [ *Mi, fa, sol, la* ] the semitone would be in the lowest place. And this is the reason why they used six syllables...

<margin>CHAPTER X.</margin>
...inventors of Music, not eight. And so, let that Belgian <note>original: "Belga ille"; likely referring to Hubert Waelrant (c. 1517–1595), who proposed a seven-syllable system called "Bocedization."</note> see what profit he gains from this increase, who made seven syllables out of six: *Bo, ce, di, ga, lo, ma, ni*. For if he judged that syllables should be used in a number equal to the strings of one octave, minus one—so that the octave, because of its identity <note>i.e., the way an octave sounds like the "same" note at a higher pitch.</note>, would be represented by the first syllable *Bo*—what, I ask, does he find lacking in the letters *a. b. c. d. e. f. g.* which have long since been accepted for this use?

<margin>The mutation of song.</margin>
Since, therefore, the six syllables were born in this way because of the triple form of the <term>Tetrachord</term> <gloss>a four-note scale segment</gloss>, there arose from this the doctrine of **Mutations** <gloss>the rules for switching between overlapping hexachords</gloss> through the modern Musical scale. This doctrine is concerned only with fitting these syllables to the letters explained above. It shows that the superfluous syllables *Sol* and *la* are sometimes equivalent to the first syllables *ut* and *re*, and sometimes to the following ones, *Re* and *mi*, so that occasionally, out of order and without a formal mutation, *fa* can be inserted after *sol* and *la*.

There is indeed another kind of "dissimilar similarity" among <term>Tetrachords</term>, which is the foundation for likening different melodies that sound together, which they are accustomed to call **Fugues** and **Phantasias** <note>Fugues and Fantasias are musical forms based on imitation, where one voice follows another.</note>. For if you take contiguous Tetrachords, separated by no interval from one another—just as the major tone was left over to fill the octave above or below—there occurs in certain systems of the octave a series of the same elementary intervals on both sides:

that is, of Semitones, Diesium, and Limmata. A major tone is added to the other so that a <term>Diapente</term> <gloss>Perfect Fifth</gloss> is created in place of a fourth, which is in some way similar to the other fourth. Thus, two melodies—the first in time running through the interval of a **Fifth** above, and the second later in time running through the interval of a **Fourth** below—the latter follows the former and, as far as it is permitted, imitates its pattern like a sort of rival.

# CHAPTER XI.
## On the composition of Systems.

Although the voice of a single human usually moves within the system of a single octave, the harmony of several melodies together teaches us to arrange several contiguous octaves. The ancients, therefore, defining everything by the properties of numbers, defined the "perfect system" as the **Octave plus a fifth** <note>original: "Diapason epidiapente"</note> with the numbers 1, 2, 3. For us, the individual harmonic sections above have each yielded individual systems, the largest of which was the **Double-octave plus a fifth** <note>original: "Disdiapason-epidiapente"</note>, with the numbers 1, 5, 6. Although for our Composers, as they are called, the limit...

# ON PROPORTIONS
## CHAPTER XII.
### On Adulterine Consonances.

From the continuation of two major tones, imperfect consonances result. For in the joining of both, two major tones (ratio 8:9) follow one after another between F–G and G–A. Therefore, in the interval F–A, the ratio is 64:81, which is larger than a just major third (ratio 4:5 or 64:80) by one comma (ratio 80:81). Following Galileo <note>The author refers to Vincenzo Galilei (c. 1520–1591), a famous music theorist and father of the astronomer Galileo Galilei</note>, let us call this a ditone. The same interval exists between C–E, because there is the same semitone interval on both sides between B–C and E–F.

<margin>Ditone.</margin>

Thus, between F and B-flat, if a semitone is added to the excessive ditone F–A, it creates the interval 60:81 (or 20:27), which is one comma (80:81) larger than a perfect fourth (ratio 3:4 or 60:80).

<margin>A from B itself.</margin>
Judge the same for E–A, because just as E is a semitone lower than F itself, so also is A lower than B <note>meaning B-flat</note>.

These imperfect consonances—or "excessive" intervals—if they are subtracted from the interval of an octave <note>original: "Diapason"</note>, leave behind imperfect remainders that are deficient by one comma. For between A and the high F, there will be a ratio of 81:128, which is a deficient minor sixth.

The same occurs between G and the high E-flat if you subtract the interval E-flat to G from the octave.

So too between B-flat and the high F: after subtracting the imperfect fourth F–B-flat (20:27) from the octave, there will remain a diminished fifth (27:40, which is the same as 81:120).

The same occurs between A and the high E-flat, by subtracting E–A from the octave.

But when the excessive ditone F–A is added to the minor third A–C (5:6), a fifth <note>original: "Diapente"</note> is produced with the ratio 160:243, <term>sc</term> <gloss>that is to say</gloss>, excessive by one comma. For 160:240 is a perfect 2:3 ratio, and 240:243 is the comma (80:81).

And when the excessive fifth F–C is removed from the interval of an octave, there remains the fourth C–F (243:320), which is deficient by one comma.

## Table of Six Imperfect Consonances.

| | | |
|----------|----------|----------|
| Instead of 4:5, it is 64:81 (excessive) | | |
| Instead of 3:4, it is 60:81 or 20:27 (excessive) | } | and 243:320 (deficient). |
| Instead of 5:8, it is 81:128 (deficient) | | |
| Instead of 2:3, it is 81:120 or 27:40 (deficient) | } | and 160:243 (excessive). |

Yet, there is no need for the Platonic Limma (243:256) <note>A very small interval used in Pythagorean tuning</note>, which Plato called a "Limma" for a different reason than I do. For when two major tones—that is, the ditone 64:81—were removed from the interval of a fourth (3:4), that Limma (243:256) remained for him in place of a semitone. But I have no need for this subtraction; for in my system, the 3:4 interval is instead increased, becoming 20:27.

# CHAPTER XIII.
## What Song is Naturally Harmonious and Fitting.

We shall say nothing of that shrill manner of singing which the Turks and Hungarians are accustomed to use for their military signals; they imitate the unformed voices of brute animals rather than human nature.

It seems altogether likely that the first author of this kind of unformed melody derived it from an ill-suited instrument and, through long habit—along with the specific construction of that instrument—transmitted it to posterity and the entire nation. I was present in Prague for the prayers which the priest of the Turkish Ambassadors used to chant at fixed hours, kneeling and frequently striking the ground with his forehead. It was easily apparent that he sang according to a discipline, and that he had acquired his skill and readiness through labor, for he never hesitated. However, he used intervals that were strange, unusual, truncated, and abhorrent, such that it seems no one, by their own natural instinct and of their own accord, could ever consistently devise anything similar. I will attempt to express something close to it through our own musical notes.

<note>Kepler provides a musical staff here intended to mimic the "strange" Turkish melody he heard, using Western notation to show irregular jumps and chromaticisms.</note>

Therefore, a song is harmonious and fitting to the judgment of human ears when, having started from a certain sound, it proceeds through harmonious intervals toward sounds that are consonant both with that first sound and, for the most part, with each other. It flies swiftly through dissonant intervals but lingers on the consonant ones—either through the measure of time and the length of syllables, or by frequent return to them—as if striving for a harmony of two voices through the movement of a single voice from one place in the system to another.

->Example.<-

<note>The following is the "Victimae Paschali Laudes," a famous Gregorian chant for Easter.</note>

Christians, offer praises to the Paschal victim. The Lamb has redeemed the sheep; the innocent Christ has reconciled sinners to the Father.

Here, the starting sound is in the key of *G*, with which the notes *B-flat, C, D, and G* harmonize in "soft" song <note>original: "cantu molli," referring to the hexachord that uses B-flat</note>. Therefore, the melody runs (after first making a downward turn) to the key of *C*, which is consonant, and plainly skips over the dissonant place *A*. It would have been the same if it had touched *A*, but only with a brief delay. Indeed, the entire remaining series sounds most strongly in the places *B-flat, D, and G*, expressing the "skeleton" of the octave in this way: returning most frequently to *D*, then to *B-flat*, and occasionally raising itself to the higher *G*. It dwells significantly on all these places, but not so on *A* or *F*, which are initially dissonant places. Finally, it returns to *G* and finishes there.

Regarding the definition of song handed down to us, many things come to our attention to be noted.

I. The parts of a song, from which all song consists (either in whole or in part), Euclid names as these four: <term>Movement</term> <note>original Greek: Αγωγή (Agoge), referring to the upward or downward motion of the melody</note>, <term>Pitch</term> <note>original Greek: Τονώ (Tonos), the sustaining of a sound</note>, <term>Composition</term> <note>original Greek: Πεττεία (Petteia), literally "the game of pebbles," referring to the choice of which notes to use and how often</note>,

<sig>H 3</sig>
<meta>catchword: Interweaving (original Greek: Πλο- from Πλοκή)</meta>

<summary>Kepler defines "natural" melody as music that emphasizes consonant intervals and structural "skeleton" notes, contrasting human-centered harmony with the "unnatural" military chants of the Turks. He uses the Gregorian chant "Victimae Paschali Laudes" to illustrate how a melody centers itself around a tonal home.</summary>

<margin>CHAPTER XIII.</margin>
The terms **Weaving** <note>original Greek: Πλοκὼ (Plokē)</note> and others like it indicate by their very names what they are. For **Leading** <note>original Greek: Ἀγωγή (Agogē); the movement or "path" of a melody</note> is the carrying of the voice from a set root to a place consonant with that root, or from one consonant to another that is consonant with either the second or the first root. **Dwelling** <note>original Greek: Τονή (Tonē); a rest or sustained pitch</note> is a lingering in the first place, or in a place consonant with it, or even in a place consonant with a previous note, even if it is not consonant with the first. **Interweaving** <note>original Greek: Πλοκὴ (Plokē); a complex melodic ornament</note>, or implication, is a certain type or "color" of **Leading**, just as **Variation** <note>original Greek: πεττεία (Petteia); literally "playing draughts/checkers," referring to the rhythmic "gaming" of a note</note> is a color of **Dwelling**. And as **Leading** is to **Dwelling**, so **Interweaving** is to **Variation**; because **Leading** passes through, as it were, directly, while **Interweaving** wanders in its passage around the **Leading**, like a dog around a traveler.

Therefore, **Leading** is a motion that is, so to speak, direct; **Interweaving** is a varied motion. **Dwelling**, however, is like the end of a motion, or a rest in a desired place of the Musical System. **Variation** consists of many ends of smaller motions, acting like little rests. In our example, the syllables *“Christ leads away the sheep”* <note>original Latin: demit Oves Christus in; from the Easter sequence "Victimae Paschali Laudes"</note> are a certain perpetual **Dwelling**, with only two syllables excepted; but the syllables *“[the guiltless] reconciled [sinners]”* <note>original Latin: cens rec li peccat</note> express **Variation**. But if you look at the bindings <term>ligatures: notes tied together or sung to one syllable</term> of the syllables in this song—*“praises,” “Father,” “Redeemer”* <note>original Latin: laud an patr tor</note>—and consider them as two-toned, then in that case there will be no pure or unmixed **Leading**. But if you consider that it was done in a rustic manner, so that from a sound that was meant to be sung longer, it became a two-note sound rising at the end; and if you restore to these syllables the simple prolonged sound (which is the first note of the binding), you will find pure **Leading** in these: *“To the Paschal [praises]”* <note>original Latin: Paschali laudes</note> also, *“let [Christians] immolate”* <note>original Latin: immolent</note> also *“Christians”* <note>original Latin: Christiani</note> also *“The Innocent [to the] Father”* <note>original Latin: Innocens patri</note> and a short one in *“[sin]ners”* <note>original Latin: catores</note>. However, pure **Interweaving**, though not a natural kind, exists in the Turkish example <note>Kepler refers back to the "unnatural" Turkish melody transcribed on the previous page</note>.

Just as the skeleton is to the body in the study of anatomy, so the octaves and the sounds that are consonant both with each other and with the root or base of the octave are to the melody or song itself in a Musical System. For just as the flesh fills the hollows of the bones and clothes them for beauty, so these parts just reviewed—especially **Leading** and **Variation**—fill the skeleton of the octave. By wandering through dissonant places cast between the consonant sounds, they shape and, as it were, give body to the Melody.

II. When song is defined as starting from a certain sound,
<insert>[A musical staff with four lines showing five square-note neumes: G, A, B, C, D]</insert> 
which is the base of the Musical System of the octave, this is not always to be understood as being the case in practice. Since variety delights and serves to emphasize, a melody very often begins abruptly from a key or some other place. Nevertheless, in potential, a certain fixed beginning is understood to be placed there, which shines out from the entire stretch of the Melody on all sides; as in this very ancient German song, it is easily understood that even if the beginning starts in *d* in practice, the root is nevertheless *G*.

III. There is a similar exception to the rule that a regular song is said to aim its **Dwelling** or **Variation** toward places consonant with the root of the Octave. For frequently these parts, in the middle of a longer stretch of melody, are occupied around...

***

He also notes that while songs have a theoretical "root" note, they often begin on different pitches for artistic variety.</summary>

<margin>CHAPTER XII.</margin>
...those locations which are dissonant from the first root; but this is done for the sake of variety. It is just as if a new melody were mixed into the previous one, in whose dissonance a certain new beginning might be fixed, or a new **skeleton of the octave** <term>sceleton octavæ; the primary structural framework of notes that define a musical scale</term> might be marked. It is like a departure in a speech, or a digression; therefore, we do not linger in such places, but quickly return to the principal skeleton. And as long as **sustaining** <note>original Greek: τονή (tonē)</note> and **variation** <note>original Greek: πεττεία (petteia)</note> occupy themselves around dissonant notes, we understand that the song is not yet finished. For at the very end, we must return not only to the consonant notes—as is the rule—but even to the root of the proper octave itself. Because of this articulation of song and this striving for consonances, the ancients seem to have called even a simple song "Harmony." This is no different than how a becoming and fit correspondence of limbs, which is the soul of form, might be called "harmony," as if it were beauty itself; indeed, **Harmony** was even a woman's name <note>Harmonia was the Greek goddess of concord and daughter of Ares and Aphrodite</note>.

IV. As for **leading** <note>original Greek: Αγωγή (Agogē); the movement or "path" of a melody</note>, it is again varied; for it does not always actually pass through all the intervening locations, but often skips some <margin>Leaps</margin> and is carried by a leap from one note to another that is consonant with it. In that case, the **leading** exists only in potential, and it is almost pure **variation** or **sustaining**. This is the habit of most of our **trumpeters** <note>original: "Tubicinum"</note> when they play a military signal or an equestrian charge; for then, almost nothing is heard except the skeleton of the octave. Consider whether the **Orthian Strain** <note>original Greek: Νόμος ὄρθιος (Nomos orthios); an ancient, high-pitched, and vigorous Greek melody used for inspiring soldiers</note> of the ancients was of this kind.

V. Since a **well-proportioned** <note>original: "Concinnus"; also translated as "apt" or "fitting"</note> song consists of its elements, which are well-proportioned intervals, those must first be defined more accurately.

<margin>How many ways intervals are ill-proportioned</margin>
For intervals are called well-proportioned or ill-proportioned <note>original: "concinnia" or "inconcinnia"</note> in a twofold sense. First, individual intervals are called well-proportioned or ill-proportioned on their own with respect to their origin. Those that nature admits in the divisions of consonant intervals are well-proportioned; however, those that do not result from the comparison of consonances are entirely foreign to the study of Harmonics, as explained in Chapter IV. Secondly, with respect to the song or melody itself, there is a distinction even among musical intervals (those well-proportioned in the first sense). Some of them, when considered together, are rejected by melodies as ill-proportioned in a certain respect, even though they are well-proportioned by nature (that is, arising from the comparison and abstraction of harmonies). **Sustaining** and **variation** presuppose and look back to the first sense; but **leading**—both the actual and the leaping kind—looks primarily to this second sense. Therefore, these intervals become ill-proportioned for two reasons: either with respect to the **Genus** <term>the type of scale, such as Diatonic, Chromatic, or Enharmonic</term> or the skeleton of the octave, because they are clearly not used in it, nor do they form it; or if they are arranged in an order other than that which nature taught above in Chapter VII. For example, if someone wanted to arrange three **semitones** <note>a half-step in music</note> in succession: a semitone is well-proportioned in the first sense, but this arrangement of semitones is not well-proportioned in this second sense. Likewise, a **diesis** <note>a very small melodic interval, smaller than a semitone</note> is well-proportioned by nature, yet it is ill-proportioned on its own whether in the "hard" <note>major-like</note> or "soft" <note>minor-like</note> genus of song. Or finally, they are not sung in succession, nor are they permitted for a leap of the melodic voice, nor are they suitable for **leading**.

<summary>Kepler explains that melodies must revolve around a structural "skeleton" of the octave, allowing for temporary dissonant digressions for the sake of variety. He also distinguishes between intervals that are mathematically well-proportioned in isolation and those that are functionally appropriate within a specific melodic sequence.</summary>

<header>ON PROPORTIONS</header>

<margin>CHAPTER XIII.</margin>

# ON PROPORTIONS

In this second sense, therefore, there are discordant and forbidden intervals, governed by these principal rules:

I. A **diesis** <term>diesis; a very small musical interval, smaller than a semitone</term> is not normally sung before or after a **semitone** <term>semitonium; the smallest interval in a standard scale, roughly half of a whole tone</term>.

II. Although two **semitones** may be arranged one after another according to the sequence of the smallest intervals in Chapter VII, they cannot, however, be sung consecutively across three pitches; instead, they must merge with two other elements into two **tones** <term>tonus; a whole tone or whole step</term>.

III. Two **semitones** are not normally sung within the span of a single **fourth** <term>quarta; an interval spanning four notes</term> or **fifth** <term>quinta; an interval spanning five notes</term> when they occur at the bottom of the **skeleton of the octave** <term>sceleton octavæ; the primary structural framework of notes that define a musical scale</term>. For if they were, the result would be that the note at the fourth or fifth position would not harmonize with the first note—neither perfectly nor imperfectly—and thus it would not truly be a fourth or a fifth.

IV. Four **tones** are not sung consecutively, except in the highest part of the **octave** <term>octava; an interval of eight notes</term>, when the **skeleton** is changed for the sake of color and variety; therefore, this is not done normally.
<note>The musical example for Rule IV is marked with "T, T. To. To." indicating Tone, Tone, Tone, Tone.</note>

V. The **seventh** <term>septima; an interval of seven notes</term> and all dissonances above the **octave** are not normally sung using notes arranged consecutively after the root; unless the preceding note acts in some way as an ending, and the following note as a new beginning.

VI. We admit **sixths** <term>sextas; an interval of six notes</term> more rarely, even though they are consonant, and then only the minor sixths.
<note>The musical example for Rule VI includes the text: "In me transierunt" <note>Latin: "They [your wrath] have passed over me," from Psalm 88</note>.</note>

VII. Two **tetrachords** <term>tetrachorda; a scale of four notes</term> within a single **octave** are more rarely sung if the **semitone** does not fall in the same relative position in both of them. This is done for the sake of color or for **syncopations** <term>syncopatio; a displacement of the musical beat</term> (which are discussed in Chapter XVI). Yet there is no absolute freedom in placing the semitone, for it is restricted to the position permitted by the **Musical Genus** <term>Genus Cantus; the specific classification of a melody's scale structure</term>.

VIII. Related to this is the fact that three **tones** are not sung consecutively at the bottom of the **octave**; however, they are permitted in the upper part according to the rules already stated.

IX. Two **semitones** do not naturally blend into a single **tone**, even though there is a small audible difference between them. For instance, if the **octave** begins from E, between C-sharp and D-sharp <note>original: "ce. dẹ."</note>, an interval of 225 to 256 would be created from the combination, which is naturally discordant (see Chapter IV).

X. In general, every system of the **octave** <term>octava; an interval of eight notes</term> is unharmonious if it does not establish both a **fourth** <term>Diatessaron; the interval of a perfect fourth</term> and a **fifth** <term>Diapente; the interval of a perfect fifth</term> below.
