Most of these laws will now serve us in establishing the number of **modes** <term>tonorum; the scales or "tones" used in composition</term> in the following chapter.

<margin>On Measures.</margin>
VI. Regarding that part of the definition, *gliding quickly through dissonances, lingering on consonances*: although it is not my purpose in this work to argue about measures <note>Kepler is referring to musical time and rhythm</note>; I nevertheless advise in general that the principal beauty of harmonic song lies in measurement. For what was stated very generally—*Dissonances quickly*, etc.—is made true in specific cases as follows. First, the Latins have a distinction between a **long** and a **short** syllable, making the latter one unit of time and the former two, and thus of double length. <margin>In Prose.</margin> Although today not only poems but also prose is sung; in which the distinction between long and short syllables is completely neglected by modern musicians; they look uniquely to the custom of pronunciation, even though it is corrupt today; any syllable usually uttered with an **acute accent** <note>stress or pitch emphasis</note> is considered long, and with a **grave accent**, short.

It is no wonder this happens in the Latin language, since the later Greeks did the same: who, although they wrote purely, embraced a most faulty pronunciation, in which there is no longer any distinction between an acute accent and syllable length, or a grave accent and shortness, even though they abound in signs for this which are not used as frequently by the Latins. <margin>Greek "Political" Verses.</margin> Therefore the Greeks, having abolished the custom of composing poetry <note>referring to Classical quantitative meter based on vowel length</note>, began several centuries ago to write so-called **Political verses** <note>original: "versus Politicos"; these are Byzantine verses based on word stress rather than vowel length</note>; in these, syllables are counted, not measured, and the verse favors the penultimate syllable, not because it is long by nature, but because it is sharpened by accent in popular speech. Our musicians also imitate this in Latin; so much so that they do not even spare poems <margin>In Meters.</margin> except very rarely, and never entirely: I believe because the perpetual duple and triple rhythms are accepted in songs, while poems mix these unequally—except for the **Hexameter**, which is content with the proportion of equality in the **spondee** <term>spondaeus; a foot consisting of two long syllables</term>, and perfect duple in the **dactyl** <term>dactylus; a foot consisting of one long and two short syllables</term>. Therefore, musicians assign a dissonant sound to a short syllable, or one in the place of a short (as when a spondee follows an iamb), if it must be passed through, but a consonance to long syllables, or those treated as such.

<margin>In modern Meters.</margin>
Secondly, the **Ionic languages** <note>Kepler uses "Ionic" here to categorize modern European vernaculars that use rhythmic stress</note>, which use rhythm—German <note>original: "Teutonica"</note>, French, Spanish, and Italian—make either the last or the penultimate syllable of the verse acute, and utter the whole verse as if alternating acute or grave syllables following one another in turn, whether this fits (as in a proper German verse) or not (as often happens in French). Therefore, every verse of theirs is either like a **Trochee** <term>trochaeus; a stressed syllable followed by an unstressed one</term> or an **Iamb** <term>iambus; an unstressed syllable followed by a stressed one</term>, and these are either **complete** <term>Acatalectic; a line of verse that has the full number of syllables</term>—*Creator of heaven and earth. Now we pray to the Holy Spirit.* <note>original: "Schöpffer Himmels vnd der Erden. Nun bitten wir den Heylgen Geist."</note>—or **incomplete** <term>catalectic; a line of verse lacking a syllable at the end</term>—*At which all the world wonders. He is the morning star.* <note>original: "Deß sich wundert alle Welt. Er ist der Morgensterne."</note> Therefore, musicians fix the seat for dissonant sounds on the grave or shortened syllables, and consonances on the acute ones.

<margin>In the beat.</margin>
Thirdly, when indeed the song <term>cantus</term> <note>Abbreviation for cantus</note> receives its measure not from the syllables of the text, but from the **beat** <term>Tactu; the "tactus" was the steady pulse used by conductors to keep time</term>; and this follows either duple or triple proportion; they reserve the first part of the beat for consonances, and the latter part—which in triple time is shorter and indicated by the raising of the hand—primarily for dissonances: 

<sig>I</sig>
<meta>catchword: cavent- (they beware)</meta>

He explains that "lingering" on consonances should align with long or stressed syllables, while "gliding" through dissonances should occur on short or unstressed ones.</summary>

...and they take care, as much as possible, that no other syllable occupies the first half of the beat <term>tactus; the steady pulse of the music</term> except the one that is to be pronounced with an acute accent <note>the stressed or higher-pitched syllable</note>, nor are two long syllables to be squeezed into the final part of the beat.

## CHAPTER XIV.

### On the Modes of Melodies, which
### they call Tones.

About to speak of modes, I first advise modern Musicians that those things they are accustomed to call "Modes"—namely, the double or triple proportions of the beat and similar things (the kind of "Modes" perhaps used long ago with pipes in Roman comedies)—will not be the subject of my discourse beyond what has already been said. I call "Modes" those things which they, following the ancients, are accustomed to call **Tones**, when asking what "Tone" a song is in. For there are certain qualities or species of harmonious Song, divided against each other by the two greatest differences of the **Genres**, the **Hard** <term>Duri; roughly corresponding to the modern major quality</term> and the **Soft** <term>Mollis; roughly corresponding to the modern minor quality</term>.

The Greeks called these *Ways* <note>original: Τρόπους (Tropoi)</note> and *Characters* <note>original: ἤθη (Ethe)</note>; the former from the form of the Scale System, the latter from the effect of the Song on a human being, because most lawgivers judged that the Modes of songs serve to shape Morals <note>ethical character or behavior</note>.

Regarding the number and differences of these Tones, there are not only great controversies among Musicians today, but there were also in the past: some of which can be seen in Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy, a 2nd-century astronomer and music theorist</note>, and many in Vincenzo Galilei <note>a late 16th-century Italian lutenist and theorist, father of the astronomer Galileo Galilei</note>. Truly, it is not my purpose to examine the opinions of everyone, nor to refute them; therefore, the Musician should expect nothing else from me in this question than that single point to which my principles, explained thus far, lead me. 

For although Tones seem to be named from the fact that one Mode begins either higher or lower than another by the interval of one Tone (or Semitone): nevertheless, I do not distinguish Tones by the height or depth of the Song itself (which Vincenzo Galilei testifies some have observed alone); but I require their number to match the number of species of a single **Octave** <term>Diapason; the span of eight notes</term> along with Ptolemy; and I say there are as many Tones as there can be legitimate and Harmonious skeletons of the Octave System, differing among themselves in Genre, the sequence of harmonious intervals, and the placement of the **Tetrachords** <term>a scale segment of four notes</term>, or the choice of the two harmonic medians <note>the mathematical "means" or middle notes that divide the octave</note>. There are, to be sure, three things that vary Tones and distinguish them from one another: Genre, the Sequence of Harmonious intervals, and the Articulation of the skeleton from the smaller Consonances.

First, the two **Genres** established in Chapter VI for the division of the Octave System provide us with two principal Tones that are first by Nature, arising with the System of a single Octave itself. Then, in both the Hard and Soft genre of the System, from the composition of two Octaves into one larger and perfect System (which we handed down in Chapter XI), the Systems of individual Octaves are given, differing by their roots or "goals" <note>the starting and ending notes that define the scale's range</note> by which they are enclosed; however, those goals are the Locations of the natural System...

<summary>Kepler defines musical "Tones" (Modes) based on the mathematical structure of the octave rather than just pitch height, referencing historical debates between theorists like Ptolemy and Vincenzo Galilei. He argues that the number of modes is determined by the possible harmonious "skeletons" or interval arrangements within an octave.</summary>

### BOOK III OF THE HARMONICS

<margin>CHAPTER XIV.</margin>
...different natural systems, or in today’s terminology, various different **Keys**, which necessarily result in different pitches relative to the natural system that begins from G. Through this, the position of the **semitone** also varies, being located in either the third, the penultimate, or the bottom place of the Octave. As for the height itself, considered in the absolute, it changes nothing about the species of the melody, since the same species can be intoned either high or low. Nor are we forced to follow **Ptolemy** <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century astronomer and music theorist whose *Harmonics* Kepler studied closely</note> in taking half of the remaining Tones lower than the principal Natural System of G, and the other half higher. For we can take them all higher, or all lower, since the same **Order of Concords** <term>concinnorum; harmonious intervals suitable for melody</term> follows in both cases—provided that the naturally composed system of the double octave begins from the key of G. But if we make some lower and some higher as Ptolemy did, the natural system must be composed so that we add a **Fifth** <term>Diapente; the interval of a perfect fifth</term> below and a **Fourth** <term>Diateſſaron; the interval of a perfect fourth</term> above; thus the double-octave system will begin from C.

Thirdly and finally, in systems established this way, there is a choice between two **Harmonic Means**, which the **stretching** <note>original: τονή (tonē); referring to the tension or pitch-height of a melody</note> and the **lowering** <note>original: πελεία (peleia); referring to the lower or concluding range of a melody</note> (the parts of the song) aim for. Or, what amounts to the same thing, the placement of the **Tetrachord** <term>a scale of four notes spanning a perfect fourth</term> is given either at the top or bottom of the Octave, or in the middle of two Thirds.

For the sake of this diversity, we must first subjoin here the **Square Grid** prepared from Chapter XI, composed of twelve orders of the twelve smallest natural intervals. This is not done so that we, like **Aristoxenus** <note>A Greek theorist who argued that the ear, rather than mathematical ratios, should judge intervals</note>, might create as many Tones as there are numbers of those intervals by starting each one a single minimal interval higher; rather, it is so that once these minimal intervals are contracted into the usual concords, it may appear whether any new species of Octave can begin from any one of these minima.

# ON PROPORTIONS

<margin>
**CHAPTER XIV.**

**Origin 14.**
Of the systems of the fourteen different species of the octave.
</margin>

You see that from the twelve distinctions of the Octave's pitches, there is none that agrees with another in the order of its elements. Let us now see how many species of Octave Systems exist if the first difference of Octaves, which is that of **Genus** <term>genus; here referring to the character of the scale, such as "hard" or "soft"</term>, is mixed in: that is, whether the 12 smallest intervals of all 12 Orders can be harmoniously contracted into the seven usual intervals of a single Octave, distinct in eight positions, and in how many ways each might occur.

Note here that **LS** or **SL** is the sign for a **Major Tone** <note>original: "Toni Majoris"</note>, **DS** or **SD** is the sign for a **Minor Tone** <note>original: "toni Minoris"</note>, and **S** is the sign for a **semitone**. Our descriptions will proceed from the **Low** to the **High** <note>original: "à Gravi ad Acutum"</note>, or from the bottom to the top.

It is certain, therefore, that in the **G** octave, two species exist because of the double position of the semitone in either the second or third place from the bottom.

### First, of the Soft Genus.
*LS. S. DS. LS. S. SD. LS.*

### Second, of the Hard Genus.

But in **G<sub>e</sub>** as also in **C<sub>e</sub>** <note>Kepler uses these subscripts to denote specific pitch alterations or 'extra' notes in his system</note>, since two semitones do not compose a single harmonious interval, nor are they sung in succession **melodiously** <term>ἐμμελῶς (emmelōs); in a musically pleasing or melodic manner</term>; therefore the bottom semitone stands alone, according to laws 8 and 2 of the previous Chapter. Therefore, the distribution would be:
Either such as *S. SD. SL. S. SD. SL. SL.* which is unharmonious according to law 3.
Or in **G<sub>e</sub>** indeed such as *S. SD. SL. SS. DS.* etc., and this is unharmonious according to law 9. Therefore, no harmonious species of the Octave begins from **G<sub>e</sub>**.

In the **A** octave, because of the three possible positions for the lower semitone, the elements are also contracted into Tones in three ways: for either it is thus *S. DS. LS. S. DS.* etc., which coincides with that which has already been rejected; or it is thus, so that from here is born:

### BOOK III ON HARMONY

In the **B-natural** <note>original: ♮</note> Octave, because it is not permitted to fuse two semitones in the second position according to Law 9, nor to arrange them in succession according to Law 2, they must therefore be distributed among the <margin>**CHAPTER XIV.**</margin> tones in such a way that the solitary semitone stands in either the first or second place.

But if it stands in the first place: it would follow that the other solitary semitone would stand either in the fourth place (which is rejected by Law 3) or the sixth, and four tones would then follow in succession in the lower part of the octave, against Law 4. Therefore, the semitone must be arranged in the second place, so that from this arises species:

Finally, in the **F** Octave <note>original: "fe"; likely referring to a specific tuning of the pitch F</note>, there are two possible places for the semitone: either in the penultimate seat or the ultimate one. Thus, if you order them as **Major Tone—Semitone—Minor Tone—Major Tone—Semitone—Minor Tone—Major Tone** <note>original: "SL. S. SD. SL. S. SD. SL." where L = Major Tone (9:8), S = Semitone (16:15), and D = Minor Tone (10:9)</note>, it will be the first species, as appears from the comparison; if otherwise, it will be the fourteenth: **Semitone—Major Tone—Minor Tone—Major Tone—Semitone—Minor Tone—Major Tone.**

The reason therefore appears why in the second, fourth, fifth, seventh, and ninth orders—namely, in the octaves of **G, B-flat, B-natural, C,** and **D**—no unique species begins.

It appears secondly that no genuine transposition can be made that preserves the same species of the Octave, except for these:
I. From **F** into **G**. 
II. From **G** into **A**, but in a rejected form. 
III. From **A** into **B-flat**. 
IV. From **B-natural** into **C**. 
V. From **C** into **D**. 
VI. From **D** into **E**, in a rejected form. 
VII. From **E** into **F**.

But if we comply with the common practice of instrumental musicians <note>original: "Musicorum Organicorum"; those who play the organ or other keyed instruments</note>, who neglect the <term>comma</term> <note>The syntonic comma (81:80), the tiny mathematical difference between a Major Tone and a Minor Tone</note> and do not distinguish between the Greater and Lesser Tones, then all fourteen of our species of octaves constitute no more than three **Modes**, according to the triple position of the semitone. This is exactly what Galilei <note>Vincenzo Galilei (c. 1520–1591), music theorist and father of Galileo</note> said was the case in ancient times, when there were thought to be no more than three Tones: the **Dorian**, **Phrygian**, and **Lydian**. These are then multiplied into many more solely by their pitch (altitude).

For as far as the third cause is concerned—the articulation of the <term>skeleton</term> <note>original Greek: "sceletôn"; the basic structural framework of the octave, usually the perfect fourth and fifth</note> of the octave—that is still held in common by us and them; because of this, even for us, more than fourteen species will be born.

Therefore, according to the common opinion regarding the Major and Minor Tone <note>Instrumentalists of Kepler's time often used "equal temperament" or "meantone" systems that blurred the mathematical difference between 9:8 and 10:9</note>, many transpositions of melodies from one letter to another can be made by means of the signs flat (♭) and sharp (♯).

It remains for us to examine which of our fourteen species of the Octave can be produced in multiple ways through the arrangement of fitting elements <note>original: "articulationem elementorum concinnorum"; referring to how the mathematical ratios of the tones are joined to form a scale</note>. For a fivefold distinction of species arises from the proximity of whole tones; for either three tones follow one another in a row, or only two. If there are three, they must either stand in the middle of the octave unnaturally, having single tones and single semitones on either side: or they must shift toward one end of the system, and in that case, a semitone must necessarily be at that end, according to Laws 8 and 3. But if only pairs of tones follow each other, with semitones coming between them, then there is no place for a semitone at the ends; and two pairs of tones stand either above or below, with a third "soft" <term>mollis</term> <note>Likely referring to a flattened or minor interval</note> tone at the opposite end—this being "upright" at the bottom, with a semitone above it, and "inverted" at the top, with a semitone below it.

# ON HARMONICS, BOOK III

<margin>CHAPTER XIV.</margin>
In this way, among our 14 species, ten others are found interspersed, coinciding with the first four or even five positions of the previous ones; but where they begin to differ, the particle *or* [original: *vel*] is placed before them.

But if the "final cause" is now added, which distinguishes the <term>Modes<gloss>original: Tonos. In this context, 'tones' refers to the musical modes or scales</gloss></term>—namely <term>intonation<gloss>original: tonē; the pitch or tension of the voice</gloss></term> and <term>melodic composition<gloss>original: peteia; the art of choosing which notes to emphasize in a melody</gloss></term>—the number will be tripled, and there will be 72 species. For every <term>skeleton<gloss>original: sceleton; the structural framework of the primary consonant intervals within an octave</gloss></term> of the Octave out of all 24 has both a third and a fourth concordant with the first, as well as a fifth and a sixth. If, therefore, these parts of the song are occupied primarily around the fourth and sixth, then they place the <term>Perfect Fourth<gloss>original: Diatessaron</gloss></term> in the lowest position. But if they are around the third and sixth, the Perfect Fourth is

---

in the middle; finally, if they are around the third and fifth, the Perfect Fourth is in the highest position.

<note>The following diagrams illustrate the three different placements of the Perfect Fourth (Diatessaron) within the octave structure described above: at the bottom, in the middle, and at the top.</note>

->[Diagram: Three musical staves showing the structural placement of the Fourth]<-

I do not say these things because such a minute division is necessary—since I know that three forms are usually mixed in a single song—but so that from this number a judgment can be made regarding the differences of the <term>Modes<gloss>original: Tonorum</gloss></term> handed down by the Moderns. Some of their distinctions seem to me to suggest as many modes as there are songs, while others belong to a single Mode. But if we observe these principles, the number of Modes, however large, is nonetheless finite. In short, the Modes distinguished by real boundaries and differences—not just in respect to the pitch of the notes on an Organ, but also in the human voice itself, which can begin a natural <term>System<gloss>original: Systematis; the organized scale of notes</gloss></term> from any pitch, high or deep—are either only 3, or 14, or 24, or 72.

With these principles of mine, I reconcile the eight common Modes which they call "Ecclesiastical"; and among the ancients, in the opinion of some, they were:

# BOOK III ON HARMONICS

### CHAPTER XV.

<margin>* The pitch of a <term>Tone<gloss>original: Toni. Here meaning a musical mode</gloss></term> is threefold: 1. Absolute and in a way material, as in the human voice and also in Organs, for example if the root of the System rises from G to G where the form of the System is not changed; of this, nothing more for now. 2. The formal pitch of each root itself within a natural System composed of two octaves. Nor is this what is understood in this place: for it implies a change of the Tone by changing the radical Key of the System. 3. Again formal, the pitch of the Melody with respect to its own radical key; while this remains, the Tone indeed remains the same, but it puts on another "schema" as it were: as if it does not ascend to the Octave of the root, but contains itself below the sixth, fifth, or fourth, or frequently drops itself below the root, returning however to the root at the end. Therefore, those <term>skeletons<gloss>original: sceleta. The basic structural intervals (like 4ths and 5ths) that define a scale's shape</gloss></term> are not to be understood as if the Melody must pass through all its joints or notes depicted here: it is enough if it touches some, or those below their octave. Those, therefore, dropping themselves below the root in this way, we could call "Plagal" according to the ancients; the others "Authentic." <note>Authentic modes typically stay above their "final" or root note, while Plagal modes range both above and below it.</note></margin>

Nothing is more manifest than that these two of the **Hard Genus** <note>original: Generis duri. In Kepler's era, "hard" usually referred to scales using B-natural, often associated with a "major" quality</note> belong to our species XI, and are to be written from **e**; and again, there is scarcely any other distinction than <gloss>*</gloss> that of pitch, unless you wish to accommodate these skeletons to them separately.

Although the intention of the inventors appears to be that they wished to write the First and Second from **d**, the Third and Fourth from **e**, the Fifth and Sixth from **f**, and the Seventh and Eighth from **G**; it is nevertheless certain from those things we discussed above, that these also of the **Doric genus** <note>Kepler is likely referring to the "Hard" or "Dorian" qualities here</note> for the First and Second ought to be written from the same key **G**, for which these skeletons are suitable from our species II.

->[Diagram: Musical notation showing the 'skeletons' for species II of the octave]<-

Therefore, by this application of the common eight Tones to my species of the Octave I, XI, XIII, and II, I can show a much more evident distinction between these Tones than our Musicians can, because they despise the <term>comma<gloss>A very small interval resulting from the difference between different types of whole tones in mathematical tuning</gloss></term>. For those which are written from **G** all have four legitimate consonances: the third, fourth, fifth, and sixth with the first. But those which use **f** and **e** employ "adulterated" <note>Imperfect or slightly out-of-tune intervals</note> consonances: below, the <term>Augmented Fourth<gloss>original: quartâ majori. Also known as the tritone</gloss></term> **e–a** and **f–b♭**, and the <term>Augmented Fifth<gloss>original: quintâ majori</gloss></term> **e–b♮** and **f–c**.

**What** then, you will ask, about the remaining ten species? Since all the used Tones are reduced to four? Clearly, they serve this purpose: so that Musicians may know that if we temper the Systems of the principal Octave described from **G** as nature persuades, then a song can by no means be transposed so easily and variedly without the loss of its own "sincerity" <note>Purity of tuning</note> as they are accustomed to doing. It is free for them, therefore, either to reject all the remaining ten species, and with them also their transpositions: or to confess that more Forms of Melodies—namely more Modes or Tones—can exist, and those different from these positions, others...

<margin>CH. XIV.</margin> ...some more, others less; just as you see the equivalences noted in the margin above. For if we have no reason for the intervals of one of the higher Octaves, surely some transpositions are possible from *G* to *c*, from *A* to *d*, and others.

Lastly, you may ask: what prevents those transpositions that I have rejected so many times? For they do not seem to offend the ears, since it is generally admitted that the excess of a <term>Comma<gloss>original: Commatis. The "syntonic comma" is a tiny mathematical interval with a ratio of 81:80, the difference between a major and minor whole tone.</gloss></term> in intervals that are separated in different parts of the <term>System<gloss>The overall musical scale or framework.</gloss></term> is not perceived by the ears. For suppose a system is tuned as perfectly as possible according to the laws of nature explained so far; let the notes *G* to *a* and *a* to *b* be struck. Ask all people who hear them which of these intervals is larger; they will say they do not know. They will not discern the difference until the intervals are joined in the same place in the Octave—that is, where the space of the string is marked out with a compass, and the eighty-first part of the string is marked off, and thus two lengths of 80 and 81, struck one after the other, are compared to each other.

I respond: although the sense of hearing does not distinguish when only three strings of the Octave are struck (the boundaries of two intervals), yet when all the strings of one Octave are struck, it finally distinguishes the "first-born" and natural Octave starting on *G* from the Octaves starting on other keys. For in all species of the Octave, the same seven <term>Harmonious<gloss>original: Concinna. Kepler's term for intervals that are mathematically and aesthetically pleasing.</gloss></term> intervals are present. Once these are expressed by the striking of the strings, they immediately stick in the memory; thus it becomes easily apparent to the hearing at which place in the natural Octave any <term>Tone<gloss>original: Tonus. Here referring to the starting note or mode.</gloss></term> begins. In this way, the sense of the Comma will be implicit in the distinction of the Octaves. For just as the Hearing approves the Consonances themselves and all Harmonious intervals by their effect—even though it does not count the physical lengths of the strings that cause the chords—so the same hearing also notices the effect of the 80:81 comma, even if it does not count it, and thus does not grasp it as a separate, discrete sensation.

# CHAPTER XV.

## Which Modes or Tones serve
## which Emotions.

So far I have dealt with the principles from which Tones consist and are distinguished from one another; now I shall say a few things about their effect, which is indeed consistent with my principles.

First, the reader must be warned that we are not dealing here with the different dispositions of the soul that cause a person to sing rather than use plain and steady speech; nor with those things that follow from singing on one hand and simple speech on the other in the listener. For just as it is the alacrity of the soul that precedes all singing in the singer and, as it were, dictates the Melody to him, so too a pleasure in the listeners follows every kind of harmonious Song.

We must separate this general disposition of the Soul, or rather,

### CHAPTER XV.

**Since** all parts of harmonious and natural song are designed to stir the emotions by imitating the sounds that animals produce to testify to their desires, it is clear that this discussion is varied, complex, and seemingly infinite. Because it exceeds my own strength, the whole matter might be more rightly handed over to the <term>Empirics<gloss>Practical musicians who learn by experience and "ear" rather than by mathematical theory.</gloss></term>—that is, the practicing musicians. These men, guided by nature alone without formal rules, frequently emerge as the authors of wonderful melodies. It is far easier for them to create such music than to explain in a long and eloquent speech what song is, what it consists of, or how it is made.

**For** just as prose oration is represented by poetry, so the voices and gestures of living beings are represented and, as it were, "painted" by song. Certainly, just as in the poetic arts, the faculty for composing musical song must be learned through use and practice alone, provided that one’s talent has also been shaped for this by nature.

**However**, because it is one of the most honorable recreations of the Mind to investigate the causes of things—or to look closely at those causes discovered by others—even Aristotle devoted a large part of his *Problems* to harmonic contemplations. Therefore, we must also attempt something here to extend the boundaries of philosophy. By applying the laws of systematic method, we must restrain that "infiniteness" of discussion and bring it back to general headings, so that through these specific categories, a judgment can later be made about similar cases.

**I.** The elements of song itself, and of the emotions that follow the various types of song, are proportional; there are roughly the same number of elements on both sides. For even the terms for the "Parts of Song"—<term>Melodic Motion<gloss>original: $\alpha\gamma\omega\gamma\acute{\eta}$ (agoge). This refers to the upward or downward movement and tempo of a melody.</gloss></term>, <term>Sustaining<gloss>original: $\tau\omicron\nu\acute{\eta}$ (tone). The drawing out or holding of a pitch.</gloss></term>, <term>Note-Selection<gloss>original: $\pi\epsilon\tau\tau\epsilon\acute{\iota}\alpha$ (petteia). Literally "game-playing," referring to the art of choosing which notes to use or avoid in a composition.</gloss></term>, and <term>Interweaving<gloss>original: $\pi\lambda\omicron\kappa\acute{\eta}$ (ploke). The weaving together of different melodic lines.</gloss></term>—allude to certain emotions. The first serves simplicity; the last serves luxury. The former is like the body, the latter like colors. The equality of the **Sustaining** tone moves one to attention; **Note-Selection**, or "playing about," is designed for delight and recreation. These are general principles across all musical modes.

**II.** Regarding **Melodic Motion**, <term>Galilei<note>Vincenzo Galilei (c. 1520–1591), an Italian lutenist and music theorist, and the father of the astronomer Galileo Galilei.</note></term> notes this specific point: there are two differences, one upward and the other downward. The former serves joy, while the latter serves sadness and weeping. The cause is natural: for below, a deep voice is produced by slow motion; above, a sharp voice is produced by rapid motion. Therefore, when the voice descends, it approaches rest; when it ascends, it advances in motion. For this reason, in choral song, we usually end at the bottom; there the voice faints away, while at the top, it flourishes. And so, in grief, the mind and all its functions languish, while in cheerfulness, it lives and is active.

**III.** There is also great power in the **Leap**, which is like a "potential" melodic motion. It possesses rashness, movement, and audacity; it is military, masculine, and shameless if it occurs frequently—especially through the <term>Fifth<gloss>original: diapente.</gloss></term>. The shape of the Fifth, the **Triangle** <note>Kepler associates musical intervals with geometric shapes inscribed in a circle. The Fifth is related to the triangle (trigonus).</note>, consists of acute angles and consumes the whole circle with three lines. Conversely, a single ascending leap through a **Soft Sixth** <note>A minor sixth.</note>, followed by a melodic motion downward, expresses the magnitude of sorrow. It is suited to wailing because of its similarity to the human voice, as seen in the song *In Me transierunt* by <term>Orlando<note>Orlando di Lasso (c. 1532–1594), one of the most famous and influential composers of the late Renaissance.</note></term>.

**IV.** It also matters a great deal how much "altitude" the primary part of the song occupies within the framework of the **Octave** from its lowest root. For if it runs through the whole Octave, or exceeds it, the song is spirited; but if it occupies only a <term>Fourth<gloss>original: Diatessaron.</gloss></term>, it is modest and pleasant. The <term>Fifth<gloss>original: Diapente.</gloss></term> possesses a middle quality. The **Soft Third**...

V. Among the general elements, we must especially include the speed and slowness of the rhythm, or <term>tactus<gloss>The steady pulse or beat that governs a piece of music.</gloss></term>. The former is suited to anger, movement, fighting, and cheerfulness; the latter to those affections we enjoy in stillness: sorrow, love, longing, and the pleasure of attainment.

VI. Add also the mode, that is, the Rhythm itself: for the power of the so-called triple meter is one thing, and that of the duple is another. Much of this power is perhaps drawn from the imitation of dancing troupes; since the alternating variety of movements in them is known to all, it immediately alerts the listeners, bringing them, as it were, into the presence of the event. Triple rhythm is therefore turbulent and active, while duple is quieter, more peaceful, and more modest. But regarding Rhythms and their signs, I shall say nothing in this book; therefore, I will let them pass.

Aristotle writes regarding the Enharmonic genus that minds are filled by it with a divine frenzy; on the other hand, the Spartan magistrates—because this type of song was considered effeminate and artificial—drove its author out of the city, marked with ignominy, for attempting to introduce it.

VII. We must now come to those things by which we said the <term>Modes<gloss>Also called "Tones," these are the musical scales or keys used in composition.</gloss></term> are properly distinguished; the chief of these is the diversity of the types of Song. And here a most abundant harvest of disputes arises: which of the three ancient <term>genera<gloss>The three types of Greek scales: Diatonic, Chromatic, and Enharmonic.</gloss></term> was assigned to which emotion? We shall pass over this untouched, since the distribution of song into three genera is not natural, nor are the ancients consistent with themselves on this matter. My discussion will be about the two natural genera of song, namely the **Hard** and the **Soft** <note>These terms, "Durum" and "Molle," are the ancestors of our modern "Major" and "Minor" scales.</note>; the names themselves reveal which emotions they stir. For just as the female is made chiefly for enduring and the male for acting, especially in the business of procreation; so the **Soft** genus is suited to the feminine passions of the soul, and the **Hard** to manly actions. The distinctions between these things will become clearer from what follows.

VIII. For not only the Genera of song, but also the Modes in general differed by the placement of the <term>semitone<gloss>The smallest interval in a standard scale, such as the step between E and F.</gloss></term>. This placement of the semitone animates and affects both the Genus and the Mode or Tone. However, this placement must be discussed differently regarding the genera than regarding all the modes. For we said that the Genera first arise in the principal Octave starting from G, in which the placement of the semitone in the next-to-last position forms the **Soft genus**, and in the third-to-last position, the **Hard genus**. In the former, the <term>third<gloss>The musical interval between the first and third notes of a scale; its size determines if a scale sounds "bright" (major) or "somber" (minor).</gloss></term> is soft at the bottom; in the latter, it is hard. What, then, is the connection of this placement with the emotions? Or what does the minor third have in common with women, with passions, and with softness; and likewise, what does the Hard Third have in common with virility, hardness, actions, and efficacy?

First, then, remember that the Hard Third arose from the **Pentagon**; the pentagon uses a division according to the <term>Extreme and Mean ratio<gloss>Now known as the Golden Ratio, a mathematical proportion found in nature and art.</gloss></term>, which forms the "divine proportion." In this proportion, a beautiful idea of Procreation is present. For just as a father begets a son, and the son another, each similar to himself: so also in that division, when the greater part is added to the whole, the proportion is continued; the composite takes the place of the "Whole," and what was previously the whole takes the place of the "greater part." Although this ratio cannot be expressed in whole numbers, a certain series of numbers is given which continually approaches the truth. In this series, the very difference of the numbers from the genuine terms (which are <term>ineffable<gloss>original: "ineffabiles," referring to irrational numbers that cannot be expressed as a simple fraction.</gloss></term>) produces males and females by a wonderful alternation, distinguished by members indicating their sex. For example, if the larger part is first 2, the smaller 1, and the total 3: here 1 is not to 2 exactly as 2 is to 3; for the difference is a unity, preventing the rectangle of the extremes (1 and 3) from equaling the square of the mean (2).

Since this is the nature of this sectioning <note>The "extreme and mean ratio," or Golden Ratio, which Fibonacci numbers approximate.</note>, which concurs with the demonstration of the pentagon; and since God the Creator has conformed the laws of generation to it—the seminal reasons of plants to the genuine and, in itself, solely perfect proportion of ineffable terms <note>Plants often show five-fold symmetry (pentagons), which Kepler links to the Golden Ratio.</note>, which were each commanded to have their own seed within themselves; but for the joined pairs of proportions of Numbers (where the deficiency of one unit is compensated by the excess of the other), He conformed the union of male and female. What wonder is it then, if even the offspring of the pentagon—the <term>Major Third<gloss>original: "Tertia dura" (hard third); the interval spanning four semitones, ratio 4:5.</gloss></term> or 4:5, and the <term>Minor Third<gloss>original: "mollis" (soft third); the interval spanning three semitones, ratio 5:6.</gloss></term> 5:6—move souls, which are images of God, toward affections associated with the business of generation? 

Here we must repeat from Chapter III: although the ratio 1:6 comes from the hexagon, the remaining part 5:6 <note>The Minor Third.</note> does not harmonize because of the hexagon, but because of its derivation from the three tenths of a circle, through the doubling and halving of terms. Thus even this Remainder, and its offspring the <term>Minor Third</term>, belongs to the Pentagonal class of figures. Therefore, once it is established that the partnership of two Thirds represents the partnership of male and female, it is no trouble to assign to each sex its own Third. For the **Major Third** emerges as masculine, and the **Minor** as feminine; since the same proportion exists even in their bodies and strengths, both of body and mind. And since the Major is from an odd-sided figure (namely the Pentagon), while the Minor is originally from the even-sided Decagon, it is also consistent with the teachings of Pythagoras, who called odd numbers male and even numbers female. This is confirmed by that speculation on excesses and deficiencies, since the odd number is also the "exceeding" one; thus the former is held to be of the masculine sex, and the latter of the feminine.

Let there be added to these reasons also a contemplation of the harmonious intervals, the smallest of which is the <term>semitone</term>. For a succeeding <term>semitone</term> always invites the voice to overcome it because of its smallness; it is like a ridge on a slope that softens. And whenever a <term>semitone</term> is encountered moving toward the higher notes, it is held as a kind of goal of the song toward which it tends; from there, as if the ridge has been crested and the effort completed, it is often accustomed to return to the lower notes. Certainly, if we sing RE, MI, the hearing is not satisfied, but expects that FA be added <note>In the "soft" hexachord, the step from MI to FA is a semitone, providing a sense of arrival.</note>. 

Therefore, since the **Major Third**, which holds the lowest place in the <term>Eighth Tone<gloss>The eighth ecclesiastical mode, or Hypomixolydian.</gloss></term>, lacks a semitone (which is only added later to complete the <term>Fourth<gloss>original: "Diatessaron."</gloss></term>), it is rightly considered active and full of effort. Its power is <term>fruitful<gloss>original: "γόνιμος" (gonimos).</gloss></term> and <term>unrestrained in its prime<gloss>original: "ἀκμή ἄσχετος" (akmē aschetos).</gloss></term>, seeking its end—namely the Fourth—whose semitone is for it like an <term>outpouring<gloss>original: "ἔκχυσις" (ekchysis).</gloss></term> sought with all its might. 

But the **Minor Third**, standing in the lowest place of the <term>First Tone<gloss>The first ecclesiastical mode, or Dorian.</gloss></term>, since it has already embraced the semitone (after the overcoming of which a return is usually made), is as if content with itself; and by its nature, being made for overcoming and for passion <note>In the sense of "undergoing" or "receiving" action.</note>, it always spreads itself on the ground like a hen, ready for the treading rooster. And behold: the causes of the "affects" in the Genera and in the Tones of the primary system arising from G.

<margin>CHAPTER XV.</margin>
Now let us consider the same position of the semitone <note>original: "semitonij" — the half-step in a musical scale.</note> even with respect to all the Tones <note>original: "Tonos" — here referring to the musical modes (like Dorian, Phrygian, etc.) rather than just individual notes.</note> indiscriminately: here I will adapt my speech, as I have done so far, to the common Tones as I have distinguished them from my own principles. As for the remaining ten species of the Octave which I added for the sake of comparison, the judgment of whether they deserve to be called Tones will rest with the musicians.

It has often been said that, by nature, larger intervals from the consonant set demand that the lowest place be given to them, so that great things may be associated with great things. For deep sounds, which are likewise at the bottom, are determined by a certain magnitude—that is, by long strings—while high sounds are determined by short ones. Or, what is the same thing, a deep sound is produced by a large and slow motion, and a high sound by a small and fast one. **The natural series, therefore, is** when in a perfect tetrachord <term>tetrachord</term> <note>A scale segment of four notes.</note>, the Major Tone is in the first place, the Minor Tone in the second, and the Semitone in the third and highest. And when all things are held according to nature, we are joyful. Therefore, the joyful Tones are those which have the lower tetrachord divided in this way; specifically, the Seventh and Eighth modes have this. People think these were called now "Phrygian," now "Mixolydian" by the ancients with a strange inconsistency; though I am more inclined to believe they were called "Lydian" by the Ancients. For they testify of their Lydian mode that it fills minds with a "divine fury" <note>original: "furore divino" — a state of inspired or ecstatic energy.</note>, that is, with alacrity and military spirits; such as are our Seventh and Eighth modes.

When, therefore, the logic is overturned so that the Semitone is in the lowest place—which happens in the Ecclesiastical Third and Fourth modes, which were the "Phrygian" to the ancients—with the order of nature reversed, it is consistent that something complaining, broken, and lamentable is sounded. But when the Semitone is in the middle place, the affect is one of middle-ground tranquility, humanity, and the pleasantness found in conversations and storytelling. The First and Second modes are suited to these, being of a soft and feminine genus; people think these were once called "Dorian." Indeed, <term>Vincenzo Galilei</term> <note>An Italian lutenist and music theorist, father of the astronomer Galileo Galilei.</note> describes the Dorian thus: that it is by nature stable, quiet, without violence, and suited to gravity and severity. This is true of these two modes according to a greater or lesser degree. For the Tones named with even numbers <note>The Plagal modes.</note> must always be softer than their Authentic <note>The primary or "odd-numbered" modes.</note> counterparts (which are named with odd numbers), for the reason brought forward a little earlier in number IV. Thus, Galilei also makes the Plagal of the First mode <note>Mode 2.</note> languid, mournful, and fearful; for motion toward the deep notes belongs to languor, and motion toward the high notes belongs to vigor. Although I would prefer to temper those adjectives and distinguish the cause: for languor, weeping, and fear are not the property of the Dorian modes themselves, but generally belong to the excursion toward the depths and the frequent descent below the root note.

IX. Thus far concerning the position of the semitone; yet we have not yet assigned their properties to all the Tones. It follows, therefore, that we must also speak of the imperfect and "adulterated" consonances by which the skeletons of the octaves are articulated. And first, their essence must be inspected, and afterward their location in the System <note>original: "Systemate" — the overall musical scale or structure.</note>.

Therefore, when the arrangement of the Octave system is natural and primeval, in which the third, fourth, fifth, and sixth intervals are perfectly consonant with the lowest string: such a Tone stirs all those things in the soul which are according to nature—soft passions, hard actions, or the affects suited to them. This property belongs to the First and Eighth modes rising from G; for which reason Galilei asserted, not without justice, that the Eighth coincides with the First; understand this, however, while preserving the property of the sixth or the genus for each. Thus, by a double name, the Seventh and Eighth excel the others, both because of the position of the semitone and also because of their perfection...

<margin>CHAPTER XV.</margin>
On the contrary, the *Fifth* & *Sixth*, and the *Third* & *Fourth* modes use "adulterated" and augmented consonances at the bottom; the former pair [the 5th and 6th] use the *Fourth* <note>original: "Diatessaron"</note>, while the latter [the 3rd and 4th] use the *Fifth* <note>original: "Diapente"</note>. This configuration grants them a power of sadness and of affects departing from a balanced human temperament.

For in the *Fifth* and *Sixth* modes, the *Fourth* is indeed <term>high-pitched</term> <note>original: ὄρθιον (orthion) — referring to a rising or high-strained quality</note>, with the natural position of the semitone at the top, no less than in the *Seventh* and *August*; but two major tones are in the lowest position, followed by the semitone. From these is fashioned a *Fourth* that exceeds the perfect ratio by a comma <note>A "comma" is a tiny musical interval, the difference between two slightly different tunings of the same note; here it implies the interval is slightly "sharp" or strained.</note>.

Therefore, these modes also promote affects of grandeur, such as *Devotion*, *Admiration*, *Amplification*, and *Sorrow*; and again *Hope* and *Confidence*, acting as an elevation of the mind above one's present lot.

In the *Third* and *Fourth* modes, however, besides the inverted form of the *Fourth* itself, there is added this fermentation of consonances, which increases the sadness and the languors of the soul.

But if it is permitted to follow this analogy beyond the commonly used tones to the third species of my own system—the "soft song" <note>This refers to what we would now call a Minor key or scale.</note> described starting from the note *A*—because that species has a semitone at the bottom but a perfect *Fourth*: I would therefore adapt this one to a "pleasant sadness," such as when we take pleasure in a certain softness of soul, in *Loves* and *Longings*, or when joy expresses itself through tears.

These things concern *Consonances* by their own nature; now let us see what they effect by reason of their place in the system.

Since, therefore, the <term>accent</term> <note>original: τονή (tonē) — the tension or pitch-accent of a note</note> and the <term>completion</term> <note>original: τελεία (teleia) — the finality or cadence</note> are chiefly occupied around the fourth and sixth strings, it appears that the *Fourth* is established by them in the lowest place. Because this is the interval of the *Tetrachord* <note>A four-note scale segment.</note>, which embraces all three species of melodic tuning, it is paramount in this "breathing of life" into the *Tones*. In such a case, this form invites the song to humility, for the same reason I used above in point number IV. But if these parts of the song are occupied around the third and fifth strings, establishing the *Fourth* higher up, the song is excited and elevated, especially if it runs up to the octave. This seems to have been the nature of the <term>Rising Tune</term> <note>original: Νόμος ὄρθιος (Nomos orthios) — an ancient Greek musical "law" or melody known for being high-pitched and stirring.</note> of the ancients. Finally, if it is around the third and sixth, so that the *Fourth* is reduced to the middle—which happens more frequently in the *First* and *Second* modes than in the *Seventh* and *Eight*—then the song will promote middle-range affects. However, these articulations of the <term>structural framework</term> <note>original: sceletôn — literally "skeletons," referring to the core structural notes of a musical mode.</note> are frequently mixed among themselves, so that different parts of the song possess different qualities, according to the variety of the text and the skill of the artist "painting" the text with song.

X. If it is true, as some say, that the odd-numbered *Tones* (I, III, V, VII) are higher, and the even-numbered (II, IV, VI, VIII) are lower—even with respect to the root of the *Octave*—then certainly height corresponds to the excitation of the Soul, and depth to its dejection. Then we can surely distribute the four classes of affects into eight classes, according to the eight tones: so that the *Seventh* has anger, violence, and fortitude; the *Eight* has cheerfulness, alacrity, and sharp pleasure; the *Third* has sharp pain and longing; the *Fourth* has weeping and love; the *First* has festivity, weddings, and banquets; the *Second* has modest cheerfulness, conversation, and storytelling; the *Fifth* has public assemblies, exclamations, confidence, and hope; and the *Sixth* has devotion, great sorrow, etc.

<page-num>80</page-num>
<header>ON PROPORTIONS</header>

And now it is time for the discourse to return to its beginning. For the philosopher-reader must be reminded of this: that our musicians express all emotions in all <term>Modes</term> <note>original: "Tonis" — in this context, the specific scales or musical systems used to organize pitches</note> indiscriminately. They do so because every song, without distinction, gives pleasure to the listener and requires energy from the composer; they are able to do so because there are many instruments for stirring the emotions (some of which were listed at the start) that can be applied across all Modes without exception. If, however, they were to strive to use all the resources at their disposal toward the same purpose, they would not easily neglect the choice of Modes suitable for a specific <term>emotional premise</term> <note>original: "hypothesin" — the intended emotional goal or subject of the music</note>. But let them see to that which is permitted in their practical work; for me, it is enough to have proceeded this far in theory.

# CHAPTER XVI.

## What Singing through Harmony, or Figured Song, Is.

Although the word "Harmony" was used by the ancients to mean "Song," it must not be understood under this name as <term>melodic modulation</term> <note>original: "Modulatio" — the artistic arrangement of sounds</note> through several voices sounding together harmonically. For the <term>ensemble</term> <note>original: "Concentus"</note> of several voices in a perpetual succession of harmonies is a recent invention, plainly unknown to the ancients; this does not require much proof. On this matter, one may look at <note>original: "Vincentius Galilæus"</note> **Vincenzo Galilei** in his Italian work on music <note>Vincenzo Galilei (c. 1520–1591) was an influential music theorist and the father of the astronomer Galileo Galilei. He argued that ancient Greek music was monophonic (a single melody) and more powerful than the polyphony of his day.</note>. To be sure, people usually object by citing the banishment of "Singing through Harmony" from Plato’s Republic, as if it were already in use back then; but that passage is understood to refer to <term>Instruments</term> <note>original: "Organis" — here meaning musical instruments in general</note>, to the **Pan-pipes**, the **Bagpipe**, and the **Lute**, where one voice either sounds perpetually or pauses, giving way to an approaching dissonance. In that ancient custom, there was no greater artistry than among our modern bagpipers.

In these recent centuries, this method of singing began to be called <term>Figured</term> <note>original: "Figurata" — referring to "musica figurata" or polyphony, where notes have distinct "figures" or shapes to indicate rhythm</note> because the first authors did not make their diagrams as simple as they are in **Plainchant** <note>original: "Chorali cantu"</note>; instead, they used various shapes, colors, and dots. Some of these signs command silence, others sound; some command a long note, others a short one; some are applied to distinguish the Modes, others for <term>rhythmic meters</term> <note>original: "Modos mensurales"</note>, for <term>Fugues</term> <note>original: "Fugas" — a musical technique where one voice mimics another</note>, for repetitions, and similar things.

Therefore, let us define a **Harmonic Ensemble** as follows: it consists of two, three, four, or more voices or well-fitted and suitable melodies (such as we described in Chapter XIII), all of the same <term>Genus</term> and the same or related Modes, moving together in such a way that they create <term>concords</term> <note>original: "concordantias" — pleasing combinations of notes</note> that are either pure or "fermented" by the very brief interruption of well-fitted dissonances. These are not identical in a perpetual tone, nor are they the same one after another; rather, they are varied for delight by the very alternation of their successions. For just as the <term>Unison</term> stands in proportion to the consonance of two voices, so is Harmonic Song to the simple song of one...

...the melody of the voice; from this principle depend all the members of the definition, which I will explain in order.

I. First, therefore, regarding the plurality of voices, it should be noted that musical craftsmen have established what is most consistent with Nature: that although many voices often sound together, they are all called by only four names, according to the number of the perfect <term>harmonic mediation</term> <note>The mathematical process of dividing an interval—here, the octave—into consonant parts.</note> within one perfect system of the **octave** <note>original: "diapason"</note>. For they call the highest voice the **Discant** <note>Also known as the Soprano.</note>, the next one the **Alt** <note>The Alto.</note>, the higher of the low voices the **Tenor**, and the lowest the **Bass**. For between two voices sounding an octave apart, only two harmonic mediations intervene that are consonant with the extremes when those extremes sound the same pitch in different octaves, as explained in Chapter III.

<margin>Discant, Alt, Tenor, Bass.</margin>

Although the origin of these words is Italian, they seem to refer more to a composite system, such that the Alt and Bass hold opposite parts—not that the Alt is the highest overall, but because these two frequently (though not at the end) create an octave, the former being higher and sharper, the latter lower and deeper. Likewise, the origin of the word **Tenor** gives the idea of a simple <term>modulation</term> <note>The flow or "holding" of the melody.</note> of the song; while the name **Discant** seems to have been given because of its constant agility and its wandering away from the region of the Tenor, which is situated an octave away. Therefore, if we compare the parts of Song <margin>Discant, Alt, Tenor, Bass.</margin> from Chapter XIII (cited from Euclid), even though those qualities belong to all voices, the Tenor is chiefly occupied in **Melodic Progression** <note>original: "Αγωγῆ" (Agoge) — movement by consecutive steps.</note>, the Discant in **Interweaving** <note>original: "Πλοκῆ" (Ploke) — the winding of the melody through leaps or figures.</note>, the Alt in **Sustained Pitch** <note>original: "Τονῆ" (Tone) — the holding of a note or extension of sound.</note>, and the Bass in leaping through harmonic intervals. Of all four, however, **Melodic Disposition** <note>original: "Πετεία" (Peteia) — the artful choice and use of musical sounds.</note> is common to all, though more notable in the Alt.

These properties of the four voices are taken from the very Nature of things. For because by the definition provided, the <term>harmony</term> <note>original: "concentus" — the sounding together of multiple parts.</note> must be perpetually changed from one to another, it was necessary for this to happen so that one of the intermediate voices, in comparison to the others, moves within a narrow space of the system. For if an equal, loose freedom were given to all, it would necessarily follow that a lower voice would frequently wander into the space of a higher one and vice versa; this would result in an insane confusion, and the distinction of the four voices would be rendered useless. It was more appropriate for one of the middle voices (the Alt or Tenor) to occupy these narrow constraints, rather than the extreme voices, the Discant or Bass.

For if such a thing were done in the extreme voices, every variation of intervals would tend toward only one region, namely either toward the high or toward the low. It was better, therefore, for the harmony to be fixed or bound in a narrow place by some intermediate voice, like a single boundary for the parts themselves; the variation of intervals would then tend from that voice partly upward and partly downward. However, the lower of the middle voices should not have been the one constricted; because the "Idea" of the song, ascribed to the Tenor (the lower of the middle voices), must be both free and proceed through the middle quantity of the entire system, so that the surrounding voices are nothing other than its colors, ornaments, or emblems. Furthermore, the lower intervals are always larger than their counterparts above. Therefore, so that the Tenor might hold the middle place of quantity, it was necessary for it to be the lower of the middle voices; and thus the Alt...

<margin>CHAPTER XVI.</margin>
...it was necessary to be reduced into a narrow space, but not the Tenor. There remain, therefore, excursions for the **Discant** and the **Bass**, but with this distinction: the **Bass**, which sounds deep and is expressed with great motion and long strings, wanders in slow and large measures and through large harmonic intervals. The **Discant**, which sounds high and "flies over" the others, is drawn out from short strings and a swift motion of narrow space; it wanders through everything in short, and therefore more frequent measures, and with the smallest agreeable intervals. This, then, is the specific nature of the voices. Now I shall also explain the remaining parts of the definition.

<margin>Dissonances.</margin>
II. Now, as for that primary and chief seasoning of Melodic Song: **Dissonance**. First, these must be taken not from just any <term>unharmonious</term> <note>original: "ἀναρμόστῳ" (anarmosto)—referring to intervals that do not fit into a musical scale.</note> interval, but from concordant intervals. For since the individual voices, coming together for a common harmony, admit no intervals except concordant ones between the notes that follow one another, and they are of the same genus and Tone (as was sent before in the definition), it is easily apparent that if any one harmony is established among such voices (since all harmony is dissolved into concordant elements), it can never happen through any wandering of the individual voices from the root of their Octave that two voices together create anything other than a concordant interval—even if that interval is not always a **consonance**. Secondly, although excellent craftsmen sometimes use larger dissonances—such that the dissonant voice is a whole tone away from the one that would make a consonance—this is not done except to express and draw out the deepest stirrings of the soul. However, the ordinary dissonance, joined with pleasantness and thus in a certain way "natural," is created by a **semitone**.

<margin>
See Giovanni Maria Artusi of Bologna, book II, on the art of composition, which is entirely about dissonances. <note>Artusi (c. 1540–1613) was a famous music theorist known for his conservative defense of traditional counterpoint.</note>
</margin>
<margin>
The power of the Quindecagon in the selection of dissonances.
</margin>
The cause of this matter, again—so that the last things correspond to the first—must be sought from the innermost foundations of Geometry, from Chapter I, Axioms II and III, and from the first book and the contemplation of the <term>Quindecagon</term> <note>A fifteen-sided polygon.</note>. For since the semitone is contained in the numbers **15:16**, and indeed not only does the <term>Hexadecagon</term> <note>A sixteen-sided polygon.</note> figure have a geometric demonstration, but also the **Quindecagon**, it was not far off that the ratio 15:16 would define a harmonic proportion for us. No less would those ratios derived from it: 15:8, 15:4, 15:2, 15:32, and 15:64—and above all 15:1—be those which composite songs very frequently admit to form legitimate dissonances. Nor did we have any other exception than this: that the demonstration of the <term>Quindecagon</term> <note>original: "Pentekædecagoni"</note> was not formed by the number of the figure's angles immediately, as the others were. Therefore, it is not "proper" to itself, but "borrowed" and of a very distant degree, being transferred from different figures, the **Triangle** and the **Pentagon**. Likewise, although an angle of the **Quindecagon** might fit with others to fill a flat space, the whole figure with all its angles would not admit such a fitting together. Since, therefore, the ratio 15:16 and its companions approach Consonances so closely by reason of their forming cause, it is no wonder that they are also mixed among the consonances by frequent use. On the other hand, the Tones **8:9** and **9:10** participate by their other terms in the <term>Enneagon</term> <note>original: "Nonangulo"—a nine-sided polygon.</note>, a figure that is entirely impossible to demonstrate geometrically. For this reason, dissonances admitted through them and their companion proportions (4:9, 2:9, 1:9, 9:16, 9:32, as well as 9:5, 18:5, 36:5, 9:20, 9:40, etc.) are not sweet, but altogether harsh; and much harsher are those which are forged from the **Tritone**, the "mutilated" **Fifth** <note>original: "Diapente"—here likely referring to the diminished fifth.</note>, and similar intervals. Concerning these, see Artu-

### BOOK III OF THE HARMONICS

<margin>CHAPTER XVI.</margin>
Artusi <note>original: "Artusium" — likely referring to Giovanni Maria Artusi (c. 1540–1613), a prominent music theorist known for his defense of traditional counterpoint against modern innovations.</note>: for they <note>dissonances</note> arise after the Tones—the Major, the Minor, and the Semitone—namely from a non-natural composition of these as if they were elements. Moreover, the further one departs from Nature, the further one departs from sweetness.

<margin>Syncopation</margin>
Thirdly, the other laws of dissonances are suggested by their other name, when they are called **Syncopations** <term>Syncopæ</term> <note>Syncopation: the shifting of the expected rhythmic accent, often by holding a note from a weak beat across onto a strong beat.</note>. Although this is a common occurrence for both dissonances and imperfect consonances, we are dealing now with dissonances. Ordinarily, they maintain this rule: that they are used like leaven, salt, or vinegar in prepared dishes <note>original: "Opsonijs" — side dishes or seasoned foods.</note>; that is to say, just as a whole course is not made entirely of those seasonings, so here, whole songs do not abound with dissonances—unless for the sake of great emphasis. Nor does any one voice, beginning at the very start of the <term>tactus</term> <note>tactus: the steady pulse or beat in Renaissance and Baroque music.</note>, run into the other consonant voices while being dissonant itself. Instead, it admits the dissonance stealthily and, as if by turning away, while in one place in the scale which it occupied when the beat was raised; and thus starting a certain sound on the later and less principal part of the beat, with the remaining voices in agreement, it lingers longer after those have finished and beyond the beginning of the following beat. In this way, all the other voices—usually those deeper than itself (so that it, being high-pitched, might obstruct less by its smallness, weakness, and speed)—occupy a place dissonant from its position at the start of the following beat, before that voice has departed from its own place. From there, they expel it as if it were slow and usually push it down into a lower position. From this occasion, the name of **Cadences** <margin>Cadences.</margin> <note>original: "Cadentiæ" — literally "fallings."</note> seems to have been born for the concords and melodic endings which consume the dissonances.

Furthermore, they observe this: that the battle of Dissonants is ordinarily joined not so frequently from a close interval, such as between seconds, as it is between sevenths. Thus the upper voice, driven from its place in this manner, may flow down through a Semitone or Tone to a sixth, or fly up to be designated as an **Octave** with those going before.

<margin>Common Dissonances.</margin>
There are also other very frequent dissonances, less artificial, when a deep voice continues its sound, remaining on the same note, but the high voice runs out from the <term>diapason</term> <note>diapason: an octave.</note> of that deep sound in swift notes to some note consonant to it through a <term>diapente</term> <note>diapente: a perfect fifth.</note> or <term>diatessaron</term> <note>diatessaron: a perfect fourth.</note>, flying through all the intermediate agreeable places, such that it alternates between consonance and dissonance. However, the one that is first in order always consonants; the dissonance is both brief (being in passage) and on the sound which is later in order. For example, if a Beat of double proportion <note>i.e., 2:1 time</note> couples five notes of the **Discant** <note>the highest vocal part</note> with one of the **Bass**, the first, third, and fifth of the Discant will consonant; the second and fourth will dissonate, or consonant less perfectly. Behold:

IV. Again, just as in the simple songs of those languages that consist of **Rhythm** and the length or shortness of syllables, not much account is taken of the short ones; but we direct the long syllables and the ends of verses to places that are consonant with the first sound. So also in a musical ensemble, there are consonances called "minor" and "imperfect" which we fly through quickly; and there are "perfect" ones toward which we strive, which for that reason are called **Cadences** <term>Clausulæ</term> <note>Clausulæ: the concluding formulas or "closing" points of a musical phrase.</note>.

</margin>
V. Furthermore, just as individual consonances considered on their own are pleasing for the reason that they do not sound exactly identical, but are shaped in a certain way and are "diverse-sounding," occupying a certain qualitative breadth in the hearing—drawing their nature from the regular plane figures <note>Kepler's central theory is that musical intervals are derived from the geometry of polygons.</note> from which they arise—so now a **Harmonic Song** (or a perpetual sequence of several harmonies) loses all its grace without variety.

<margin>
Why two fifths etc. [cannot be] placed consecutively.
</margin>
From this explanation of the definition, the reasons can be given for the laws that **Composers** observe in fitting concords together. For one may ask: What is the natural cause why they think it permissible for themselves to arrange several natural **Thirds** and **Sixths** in a row, yet they do not admit several **Fourths**, **Fifths**, **Octaves**, and the like, from any single species in succession?

I respond that the cause is this: Thirds or Sixths following one another in pitch are mostly, in reality, diverse—one being Major, the other Minor. And although sometimes two Minor Thirds may follow each other closely, they are nonetheless the smallest and "imperfect" consonances. For suppose the first person sings <term>Do Re Mi Fa</term> <note>original: "Vt Re Mi Fa" — the first four notes of the hexachord.</note> and the second person, at the same moments of time, sings <term>Mi Fa Sol La</term>. Four Thirds follow one another; of which the first, **Do–Mi**, is Major; the second, **Re–Fa**, and the third, **Mi–Sol**, are Minor; the fourth, **Fa–La**, is again Major. On the contrary, all Fourths are commonly held to be intervals of the same magnitude, as are Fifths, and most especially Octaves. Therefore, if several of these perfect concords of the same species were arranged in succession, differing in pitch, the song would not be varied in its consonances.

But another principal cause prevents several **Fifths** from being sung in order going upward, which does not prevent **Octaves** from being sung; about which **Aristotle** thought he should inquire in his *Problems*: "Why do they sing in Octaves (for example, men with women, or men with boys), but they do not sing in Fifths and Fourths?" The cause, therefore, is this: That while two Thirds make the consonance of a **Fifth** <term>Diapente</term>, and two Octaves make the consonance of a **Double Octave** <term>Disdiapason</term>, by contrast, two Fifths make a **Ninth**, and two Fourths make a **Seventh**—which are dissonant intervals. Therefore, a voice running equally through Octave and Third consonances remains within the **Tone** or **Mode**, observing the same species of the Octave; but here, if it should run through equal [Fifths or Fourths], it changes the Mode or Tone significantly, which is against the definition.

VI. Regarding the choice of concords, some things must also be noted: first, that in general, large intervals express great emotions of the soul (as in those works of **Orlando** <note>Orlando di Lasso (c. 1532–1594), one of the most famous and influential composers of the late Renaissance.</note>, *Where is Abel?* and *My soul is sorrowful*); small and high intervals express joy; low and small intervals express sadness.

-># BOOK III ON HARMONIES<-

<margin>CHAPTER XVI.</margin>
Furthermore, since harmonic singing usually ends in **Identity of Sound** <note>original: "Identisonantiam" — Kepler's term for the unison or octave, where notes sound "identical."</note>, if we are to include a large interval at the end (following the logic of the text), it is necessary for the Bass not only to descend, but for the Soprano <note>original: "Discantum"</note> to also ascend—contrary to the usual nature of finishing a song—in imitation of the pipes and the strings of the **Pandore** <term>Pandura</term> <note>A long-necked, plucked string instrument popular in the Renaissance.</note>. It is then that the power of the **semitone**, explained in the previous chapter, shines most brightly. This is because the natural and ordinary conclusion of a song through an ascent loves to overcome a semitone at the finish, at least in those **Modes** <note>original: "Tonis"</note> that do not already have a semitone immediately above the root of their Octave.

<margin>Why large intervals are more pleasing.</margin>
Thirdly, Galileo <note>referring to Vincenzo Galilei, the father of the famous astronomer Galileo Galilei, who was a prominent music theorist</note> considered it a question worthy of study: why a **Fifth over an Octave** <note>original: "Diapente epi diapason" — a compound interval of a twelfth.</note> sounds more pleasant than a simple **Fifth**, and why, by extension, one Harmony is always more pleasant than another. It is not worth the effort to examine the causes he himself brought forward, as they are obscure and uncertain. From my own principles, however, the causes of this matter appear very clearly. For because of Axiom II in the first chapter, the degrees of knowledge by which the sides of geometric figures differ from one another are also transplanted into the proportions themselves, which are the offspring of those figures. It is therefore reasonable that those degrees—by which the demonstration of the **Part of the circle** and the **Remainder** <note>Kepler's theory relies on how a circle is divided by regular polygons to create harmonic ratios.</note> differ—should also distinguish the sweetness of both that Part and that Remainder. Therefore, those Harmonies that exist immediately through the sectioning of the circle itself—namely, those between the Whole and the Part cut away—are more perfect and pleasant than those between the Remainder and the Whole. These latter are eventually derived from the former through the mixing of **Identities of Sound** <note>octaves/unisons</note> resulting from the halving or doubling of strings. Thus, the ratio 1:3 <note>the compound fifth or twelfth</note> holds the first rank and is therefore more pleasant than 2:3 <note>the simple fifth</note>; and 1:6 <note>compound major sixth</note> more than 5:6 <note>minor third</note>; and 1:5 <note>compound major third</note> more than 4:5 <note>major third</note>; and 1:4 <note>the double octave</note> more than 3:4 <note>the fourth</note>; and 2:5 <note>compound major third</note> more than 3:5 <note>major sixth</note>; and 3:8 <note>compound fourth</note> more than 5:8 <note>minor sixth</note>. For first, a Part is made consonant through itself, not because of the Remainder; only later, and thus more imperfectly, is the Remainder shown to be consonant because of its partner or an outside part.

<margin>The goal of this entire work.</margin>
The remaining rules of the art of Composition I leave to the Craftsmen themselves to prove or to provide the reasoning behind them. For the things I have discussed up to this point are quite sufficient for me, both for illustrating the nature of Song (having shown at least its first and general foundations in Nature) and especially for the speculations of the following Book V. The subject matter of that book is the single goal I have set for myself in this entire work. For as an **Astronomer**, I discuss regular figures not so much geometrically (except where that geometry seemed incomplete) as **astronomically** and **metaphysically**. In the same way, I write about the proportions of song not so much musically as **geometrically**, **physically**, and finally, as before, **astronomically** and **metaphysically**. Just as I have need of the five regular solids from Geometry, so too I need the Proportions and the whole Harmonic apparatus from Music to explain the causes of the proportions of the heavenly Orbs, their **Eccentricities**, and their motions at the **Apsides** <term>Apsides</term> <note>The points in a planet's orbit where it is closest to or farthest from the Sun.</note>. Indeed, I by no means profess the art of composing songs, which is the practice of Music; anyone who wishes will more correctly seek that from the books on the art of composition published by the aforementioned Artusi and by Seth Calvisius, a former friend of mine. I name these authors not because I think they are the best, but because I have not seen others.
