# On the Three Means
## A Political Digression.

<margin>See a most beautiful passage in Bodin's *On the Commonwealth*:</margin> <note>original: "Bodino de Repub" — referring to Jean Bodin (1530–1596), a French jurist and political philosopher whose work *The Six Books of the Commonwealth* argued for different types of justice based on mathematical proportions.</note>
**F**olios 29, line 9: the following paragraph was excluded from its proper place because the workers had incautiously distributed the leaves of the manuscript (specifically folios 7 and 10).

However, those authors should not be blamed who admit proportions of this kind into the Commonwealth <note>original: "Rempublicam" — the State or Republic</note> under the title of "Harmonic Proportions." For even if few of those formed in this way define pure Harmonies, and all the rest are foreign to Harmonies, they all share this part of the definition: they are tempered from both proportions, the Arithmetic and the Geometric. From this tempering, they possess an aptitude within the Commonwealth. Conversely, if there is any power of Harmonies as Harmonies within the Commonwealth, our "Harmonic Means" <note>original: "medietates Harmonicæ" — the mathematical average or midpoint between two values</note> cannot be despised, which I hand down with this looser definition:

<margin>What a Harmonic Mean truly is.</margin>
> *That it is everything which comes between two consonant voices, being itself consonant with each of them.* In the sections, therefore, etc.

*The portions omitted until now. Since I had mentioned Bodin in the margin, and having now finished the third book, I judged that I had labored enough over mathematical speculations. With this thorny matter finished, I decided to transcribe from Bodin himself the principal heads of this political dispute, with the words and order mostly shaped by my own understanding of that passage. I do this both to bring some light to a place obscure in itself—since Bodin did not bring enough support from mathematical disciplines to this speculation—and to soothe the boredom of the morose mathematical demonstrations of which this whole book consists, by interposing pleasant, popular material, and to offer a taste of its significant use in understanding the Commonwealth. I shall begin, however, with a fuller explanation of the mathematical matter, more accommodated to the grasp of the non-mathematical reader.*

When equal amounts are added to several numbers, without considering their magnitude, it is an Arithmetic proportion. As:

<margin>For just as 6 is greater than 3, so (by that many units, namely 3) 12 is greater than 9.</margin>

| | | | | | | |
| :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| | 3. | 9. | 5. | 10. | 17. | 38. |
| **Add** | 3. | 3. | 3. | 3. | 3. | 3. |
| | **6.** | **12.** | **8.** | **13.** | **20.** | **41.** |

This proportion in this example is "disjunct." Therefore, a "conjunct" proportion or an arithmetic progression occurs when, starting from any number, equal amounts are added to it continuously.

| **As** | **3** | **or** | **38** | |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| | 3 | | 3 | Since, therefore, between 3, 6, 9, 12, and likewise between 38, 41, 44, 47, there is a continuous arithmetic progression, it happens that the middle of three such numbers placed in order is called the Arithmetic Mean; as between 6 and 12, the Mean is 9; between 38 and 44, the Arithmetic Mean is 41. |
| | **6** | | **41** | |
| | 3 | | 3 | |
| | **9** | | **44** | |
| | 3 | | 3 | |
| | **12** | | **47** | |

When, however, similar amounts <note>meaning proportional ratios rather than fixed units</note> are added to several numbers, with attention to their magnitude, then it is a Geometric proportion.

# BOOK III ON HARMONICS

<margin>POLITICS</margin>

->9. 27. 51. 114.<-

For just as the triple of 3 (which is 9) is added to 3, so to 9 is added its triple (27), which is as much greater than 9 as 9 is greater than 3, and as 15 is greater than 5, and so on. Therefore, as 3 is to 12, so 9 is to 36. And as 3 is to 9, so 12 is to 36.

Again, this proportion in this example is *disjunct* <note>original: "disjuncta" — a proportion where the four terms are distinct (a:b = c:d) rather than a continuous chain (a:b = b:c)</note>. Therefore, a *conjoint geometric proportion* or progression occurs when, after starting with any number, either a part or a similar multiple is always added to it.

| For example | 3 | 10 | 8 |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| | 9 | 30 | 4 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| | 12 | 40 | 12 |
| | 36 | 120 | 6 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| | 48 | 160 | 18 |
| | 144 | 480 | 9 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| | 192 | 640 | 27 |

In the first two examples, the triple is added to the initial number; in the third, the half is added. And again, to the number resulting from this, the same multiple or part is added. Therefore, as 8 is to 12, so this same 12 is further related to 18, and 18 likewise to 27. Here, 12 is the **geometric mean** <note>original: "medietas Geometrica" — the middle value in a geometric progression where 8/12 = 12/18</note> between 8 and 18. Likewise, 18 is the geometric or proportional mean between 12 and 27, etc.

These things must be understood first so that it may be grasped what a **harmonic proportion** is. For it is defined by Bodin <note>Jean Bodin (1530–1596), a French jurist whose work *The Six Books of the Commonwealth* compared types of justice to mathematical proportions</note> thus: *that in it the ratios of equals and likes are moderately blended* <note>original: "quòd in ea Rationes æqualium & similium sint modicè confusæ"</note>—that is, the prior ratios are arithmetic, and the subsequent ones geometric.

Furthermore, this definition is not true. **1.** For there are many ways, even in non-harmonic numbers, in which the ratios of equals and likes can be moderately blended; yet this does not suffice for it to be a harmonic proportion. Indeed, other relationships of numbers must also be included, which are to be sought from Chapters 1, 2, and 3. **2.** Conversely, there are many harmonic pairings of numbers in which neither the ratios of equals nor of likes are contained. **3.** Moreover, there are harmonic proportions in which there is a simple geometric proportion, such as 1, 2, 4. Even if these are identical <note>meaning they share the same ratio, such as the 1:2 octave</note> and do not by themselves produce any special beauty—so much so that Bodin denies they produce any **concord** <note>original: "concentum" — a musical harmony or sounding together</note> on their own (meaning a figured one)—there are, in turn, other harmonic proportions in which there is a simple arithmetic proportion, such as 1, 2, 3 and 2, 3, 4. Bodin, forgetting his own principles, acknowledges these as harmonic, even though they have no geometric analogy mixed in. So too 3, 4, 5; so 4, 5, 6; so 1, 3, 5; so 2, 5, 8, etc. Bodin wrongly denies that these latter ones produce harmonic concords, rising up on the authority of the ancients against the very **sense of hearing**. <note>original: "sensum auditus"</note>

<page-num>88</page-num>
# ON PROPORTIONS

<margin>DIGRESSION.</margin>
However, the assertion is true to a certain extent regarding that proportion which the ancients, through a false persuasion, called **Harmonic** <note>original: "Harmonicam" — Kepler distinguishes between the ancient mathematical definition and the true musical "harmonic" ratios he has discovered</note>. I say "to a certain extent" if, indeed, instead of the **ratios of equals** <note>original: "Rationibus equalium" — refers to arithmetic equality where the differences between numbers are the same</note>, you understand **Arithmetic Means** transformed into other numbers. In these transformed numbers, the actual equality of the differences—which existed in the first three numbers—is no longer explicitly expressed. For the **Harmonic Mean** of the ancients is most properly defined as follows: *it is when the proportion of the differences between three numbers is the same as the proportion of the extremes* <note>original: "excessuum inter tres numeros, eadem proportio, quæ extremorum"</note>, as in the numbers 3, 4, and 6 <note>The difference between 3 and 4 is 1; the difference between 4 and 6 is 2. The ratio of these differences is 1:2. The ratio of the outer numbers (the extremes), 3 and 6, is also 1:2. Thus, it is a "Harmonic Mean" by the old definition.</note>. Whatever three numbers are of this kind—whether they are truly musical or not—it is always true that the **ratios of equals** (or rather, the arithmetic) and the **ratios of likes** (the geometric) are blended in one certain way.

The method is this: Given the extremes, such as 2 and 5, the arithmetic mean is provided. So that it does not involve a fraction <note>The arithmetic mean of 2 and 5 is 3.5</note>, let the doubles of the extremes be taken: 4 and 10. Their arithmetic mean is 7. Now, in such an arithmetic mediation—4, 7, 10—with equal differences of 3 and 3, two proportions are always established: one larger, between the smaller terms 4 and 7; the other smaller, between the larger terms 7 and 10.

<margin>
7 to 10
———
4 to 7
</margin>

Whoever now wishes to create a **Harmonic Mean** from this arithmetic mediation, and mix into it something of a **Geometric Mean**, should place the smaller ratio in the first position and the larger ratio in the second position. Then, seek a number that stands in the same relation to 10 as 4 does to 7. The three numbers would thus be 7, 10, and 17 and 1/7. Expressed in the smallest whole numbers <note>original: "integris inter se primis"</note>, these are 14, 20, and 35. In this triad <note>original: "trigæ"</note>, something of an arithmetic progression is mixed in, though its explicit equality does not remain. For both ratios of the arithmetic mediation between 4, 7, and 10 have been brought here, merely with their positions swapped: just as the earlier terms were there (4 to 7), so here the later terms are (20 to 35). And just as the later terms were there (7 to 10), so here the earlier terms are (14 to 20). 

Turn by turn, something of a **Geometric Mean** is also mixed in. For the smaller ratio, 7 to 10, is placed with the smaller terms 14 and 20; the larger ratio, 4 to 7, with the larger terms 20 and 35. Finally, it results that just as the smallest term (14) is to the largest term (35), so is the smaller difference (6) to the larger difference (15) <note>14/35 = 2/5 and 6/15 = 2/5. This satisfies the "Harmonic" definition.</note>. All these things, however, smack of a likeness familiar to geometric proportion; because in that, as the smallest term is to the middle, so the middle is to the largest.

These things must be understood from mathematics. **Bodin** <note>Jean Bodin (1530–1596), author of *The Six Books of the Republic*</note> does not seem to have perceived them sufficiently when he proposes a **Harmonic proportion** in five numbers: 3, 4, 6, 8, and 12. He affirms of them that *equal and similar spaces exist there in a somewhat tempered way.* For when he saw the differences were 1, 2, 2, and 4, he recognized an explicit "equality" in 2 and 2, and a "likeness" <note>a geometric ratio</note> in 1, 2, and 4. But in the definition of the ancients, three numbers are sufficient; moreover, that definition contains no "tempering" of explicit equality with likeness. For in 3, 4, and 6, there is no explicit equality of the differences.

Now it is worth the effort to see how Bodin, who is most verbose on this subject, applies these things to Morality and Politics in various ways. It frequently happens to him that, instead of the harmonic mediations of both the ancients and the true ones, he seizes upon mere combinations of arithmetic and geometric proportions, relying on his own faulty definition. Just as this had to be stated at the beginning, it will have to be repeated more often in what follows.

**I.** Since there are three forms of government <note>original: "Politiarum formæ"</note>: **Popular** <note>Democratic</note>, **Aristocratic** <note>original: "Optimatum" — government by the "best" or nobility</note>, and **Royal**;

# ON THE HARMONICS. BOOK III.

<margin>POLITICAL MATTERS.</margin>
...He [Bodin] <note>Jean Bodin (1530–1596), a French jurist and political philosopher whom Kepler is critiquing</note> compares the popular state <note>a democracy or republic</note> to **Arithmetic proportion**, the Aristocratic to **Geometric**, and the Royal to **Harmonic**. For just as in Arithmetic, the increments of all numbers are equal, whether they are large or small, so in a Republic, the people want the burdens, benefits, honors, and magistracies of all to be equal. They do not want to tolerate any respect of persons; for example, they want the right of hunting to belong to everyone, whether they are nobles or commoners, rich or poor. But if there is something that cannot be divided among many, the people want it to be decided by lot; for chance is blind, and does not distinguish a noble from a commoner, a rich man from a poor man, a well-deserving man from an unworthy one, one dedicated to virtue from one who is vicious, or a genius from a fool. For then, finally, a man thinks himself equal to the rest if he draws lots with them over such matters, whether he obtains them by good or bad luck. In place of a lot, there can also be other means of acquisition; for instance, if the choice is permitted to someone who has no personal interest, or who is believed not to show favoritism. Thus at Rome, the Consulship was common to everyone of a certain order; and it was permitted to seek it from the people, but not through bribes, lest the people be corrupted and the wealthy preferred over the poor. Although in this case, by a silent consensus, virtue is respected, and the judgment concerning it and those who have served well is left to the people.

On the contrary, just as in Geometry the differences <note>original: "excessus" — refers to the mathematical difference between values</note> of the numbers are proportional to the numbers themselves, so that a large number has a large difference and a small one a small difference: so in an Aristocratic Republic <note>original: "Optimatum Rep." — a state ruled by the 'best' or the nobility</note> persons are distinguished, as are the burdens, rewards, Magistracies, and duties; and the most excellent things are reserved for the Nobles, while the rest are left to the people. Here it is necessary that, separately within the individual factions, an arithmetic proportion is also admitted: for regarding those things which belong to the people, all who are among the people will draw lots; and regarding those things which belong to the Nobles, all the Nobles will draw lots. For unless this is done, there will be constant levels of "nobility" even among the common people, right down to the lowest dregs; and constant levels also among the Nobles, up to the Prince of the State; by which reasoning it would not be a Republic, but a Royal type of city-state.

<margin><unclear>Distributive</unclear> <unclear>Justice</unclear></margin>
The Royal state, however, although it most closely resembles Geometric proportion—because all the rights of Majesty are reserved for the King, just as he himself excels all others by noble lineage, by arms, or by virtues—nevertheless, the method of governing in this state can most rightly be tempered by both types of proportion. For one King, the arbiter of all, distributes everything between the Nobles and the people, not by a blind impulse like chance, but by considering virtue, merits, order, and rank. He carries out all the parts of **distributive** and **commutative justice** <note>Distributive justice deals with how a society shares its goods/honors; commutative justice deals with fair exchange and contracts</note>; this union of both proportions is sufficient for Bodin to establish a **Harmonic proportion**. Yet, according to all his advice, the King refers not so much to individuals or specific Orders of men, as to the whole body of the City, its safety, and its mutual charity and concord. This is no different than if, in numbers, proportions were deflected somewhat from equality and similarity—so that they are destroyed if necessary—and referred back to the common harmony of all: which is how he will use my Harmonic means.

II. From the *Cyropaedia* <note>Xenophon's famous biography "The Education of Cyrus"</note>, Bodin proposes an example by which all three types of proportion can be explained. When Cyrus was a boy, and a man...

# ON PROPORTIONS

<margin>
**DIGRESSION.**

**The judgment of the boy Cyrus.**
</margin>
...when [Cyrus] <note>The story of the young Cyrus the Great, from Xenophon’s *Cyropaedia*, was a standard educational anecdote about justice.</note> had seen a tall boy wearing a short tunic, and next to him a short boy in a loose, long tunic, he judged that they should exchange tunics so that each would have what was suitable for him. His teacher, however, declared that each should be left with his own property. Now, if the tall boy had been ordered to pay some money to the short boy, and only then the exchange were made, the teacher would have been perfectly reconciled with the pupil. In this case, Cyrus urged **Geometric proportion**, measuring the garments to the bodies; the teacher urged **Arithmetic proportion**, protecting what each already possessed. But a third person would have looked at both simultaneously: both the physical need and the preservation of each person's goods. Thus, he would have asserted **Harmonic proportion** in Bodin's sense, as it is mixed from both of the former. Indeed, it is also Harmonic in my own sense; for such a judge would not hesitate to take the surplus cloth from one and money from the other so that both are provided for, because the common benefit of both is comparable to the sweetness of a musical harmony. However, I have said that it happens that sometimes a Geometric proportion is also Harmonic, such as 1, 2, 4 <note>In music, these ratios represent octaves, which are the most harmonious intervals.</note>, just as here it is suitable for a tall man to have a long garment; but sometimes an Arithmetic proportion is also Harmonic, such as 2, 3, 4 <note>This represents a perfect fifth and a perfect fourth, the building blocks of harmony.</note>, just as here it is suitable for the short owner of a long garment to keep his property, but changed into money, which he can use more rightly than a surplus of cloth.

<margin>
**Types of Justice.**
</margin>
III. Since justice encompasses all methods of governing, [Bodin] cites two parts of it from Aristotle: **commutative justice**, which deals with Arithmetic equality, and **distributive justice**, which deals with Geometric similarity. He himself argues for a third type of justice, forged from both of the former, which desires that an abundance of goods be sold to certain people at a lower price than to others, and that great things should not always be distributed to the great. Thus, both types of "the just" are violated to some extent if the safety of all requires it, or if a public benefit emerges from it. A proportion is not well-forged from two other types if it destroys both; therefore, this application is better suited to my **Harmonic means**. Just as in the numbers 2, 3, 5, there is neither an Arithmetic equality of differences, nor a Geometric progression, yet there is a Harmonic relationship between them <note>Kepler defines the Harmonic mean here as a specific mathematical relationship where the differences between terms are proportional to the terms themselves.</note>.

Toward the end of the book, he adapts the Poets, who imagine three daughters of Themis <note>Themis was the Greek titaness of divine law and order.</note> (who is Justice): *Eunomia*, *Epieikeia*, and *Eirene* <note>original: "Εὐνομίαν, ἐπιείκειαν, εἰρήνην"</note>—Good Law, Equity, and Peace—as if they were the guardians of the three proportions: Arithmetic, Geometric, and Harmonic.

<margin>
**Marriage laws.**
</margin>
IV. Marriage laws, the primary bond of a state, provide a brilliant example of the three proportions. If Patricians <note>the noble or upper class</note> are ordered to marry Patrician women, and commoners to marry commoners, this is a **Geometric similarity** <note>matching like with like</note>. But if the law allows everyone to seek marriage indiscriminately, whether by lot or by competing as much as possible in beauty, wealth, virtue, or lineage without regard for status, and no condition is forbidden, this will be **Arithmetic equality**. However, in the first case, the minds of the citizens are torn into factions, and in the second, the social orders are thrown into confusion; both are ruinous to the Republic. Therefore, Bodin suggests that impoverished Patricians should sometimes be permitted to marry wealthy commoners, and rich commoners to marry poor Patrician women. For this is beneficial to both orders: to the nobles, so that, increased in wealth, they may protect the rank they hold and the women of this order may be married; and to the common people, so that with the path to honors opened, they might give [effort] to virtue...

### Book III of the Harmonics

<margin>POLITICS</margin>
...they should devote their efforts, finally, to the Republic itself, so that the different social Classes may embrace one another with mutual charity.

Once again, here he has destroyed the <term>Geometric Proportion</term> <note>original: "Geometricam Analogiam"; a proportion where the ratio between terms is constant, like 1, 2, 4</note> in order to produce a <term>Harmonic</term> one; yet he did not reduce it to the mere equality of an <term>Arithmetic progression</term> <note>original: "Arithmeticae progressionis"; where the difference between terms is constant, like 1, 2, 3</note>. For example, if the Geometric series 1, 3, 9 is destroyed and becomes 1, 3, 8: as much as the 8 has receded from the 9, so much has been taken away from the patricians <note>The "patricians" are the upper class; in this mathematical metaphor, they represent the larger number or greater share</note>. And insofar as the differences in 1, 3, 8 are 2 and 5 (whereas previously they were 2 and 6), we have moved closer to the arithmetic progression 1, 3, 5 (where the differences are equal at 2 and 2). That gain is what was given to the common people. Thus, in numbers, a <term>Concordance</term> <note>A musical agreement of sounds</note> is established among 1, 3, 8; but in the Republic, <term>concord</term> <note>social harmony</note> is established between the Patricians and the commoners, while the distinction between the classes remains. This change of 1, 9 into 1, 8 will also be found in Book V, occurring even in the heavens themselves.

<margin>The Law of Banquets.</margin>
V. <term>Arithmetic equality</term> is foolish in <term>Symposia</term> <note>A Greek-style drinking party or banquet</note> if everyone reclines together indiscriminately, without regard for sex, status, age, or character. Conversely, a mere <term>Geometric</term> similarity is dull. For if the learned are joined only to the learned, how will they benefit the unlearned? If women are only with women, where is the pleasure? If the loud are with the loud, who will teach them modesty? But if you admit neither a blind equality nor a stubborn similarity, but mix both—yet moderately and with the judgment of reason—the proportion will be <term>harmonic</term>. For you will ensure that the old enjoy the sight of the young, and men the sight of women; that the young are guided by the wisdom of the old, and women by the authority of men; that the witty rouse the gloomy, and in turn respect them, without dissolving into buffoonery. Again, this is not a simple composition of whole types, but a certain breaking of the rules so that a <term>Harmonic</term> state may exist.

<margin>Seating at the Games.</margin>
VI. It pertains to arithmetic equality that in ancient times the Fathers <note>The Senators or Patricians</note> used to watch the games in a crowd mixed with the commoners. It pertains to geometric proportion that later the Fathers were separated from the commoners. This is true if you consider the games alone. But if you hold all the benefits of the Republic in one mental embrace: since most of these benefits were claimed for the Fathers by geometric reason (with the people excluded), this very equalization of both orders at the games pertained to that tempering which <term>Bodin</term> <note>Jean Bodin (1530–1596), a French jurist and political philosopher whose "Harmonic Justice" influenced Kepler</note> calls the "harmonic" form of the whole government. By this means, the commoners were soothed—as children usually are by trivial things—and were invited to love the higher Classes, yet nothing was taken away from the dignity of those classes. This also fits my <term>Means</term> <note>original: "Medietates"; mathematical middle points between extremes</note>, insofar as a strict proportion is not maintained, so that concord may be maintained. Previously, in the case of specific persons in the Classes, the Proportion was set aside; now it is set aside in the case of specific rewards.

<margin>Friendship.</margin>
VII. Harmonic tempering animates friendships. For what <term>Concordance</term> is in proportion, <term>Love</term> is in the whole span of human life, and Love is the foundation of Friendship. But if a mere equality of duties is introduced by arithmetic law, there will be no friendship except between equals. And if there is a mere and exquisite Geometric similarity of duties between unequals, there will be friendship in neither case. Instead, in the first case, there would be a perpetual business transaction and a "haggling" <note>original: "nundinatio"; literally a market-fair trade</note> of duties for the sake of one's own profit; in the second, a necessary association of Patron and Client, with no freedom to demonstrate Love and nothing spontaneous. Although friendship cannot stand alongside frequent injuries, it nevertheless rejects strict laws and refers everything to the sober and sound judgment of Love, now equalizing...

He uses mathematical ratios to illustrate how giving small concessions to the lower classes creates social concord, mirroring musical harmonies.</summary>

## ON PROPORTIONS

<margin>Digression.</margin>
...repaying such proportional things now, where neither [extreme] exists, but always such things that seem to serve the preservation of Love according to the occasion. For Love—just as Harmony is stirred by dissonances, or as iron is carved by a stylus—is provoked by certain injuries, and renews its strength through their free forgiveness.

<margin>The Lesbian Rule.</margin>
VIII. <term>Bodin</term> <note>Jean Bodin (1530–1596), a French jurist and political philosopher whose work *The Six Books of the Republic* Kepler is citing</note> beautifully compares <term>Arithmetic Equality</term> <note>A system where the difference between units is constant, e.g., 1, 2, 3</note> to the iron rule of <term>Polycletus</term> <note>A famous Greek sculptor; his "rule" refers to a rigid, unbending standard of measurement</note>, which would sooner break than bend. He compares <term>Geometric similarity</term> <note>A system based on ratios, e.g., 1, 2, 4, which Bodin links to social status</note> to the leaden <term>Lesbian Rule</term> <note>A flexible mason's rule used on the island of Lesbos that could be bent to fit the curves of a molding; a classic metaphor for flexible justice</note>, which was adapted to all angles. He himself describes <term>Harmonic proportion</term>, by his own definition, with the image of a wooden rule, which indeed bends, but immediately springs back to its shape.

<margin>Laws and Equity.</margin>
IX. In the governance of all types of <term>States</term> <note>original: "Politiarum"</note>, the rigor of the laws and the duty of the Judge are compared to Arithmetic equality, by which not only is each person given exactly what is theirs, but punishments are also imposed on offenders equally, without respect for persons. By this, Judges are bound to the laws and to the evidence and testimonies presented, so that they may judge according to them, even if the laws seem unfair. Conversely, <term>Equity</term> and the pure discretion of a Magistrate—provided he is good and acts from conscience—takes on the nature of <term>Geometric Analogy</term>. But Bodin, using the example of <term>Harmonic</term> tempering, places in the middle the duty of either the superior Courts, or of all courts, or of the supreme Magistrate. To these, it is not permitted to act by pure whim; yet it is permitted that they bend the laws (not break them) according to the reason of the circumstances, and interpret them in judgments according to equity, so long as the law is not undermined by the individual rulings of the courts. He wants the laws to be held like his wooden Rule: they should yield to the curve, but return immediately. 

However, in this passage, Bodin has demonstrated by his own example the truth of what he had previously affirmed regarding legal experts: that they understand these mathematical matters less because of their obscurity. For his discussion of Numbers does not fit the standard of our discipline when he says it is impossible for a <term>Geometric Proportion</term> (which exists between four terms) to be destroyed by any transposition of terms; and he asserts the same analogy exists in 6, 3, 4, 2 as in 3, 2, 4, 6. Not at all! For 3 is to 2 as 4 is to 6 <note>Kepler is correcting a mathematical error: 3/2 = 1.5, while 4/6 = 0.66; they are not the same ratio, thus the proportion is destroyed by the move</note>. Conversely, he thinks Harmonic Proportion is disturbed by transposition. To be sure, if he recognizes no proportion between only two terms, he wins his point.

<margin>What proportion means to me.</margin>
This is the subtlety of speech used by some, combined with the greatest obscurity: that what the Greeks call *logos* <note>original: λόγον; reason or ratio</note>, they wish to call *Ratio* in Latin; but what the Greeks call *analogia* <note>original: Αναλογίαν; proportion or comparison</note>, they call *Proportion*. I would indeed wish to be able to imitate that distinction, as I remember doing before this; but among the Greeks, *logos* is never used in common speech for the word *aition* <note>original: αἴτιον; cause or reason</note>, whereas in Latin, *Ratio* very frequently sounds like "cause" or "method." It is therefore necessary to keep to the custom introduced by the <term>Barbaric</term> <note>Medieval or non-Classical</note> translators of Greek elements, and use the word "proportion" for both *logos* and *analogia*; which I do frequently throughout this book.

Now, therefore, <term>Proportion</term> and <term>Concordance</term> have been distinguished: the latter is, as it were, a certain quality of the former, and the former is the subject of the latter. Indeed, Concordance is present in Proportions primarily and by itself, insofar as they are between two terms; not insofar as there is a certain continuity between several terms...

## HARMONICS BOOK III
->93<-

<margin>POLITICS.</margin>
...of proportion. And two terms of a proportion are consonant not because of their position—in which one is first and the other second—but insofar as two strings are struck simultaneously at the same time. Nor is this concord changed if the position of the characters in the musical notation is moved, or if the <term>Lute</term> <note>original: "Testudine", literally a tortoise shell, referring to the stringed instrument</note> is turned upside down. Regarding the proportion that exists between three or more terms, concord happens secondarily because of the specific pairs of terms. In these, even if the <term>Analogy</term> <note>The mathematical relationship or ratio between the parts</note> can be changed by moving their positions—that is, the part of them that is an admixture of <term>Geometric proportion</term>—the **Harmonic quality** cannot be changed at the same time.

Therefore, as for what **Bodin** <note>Jean Bodin (1530–1596), whose political theories Kepler is scrutinizing</note> argues—that those four things, **Law**, **Legal Action**, **Equity**, and the **Magistrate**, are compared to four numbers joined by a Harmonic proportion; and that just as the harmony perishes when the numbers are transposed, so too if legal proceedings and execution are held as more important than the Laws, or if the Magistrate is placed before Equity, the harmony of the state is disturbed—that argument is to be referred in no way to what is truly **Harmonic** in proportions. Rather, it refers simply to the nature of the proportions themselves, whether **Geometric** or **Arithmetic**. That is, it belongs to that genus of proportion which is tempered from both, and which the **Ancients**, based on some weak conviction, called "Harmonic." For it is common to all Analogies, whether simple or mixed (contrary to what Bodin teaches), that they are either changed into other types when the terms are transposed, or are completely destroyed. But I return to the matter at hand.

<margin>The necessity of laws.</margin>
If a **Magistrate** has pure discretion to govern without laws, and observes neither the law of Nature nor performs the duty of a good and innocent man, he will not be a magistrate, but a **Tyrant**. And since the number of good Princes is exceedingly small, it is not advisable for a Republic to commit itself to this danger every time a magistrate is replaced. Even if it should happen that a state receives a good magistrate at some point, such a status cannot be lasting. Nor is it healthy for the Republic; for even if a Governor is good, he will not always be prudent enough to see what is equitable without the standard of laws. And even if he himself sees and follows what is right, the citizens will still find fault with even the best actions, unless there are laws by which he can defend his deeds to the people. Citizens must be educated by the discipline of laws and deterred from wrongdoing by the specter of punishments prescribed by those laws. Therefore, a Republic cannot do without laws.

<margin>And of Equity.</margin>
In turn, laws—referred to by the Greek word <term>Nomoi</term> <note>original: "Νόμοι"</note>—signify the distributive part of justice, which in a popular state <note>A democracy or republic</note> follows **arithmetic equality**. But if everything is examined according to the strictness of the laws, injury will be done to many. For laws decide on deeds without defining them by any variety of circumstances; yet individual deeds are described by their own circumstances, by which they are either mitigated or aggravated. Since there is such a variety of these circumstances, they can never be encompassed by any laws. Therefore, neither principle by itself preserves a Republic; rather, Bodin teaches that they must be mixed, so that there are laws, but few of them (since a multitude of laws is a most fertile harvest for lawsuits), and many things should be reserved for the **Magistrate's discretion**—not only individual deeds, but also some entire types of deeds and certain other matters of law, especially

# ON PROPORTIONS
->94<-

<margin>DIGRESSION.</margin>
...the intensification and lessening of punishments, the interpretation of the laws themselves, and their application to the circumstances of the deed. Here we are not dealing with a threefold form of the State <note>Latin: *Respublica*</note>, but with the threefold form of governing any one state. A mere principle of equity, unbound by laws, is an **aristocratic** method of governing, even in a Popular or Royal state. The chains of laws create **popular** government, even in a Monarchy. But if there are indeed laws, yet they are set aside in certain times and places at the discretion of the governor appointed by the supreme power; that governor, although appointed by the people, acts as a sort of Petty King <note>Latin: *Regulum*</note>. Such are usually the Governors of Provinces. He, therefore, either observes the laws or judges based on equity, so long as the safety of the State allows; if otherwise, he does not hesitate to deviate. It is as if someone should accept the types of proportions that create harmony, such as 2:3:4 or 1:2:4, but should disturb those that create dissonance, changing them into consonances—for example, changing 1:3:9 <note>a dissonant geometric progression</note> into 1:3:4 <note>a consonant harmonic progression</note> or 3:5:7 into 3:5:8.

<margin>Fines.</margin>
**X. In the laws themselves concerning monetary fines, for the most part, arithmetic equality is maintained, so that whoever commits a crime pays the fine established by law, whether rich or poor. Yet one can see where there is also a Geometric similarity, as when a fine is imposed on someone in proportion to their wealth <note>Latin: *census*</note>, or if a reckless litigant loses a specific portion of the estimated value of the lawsuit. But if, among all the wealthy, a larger fine is named, and among the poor a lighter one, and that fine is exacted equally from each individual of each class; that will be a tempering of the proportion which Bodin calls Harmonic. Here the types of proportions are not changed, but are composed—or rather distributed—into distinct subjects belonging to the same whole.**

<margin>Sumptuary laws.</margin>
**XI. Laws regarding clothing <note>Sumptuary laws, which regulated luxury and consumption to maintain social hierarchy</note> have a great deal of Geometric proportion; for the higher the rank of dignity someone holds, the more precious the decoration of their garments is permitted to them. Arithmetic equality is intolerable here. However, because the variety of ranks alone does not demand a distinction in dress, but some consideration must be had here for wealth, and some for merit; and because all Ranks cannot easily be declared under one law: some tempering of both proportions is usually inserted into the laws themselves, or is partly left to the discretion of the Moderators. Bodin considers this tempering to be "harmonic" because he defines Harmonies by the joining of two types of proportion. To me, it is not truly harmonic when one proportion is merely sought after and would be expressed perfectly if it only could be.**

<margin>Punishments.</margin>
**XII. Nearly the same should be said about those laws which, since they concern punishments, exempt illustrious persons from the danger of execution and Nobles from hanging, changing the type of punishment according to a custom received by most nations. For a defendant losing the dignity he held is punished more severely by this disgrace (observing Geometric law) than if someone who held no dignity were publicly beaten with rods. And so there can be a certain equality of dissimilar punishments, and a Harmonic distribution in the sense used by Bodin. Here Bodin rejects Aristotle, who had taught that Geometric proportion should be maintained in rewards, but Arithmetic equality in punishments.**

<margin>Restitution.</margin>
**XIII. There is also another observable proportion in penal laws with the same tempering; it does not concern the offender, but the honor and vengeance of the person harmed. For he who [harms] the Prince of the State is punished more severely...**

# BOOK III ON HARMONICS

<margin>POLITICAL MATTERS.</margin>
...[it is considered a more serious crime] for one who kills a member of the College of Electors <note>The high-ranking princes who elected the Holy Roman Emperor</note> than one who kills a farmer; more serious for one who kills a free man than a slave. For although this variety is to be referred to a **Geometric similarity** between the person and the retribution for the injury inflicted upon them, such a distinction is nonetheless rare. On the other hand, in the punishments for homicide, there is for the most part an **Arithmetic equality**, especially among Christians, based on divine law, by which man is equated to man and blood is repaid with blood. This blending of both types of ratios, therefore, pertains to what Bodin calls the **Harmonic**. Primarily, this is seen in the fact that in divine law all assassins are punished with death by arithmetic equality, yet the *type* of death is in the power of the judge, to be imposed by a **Geometric response**, according to the facts and the variety of dissimilar circumstances; as Bodin reports, I believe, from the writings of the Rabbis.

Nor is this inequality of punishments attributed so much to the individual persons harmed as it is to the safety of the whole state <note>Latin: *saluti totius reipublice*</note>, which allows all enemies of the fatherland to be killed with impunity, and protects the safety of all citizens collectively through the safety of the Prince and the Nobles, and through the preservation of public tranquility. It has been said quite often that the **Public Good** has a certain correspondence to the sweetness of a Harmonic concord. If this one supreme law, the mother of all laws, is observed—so that whatever is commanded as holy and lawful is that in which the safety of the State turns <note>A reference to the legal maxim *Salus populi suprema lex esto*: "The health of the people shall be the supreme law"</note>—then its similarity to Harmonic ratios is immediately clear, even according to my own described opinions, even if that law otherwise contains nothing similar to either Geometric or Arithmetic proportions. For neither do these numbers **15, 20, 24, 30**, which contain the sweetest Harmony <note>This sequence of numbers represents a major chord (C-E-G-C). The ratios are 3:4, 5:6, and 4:5</note>, observe one proportion or the other: for the differences between them are **5, 4, 6**, which are neither equal (as in arithmetic) nor similar in proportion (as in geometric) to the ratios of the terms themselves, nor do they increase in the same order as the terms.

<margin>The assessment of a fine.</margin>
XIV. Bodin brings forward another example, more familiar to the Geometric discipline, in the interpretation of laws concerning fines; specifically, that monetary fines established in antiquity should be assessed according to the ratio of present public wealth or poverty. In this case, a strict **Arithmetic equality** for all times would be intolerable; yet a strict **Geometric proportion** is not easy to observe in every instance. Therefore, according to his own prudence and the circumstances of the matters, a judge will seek a **harmonic mean**. He will take care lest he should seem to have violated the laws, or that by a malicious interpretation of the laws the poor are oppressed while the wealthy and more powerful are given license to sin. Indeed, out of a desire for this same harmony, he will sometimes exchange a monetary fine, which might be treated with contempt by the rich, for a physical punishment.

<margin>The punishment for theft.</margin>
XV. Bodin approves of the law that punishes thieves by hanging insofar as it relies on the reasoning that "thieves should not increase," so that crimes likely to be frequent are punished more severely; this smacks of **Geometric proportion**. However, he criticizes the same law on account of its **Arithmetic equality**. For indeed, the legal action for theft is very frequent throughout all towns and villages, and it mostly involves common judges. While they drag everyone equally to execution, they do not understand that they are introducing a most unjust inequality of punishments, for they impose the same penalty on crimes that are most unequal due to the variety of circumstances. Most defendants lack the steadiness of judgment by which they ought to guard themselves more against misfortune than against the magnitude of the crime: those whom opportunity, hunger...

# ON PROPORTIONS

<margin>DIGRESSION.</margin>
Want, the zeal for one’s children, the confidence of staying hidden, or the perception of another's wealth makes thieves; yet the crime itself, when compared to others, is held in low esteem by natural judgment. This even seems to be confirmed by divine law, which punishes theft with only fourfold restitution <note>A reference to Exodus 22:1, where a thief pays back four or five times the value of what was stolen, rather than facing death</note>. If, however, it is considered equitable and holy that that portion of humanity—born for trickery and darkness, reflecting the nature of mice, digging through walls—disturbs the public security not only of fortunes but of life itself, then they should be reduced for the sake of the Commonwealth rather like other rapacious beasts. Certainly, the respect for the Commonwealth, as often stated, corresponds to a **harmonic concord**. Yet this question must not be weighed without the most accurate **harmonic** tempering; lest, while the Commonwealth is being consulted, life be rashly snatched away for this kind of crime from many who might otherwise offer hope of being good citizens in the future.

<margin>Punishment of the excused.</margin>
XVI. Even this pertains to **Geometric** equity in the imposition of punishments: that the punishment for a child is lighter than for an adult, for a youth lighter than for an old man, and for a woman lighter than for a man. In these cases, nothing is more inequitable than a perpetual **arithmetic** equality. If such discretion were taken away from the prudent judgment of the judge to be used as the situation requires, the **Harmonic** proportion would nevertheless be disturbed.

<margin>Repeat offenders.</margin>
XVII. **Bodin** <note>Jean Bodin (1530–1596), a French jurist and political philosopher whose work *The Six Books of the Republic* Kepler is critiquing here</note> demonstrates the **Harmonic** proportion in those laws which punish the first act of a crime equally in all people with a light fine, as a kind of warning, but later punish repeat offenders more severely, those sinning a third time more severely still, and finally punish with death. For there is a mixed **arithmetic** equality in the first act, joined to a **Geometric** proportion in the repeated offense, so that a heavier punishment meets a heavier crime. To **Bodin**, this composition of two proportions into one seemed to constitute a **harmonic** proportion.

<margin>Retaliation.</margin>
XVIII. In general, because punishments are dispensed—whether by laws or by the judge's discretion—according to the diversity and magnitude of crimes, the entire law of Retaliation <note>Latin: *jus Talionis*, the principle of "an eye for an eye"</note> must be attributed to **Geometric** analogy. Some legislators punish unequal types of sins equally; this **arithmetic** ratio has no place among men. In God, whose creatures we all are equally, it is not lawful for us to rebuke Him with our complaints. But because legislators, for the sake of the Commonwealth, equalize certain crimes (which are lighter in themselves) with the gravest ones by the imposition of punishments, and because in the law of retaliation it is not "a tooth for a tooth" <note>original: *dens pro dente*</note> but rather an estimated price is repaid in place of the tooth (which can be agreed upon between the litigants); and because absolute blindness is not inflicted upon a man who tore out one of my two eyes when he himself only had one eye to begin with—that is a result of **Bodin's Harmonic** tempering. For in this way, individual sins have **arithmetically** equal punishments, yet different sins are distinguished by different punishments.

<margin>Of intent.</margin>
XIX. Those who punish the attempts of the mind <note>The intent or "mens rea" behind a crime</note> with a punishment no lighter than if the result had followed the will, and those who punish a deed from which the mind was absent, establish a common **arithmetic** equality with no small fault—in the first case among dissimilar mental attempts, and in the second among dissimilar deeds. A judge who distinguishes here between the various forms of attempts acts rightly: so that he who did everything that a mind could meditate to bring about an outcome receives the punishment for the crime, whether he actually perpetrated it or missed the mark; yet he who merely lay in wait for opportunities does not receive it; for regarding the matter <note>Latin: *ad rem*</note>, the wicked image of which...

### ON THE HARMONICS. BOOK III.

However, the act itself, the criminal image of which could have served as a deterrent, did not occur: <margin>POLITICS</margin> here observes **geometric equity**. Politics does not punish someone who merely persuades another to commit a crime less than the perpetrator himself; and conversely, it punishes the author and instigator more severely than the servant, as one who has brought about another’s crime. Finally, it punishes more lightly the one who was swept away by a great force of lust or anger than the one who, being calmer than those, performed everything with a premeditated mind. The same must be held regarding the variety of outcomes. He who robs a traveler of three obols <note>original: "triobolo"; a small Greek coin, here representing a trivial amount</note> deserves the same punishment if he gaped with a mind for great plunder as he who snatched a talent <note>A very large sum of money</note>. Conversely, he who could have carried off a whole weight of gold but took only a modest amount deserves a smaller punishment than he who snatched a purse in which there were only a few small copper coins <note>original: "pauculi asses"</note>. Indeed, Bodin refers these **Geometric** distinctions to the philosophical estimation of crimes; yet punishments, by which public examples are set, pertain to public tranquility and are exempt from that absolute equality. Thus, it is more frequent for the public to take notice of deeds that strike the eyes of the citizens, while attempts that miss their mark are frequently passed over—being generally inconspicuous—either unpunished or punished more lightly than **geometric** fairness would dictate, so that less cruelty is found on the part of the judge. So many respects for the public good savor of something **Harmonic**.

<margin>The Law of voting.</margin>
X. In judgment and in consultations, **Arithmetic** is the ratio of votes if they are numbered; **Geometric** if they are weighed, whether by the importance of the one casting it or by the quality of the arguments. There was a **harmonic** mixture (in Bodin's sense) among the Romans, whose Consulars explained their opinion in a speech, while the others "went with their feet" <note>original: "pedibus in eam ibant sententiam"; a Roman legal phrase meaning to vote by moving to a certain side of the chamber</note> into the opinion they approved of. To me, what was done by the law of necessity (for there would not have been enough time for hearing everyone) does not seem comparable to **Harmonic** proportion.

<margin>Commutative justice</margin>
XI. In **commutative justice** <note>The branch of justice concerning fair exchange and restitution between individuals</note>, Aristotle required **Arithmetic** equality. Bodin says that **Geometric** analogy does not go into exile here either, even if the examples seem confused. 1. For instance, if someone who caused a public scandal also injured a private person: he shall indeed satisfy the private person separately with **arithmetic** equality, and no more shall be restored to that person for his property by a nobleman than by a farmer. Yet that person will pay for the very bad example in one way, and this person in another, the **Geometric** proportion of their social standings being preserved. In this place, Aristotle is reconciled to Bodin.

<margin>Creditors</margin>
2. As for the fact that the goods of a person who is insolvent <note>original: "non est solvendo"; unable to pay</note> are distributed according to the size of each person's credit, without respect for the creditors themselves (provided they were equal in the time and quality of the credit), that is indeed done by a purely **geometric** proportion. Just as Aristotle did not deny this, so it seems to have been omitted by him through lack of thought and rightly supplied by Bodin. Although this is founded on the **arithmetic** equality of the paid and the credited, if the assets were sufficient. Yet a superior magistrate is not entirely forbidden from using **harmonic** tempering and preferring poor creditors to some extent and according to the circumstances over the wealthy ones.

<margin>Restitution for theft.</margin>
3. That also savors of something **harmonic** (in Bodin's sense): that by the custom of certain nations, things taken by theft are not compensated by the simple amount, but by fourfold, and other things by fivefold. This is done equally by all, yet unequally for different things, in which the different magnitude of the injury is estimated by a **geometric** reasoning, not merely the raw price of the object.

# ON PROPORTIONS

## ON PROPORTIONS

<margin>Digression. Damages.</margin>
4. Harmonic reasoning is even more evident in the compensation for damages that were not caused by malicious intent <term>dolo malo</term> <note>original: "dolo malo"; a legal term for "evil intent" or fraud</note>. In these cases, much depends on the circumstances of the actions of both parties involved in the contract. Sometimes, whether by law or by the command of a Magistrate, these circumstances require an equal and **arithmetic** compensation; at other times, they require none at all; and in certain instances, they require a moderate compensation based on **fairness and equity** <term>ex æquo et bono</term> <note>original: "ex æquo et bono"; a legal principle of deciding a case based on what is fair rather than strict law</note>.

<margin>Arbitrators</margin>
Of this same kind, it seems, is the fact that a higher magistrate does not allow everyone to litigate against each other with equal rights in every case. Instead, according to the circumstances, he either appoints arbitrators himself or allows the litigants to choose them, so that either the interests of both parties or the interests of the Republic are served.

<margin>Interest.</margin>
5. Even **usury** <note>interest charged on loans</note> pertains to the commutative part of justice. However, legislators do not permit equal rates of interest to all classes of men. Instead, through a **geometric mixture**, they allow unequal rates for persons of different ranks, but equal rates for those within the same rank. To Bodin, this composition is **harmonic**.

<margin>Remuneration.</margin>
6. I shall transcribe a remarkable exception to the arithmetic equality of exchange in Bodin’s own words: *A doctor often receives (indeed, demands) 500 gold coins to remove a stone from a rich man, but from a poor man he takes 10 or 5 (indeed, nothing at all, according to the formula of the Hippocratic oath). If they were to follow Arithmetic or Geometric Proportion in every case, one would die of the stone and the other of hunger. But by **harmonic reasoning**, wealth is provided for the doctor and health for the patient (though not, to be sure, with the same certainty).*

<margin>The judge’s fee.</margin>
7. According to this same reasoning, judges have also been accustomed to demand their labor and an **honorarium** <note>a fee for professional services</note> in deciding cases. For the difficulty of very trivial disputes is often greater than if the inquiry were about the gravest matters, yet they remain unprofitable for the judges. It is therefore fair that a bit more of a fee be demanded from the adjudicated claims of very wealthy estates—specifically in cases where the judges do not receive a sufficient salary from the Republic, but are ordered to seek compensation for their labor from the taxes of the litigating parties as a strategy to reduce the number of lawsuits. However, I leave this "Harmonic harmony" to the author, the Frenchman Bodin. Among us Germans, the courts in our principal cities and provinces are kept far away from such sordid practices; nothing is permitted to be demanded beyond what is prescribed by law.

<margin>Division of inheritances.</margin>
8. An equal distribution of inheritances among individuals of both sexes is carried out according to **arithmetic** laws, so that those who are equal in origin are also made equal in the proportions of the substance left by the same father. But when the interests of the Republic are considered, estates devolve to males (who are fit for necessary military service), and money to females and to persons consecrated to God. Furthermore, when the firstborn is preferred over the others either by a larger portion or by possession of the whole estate <note>original: "totius assis"; a reference to the 'as', a Roman unit of currency or weight, used here to mean the entire inheritance</note>, the others are provided for by unequal portions, by a legacy, or by right of use alone. This is done so that a certain image of leadership, useful to the Republic, may be established within families. This is achieved through **harmonic ratios**, which are sometimes quite harsh and dissonant regarding individuals (since arithmetic equality is disturbed), yet they harmonize toward the preservation of the entire state.

<margin>Forms of Government.</margin>
XXII. In a popular government <note>a democracy</note>, which is shaped by **Arithmetic equality**, and in an aristocratic government, which is shaped by **Geometric similarity**, some method of tempering <note>blending or moderating</note> is nevertheless often employed. For instance, when the People themselves...

### HARMONICS BOOK III

<margin>POLITICS</margin>
The ruler of affairs, of his own accord, entrusts honors, magistracies, and priesthoods primarily to the <term>patricians</term> <note>the hereditary aristocratic class of ancient Rome</note>; or, when the <term>Optimates</term> <note>the "best men" or aristocratic faction</note> allow the <term>plebs</term> <note>the common people</note> to share in some honors, they grant the most profitable offices to the commoners alone. They most severely avenge injuries inflicted upon them by the elites, and grant them the freedom to enjoy pleasures—which in itself tastes of a popular state. They permit the common people a certain right of suffrage in nominating a fixed number of candidates from the ranks of the elites, from which number the elites themselves later entrust the magistracies to whomever they wish.

As long as this sharing exists by the free will of that Order which holds supreme power, a most sweet harmony of consensus among the citizens endures. But if it is revoked, first the complaints of the penalized party emerge, then discords follow—as if the harmony has been disturbed—and finally, either the power is transferred, or the entire city falls to enemies. The same must be held regarding the Royal state, to which the <term>harmonic proportion</term> <note>original: "harmonica ratio"; a balance between strict equality and proportional merit</note> is familiar. In this state, just as one individual stands above all others, so too does he alone possess the supreme right of command; the rest live under him in <term>arithmetic equality</term> <note>original: "arithmetica aequalitate"; where everyone is treated as a simple equal without regard to rank</note>.

Therefore, in this form of Politics, there can be a method of governing of three kinds, which we touched upon above in Note IX; however, there we dealt with things, while here we deal with persons, or the Orders that are the members of the Republic. For if a King shares all duties equally, with no distinction between the nobility and the commoners, the moderation will be popular and similar to the **arithmetic** style—which is not becoming of the highest majesty. Indeed, the highest person would be joined with the lowest dregs with no intermediate order placed between them, which is something Nature, however, loves. Furthermore, citizens of a noble character will depart the kingdom if there is no respect given to their lineage.

On the other hand, if he confers everything upon the nobility, entirely excluding the common people, this will be a **Geometric** form of commanding, but a dangerous one, lacking in **harmonic sweetness**. For the people, empowered by their great numbers, will eventually be offended and strip the Nobility of their magistracies and honors, and the King himself of his command. And even if the Governor distinguishes the Orders into many degrees and distinguishes their duties with great subtlety, if he nevertheless reserves for each order its own duties exclusively—as in Rome, where the Tribunate belonged to the commoners alone and the Consulate only to the patricians—the Orders will become alienated from one another and will not grow together into one body with firm concord. For the duties of the inferiors will be despised along with the order itself; so much so that in Rome, a patrician could not hold the Tribunate unless he renounced his nobility. And when the commoners eventually extorted the consulate, those few commoner Consuls themselves thereafter looked down upon the common people.

<insert>Bodin</insert> <note>Jean Bodin (1530–1596), a French jurist and political philosopher</note> proposes the idea of these disputes in numbers: and first in these: **4, 6, 7**. Here **4** represents the King, and **6** the Nobility, and he advises that there is a harmony between them. But **7** represents the commoners, a number which he correctly asserts is discordant with both of the former. He could have better used these: **4, 6, 9**. For just as **6** makes a harmony with **9**, while **4** makes none with that same **9**, so the Nobility finds association with the commoners easier than the King does. And as **6** is the <term>Geometric mean</term> <note>original: "Geometricum"; here, the middle term in a proportional sequence</note> between **4** and **9**, harmonizing with both: so the Nobility is placed as a bond between the King and the lowest commoners.

But he represents the Aristocratic form of governing a Kingdom with the numbers of a <term>disjunct Geometric proportion</term> <note>original: "proportionis Geometricae disjunctae"</note> **3, 6, 5, 10**. He compares this disjunction to the dissensions in a City resulting from an overly rigid exclusion of the orders.

# ON PROPORTIONS

<margin>Digression.</margin>
...not unsuitably. But this is poorly handled: he treats this disjunction as the culprit for discord. For all these numbers—3, 6, 5, 10—create a common harmony. As has often been said, **Geometric Analogy** <note>original: "Analogia Geometrica"; a sequence of numbers with a constant ratio, like 2, 4, 8</note> has nothing to do with the quality of Harmony, nor does the difference or disjunction of that analogy affect it. And although, as if correcting himself on the same page, he provides another example of numbers in a disjunct proportion intended for the same purpose—namely 2, 4, 9, 18—in which the sounds denoted by 2 and 4 truly clash with the sounds 9 and 18, this musical discord does not arise from that Geometric disjunction. Rather, it arises from its own proper causes: specifically, because the side of a **Nonagon** <note>a nine-sided polygon; Kepler believed certain polygons were "unharmonic" because they cannot be constructed with a compass and straightedge</note> is not among the **Middle Notes** <note>original: "Μέσαι" (Mesai); the central notes in the ancient Greek musical system</note>. Finally, there is the **temperament** <note>a "tuning" or balancing of different elements</note> of both

<margin>The Temperament of Royal Governance.</margin>
forms of governing in a Royal state. For instance: some **plebeians** <note>commoners</note> should be mixed into the duties of the **Nobility**, but only a few, and those who are equal to the burden by their wealth, or commended by virtue or some other quality. Likewise, occasionally one of the poorer Nobles might be placed in charge of a productive commoner's function, casting a certain dignity upon it by the splendor of his lineage, so that the role becomes more respectable to the common people in the future. Or, a **Duumvirate** <note>a magistracy held jointly by two men</note> might be formed of a Noble and a commoner, providing solace to both classes. Courts should be composed of persons from all ranks; in deliberations concerning the public good, the poor should be mixed with the wealthy. It is not that the mere cultivators of virtue and piety should possess everything; rather, some things should be reserved for the brave, some for the ingenious, some for the prudent, and some for those excelling in experience. Each person should receive that for which their talents are suited and where they can offer the most protection. 

This temperament, I say, Bodin expresses with the numbers 4, 6, 8, 12, believing that he is providing an example of what he calls "contained Analogy," or what geometers call **continuous proportion**. Again, he is mistaken: for 4 is not to 6 as 6 is to 8 <note>4:6 is a 2:3 ratio, but 6:8 is a 3:4 ratio</note>. Yet this much is true: among all four numbers 4, 6, 8, 12—or in their simplest form 2, 3, 4, 6—there is a common **concordance**, even though 2 and 3 sound together in one way, 3 and 4 in another, and finally 2 and 4 or 3 and 6 in yet another. Therefore, whatever similarity exists between numbers and the Republic exists only insofar as they are associated through geometric or arithmetic progressions (separated from Music), or a mixture of both. Conversely, if **Harmonic proportions** of numbers shed any light on understanding politics, they do so through their own nature, separate from any consideration of geometric proportions.

<margin>True Harmonics: the idea of the Best Republic.</margin>
And truly, if I had acquired a knowledge of the Republic and were acting as a political theorist in this book, I would use a distinction of things to revise Bodin’s entire passage. I would do this so that **Aristotle’s** decrees would remain unshaken, and Bodin might learn to philosophize better regarding the state from this **Harmonics** of mine, treated separately from Aristotle. I would say that the status of a City and its form of government is one thing, and the administration of justice is another; they differ as a part differs from the whole. This is just as in Mathematics: the Geometric and Arithmetic proportions of numbers are one thing, while musical **consonances** <note>original: "concentus"; sounds that harmonize together</note> expressed by numbers are another. Certainly, those who hold power—whether it be one, a few, or all—establish the judgments. Yet these same people are occupied with the protection of the Republic; they rarely exercise judgments themselves unless they are permitted to use their own discretion, free from laws. Conversely, the higher duties of state are rarely entrusted to Judges; rather, 

<margin>Geometric and Arithmetic proportions do not pertain to the Reason of State, as Harmonics do, but only to judgments.</margin>
prescribed laws are laid down for them, by which they are bound. Therefore, I would relegate Geometric and Arithmetic progressions to legal judgments along with Aristotle, without mixing in the respect for harmonic consonances that happens to coincide with them. For those "temperaments" which Bodin has desired in judgments thus far are ultimately referred by appeals to the supreme moderator of the Republic himself. And then, when that ruler derogates <note>detracts from or modifies</note> the proportions that Aristotle gave to Judgments and justice;

<meta>This page continues Kepler’s critique of Jean Bodin’s "Six Books of the Republic." In the previous section, Kepler examined how geometric ratios relate to social classes; here, he argues that "Harmonic" proportions—which are more flexible and "expressible" than rigid geometric ones—are the best model for a ruler's governance.</meta>

<page-num>101</page-num>
<header>HARMONICS BOOK III.</header>

# HARMONICS BOOK III.

...does not judge now, but performs a higher office, protecting the Republic and its individual members. <margin>Politics</margin> To this Moderator, whether it be a king, the nobles, or the entire people, I would certainly recommend Harmonic proportions—not with any regard for **Geometric Analogy** <note>a sequence of numbers with a constant ratio, such as 1:2:4</note> or **Arithmetic equality** <note>a sequence with a constant difference, such as 1:2:3</note>, but for pure consonance. I would order those subtle analogies to give way to Harmonic consonances, and thus the rigid administration of both types of justice <note>referring to "distributive" justice (geometric) and "commutative" justice (arithmetic)</note> should yield to the supreme commands and the safety of the Republic. Oh God, what a harvest of debates would arise here if someone wanted to go through every detail for comparison! For consider the nature of each thing. Geometric analogy is common to numbers and continuous quantity, so that it later enters into numbers only when the shapes given to quantities allow them to be expressed numerically. Now, it very frequently happens that the terms encompassing a Geometric Analogy are **ineffable** <note>original: "ineffabiles"; irrational numbers that cannot be represented as a simple ratio of whole numbers</note>, and the further we progress, the more they degenerate from expressibility. On the contrary, every Harmonic proportion can be expressed in numbers. What else does this mean when applied to politics, other than that the most just sentences of judges—exactly weighted by the experts of the law according to the rule of equity—ought to be precise; but on the other hand, the moderation of the Republic, released from such strict necessities as the times require, should be adapted by the ruler’s judgment for the safety of all, without much public outcry. 

Here the question would be divided into parts: how the method of Arithmetic progression—which is crude, lacks any noble form, and insists only on the dimensions of matter—might be likened to commerce, trades, and the livelihood of the common people. Geometric similarity (observing only one law and caring nothing for whether the line it considers is the side of a pentagon or a triangle, or whether it is expressible or ineffable) mirrors the simple duty of the judges. But Harmonic ratios, arising from many knowable **regular figures** <note>polygons like the square or triangle that Kepler uses to derive musical intervals</note> and joined together from different kinds into one structure, represent the many distinct duties of an empire, to each of which belongs its own proper law, separate from the others. Here, following **Ptolemy** <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century astronomer whose work on music Kepler is updating</note> (further down in the appendix to Book V), regarding the genera of harmonies and song, <margin>Peace from the Soft genus; War from the Hard genus</margin> the **Soft** <note>original: "Molle"; a musical genus associated with more complex or relaxed intervals</note> would be given to Peace, and the **Hard** <note>original: "Durum"; the diatonic genus, associated with vigor</note> to War; and the disagreements between these musical types would be the same as those between those two types of times in a state. Truly, I leave these things to be handled by others whose way of life is better suited to them; I myself now hasten to the following matters of my own profession. Therefore, I shall first settle the matter of Bodin. For I am reaching the end of his book, and at the same time, the beginning of this third book of mine.

### XXIII. 
For now **Bodin** <note>Jean Bodin (1530–1596), a French political philosopher</note> passes entirely over to music, as it has been described by me separately from Geometric proportions. And, adapting it to politics as I also prefer, <margin>The idea of a Kingdom in Numbers</margin> he disputes nothing more brilliantly in his whole book than the form of a Kingdom expressed by the numbers **1, 2, 3, 4**. These are the first numbers by nature, and Unity is the principle of numbers. Thus, they are compared by a pleasant play of wit to the principle of quantities—the Point—and then to the three types of quantity: **2** to the line, **3** to the surface, and **4** to the body <note>a three-dimensional solid</note>, in almost the same way I recounted from the **Pythagoreans** <note>ancient Greek followers of Pythagoras who believed the universe was built on the first four numbers, called the Tetraktys</note> at the start of this third book. Furthermore, to him, Unity is the King, the representative of the Almighty God in the Republic. **2** is the Sacred order <note>the clergy</note>. **3** is the Military or Knightly order. **4** is the People, and they are fourfold: Farmers, Scholars, Merchants, and Artisans. Here, among these numbers, he recounts the harmonies contained within them in the same way I used above; however, he has a vain reason for fearing to proceed to the **number five** <note>original: "qunarium"</note>, as if the harmony would be disturbed—which is clearly false from this entire book <note>Kepler believed the number 5 was essential for harmony because it creates the "major third" interval</note>. Certainly, let there be other valid reasons for stopping at the **Quaternary** <note>the grouping of the first four numbers</note>. Indeed, he even demonstrates that this form of the Republic shines forth in Man himself.

<margin>
DIGRESSION.
The Soul.
</margin>
...from Plato, in which there are 1. The Mind, 2. The Reasoning faculty, which spreads itself out into syllogisms, 3. The Irascible <note>The "spirited" part of the soul associated with anger and courage</note>, and 4. The Concupiscible faculties <note>The part of the soul associated with basic desires and appetites</note>; Plato demonstrates that their seats—in the brain, the chest, and the belly—are even set apart by harmonic intervals. To these are compared: the Command to the first, Counsel to the second, the Military order to the third, and the Common People <note>original: "Plebs"</note> to the fourth, who possess the greatest share of it. From this arise the four pillars of the Republic: Justice, Prudence, Fortitude, and Temperance—rightly called the "hinges"—with each being especially entrusted to its own Order. Jean Bodin <note>A French jurist and philosopher (1530–1596) who argued that the state should be balanced like a musical harmony</note> has become so musical, setting aside Geometry and Arithmetic, that he did not even forget dissonances. Using this as an image, he suggests that a magistrate ought sometimes to allow honors and other rewards of virtue to be given even to someone undeserving, without being troubled by it; for just as the remaining harmony is recognized much better and enjoyed more eagerly through the opposition of a single dissonance, so too may everyone who sees and loathes such a "painted-on" <note>original: "fucum"; a deceptive or superficial appearance</note> benefit to the Republic become more and more accustomed to fleeing similar vices and pursuing virtues.

<margin>The World.</margin>
XXIV. Finally, Bodin compares the State he described to the World itself, showing how God the Creator adorned his work by joining ratios of equals and similars into one Harmonic harmony. In this intention, I agree with him most strongly; and what he or preceding philosophers did not even touch upon—concerning the most accurate harmonic tempering of certain motions—I supply in the following books and bring to light with the clearest demonstrations. Nevertheless, I do not cease, even at the very end, to speak against the hallucinating Bodin: for true Harmonies do not arise from mixed ratios of equals and similars, as has been said quite often. Therefore, Bodin, thinking he is demonstrating Harmonies in the world, demonstrates instead geometric means, equalities, and similarities: 1. Indeed, he finds Harmonic ones in the faculties of the Soul; but these are only Symbolic, expressed with no evidence of demonstration in any solid form (as mathematical things prefer); for it cannot be understood how quantities, which are the next and immediate subject of harmonies, can exist in the Soul. 2. He shows Equality between the body of the World and the universal power of matter. 3. He shows Similarity (qualitative, based on shapes, rather than a relative similarity of quantitative terms) between the eternal Archetype and the form of the World; at this point, Bodin touches my heart, for he has hit upon the subject matter of my *Cosmographic Mystery* <note>Kepler's first book (1596), which argued that the spacing of the planets was based on the five Platonic solids</note>, albeit through ignorance.
<margin>Namely, in any of its faculties, that very number which Bodin assigns to it.</margin>

But how much more plausibly is this mixture of equals and similars demonstrated regarding the principal parts of the World in Book IV of my *Epitome of Copernican Astronomy*: concerning the Sun as the Mover, the sphere of fixed stars as the Placer <note>The "Locans" or container of the universe</note>, and the Intermediate space granted to the movable bodies. For Equality is established in the parts of matter, so that there is as much of it in the Sun as there is in either the orb of the outermost sphere or in the intermediate space. To matter, however, as to the common people, is owed an arithmetic equality. Conversely, there is a Geometric similarity of proportion in the density of these three bodies; and again another between the diameters of the Sun the Mover, the region of the Movables, and the final sphere of the immobile Placer. 4. Furthermore, there are Geometric means in a certain way: as between the two types of motion, one toward the east, the other toward the west, and a third of Trepidation...
