> *On the use of Mathematics in Natural Science and Politics: which especially concern the Harmonic part of that [subject] regarding Radiations.* <note>Proclus (412–485 AD) was a Neoplatonist philosopher whose ideas about geometry being "inscribed" in the soul deeply influenced Kepler.</note>

For the contemplation of Nature, [Mathematics] supplies all the primary things, declaring the most beautiful order of Ratios <note>original: "Rationum," referring to the mathematical relationships or proportions</note>, according to which this whole Universe was fabricated; and the Analogy of proportions, which connects all mundane things among themselves, as Timaeus <note>A reference to Plato's dialogue "Timaeus," which discusses the mathematical construction of the universe</note> speaks of somewhere, and which reconciles friendship between fighting things, and harmony <note>original: "responsum," meaning a correspondence or "answer"</note> and mutual affection between those very far apart. *And after a few words:* From there, it is also possible to hunt for suitable angulations <note>The geometric angles formed between planets, known in astrology as "aspects"</note> by reasoning. *Again:* This, I think, Timaeus also wanted to mean, when everywhere through mathematical words he hands down the contemplation of the Nature of the whole universe, and depicts the origin of the elements with Numbers and Figures, and attributes their faculties and affections, and also their effects, to these <gloss>(figures)</gloss>; establishing the sharp or obtuse angles of their corners, and the rough or smooth textures of their sides, etc., as causes of all various mutations.

To the field called Politics, who could deny that this doctrine contributes many and wonderful things; while it measures the opportunities for conducting affairs, and the various circuits of the whole universe, etc. And Harmonic Numbers, the rulers of life, or the authors of incongruity, and the helpers of effort or relaxation in the universe, etc.

ON CONFIGURATIONS

# Preamble & The Logic
## Of the Order.

We have shaped the Harmonic proportions considered in the abstract in the first three books, of which the first showed the Geometric properties of individual figures, the second the Congruencies <note>The way shapes fit together to fill a space without gaps</note> of joined figures, and the third propagated harmonic proportions from those figures.

It remained for us to introduce the Harmonic ratios described so far into the World in three other books, of which the first would attribute Harmonies to God the Creator of the heavens, the second to Nature as the administrator of various motions, and the third to Man, who possesses the voice that is born from motion. However, the condition of the subjects to be discussed persuaded us not only to change the order—beginning with human song, passing from there to the works of Nature, and so finally to the work of Creation, which was the first and most perfect of all—but also to join the end of the abstract speculation with the beginning of concrete Harmonies in Song, in that same third book. Therefore, since the beginning of this introduction into the World was made in the preceding book, and the Harmonies were transcribed to human song (which others are accustomed to embrace with the general term of "Art"), there now follows the fourth book, which in this reversed order assigns to Nature the second parts of concrete Harmony.

<margin>
And yet Socrates in Plato, as cited by Proclus in Book I on Euclid, defines that Musician as one who proceeds from those Harmonies which are in the senses to insensible harmonies and the investigation of their proportions. He finally emerges as a Philosopher, having been awakened by both harmonies to the contemplation of the First true Being and truth itself.
</margin>

Although I touched upon the dispute concerning the Essence of harmonies here and there in Book III, I nevertheless decided that a full treatment of this metaphysical dispute should be reserved for the beginning of this fourth book with the same purpose. For since the common run of philosophers seek Harmonies nowhere else but in song, and for most people it is an unbelievable teaching <note>original: "Acroama," a Greek term for a lecture or something heard</note> when they are taught that sounds are one thing and the Harmonies—which are thought to be in the sounds—are another; something had to be granted to the weakness of understanding, and the origin of Harmonies had to be explained in musical terms commonly known, rather than disturbing the reader's eagerness with the untimely subtlety of metaphysical questions.

But now, furthermore, since the intention is to reveal Harmonies in Nature and in the motions of the Heavens—whereas the common crowd of philosophers, at the first mention of Harmony, immediately conceives of the vocal Music of the stars to be perceived by hearing, and stands with ears pricked like Cicero's Scipio <note>A reference to "The Dream of Scipio" by Cicero, a famous text describing the celestial music of the spheres</note>, expecting to catch *so great and so sweet a sound*; and since it is easy for those unskilled in things to argue with that same dreamer Cicero that *such great motions cannot be stirred in silence*, and with the Pythagoreans (according to Aristotle) to give a reason why the celestial sound is not heard on Earth—these preconceived opinions greatly obstruct readers striving toward the inner secrets of Nature. Indeed, they could even deter many who are strong in judgment and seekers of truth, who, despising these Pythagorean trifles recognized from afar, might throw away the book unread. For these reasons, this very place seemed suitable to me for conveying this most necessary discussion.

<meta>catchword: Chapter I</meta>

I was also moved by the example of Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century Greco-Egyptian polymath whose work on music theory and astronomy served as a vital foundation for Kepler</note>. When he had completed the harmonic doctrine regarding song in the first two books of his own work on *Harmonics*, and had undertaken in the third book to demonstrate that all perfect natures participate in harmonic power, he himself began his discussion with this very question: *Under what category of things should the Harmonic Nature or power, and its science, be placed?* <note>original: "Sub quod genus rerum referenda sit Natura seu vis Harmonica, ejusque scientia"</note> Therefore, although I have relegated my specific examination and critique of Ptolemy to the appendix of this work, the answer to this question based on my own principles ought to be placed at the beginning of this fourth book for the reason I have stated. This serves not only to prepare the reader and turn away unfavorable opinions, but also to provide a fundamental explanation of the entire fourth book. 

Since we are going to speak about the Harmonies of the rays of the stars <note>In Kepler’s view, the angles formed by light hitting the Earth from different planets create "harmonies" that affect the world</note>—how many there are, and by what geometric principles they are formed—we must first know the essence of Harmonies, setting aside both sounds (which are not present here) and even the rays themselves. We must ask: what is their proper subject, and what are their limits? Do they exist in things outside the intellect, or only in the soul? By what means are they perceived and received within? By what standard are they judged? What effect follows this perception and recognition, and by what author or "prime mover"? Once these things are explained, both in general terms and through a comparison of specific subjects, it will then be easy for us to discuss Metaphysically the essence and properties of Souls and of the **sublunary Nature** <term>Sublunary Nature: The Earthly realm "beneath the moon," which was thought to be changeable and influenced by the heavens</term> itself, and to place the secrets of Nature in a slightly greater light than they have been until now.

*Chapter VII. The Epilogue contains a contemplation of sublunary Nature and the lower faculties of the Soul.*

# CHAPTER I.

## On the essence of harmonic proportions, both sensible and intellectual.

**A**s I prepare to discuss the essence of harmonies, I find myself in doubt: would it be clearer to first seek out the opinions of the ancients and then compare them with my own, or to begin with the explanation of my own view? The former method of philosophizing is accepted by everyone and is frequently recommended by Aristotle <note>Aristotle often reviewed his predecessors' views before presenting his own, particularly in his *Metaphysics* and *Physics*</note>; yet the latter seems more suitable for the present subject. Indeed, few have specifically touched upon discussions concerning the Essence of Harmonies; and if they said anything regarding the existence of mathematical Genera and species <note>Kepler refers here to the "subsistence" or reality of mathematical categories</note> that could be applied to Harmonies specifically, it is necessarily full of obscurity in the philosophy of the Gentiles <note>original: "philosophia Gentilium," referring to non-Christian ancient philosophers like the Pythagoreans or Platonists</note>. Thus, the reader's mind fluctuates in doubt between a love for these most beautiful doctrines and the suspicion that they are merely fictional. Among Christians, if one embraces with firm faith the most holy Mystery of the Trinity and the origin of all things from the Mosaic history <note>The creation account in the Book of Genesis</note>, the main points of the discussion can be proposed more clearly and find readers more inclined to believe.

To proceed with our method <margin>Division of Harmonies.</margin> of explanation, we must begin with a division. For a sensible Harmony—or one analogous to it—is one thing; a secret Harmony, pure and separate from sensible things, is another. The former are many, both by reason of their subjects (which differ in species) and by reason of individuals. But pure Harmony, separated from sensible subjects, is one and the same within any given species. For example, there is one and the same species of Harmony that arises from a double proportion <note>A 2:1 ratio</note>. If this is found in sounds, it is called a <term>Diapason: the Greek name for an octave</term>; if it occurs in radiations <note>astrological light rays</note>, it is called an Opposite Aspect <note>An aspect of 180 degrees, where two planets are on opposite sides of the Earth</note>. In a musical system, it is either higher or lower, more acute or more grave, whether produced by human voices or by the sounds of instruments. It is no less varied in Meteorology <note>Kepler believed planetary aspects influenced weather through the "Earth's soul"</note>; for it may involve the pairing of Saturn and Jupiter or another pair, and arise either from the equinoctial signs or from the Tropics.

Therefore, we must ask how both kinds exist: whether they exist of themselves, in themselves, or within other things. Regarding sensible harmonies <margin>Sensible harmonies.</margin>, four things must concur for them to have "Being": 1. Two sensible things of the same kind and of a certain magnitude, so they can be compared to each other on account of quantity; 2. A comparing Soul; 3. The inward reception of these sensible things; 4. A suitable proportion, which is defined as Harmony. If one of these is removed, the sensible Harmony is destroyed. For it is easy to understand that the Nature of Harmony must not be defined <margin>Order is required for the Being of Harmonies.</margin> by sensible things alone, such as by a sound or the ray of a star. For a sound is one thing, but a specific order between different sounds is another. In this context, I mean "order" not in terms of position in physical space, nor in terms of time, but in terms of high and low pitch <note>original: "acuminis & gravitatis"</note>. Thus, there can be different sounds, but unless there is a specific order between them defined by certain proportions (which are mathematical things), there will be no Harmony between the voices. Conversely, if the sound is removed, what audible Harmony could be imagined? And if the rays of the planets are removed, what Harmony could be configu-

# BOOK IV OF HARMONIES

<margin>CHAPTER 3</margin>
...of configurations? Furthermore, because musical Harmony is not sound, but an **Order** of several sounds, it follows that it belongs to the <term>Category of Relation</term> <note>In Aristotelian logic, "Relation" is one of the ten categories used to describe how things exist; it refers to things that are defined only in reference to something else</note>. For the Order we are speaking of here is a relation, and things that are ordered are related to one another. Therefore, the fact that sounds are a harmony is an **accident** <note>In philosophy, an "accident" is a quality that a thing possesses but which is not essential to its nature—like the color of a car</note>, since it exists within the subjects and does not exist separately, and it can be absent without the destruction of the subjects themselves. 

Next, just as quantity in general cannot be separated from its own bodies, yet can certainly be increased or diminished along with those bodies while still remaining an accident; so too this **Order** of sounds—under which we categorize Harmony as a species—cannot be removed from sounds (provided there is more than one) which are distinct from each other by the quantity of highness and lowness. For either they will cease to be "several," or if they are several, there will be an order between them according to their excess and deficiency; though that order is changeable if either of the related subjects is changed. Therefore, Order travels at the same pace as quantities, and specifically with number. 

Thirdly, just as **Number** is defined as a multitude composed of units—in which Aristotle recognizes something analogous to matter (namely, its units) and something formal (the concept of the mind, which recognizes that multitude of individual units as "one" when separated from others in any respect)—so the same philosopher says elsewhere that if the **counting Soul** were removed, all number would be removed, though not the individual units. Thus, number exists "materially" in the things themselves and is nothing besides them, unless a **counting Mind** is added. For only then is number something distinct from the things themselves and abstracted from them; that is, it is a concept in the mind of a plurality of individual things. 

In the same way, the very order of sounds and other perceptible things which we are treating here is nothing other than the several sounds themselves, unless a **Mind** is added which compares the sounds to each other as they differ in pitch. Indeed, every relation in general is nothing without a Mind, except for its own related terms; because related things are not what they are called unless some mind is presupposed to relate one to the other.

<margin>Harmony is incidental to sensible things</margin>
<margin>A Soul is required for the existence of Harmony.</margin>
Therefore, what is true in general regarding order and relation must be applied most especially to Harmony, which consists in proportion and in the counting of equal parts of a quantity. Namely: for any **sensible harmony** <note>That is, a harmony that can be heard or perceived by the senses</note> to subsist and be able to exist, there must be a comparing **Soul** in addition to the two sensible terms. For if the soul is removed, the terms will indeed be two sensible things, but they will not be a single Harmony, which is a <term>being of reason</term> <note>original: "ens rationis," a philosophical term for something that exists in the mind rather than as a physical object</note>.

<margin>The reception of external things into the Soul is required for the existence of sensible harmony.</margin>
We must now also look at a third point: the reception of sensible things into the soul, its necessity, and its manner. 
Undoubtedly, Harmony is one thing, but the sensible terms outside the Soul are not one thing; they cannot be united anywhere except inside the soul. However, they cannot be inside unless they are received within, which does not need to be proven by many words of experience. To be sure, a Musician—a craftsman of symphonies—can meditate on a Harmony of two or more voices within his own soul without receiving them from outside; yet that harmony is not **sensible** in that act. We, however, are speaking of the essence of sensible harmony. 

But what is the nature of that reception? Do not sounds (to use the most well-known example for all of them) persist outside the ears in the air? And before the sounds, the movements of bodies, which the sounds follow according to their quantity? Do they not remain in their own bodies? How, then, do they enter? I respond,

<margin>CHAPTER 1.</margin> ...partly by acting, and partly by <term>being acted upon</term> <note>original: "patiendo." In older philosophy, "passion" isn't just an emotion; it is the state of being the recipient of an action, like a catcher receiving a ball</note>. They act when they emit their <term>species</term> <note>original: "species." Kepler uses this to mean the "form" or "image" that an object sends out through the air to reach our senses</note>: for instance, when objects are struck, they emit the sounds of their own motion; when bright things emit the rays of their own light and color; and as we say when we remark that objects "move" the senses—for to move is to act. 

Yet they are "acted upon" as well—not the things themselves in their essence, but through their <term>species</term>. When these forms are sensed, remembered, and compared, they must always "suffer" or undergo something according to common usage. Indeed, this very joining of two boundaries within the **Mind**, through which the **Essence of Sensible Harmony** results—that is, the act of being related and compared—is, when taken together, the same sort of thing that happens to individual objects when they are seen or heard, or even less than that. For all these things are certain types of <term>passions</term> <note>acts of being affected</note>, though the word is used in a broad and varied sense.

<margin>Degrees of various "passions"</margin> But let us establish the degrees of these <term>passions</term>. First, for example, **Water** is "acted upon" when, starting out chilly, it grows warm when fire is brought near. In a second sense, we say moisture is "acted upon" when it acts on something else—namely, by moistening dry things. For a part of the water is snatched away into the dried-out passages and mixed with them, which is a way of being acted upon. In this way, water is also acted upon when it is tasted; for the thirsty person swallows a part of it and digests it. 

But in a third sense, water is acted upon in the act of tasting when it is merely touched by the tongue—not just because it is warmed by the heat of the tongue (while it simultaneously cools the tongue with its own coldness), and not just because some water clings to the tongue, but simply because it is touched by the tongue. This is like being very gently struck, or pulsed, or pushed, which causes a local motion of the parts within the whole; and to be **Moved** is to be **Acted Upon**.

Let there be a fourth sense: water is said to be acted upon when it emits a vapor that strikes the nostrils and is perceived by smell. To be perceived is to be acted upon; and here, it is not the water itself that is acted upon, but its corporeal outflow, and by this "passion" some part of it is actually consumed.

A fifth degree: water is understood to be acted upon when the noise of it is heard. First, the water itself is in motion; then, the **immaterial form** <note>original: "species immateriata"</note> of the water, as it moves, is spread out from it in every direction and is received into the passages of the ears. This reception is a "passion"—not of the water itself, but of its <term>species</term> or its immaterial outflow. In this reception, something is lost over time and through the sheer number of receptions. For a sound is more muffled when it reaches the ears of a large crowd, or hits clothing, or is emitted amidst falling snow.

Sixth, water also undergoes something when it is seen. It emits from its surface (or thereabouts) rays to the eye—specifically from its colors, insofar as it is colored. These rays are touched, reflected, refracted, brought to a point, and gathered by the <term>retiform tunic</term> <note>original: "retiformi tunica." We now call this the retina. Kepler was one of the first to realize the retina, not the lens, was the part of the eye that actually "sees"</note>. All these are "passions," not of the water itself, but of the immaterial form or the rays. And these rays, in this reception, lose nothing—neither in space nor in time. For once the thing that touches them is removed, they proceed further, completely undiminished, which is something sound does not do.

Seventh, after these <term>species</term>—and indeed the very body of the water—have first acted upon the corporeal instruments of the senses (that is, they have affected those instruments to match themselves and made the instruments like them), the membranes of the tongue and skin perceive the cold and flavor, the "spirit" of hearing rings with its sound, and the "spirit" of sight shines with its light. Thus, a **sensory image** or type has been formed, which the eyes certainly carry around, even after the object is removed, often against a person's will. Now, these sensible forms [move] from the entryways of the senses...

<summary>Kepler categorizes perception into seven degrees of "passion," ranging from physical changes like heating water to the immaterial reception of light and the formation of mental images.</summary>

# ON BOOK IV OF THE HARMONICS

...or orifices, they are received inward through a **representative** or **imaginative** power, recognized by the **common sense**, stored by **memory**, brought forth by **recollection**, and judged by a **higher faculty**: all of which the <term>water</term> <note>Continuing the analogy from page 110, where water represents the medium of the soul being "acted upon."</note> is understood to undergo, not in its own substance, but in its sensible and mental <term>species</term> <note>The "forms" or "images" of things that travel to the senses.</note>. Then, therefore, even the supreme faculty of the soul—which presides over number and comparisons—constructs and forms for itself one single <term>species</term> of relation, order, and comparison out of many mental forms. It compares the things existing outside with one another. This comparison, as we said above, although it is performed upon the things themselves without their own labor, is understood to be a certain <term>passion</term> <note>original: "passio." An "undergoing" or being acted upon.</note> of theirs. It is in much the same sense as when a legal case is conducted regarding the reputation of someone who is absent and unaware, or when someone is condemned to death or proscribed in their absence. 

This is indeed an entirely fitting likeness; for just as such a person, even if they feel nothing of the evil at that moment and thus "suffer" nothing in their person, yet a little later they experience the force of what they have "suffered" in actual reality. In the same way, voices—and whatever is entirely a participant in congruence—accordingly as they have pleased the **Mind** in this comparison, are either continued, or rejected, shunned, prohibited, hindered, suppressed, or ended. However, I do not say that sounds "suffer" only in respect to this subsequent result, but in that very act when the mind compares them with each other. It is sufficient to have explained at length by what degree of <term>equivocal meaning</term> <note>Meaning the word is used in a specific, non-standard way.</note> I call this mental comparison a "passion." But I have not been lengthy in listing these meanings in vain: for by this path we shall henceforth be wonderfully aided in recognizing the **Nature of the Harmonic Faculty** and in completing this part of **Metaphysics**, which **Aristotle** did not even glimpse <note>original: "ne per transennam quidem aspexit," an idiom meaning "not even through a lattice-window" or "not even a passing glance."</note>.

<margin>Are sensible Harmonies **concrete** or **abstract**?</margin>

From these points it is also clear what I was previously contending: namely, that the very "formal" part of sensible **Harmony** (insofar as it is harmony) happens to the sensibles, just as it happens to them to be seen, heard, and so on. Secondly, it is clear that sensible **Harmonies** are also things that are in a way **abstracted** from the objects themselves—insofar as it is not the objects outside, but the <term>species</term> of things entering through the senses and led to the tribunal of the soul, which become the "terms" or boundaries of the harmonic proportion. 

But conversely, these harmonies are still **concrete** for a twofold reason: first, because these species of sensible things are not species of their bare quantity alone, but also of their sensible quality (such as sound or light, etc.). Secondly, because these sensible species, as sensibles, cannot shine back within the mind unless the objects themselves, of which they are species, are also present and remain outside. For if the objects are taken away, their species inside also cease—light, in terms of its radiation, in that very instant, and sound within a very brief moment of time. To be sure, some impression is left behind in the sensory instruments, as light leaves an impression in the eye, but that is not the external thing itself. It is rather a "second species" of the species, impressed into the body, having now become a momentary quality of the body. This is just as in optics, where colors—by means of the pure and least-colored light of the sun—conceive the power of radiating color in every direction. And this is what we were contending at the beginning: it is necessary for the sensible terms and the **Soul** to be present together and to exchange mutual operations through acting and being acted upon—the former by moving the senses, the latter by comparing—so that the essence of **sensible Harmony** may be established.

Here someone might object that the **Soul**, by comparing, does not "make" or create, but in-

...to reach a suitable proportion: which was the fourth and formal principle of sensory harmony mentioned above. Therefore, it might seem that the soul could be absent while the Essence of Harmony remains intact.

<margin>
CHAPTER I.
To what extent the Soul makes Harmonies and to what extent it finds them.
</margin>

I respond by inverting the argument: to find a "suitable proportion" in sensory things is to uncover, recognize, and bring to light the similarity of that sensory proportion with a certain Archetype <note>An "archetype" is a foundational, ideal pattern or original model that Kepler believes God placed within the human soul.</note> of the truest Harmony which exists within the Soul. Just as the Athenians found some virtue in Zeno <note>Zeno of Citium, the founder of Stoic philosophy, who was highly honored by Athens despite being a foreigner.</note>, yet they did not "find" the right to their **Prytaneum** <note>The Prytaneum was a public hall in ancient Greek cities where distinguished citizens were fed at public expense; the Athenians conferred this honor upon Zeno.</note> in him, but rather conferred it upon him—something Zeno could not have achieved without the Athenians—so the Soul finds order and proportion in sounds and light rays. (Though it does not even find this order entirely outside itself, but at least finds the "terms" or limits of the proportion, as was said). Yet, for this proportion to be *harmonic*, the Soul itself makes it so by comparing it with its own internal Archetype. It could not be called harmonic, nor would it obtain any power to move minds, if this Archetype did not exist. Enough, then, regarding Sensory Harmonies.

<margin>
What is insensible Harmony?
</margin>

For now we must move on to the pure and secret Harmonies, the second part of our division: namely, those which we have just established as the Archetypes or **Paradigms** <note>Ideal patterns or examples.</note> of sensory harmonies. For if these Archetypes had their own existence outside the Soul, I would indeed admit that we would be deprived of a great argument for asserting the necessity of the Soul in establishing the essence of Harmony. And yet, to place them outside the Soul is a **contradiction in terms** <note>original: "oppositum in adjecto." A logical error where the definition contradicts the subject.</note>, as we shall hear.

<margin>
Its limits.
</margin>

For the principles of true and archetypal Harmony—which exists without being mixed with any sensory **species** <note>The outward appearance or form of something perceived by the senses, like a sound or a color.</note>—are nevertheless divided and multiple in number. Since it too is a proportion, it requires its own two **terms** <note>In a mathematical ratio, the "terms" are the two quantities being compared to one another.</note>. These terms, as we employed in the previous books, are the **whole Circle** and its **Part** or parts (whether a single divisor or multiple parts), where the arc is cut away in a demonstrable way. This is the specific difference of a harmonic proportion, by which harmonic proportion is distinguished not only from other proportions of the same kind, but also the pure and archetypal is distinguished from the sensory—except insofar as by common and trite usage, only the "Agreement" of sounds is called "Harmony." For in this very thing, the clearest difference appears between pure Harmony and sensory (or "concrete") Harmony: that in pure harmony, the terms belong to mathematical categories—the Circle and the Arc—formed in a specific way. For the circle has its formation or shape from itself; the arc has its limits from the **chord** <note>original: "subtensa." The straight line connecting the two ends of a curved arc.</note> and its shape from the circle. In sensory harmonies, however, there is no need for this special formation; for they can be straight lines or other shaped sensory quantities, provided they are faithful examples of this archetypal Harmony in whatever quantity they possess. This is to the extent that faithful imitation is possible in sensory things; because in such things, whatever is close to the truth (by degree of "more" or "less") is accepted as the truth itself. These, therefore, are the terms of archetypal Harmony.

<margin>
For the BEING of abstract Harmony, Mind is required.
</margin>

Next, besides the terms—again, as was said before regarding sensory things—a **Mind** is also required, which compares the terms and judges whether they (namely the arcs of the circle) are such that some side of a demonstrable figure might cut them from the whole circle. And so, in a way, there are three principles of Harmony...

He defines the mathematical basis of these pure harmonies as the relationship between a circle and its arcs.</summary>

# HARMONIES, BOOK IV

<margin>CHAPTER I.</margin>
...of Archetypal Harmony, there are two elements on the part of the terms: the **Material**—to speak by analogy—which is the Circle and its part; the **Formal**, which is the cutting of the part by means of a demonstrative figure; and one element on the part of the relation itself, namely the **Efficient** cause, which is (in a certain way) the Mind.

<margin>Harmony is a qualitative Relation.</margin>
And since every proportion—and thus also this proportion of a part of a circle to the whole—falls under the category of **Relation**, this specific and described form of proportion conducts itself as a quality of the "fourth species" <note>Kepler refers to the Aristotelian categories of quality, where the fourth species includes "shape" and "mathematical figure."</note>. For Harmony is a qualitative or "figured" Relation, in that it is formed by regular figures.

But if it previously belonged to the Essence of sensory Harmony that sensible things should flow into the soul through a "species" <note>In medieval and Renaissance philosophy, a "species" was an image or likeness of an object that traveled from the object to the senses.</note>, how much more is it necessary that those secret terms of Harmony we mentioned—the Circle and its Arc—be within the mind itself? This is true whether one says it happens through species received from the outside, or whether they have endured with the Mind itself, present within before any reception. Regarding this, we must now investigate with all our intellectual powers.

<margin>How the Genera and Species of Mathematical things exist in the Soul.</margin>
Now that we have reached this point, we cannot hide the views of the Ancients who trod this path of philosophy before us, insofar as they are known to us; to do so would be a slight to the reader eager for philosophy. I believe only one thing must be established first: a distinction must be made between the mathematical species themselves—the Circle and its Arc—and the comparison between them. This is because if the species themselves, as the "terms," are to be placed within the soul without being received from outside, then Harmony (which is the relationship between those parts) must even more certainly be placed in the mind. Harmony does not have its essence outside the mind, since its essence consists in a specific action of the mind regarding those species. While the circle and its arcs are in the Soul in such a way that they are also, beyond controversy, in sensible things; Harmony, which exists between the circle and its part, is—in terms of its **formal** nature—in no way outside the soul, as was shown above by the example of Number. Now, the arguments of the ancients are primarily about the species themselves, which are simpler; Harmony is a more composite thing.

And this is the difference between Aristotle, Plato, and Proclus on one side, and Ptolemy on the other. For the former group disputes the "Being" of the species, while Ptolemy disputes the "Being" of Harmony. However, we shall relegate Ptolemy’s text to the Appendix of the entire work, lest he stir up the confusion we feared at the start of this chapter; instead, we shall now listen to those who speak most appropriately to the present speculation.

<margin>Plato’s dogma on the subsistence of Mathematical things.</margin>
Plato’s opinion regarding Mathematical things was this: the human mind is self-taught in all species or figures, axioms, and conclusions; when the mind seems to be "taught," it is actually nothing other than being reminded by sensory diagrams of those things which it already knows within itself. He represents this with singular skill in his dialogues <note>Specifically the *Meno*, where Socrates guides a young boy to solve a geometry problem without teaching him.</note> by introducing a boy who, when questioned by a teacher, answers everything according to his wish.

<margin>Aristotle’s contrary dogma.</margin>
Aristotle, on the contrary, in his *Metaphysics*, calls this invention **a fictitious discourse, forced to fit the hypothesis** <note>original Greek: "λόγον πλασματώδη, πρὸς τὴν ὑπόθεσιν βεβιασμένον"</note>. For he argues that these Mathematical things do not exist anywhere separately from sensible things; nor...

...that their existence is no different, not even in the Mind, except in the same way that other universals are in the Mind: when the species <note>In this context, "species" refers to the mental form or essential image of an object.</note> of the essence of singular sensible things is formed in the Mind through definition. Therefore, they [mathematical objects] are indeed prior to sensible things and are abstracted from sensible things, but not in reality—only in the concept of the mind. Here it must be noted that Aristotle, almost as often as he happens to <margin>What harmed Aristotle.</margin> name one of the mathematical genera for the sake of an example, always names either the **Point**, or the **Line**, or the **Surface**, or the **Body**, or **Number**; these are the highest genera in the category of Quantity. However, regarding quantities insofar as they are **figures**, which belong to the "fourth species of quality" <note>Aristotle categorized "shape" and "mathematical figure" as a specific type of quality rather than just quantity.</note> (where one part is their material—quantity—and another their formal—figure), mention is very rare throughout these discussions. Insofar as they are **Relations**, there is absolutely no mention at all. Indeed, he even posits that the science of Harmonics speculates about nothing except voices; and about them only insofar as they are lines, clearly just like Optics. But about the intervals of lines, which are proportion (certainly a relation, and specifically a qualitative and figured one), Aristotle never even dreams. Therefore, there is no doubt that he would have progressed further in this speculation if he had been imbued with deeper mathematics (concerning the intellectual difference between possible and impossible figures, which we dealt with in Book I). Insofar, then, as he disputes concerning the highest genera of quantity, he easily wins, with no one <margin>* also concerning individual species (formally), such as the circle, Triangle etc. Aristotle's blank slate, the mind's idea</margin> opposing him. But because he concludes *universally*, and finds Plato guilty of this foolishness which he himself imagined; and finally, because he opposes the Platonic picture of the **self-taught boy** <note>original: αὐτοδιδάκτῳ. This refers to a famous scene in Plato's dialogue *Meno*, where a slave boy "remembers" geometric truths he was never taught, suggesting they are innate.</note> with a contrary picture, asserting that the Mind is empty of itself—not only of other knowledge and mathematical genera, but even of species—and is clearly a **Blank Slate** <note>original: Tabula rasa.</note>, in which nothing is written, not even mathematical things, but in which everything can be written: in this part, I say, he is not even to be tolerated in the Christian religion. And after some centuries, he found many other **direct thinkers** <note>original: εὐθυΐας. Literally "straight-mindedness" or "directness."</note> as Proclus says, and Proclus himself as an adversary; although Proclus does not cite Aristotle himself by name, he openly professes that Plato, whom he defends, is his leader.

<margin>Proclus's Philosophy on the Essence of Mathematical things</margin> It is worthwhile, therefore, to transcribe here word-for-word from his first book on Euclid the philosophy of this Proclus concerning the species of mathematical things, which I profess to be the terms of pure Harmonic proportion, hidden from the senses.

<margin>CHAPTER I</margin>
From where does that immense certainty and precision in these Ratios <note>The Latin "ratio" here refers simultaneously to mathematical ratios, logical reasons, and definitions.</note> (or definitions) arise? It must come either from sensible things <note>Things perceived by the five senses.</note> or from the soul itself. But it is impossible for it to come from sensible things, for a much greater subtlety and exactness exists in these Ratios. Therefore, it comes from the soul, which bestows that precise subtlety upon imperfect and imprecise things.

<margin>The true essence of mathematical things is in the Soul.</margin>
For say, where among sensible things is found a nature that cannot be divided (the **point**), or one lacking width (as a **line**), or depth (as a **surface**)? Or where is that equality of lines from a center [a circle], or where are the always constant Proportions of sides (the subject of my Book I), or where is the perfect rectitude of angles? Indeed, I do not see them, since all divisible things are mixed and confused with one another; nothing is pure, nothing is free from its opposite; all are divisible, both those separated by space and those joined together. How then shall we obtain a durable essence for immobile things from things that are mobile and constantly changing? For even they [the Aristotelians] concede that whatever derives its existence from moving essences must itself be changeable. And how shall we obtain accuracy for precise and certain forms from those that are not accurate? For everything that is the cause of an ever-changing notion is itself much more so.

We must therefore suppose that the Soul itself is the mother of **Mathematical forms** and **Ratios**. And if she, containing them within herself as primary patterns or Paradigms, brings them into essential existence, then generations <insert>a Christian understands this as the creation of sensible things</insert> are nothing other than the propagation of forms that were already within her. <note>Kepler adds a theological gloss here: "Christians know that the mathematical reasons for creating bodies were co-eternal with God, and that God is Soul and Mind in a super-excellent way; and that human souls are images of God the Creator, even in their essentials in their own way."</note> In saying this, we agree with Plato, and the true Essence of Mathematics will have been found by us. 

But if the Soul—lacking these Mathematical Ratios and not having previously received them from anywhere (as if they had not been created within her)—nevertheless wove this wonderful, immaterial adornment and labored at this most beautiful speculation, how then would she discern whether the things thus produced were substantial and constant <note>Kepler notes: "I read <term>monima</term> (permanent/stable) not <term>gonima</term> (generative)."</note> or vanishing into the winds, and specters rather than true things? What standards would she use to measure their truth? Indeed, how could she beget such a variety of ratios when she did not possess their essence? For in this way, we would make their existence accidental, tending toward no goal or limit.

<margin>Mathematical forms are not gathered into one from singular quantities.</margin>
Thus, **Mathematical forms** are the offspring of the Soul itself; she does not derive the Ratios she establishes from sensible things. Rather, the sensible things are propagated from the soul's forms. These labors and births of the soul are the evidence of permanent and eternal forms.

<margin>Arguments from Aristotle.</margin>
Secondly, if we gather the Ratios (or definitions) of mathematics "from below" and from the senses, why would the demonstrations constructed from sensible things not be superior to the demonstrations of more universal and simple forms? For we say that in the investigation of a sought-after thing, the principles and propositions are everywhere related to the demonstrations or conclusions. If, therefore, singular things are the causes of universals, and sensible things the causes of rational ones, how can it be that the conclusion of a demonstration refers to the more universal rather than the specific parts? And how can we prove that the essence of intellectual things is more closely related to demonstrations than that of sensible things? For thus they speak: "Not if someone demonstrates that an Isosceles <note>Original: "Aequicrurum."</note> triangle has ang-" <note>Catchword for the next page.</note>

<margin>CHAPTER I</margin>
[To know that a triangle has] angles equal to two right angles—and that this is true whether it is equilateral, isosceles, or scalene—is legitimate knowledge; but he alone possesses science properly so-called who demonstrates this simply for every triangle. Likewise: universal things are better for demonstration than particular ones. Furthermore, demonstrations belong to the more universal; those things from which demonstrations are constructed are prior, and precede singular things by nature, being the causes of the things which are proven. Therefore, **demonstrative** <note>original: "Apodicticæ". These are sciences based on absolute logical certainty, like geometry.</note> sciences are far from gathering their propositions like beggars from things born later and more obscure to the senses. I will say this third thing besides: those who claim this make the Soul more base than the forms themselves. For if matter receives from Nature those things which are essential, more "Being-ful," and more evident, but the Soul receives them by a later act from them—fashioning in itself examples and images of a later birth, looking toward baser essences and abstracting from matter things which by nature are inseparable—do they not make the Soul more obscure and more needy than matter itself? For if matter is the place for the **principles** <note>original: "rationibus". Here meaning the formal, mathematical structures within physical things.</note> of materialized things, just as the Soul is the place for the forms (of the *immaterial*), then matter would be the place for the primary things, and the Soul for the secondary; matter would hold the leadership in existence, and the Soul would have its substance from matter; finally, those things in matter would be made according to essence, while those in the soul would be named only according to intention. How then shall the Soul—a participant in the **Mind** <note>original: "Mentis". Kepler uses "Mind" to refer to the Divine Intellect or the higher part of the soul.</note> and the first intellectual Essence, which has perfected knowledge from that source—how, I say, will it be the receptacle for even the most obscure forms of all life, namely the lowest grade in things, and the most imperfect of all in terms of being? But I think it is superfluous to attack this opinion with more arguments, as it has long been deservedly lashed by many.

<margin>By "Soul" he understands here the Soul of the World especially, Plato’s "created God": but by "Mind," what Christians would call the Creator God Himself, of whom all created Souls are images, set over the task of bringing life to bodies. To Christians, Souls are both patterns of the Creator and are even now sustained by Him through a certain irradiation of the divine countenance upon them.</margin>

If, therefore, mathematical forms do not exist through the abstraction of materialized things, nor through the collection of those things which are common in singulars; nor are they at all later in birth or derived from sensible things: it must certainly be necessary that the Soul takes them either from itself or from the Mind, or finally from both itself and the Mind at once. But if from itself alone, how will they be images of intellectual forms? How will they be intermediaries between divisible and indivisible nature, since they obtain no perfection for existence from the first things? Finally, how are the First Examples, **Patterns** <note>original: "Paradigmata". This refers to the Platonic Ideas or Blueprints used by God to create the world.</note>, or **Ideas**, which are in the Mind, the Principles of all things?

But if they are transferred into the Soul from the Mind alone, how will the Soul remain active within itself and self-moving, if the **Principles** <note>original: "rationes"</note> which are in it flowed into it from elsewhere, according to the standard of existence of those things which are moved by another? And how will the Soul differ from Matter, which is only potentially all things, but generates nothing of the forms of materialized things?

It remains, therefore, that the Soul takes these both from itself and from the Mind, and that it is itself the absolute completion of forms, which have their existence from the first intellectual Examples or **Patterns** <note>original: "Paradigmata"</note> generated from themselves, and obtain access to **BEING** itself. Therefore, the Soul is by no means a **blank slate** <note>original: "Tabula rasa". Kepler is explicitly rejecting Aristotle's view that we are born without innate knowledge.</note> empty of all principles; but is always a written tablet; and it writes upon itself, and is filled with writings by the Mind. For the Soul is a Mind, or a certain Intellect, which revolves itself according to an Intellect prior to it, an image of that, and a figure or type made outwardly. If, therefore, that [Divine Mind] is all things intellectually...

<summary>Kepler argues that mathematical truths are innate to the Soul and derived from the Divine Mind, rather than being mere abstractions from physical objects. He rejects the "blank slate" theory, asserting that the Soul contains the essential patterns (Ideas) used by God in creation.</summary>

# BOOK IV OF THE HARMONIES 117

<margin>CHAPTER 1</margin>
<margin>In the *Timaeus* <note>Plato’s dialogue concerning the creation of the universe.</note>, which is beyond any shadow of a doubt a certain commentary on the first chapter of Genesis, or the first book of Moses, transforming it into Pythagorean Philosophy, as is easily clear to the attentive reader who compares it repeatedly with the words of Moses themselves.</margin>

*...is three times, and the Soul will be all things in the manner of a soul; and if He [the Creator] is the archetype, the Soul is in the manner of an image; and if He is contracted and unified, the soul is divided. Since Plato understood this, he constituted the Soul from all things, and divided it according to numbers, and bound it back together with Analogies and Harmonic Ratios; and into it he brought the first Principles, the shapers of Figures, namely the Straight and the Curved, and he moves the circles which are in it intellectually. Therefore, all Mathematical things are first in the Soul; and before Numbers, there are Numbers that move themselves; and before apparent figures, there are vital figures; and before things that are Consonant or well-ordered, there are the very Ratios of the concords, or Harmonics; and before the bodies which are moved in a circle, the invisible cycles themselves were established. The Soul is the Consummation of all things; and this is a certain other adornment (beyond the sensible one) which even now leads itself (to things) and is led from a familiar and kindred principle; and which fills itself with life, and is filled by the Creator, in an incorporeal and non-spatial way. (He is not far from each one of us; in Him we live, move, and have our being.) And when the Soul brings forth and unfolds His Ratios: then it also discovers all Sciences and virtues. It is therefore given its essence in these species of the Soul; nor should it be thought that the Number which exists within it is a multitude of units; nor should the form and idea of those things which can be displaced from their locations be understood as corporeal: but all things must be supposed vital and intellectual, the first examples of apparent Numbers and Figures and Ratios and motions. Here we must follow Timaeus, who completes and perfects every origin and fabric of the soul from Mathematical Genera, and places within it the causes of all things. For those seven terms of all numbers existed beforehand within it according to their cause.* <margin>I think [he means] 1, 2, 4, 8, 3, 9, 27.</margin> <margin>Timaeus understands the Soul of the World.</margin> *Again, the principles of Figures were placed within it in an architectonic or craftsmanlike way; and the first and most principal of all motions, which surrounds and incites all remaining motions, existed together with it; for of all things which are moved, the principle is the circle and circular motion. Therefore, there are essential and self-moving Ratios of Mathematical things which complete the Souls: which the Soul, bringing forth, propagating, and unrolling, causes the whole variety of Mathematical sciences to exist. Nor will it ever happen that it ceases to produce and bring forth always one after another; while it strips its indivisible Ratios of their simplicity. For it received all things beforehand, in the manner of a principle of species and primeval things; and according to its infinite power, from anticipated principles, it builds the propagations of every kind of speculation.* Thus far, Proclus.

I wanted to copy out this entire passage because it establishes that the genuine terms of Harmonies—the Circles and arcs cut from figures—exist essentially within the Soul and within the mind, among other mathematical things. Thus, these mathematical things become the Soul's own, and in turn, the Soul becomes a kind of Essence for them (insofar as they are separated from individual physical things). But also, I quoted it because by bringing forth similar views, it removes the "envy" or hostility of those who follow Aristotle (who is rejected on this point), and it excellently commends this whole philosophy.

Regarding Numbers, I would hardly contend; indeed, Aristotle rightly refuted the Pythagoreans: for numbers are, in a way, of the <term>second intention</term> <note>original: "secundæ intentionis". In scholastic logic, this refers to concepts that the mind creates to categorize other concepts, rather than things that exist independently in nature.</note>, and even the third and fourth, and there is no limit to their naming. Nor do they have anything in themselves which they have not received either from quantities, or from other true and real beings, or even from various intentions of the Mind—

# ON CONFIGURATIONS

<margin>
**CHAPTER 1.**
**Climacterics.**
</margin>
...[they] have been; therefore, I do not attribute anything to the **Platonic Numbers** assigned to the turning points of Republics—which **Bodin** <note>Jean Bodin (1530–1596) was a French jurist who sought mathematical patterns in the rise and fall of states.</note> uses in his *Method for the Easy Comprehension of History*—nor to those called **Climacterics** <note>Critical or dangerous years in a person's life, traditionally multiples of 7 or 9, thought to be governed by numbers alone.</note> for their own sake. I only value them insofar as they count the revolutions of the stars and their <term>Configurations</term> <note>Also called "aspects," these are the significant geometric angles (like 90° or 180°) planets form with each other as seen from Earth.</note>, as I clearly indicated recently in the Introduction to the *Ephemerides* <note>Kepler’s published tables of planetary positions.</note>.

But regarding continuous quantities <note>Geometric shapes and lines, as opposed to "discrete" numbers like 1, 2, 3.</note>, I agree entirely with **Proclus** <note>A 5th-century Neoplatonist whose commentary on Euclid influenced Kepler’s view that geometry is innate to the soul.</note>; even if his speech flows like a torrent, overflowing its its banks and hiding blind shallows and whirlpools of doubt, while a mind full of the majesty of such great things struggles within the narrowness of language, and his conclusion, never satisfying itself with the abundance of words, exceeds the simplicity of his propositions. I believe, therefore, that if I now add my own reasons (conceived before I had read Proclus) for why I establish the **intellectual Circle** and its parts as the terms for "insensible" <note>Mathematical or "silent" harmonies that exist in the mind rather than as audible sounds.</note> Harmonies, I will not only say things consistent with Proclus but also provide a summary of the passage described, insofar as he serves my purpose.

<margin>
**The terms of insensible Harmonies are abstract quantities.**
</margin>
I will not say, among the reasons, that those things being compared were first outside the mind, then in the senses, and finally abstracted from the things and their sensible appearances—which is the sense the word "abstracting" usually creates. For as said above, this method of abstracting pertains to the sensible Harmonies of Sounds and Rays. It only takes place when—just as the good or bad deeds of citizens are judged by laws passed in ancient times—Sounds and Rays are judged by the <term>Archetypal Harmony</term> <note>The original, divine blueprint of harmony that Kepler believes God used to create the world and placed within the human soul.</note> already present within.

But this is the reason why a quantity is said to be "intellectual" when it provides the terms for harmonic proportions: because that quantity must be capable of a far more subtle demonstration. Truly, that demonstration is never obtained from sensible diagrams, though it may be aided by them; nor does it arise from collecting many individual sensory experiences into one Axiom, but it is obtained <term>a priori</term> <note>Derived from theoretical deduction or innate knowledge rather than from observation or experience.</note>. Since Proclus correctly objected to **Aristotle** <note>Aristotle believed the mind was a "blank slate" and all knowledge came from the senses; Kepler and Proclus argue that geometric truths are born within us.</note> on this point regarding the intellect in general, I can make it very firm with most brilliant arguments taken from my first book regarding this specific case. For the specific difference of the Figures which cut off a harmonic arc of a circle—which is explained as part of their definition—is that they must be **knowable**. Now, what "knowability" can there be without a Mind capable of knowledge? And do not say that a thing can exist even if there is no knowledge of the thing itself: for knowledge consists in comparison, such as when the side of a figure is equal to the **Semidiameter** <note>The radius.</note>. Now, equality that occurs without a mind—especially in things separated by location—cannot be understood; and we are rolled back to the argument already brought forward above for even the sensible Harmonies.

Not only must they be "knowable," but they must also be **known**, so that the Archetypal Harmony may shine forth in action within the soul. For the mere possibility of knowing is not enough for us to have a criterion for sensible harmonies. Therefore, the thing whose essence is partly within the soul—and thus in its Operation or Energy—must be established within: namely, the terms of the Harmonies, the **Circle**, and its **Part**.

He critiques the "blank slate" view of Aristotle, siding with Proclus in the belief that the soul uses these internal geometric blueprints to recognize harmony in nature.</summary>

<margin>
**CHAPTER 1.**
The soul possesses knowledge of mathematics by instinct.
</margin>
You may ask how there can be knowledge of a thing which the mind never learned, and perhaps could never learn if it were deprived of the perception of external things? **Proclus** <note>Proclus (c. 412–485 AD) was a Neoplatonist philosopher who argued that the soul contains all mathematical truths within itself from birth.</note> answered this above in words common to his philosophy; today, if I am not mistaken, we use the term **Instinct** most correctly. Indeed, quantity is known to the human mind and other souls by instinct, even if they were deprived of every sense for this purpose. The mind understands the straight line by itself; it understands an equal interval from a single point by itself; and through these, it imagines a circle for itself. If it can do this, it can much more easily find a demonstration <note>A logical or geometric proof.</note> within it, and thus fulfill the office of the eye in looking at a diagram (if indeed it has need of one). 

In fact, if the mind itself had never possessed an eye, it would demand an eye for itself to comprehend things placed outside of it, and it would prescribe the laws for forming it, drawn from within itself (provided it were pure, healthy, and without impediments—that is, if it were only what it is). For the very recognition of quantities, innate to the mind, dictates what the eye ought to be; and therefore, the eye was made such as it is because the mind is such as it is, and not the other way around. Why say more? **Geometry**, co-eternal with the Divine Mind before the beginning of things—God Himself (for what is in God that is not God Himself?)—supplied God with the patterns for creating the world, and passed into man with the image of God; it was not, in the end, received inside through the eyes.

<margin>
Proclus says almost the same thing shortly after the previously cited passage: **Mathematical Essences** are likened to the truth regarding the gods, and the Architect of the entire universe used mathematical archetypes, co-eternal with Himself, in the shaping of the World.
</margin>
Since, therefore, demonstrability exists in quantities—not insofar as figures are subjected to the eyes, but insofar as they are open to the eyes of the mind (that is, insofar as they are not so much "abstracted" from sensory things as they were never "concrete" with them)—we rightly establish that **abstracted quantity** defines the terms for **Archetypal harmonic proportions**, since these are derived from the demonstrable divisions of the circle.

There is another reason why I choose abstract quantities: because the circle, which is a figure—specifically a species of the "fourth quality" <note>In Aristotelian logic, "quality" was a category of being; Kepler is categorizing the geometric nature of the circle here.</note>—is considered in this business purely as a figure, without distinction between "large" or "small." Thus, it is in a sense abstracted even from quantity itself as if from its own subject, and its nature can be recognized even in the narrowness of a single point. I believe this is what Proclus meant when he said that mathematical things exist in the soul in an **incorporeal and non-extended way**.

<margin>
The **Symbolism** of divine and human things in quantities.
</margin>
Finally, there is this supreme and most powerful reason: that there is a certain wonderful and clearly divine "polity" <note>A system of governance or organized structure.</note> of quantities, and a common symbolism in them for both divine and human things. I have written everywhere about the foreshadowing of the most **Holy Trinity** in the sphere—in my *Optics*, in the *Commentaries on Mars* <note>original: *Commentariis Martis*, referring to his 1609 work *Astronomia Nova* (The New Astronomy).</note>, and in the *Doctrine of the Sphere*—which I wish to repeat here. 

There follows, therefore, the **straight line**, which, from the flow of a point in the center to a single point on the surface, outlines the first rudiments of creation. It rivals the eternal generation of the Son (by the departure from the center toward the infinite points of the entire surface, through infinite lines, under a most perfect equality for all, figured and depicted). This straight line is the element of corporeal form. This line, drawn into width, now foreshadows **Corporeal Form** itself by creating a **Plane**. Moreover, a sphere cut by a plane represents a **Circle** by that section—a genuine image of the created mind, which is appointed to rule the body. This is in the same proportion to the sphere as the human mind is...

CHAPTER I.
</margin>
<margin>
A certain definition of the Soul.
</margin>
...to the divine [nature], as a line is to a surface; yet both are circular. Toward the plane in which it exists, however, it relates as the curved to the straight, which are incommunicable and incommensurable <note>original: "incommunicabilia & incommenſurabilia." Kepler refers to the geometric fact that a curved line (the soul/divine) cannot be perfectly measured by a straight line (the body/material), just as one cannot perfectly "square the circle."</note>. And the circle exists beautifully both in the intersecting plane, circumscribing it, and in the sliced sphere, by the mutual meeting of both; just as the soul both exists in the body, giving it form and connected to the bodily shape, and is sustained in God, like a certain <term>irradiation</term> <note>A Neoplatonic concept where light or divine influence flows from God into the universe.</note> derived from the divine countenance into the body, drawing from there a nobler nature. This cause, just as it establishes the Circle as the subject and source of terms for harmonic proportions, so it most highly commends abstraction. Since the foreshadowing of the soul's divinity resides neither in a circle of a certain quantity, nor in an imperfect one (as material and sensible ones are); and what is most important, the circle ought to be as far removed from bodily and sensible things as the principles of the curved (the symbol of the Soul) are separate and, as it were, abstracted from the straight (the shadow of bodies). We are therefore sufficiently armed so that, for harmonic proportions—objects of the soul alone—we may seek their terms chiefly from abstract quantities.

To conclude this topic, let us gather the main points into a bundle. Sensible harmonies <note>Harmonies we can hear or see in the physical world.</note> have this in common with Archetypal ones <note>The "Archetype" is the original blueprint or perfect idea of harmony existing in the mind of God.</note>: they require terms, their comparison, and the energy of the Soul itself. The essence of both consists in this comparison. But the terms of sensible things are sensible and must be present outside the Soul; the terms of Archetypal harmonies are already present within the Soul beforehand. Therefore, sensible things additionally require reception through an image <term>emitted from themselves</term> <note>In 17th-century optics, it was often thought objects "sent out" species or images of themselves to the eye.</note>, which reception is performed by the senses, the servants of the Soul. They also require another comparison of each sensible term with each Archetypal one—for instance, a circle and its knowable part. But the Archetypal harmony requires neither, since the terms are already present in the soul, being innate to it and indeed being the Soul itself. They are not an image of their true <term>Paradigm</term> <note>A perfect model or pattern.</note>, but are, as it were, their own Paradigm. Thus, only the simple comparison which the soul institutes between its own parts, so to speak, completes the entire essence of Archetypal harmony. Finally, the Soul itself, engaged in this activity, is the Harmony proposed to us; just as, without regard to this activity, it is the circle and its part (namely, the terms of Harmony). And finally, Harmony is thoroughly "ensouled" and thus "deified."

### CHAPTER II.

We have dealt with proportions for the sake of their Essence; now we must deal with them for the sake of the Soul itself.

<margin>How many faculties of the Soul are occupied with Harmonies?</margin>
There exists a twofold faculty concerning harmonic proportions: one through discourse <note>Discourse here refers to "discursive" reasoning—the step-by-step logical process of the mind.</note>, which is mental or nearly so; the other is operative. The mental faculty is again twofold: it is either the invention of proportions from abstract quantities, or the recognition and noticing of chosen proportions in sensible things <note>Sensible things: objects that can be perceived by the physical senses, like sounds or sights.</note>. Therefore, the faculty that investigates harmonic ratios is the same one that embraces the rest of the sciences and arts—namely, the superior part of the human Soul. We say nothing of God here, for He does not investigate anything by discourse and study, but knows all from eternity.

<margin>Harmonic ratios are born within souls.</margin>
That faculty which notices and recognizes noble proportions in sensible things (or even in other things established outside itself) is a lower faculty of the soul, directly informing the senses—or even lower still, namely, merely the vital faculty of the soul. For it does not use discourse, as Philosophers are accustomed to do, nor does it use a method for this; nor is it present in man alone, but also in wild animals and cattle, and even in the sublunary Soul <note>The "sublunary soul" refers to a vital spirit Kepler believed inhabited the Earth and its atmosphere, responding to the movements of the heavens.</note>. You may ask: if that faculty is not capable of discourse, and therefore cannot grasp the science of Harmonic proportions, from where does it get the ability to recognize those offered from the outside? For to recognize is to compare an external sensible thing with internal Ideas, and to judge it to be congruent with them. *Proclus* expresses this beautifully with the word "awakening," as if from sleep. For just as sensible things occurring outside make us remember those things which we had known before, so sensible mathematical things, if they are recognized, elicit intellectual ones that were previously present within: so that those things which previously lay hidden in the Soul like potentiality under a veil now shine back in actuality. How, then, did they break in? I answer: the Ideas or formal ratios of harmonies, as we discussed above, are entirely present in those things that possess this faculty of recognizing; but they are not ultimately received into the interior through discourse. Rather, they depend on natural instinct and are born with them—just as the number of leaves in a flower or the arrangement of cells in an apple (an intellectual matter) is born with the forms of plants. This evidence in plants, similar to harmonic ratios (for number and proportion are kindred things, as shown above), makes it so that I cannot confidently take away from even the vegetative faculty of the soul, and from the Plants themselves, the faculty of recognizing the harmonic proportions of the stellar Rays; although I establish nothing without my own experiments. So it happens that children, the unlearned, farmers, barbarians, and even wild animals themselves perceive the harmonies of voices, even if they know nothing of harmonic science. If you ask from where they get this instinct? I will either flee to God, who forms and presides over all these shapes in bodies—all of them images of Himself, though in greater or lesser degrees—and makes them carry harmonic ratios around with them, just as He Himself embraced them in His mind from eternity and expressed them in creation, as said above; or, what amounts to the same thing, I will cite the kinship (touched upon in *Chapter I*) of these souls—even the lower ones—with the circle, according to which they were composed and shaped as if to a pattern and law; and with the circle itself and its demonstrability, they took on the Idea of the harmonic proportions depending upon it.

<margin>CHAPTER II.</margin>
...of celestial rays toward the same point, as if from a common circle, are imprinted into the soul of the newborn; of which more will be said below in Chapter VII.

<margin>The means by which the Soul perceives Harmonies</margin>
Furthermore, the means used by these lower faculties of the Soul to perceive the harmonies of external things are the same means by which they receive the external objects themselves inward. If they are sensible things <note>Sensible things: objects perceptible by the physical senses, such as sounds or light.</note>, they are perceived through the senses—specifically by the faculties of the soul that inform the senses. These faculties, no less than the higher ones, are engaged in the comparison of certain things, but they do so by instinct, not by discourse <note>Discourse: the step-by-step logical reasoning of the conscious mind.</note>. Thus, through the sense of hearing and the power presiding over it, **consonant** sounds are distinguished from **dissonant** ones. Thus architectural proportions are perceived by the eyes, and by that faculty presiding over vision, the **beautiful and congruent** are distinguished from the **incongruous**. But if the things themselves in which the harmonic ratio exists are not sensible, but perhaps perceptible by some other faculty, these same proportions of things shine forth in the soul: as is the case with the proportions of sidereal rays <note>Sidereal rays: light or astrological influence from the stars and planets.</note>. How these are perceived by the sublunary soul <note>Sublunary soul: The vital spirit of the Earth itself, which Kepler believed responded to planetary alignments just as a human soul does.</note> we shall investigate below in Chapter VII.

<margin>What kind of perception?</margin>
Yet this perception of Harmonies in the lower faculties of the Soul is dull and obscure, and in a way material, and under a cloud, as it were, of ignorance. For they do not know that they are perceiving; just as when we see something, yet we do not notice that we are seeing it. Such are those movements and fears celebrated by the Stoics <note>The Stoics identified "propatheiai"—involuntary, pre-rational emotional responses like a sudden shudder or a racing heart.</note>—natural, without deliberation, and even against the will. Such also is the affection of natural Hate or Love, primarily of a wondrous nature,

<margin>The instinct of Love.</margin>
which, by judging the goodness or similarity of another's Soul to its own through the symmetry <note>original: "commensu"</note> of limbs, voice, and the qualities of temperament, flares up marvelously toward that person. Thus a maddened young man loves a girl; he does not know why, or what she can offer him that any passing prostitute (if it be an indecent love) or any marriageable girl (if it be legitimate) could not. But a physiognomist <note>Physiognomy: the practice of judging a person's character from their facial features or body structure.</note> arriving on the scene finds in both persons some similarity of character; which, if base, provides occasion for perpetual quarrels in marriage; but if good, for a life of tranquility. 

<margin>The physiognomic instinct.</margin>
And so, to this should be referred the entire physiognomic instinct; which, although mute and in a way "brute" (and not at all acquired by art, though it can be refined through it), is nevertheless the sole interpreter and judge of human affairs. For anyone obtains as much prosperity (naturally speaking) as their face, the symmetry of their body, their gait, and the movement of their limbs appeals to those in power, and as much as they creep into their favor—even though those in power use no deliberation in the matter, as if it were hidden; so that they often testify that they love or hate someone, not knowing for what cause. 

<margin>The Charm of the Gaze.</margin>
Such, I say, is the sense of proportions in the lower faculties of the Soul, without the conscious *awareness* <note>original: "sine sensu"</note> of them. To such an extent they neither distinguish the proportion from its "Terms" or subject matter (as when, having heard a pleasant song, we think of nothing regarding the art itself beyond the sounds themselves), nor do they clearly distinguish different Harmonies from one another; for they only notice *that* they are, but they do not know *what* or how varied they are. For even the **Ideas of Harmonies**, which these lower faculties of the Soul have within them, are not instilled in them in a completely pure state, but are wrapped in the "shrouds" of the subject species—namely, whatever object belongs to each faculty. To be sure, the faculty of hearing (to use the example of concordant sounds in place of all others), standing closest to the body, was too coarse, and therefore unsuited to receive the purest Idea of proportion, as I will now explain at greater length.

<summary>Kepler explains that lower faculties of the soul perceive harmony through instinct rather than reason, manifesting as unconscious attractions (love), character judgments (physiognomy), or sensory preferences. He argues these perceptions are "clothed" in physical matter rather than being pure abstract mathematical ideas.</summary>
