ON THE HARMONIES, BOOK IV.

<margin>CHAPTER II.</margin>
For now I come to the <term>active faculties</term><note>Latin: "energeticas Facultates." In Kepler’s terminology, these are the powers of the soul that do work or produce effects, rather than just perceiving.</note>, which are occupied with harmonic proportions. For this power is also twofold: it is either busy within itself, or in things outside of itself; in both cases, it either likens its own works to these proportions or introduces proportions into those works. The former is similar to a passive state, while the latter is beyond controversy exercised in action. The former is a descendant of the lower faculties of the Soul, and the latter of the higher. The former is subject to the forces of Nature; the latter to the human will. Indeed, the former prevails through a motion of alteration, which it brings upon its own body, so that it is entirely subject to the vital faculty. For the fact that we are delighted by the harmonies of sounds has the appearance of a <term>passion</term><note>In the classical sense, a "passion" is something that happens to you, or a state of being acted upon by an external force.</note>, namely of a soothing <margin>How the Soul is acted upon according to Harmonies.</margin> and a softening; hence it is even called by philosophers a "sympathy" of souls with Song (from "suffering together"). Yet, in truth, it is an operation of the soul, acting upon itself by a natural motion and arousing itself. To this, the soul is carried not by deliberation or will, but by a natural instinct. From its very birth, the soul has <term>Ideas</term><note>Platonic Archetypes or blueprints inherent in the mind from birth.</note> already connected and, as it were, fused into one: both the Ideas of harmonies embodied in sounds and the corresponding emotions of the soul. Thus, the Idea of Harmony is implanted in the soul in no other way than insofar as it gives joy and is something delightful, and insofar as it is intertwined with a motion conforming to that Idea. 

I believe this is what Proclus intended above when he asserted that the <term>Paradigms</term><note>The original models or patterns of things.</note> of mathematical things (and thus also, and much more so, of Harmonies) exist in the Mind <margin>intellectually, vitally</margin> **intellectually** <note>original Greek: "νοερῶς" (noerōs)</note>, but in the Soul **vitally** <note>original Greek: "ζωτικῶς" (zōtikōs)</note>. For in this way, they will also exist in the faculty of hearing "sonorously," and in the vital faculty of the <term>sublunary</term><note>Pertaining to the Earthly realm below the moon. Kepler believed the Earth itself had a soul that responded to the "rays" of the planets.</note> world "radiantly" and "operatively." That is to say, these are not the pure internal Paradigms themselves, but their "Icons" or images, derived outwardly.

<margin>That Souls act according to harmonic ratios.</margin>
Indeed, we are not only delighted by the Harmony of a song, but we also adapt the movements of our fingers, mouth, feet, and body to it; this we now perform by the animal faculty, joined with the will. But when we also adapt the voice to intelligible Harmonies, meditating on a melodic song never heard before, here we use all faculties, from the highest to the lowest. We use the highest because we both will it and use deliberation; but we use the lower because we are able to do so, and because even without an intellectual understanding of proportions, we express through song the alone-implanted Ideas of intervals, excluding all discordant ones and wandering only through concordant intervals.

<margin>From where the Harmonic faculties in Souls originate.</margin>
Therefore, that <term>Essential Harmony</term><note>Referring to God as the ultimate source of order.</note>, God Himself, breathed out these explained harmonic faculties in the act of creating, He who is **essence in actuality** <note>original Greek: "οὐσία ἐνεργείᾳ" (ousia energeia)</note>. He inspired this small portion of His own image into all souls without exception, though according to a greater or lesser degree. With this final point, I bring an end to this chapter.

# CHAPTER III.

### What are the Classes of "Fitted Things" <note>original Greek: "τῶν ἡρμοσμένων" (tōn hērmosmenōn) – things that have been harmonized or joined in proportion</note>, that is, of things whether sensible or immaterial, in which Harmonies are expressed, whether by God or by man, and in what manner?

It is easily apparent that the questions are distinct: 1. In whom do Harmonies reside as the Agent, the Shaper, or the Craftsman? 2. In what do they reside as the formed work? We have dealt with the former up to this point; we must now deal more accurately with the latter.

<summary>Kepler explains that the soul has an innate, "vital" response to harmony that functions by instinct, but it also possesses an "active" power to create harmony through music and movement. He concludes that these harmonic powers are a divine imprint of God’s own image placed within all souls.</summary>

<margin>CHAPTER III.</margin>
<margin>1. In the Soul</margin> All things, therefore, are either immaterial or participate in matter. The Soul is immaterial (at least in respect to the body) and hence, as we have used the term so far, it is described by God—entirely in respect to its essence—in these Harmonic proportions; and those proportions which previously existed in the Soul as a Craftsperson—that is, as it is <term>Energy</term><note>Latin: *Energia*. Here Kepler uses the term in the Aristotelian sense of "actuality" or "active power."</note>—now exist in the same as a work of God. However, those things which participate in matter participate at the same time in both Number and Magnitude. But their position in space follows magnitude; and finally, local Motion happens to these things. Number, <margin>2. Whether in the Number of the Planets.</margin> therefore, is something prior by nature to Harmony, because it is necessary for the terms of any harmony to be more than one in number. Yet even the Number of the primary bodies of the World has its causes from Geometry, which I repeat below in Book V from my *Cosmographic Mystery*<note>Kepler refers to his 1596 work, *Mysterium Cosmographicum*, where he first proposed that the orbits of the planets are nested within the five Platonic solids.</note>. Figure follows quantity as its individual property; why a spherical shape should be owed to the stars, and indeed to the World itself—namely, from the <term>Archetype of the Sphere</term><note>Kepler believed the sphere was a symbol of the Holy Trinity: the center for the Father, the surface for the Son, and the intervening space for the Holy Spirit.</note>—is usually explained elsewhere in various places. A certain proportion immediately follows the figures of different bodies, and that is threefold: one of diameters, a second of surfaces, and a third of space or bodies [volumes]. Therefore, <margin>3. Whether in the motions of bodies.</margin> if other causes for these Proportions were not available, we could probably affirm that they were taken from the Harmonies. Whatever those causes may be, the celestial globes preserve them without any change; for they do not become larger or smaller by any motion or the passage of time. It is otherwise with those Proportions which are in bodies by reason of their position and by reason of local motions: for these retain the character of Motion itself; which, as it is in a continuous state of **BECOMING**, is never in a state of **BEING**; likewise, the Proportions of motions are <margin>4. Whether in intervals.</margin> inconstant, being one way at one time and another at another. It is true, indeed, that if the motion of the celestial bodies did not vary their intervals from the common goal or Base of the world—that is, if there were no motion of theirs in altitude or depth, but all were in a purely concentric circle—then not only would the proportion of the intervals have been constant, but also purely Harmonic, if other causes had not been available. The same must be said of motion, regarding the cause of its es-<margin>5. Whether constantly in the speed of motions.</margin> sence, that is, the cause of its true speed through the ether: if this were constant and perpetual for each, there is no doubt that these various speeds and slownesses would have been tempered according to Harmonic laws. Finally, the same must be said of that same motion regarding the cause of the space traversed, as it appears under the Zodiac. For if all the planets were meant to proceed with the same apparent motion under <margin>6. Whether constantly in the apparent motions under the Zodiac.</margin> the Zodiac, and never be separated further from one another: there is no doubt that God would have established such a position for them relative to each other under the Zodiac from the beginning (provided that their arrangement had been free and not bound by other laws of necessity) which would everywhere divide the Zodiac <margin>7. Whether in their initial apparent position under the Zodiac.</margin> into Harmonic ratios. It is even consistent that this happened at the beginning of the motions (since the beginning of time is considered without time); so that from a common position and Harmonic configuration (such as could appear either from the Earth or, more likely, from the Sun), each might have rushed forth into their own spaces or paths as if from the starting gates. But because the planets move in altitude and <margin>In many things, not constantly.</margin> depth, changing the intervals of their position; and because a real intensification and remission of motions follows this motion by physical necessity, for the sake of speed; and finally, because through the unequal apparent speeds of different planets, the space of the Zodiac which they seem to traverse is divided differently at different times: for these three reasons, the same thing happens to positions as to motions by reason of time, as happens to the quantities themselves without respect to time. Just as in a whole circle, or in a straight line, the terms or goals of Harmonic ratios are not found at every single point, but only in certain specific ones: so too here, Harmonies cannot exist at every moment of a motion, nor in all intervals, nor in every speed of motion, nor in every space of the Zodiac intercepted between planets. However, they can certainly exist at specific moments of time, and this can happen without further labor from God, once the motion was granted at the beginning. For He who prescribed the extremes to the motions and allowed for change from one extreme to the other, also bestowed all the intermediates—both the incongruous ones, which are infinite, and the congruous and Harmonic ones, which are placed among the incongruous in a certain number. Nor did God leave these changeable things without <margin>8. In the speeds of their paths.</margin> every care for Harmonic adornment; rather, He reduced some of them (such as the proper motions of the Planets) into a Harmonic order by prescribing their very extremes—which will be the subject of Book V. In others, where <margin>7. In the lengths of paths through the Zodiac.</margin> extremes are not given, but the quantity of motion in a circle is connected with itself, the Creator found it sufficient to so shape the souls placed over mundane creatures that they would expect, observe, and notice the harmonies arising throughout the whole circle at their specific moments of time, and would accommodate their operations to those prescriptions. This is what happens with the motions of the planets as they appear from Earth under the Zodiac; the proper subject of this fourth book.

<margin>
10. In Song
Difference between celestial harmonies and human song
</margin>
Therefore, regarding the works of God known to us, the matter stands thus; if we now compare these to the things which Men arrange according to harmonic laws, we must say some things are the same and some are different. First, in Songs, although there is no less a continuous increase and decrease of quantity than in the heavens, this is necessary in the motions of the heaven by certain laws of nature; in the human voice it is neither necessary nor even easy. For the throat <term>guttur</term><note>Latin: *guttur*. Kepler refers here to the physical anatomy of the human vocal apparatus.</note> was made for articulate voices by the distinction of circles; and we arrive from high pitch to low, and vice versa, more easily through intervals, as if by leaps or discrete sounds, than if we were commanded to use continuous tension. It is no <margin>Why the human voice cannot be stretched by continuous increases, like an instrument or a string?</margin> wonder, then, that in celestial motions—along with that continuous increase and decrease which could not be avoided—there also remained unmelodious intervals mixed with melodious and consonant ones; whereas in human song, all unmelodious sounds having been eliminated, only the melodious and consonant are observed. Yet Song has no reason to boast over celestial motions on this account; for those motions are assigned a different duty to perform, and harmonic tempering is only incidental to them. Song, besides Harmonies, has nothing else to look toward; it requires nothing <margin>Why are there not pure harmonic configurations, as there are pure concordances in song?</margin> outside itself, being intent on the single end of delight.

There are also other human works into which the mind introduces harmonic proportions, though more obscurely and lowly: as when Song is formed not only by the quality of high and low pitch, but also by the measure of the beat <term>tactus</term><note>The *tactus* was the basic unit of time or "pulse" in Renaissance and Baroque music, often corresponding to a heartbeat.</note>, participating in double and triple proportions. <margin>Why among human harmonies is song alone the most exact?</margin>
So much so that Poets and Grammarians delight even in the names of proportions, using them in a peculiar way by calling four-syllable feet with one short syllable <term>Epitrites</term> <note>From the Greek 'epitritos', meaning 'one and a third', corresponding to the 4:3 ratio.</note>—that is, <term>Sesquitertials</term> [4:3]. They do this because, as in a 4:3 proportion expressed by parallel lines, the first three units are represented by a double line while the fourth exceeds them by only a single line; thus in this poetic foot, three syllables are of two beats [longs], while the fourth is of only one [short]. And since the word "Feet" itself alludes to the Choirs, a part of Comedies and Tragedies, it seems that actors also expressed all these proportions through the movement of their feet, no less than <term>duple</term> [2:1] and <term>triple</term> [3:1] rhythms are expressed today. In Architecture, whatever proportions of length to width or thickness are most approved—even by spectators who are not mathematicians—are found to be those closest to harmonic ratios. However, the proportions of sounds are more exact than all of these, and human Nature delights more intensely in expressing them. This happens because every living creature has the greatest power over sounds; indeed, they are formed within the self, sent out from the very heart, and are most ready to follow every nod of the mind and every movement of the heart. Furthermore, as was said before, humans have obtained the most suitable instrument: the Throat, stretched out in length like a string or rather a pipe, through which the voice wanders up and down most nimbly in a straight-line length.

<margin>
Why harmonies are not clearly present in the quantities of things at rest.
</margin>
<margin>Why proportions shine forth most through motion.</margin>
Generally, however, in all things where quantity exists and where Harmonies can be sought according to it, those harmonies are much more evident through motion than without motion. For even if a single straight line contains within it its own half, third, fourth, fifth, and sixth parts, and their multiples, these remain hidden among other parts that are <term>incommensurable</term> <note>Ratios that cannot be expressed as a simple fraction of whole numbers.</note> to the whole. They are so hidden in a single confusion with the whole that even if a second line, equal to one of those fractional parts, stands next to the whole—for instance, a lintel beam of three feet next to a doorpost of five feet—its proportion to the whole does not become known as easily as if some motion were to discern, establish, and determine those comparable lengths. The cause is this: where quantity exists without motion, everything within that quantity exists simultaneously at the same time—namely, all proportions of all parts to the whole. But if a quantity is traversed by a certain motion, then (as is the essence of motion) the proportions that have been traversed no longer exist, and those not yet traversed do not yet exist; thus, any single proportion exists alone at the moment the motion reaches its mark. Thus, through a succession of movements, harmonic proportions are "shelled out" <note>original: "enucleentur"; to extract the kernel from a nut.</note> from the incongruous ones and separated from the mixture of others, as if placed in pure light and held out to the senses to be grasped. So much so that not even the mind itself discerns harmonic proportions within a given quantity from the infinite incongruous ones standing before and after them without some mental image of motion. For example, in a circle, the mind is busied with the infinite <term>subtenses</term> <note>The geometric term for chords, or lines connecting two points on a circle's arc.</note> that have been passed through until it reaches the subtense of a third or fourth part of the circle and the like, and it seeks the demonstration of it. The mind performs in thought what the hand performs by drawing a line: by this act, it separates that specific proportion from the infinite ones it has not thought of.

<margin>Why do proportions shine forth most especially through motion?</margin>
<margin>Nevertheless, this will serve us below as an example for sketching out, to some extent, the harmonies of the rays.</margin>
The mind indeed is capable of this, because it employs its will and dances at its own discretion in that infinite division of quantities, all of which is simultaneously available to the mind for thinking. Natural sensations and other perceptions, however—and finally the motions of bodies, through which perceptions are assisted—are not under the power of a living being in such a way. For if infinite sounds, or the infinite angular positions of two planets throughout the whole circuit of a circle, were confused together at the same time, the senses would not be able to withdraw themselves from the rejected ones and take refuge in only the pleasing ones. Therefore, they have need of motion, by whose mediation everything that was confused because of quantity may be unfolded through successive periods of time, so that each thing may strike the senses individually. But if the eyes are able to do something similar to the mind—choosing the more excellent things from an infinite confusion of things present at once without motion (as if, using the service of the hands, they chose and drew the chord of a third part, namely the side of a triangle, from the infinite possible chords of a circle)—this itself should be considered the work not so much of the eyes as of the mind itself acting through the eyes, and not entirely without the motion of the hands, as I have said.

<margin>How sensible things ought to be arranged so that harmonies are present in them.</margin>
Therefore, to apply this observation to the previous statements: if a thing is to be a genuine subject of harmonic proportion, it is necessary both for quantity (namely length) to be present in that thing, and for there to be at least two markers if the length is a circle, or three if it is a straight line. One or all of these markers must traverse the length of the object through a certain motion and become the boundaries of the parts of the length between which the proportion arises; and this is at the minimum. This occurs in part in the configurations <note>In astrology, a "configuration" or aspect is the angular relationship between planets.</note>, which are the proper subject of this Book IV. For as will be said in the following chapter, harmonies in the angles measured by the Zodiac are indeed considered without motion; nevertheless, those very angles are established one after another by the motion of the radiating bodies through the Zodiac. There are, however, more excellent ways tending toward the same end: as when bodies that have length are themselves determined by such signs wandering up and down, and the pieces intercepted at any given time are moved simultaneously. Thus, not the bodies themselves, but the motions of the bodies, are compared with one another—not for the sake of temporal length and shortness, but for the sake of physical length (since these are the motions of incorporeal things, or rather of bodies established in motion).

<margin>How sounding things become the subject of harmonies</margin>
Just as is the case with sounds: for sound is a <term>species</term> <note>Kepler uses "species" here in the Aristotelian sense of an emanation or sensible form that travels from an object to the sense organ.</note> emitted from a body, both as a quantity, as something shaped to some extent, and as something established in motion; because both motion and sound depend on the suitability of the shape.

<margin>What the windpipe contributes to sounds for expressing harmonies.</margin>
And this is now a second and more evident reason why human nature is especially devoted to the harmonic proportions of sounds. For this happens again because of the conformation of the human body: in which that throat is the body which, according to the constriction of the upper or lower cartilaginous circle in the <term>rough artery</term> <note>original: *aspera arteria*; the classical name for the trachea or windpipe.</note>, is now long, now short. Driven by the breath expressed from the bellows of the lungs, it produces a motion through its cavity (that is, its shape) that is similar to the sound, whose form reaches the ears, and the sensation of it (of the trachea itself, as it is established in motion) is available to the perceiving soul. Indeed, this can be felt by the <term>common sense</term> <note>The "common sense" (sensus communis) was believed to be the faculty that unified the data from the five individual senses.</note>: to enjoy the forms of the limbs of the body as they are affected and, as it were, shaped by various motions. These forms, as I explained in the *Dioptrics* <note>Kepler's 1611 work on optics and the physiology of vision.</note>, are carried from the members of the body by the continuity of the spirits...

## CHAPTER IV.
### What the difference is between the Harmonies considered in the Fourth Book and those in the Third.

**Of how** great importance it is for sound philosophizing to distinguish the boundaries of things; to compare related things so they are not mistaken for the same; to set opposites against each other so they may be clarified—it is not necessary to introduce this with a longer speech. Therefore, it will be worthwhile to bring under a single view everything useful for this purpose that has been said so far, whether scattered, obscurely, or in passing, and to illustrate them more fully where necessary, and to adapt them explicitly to the prescribed title <note>Latin: *lemma*</note> of the chapter. There is, therefore, a fivefold difference between the harmonic contemplations of this book and the preceding one: first, in the Harmonic thing itself, because of its scope; second, in its perceptible terms <note>The 'terms' are the individual values or quantities that form a ratio or proportion.</note>; third, in the cause that grants Harmony its essence; fourth, in the mode of being inherent; and fifth, in the order of causes that form the terms of harmonic proportion.

<margin>Harmonies are narrower in this book.</margin>
I. As for the thing itself which is called Harmonic proportion: those in the third book first arose from sections of a circle demonstrable through regular plane figures, were soon transferred to straight lines, and, being joined and conjugated among themselves, produced no small abundance of harmonic parts (such as harmonic sections, tones, genera, modes, systems, and the like), and among them a certain admirable organization <note>Latin: *politia*</note>. Almost that entire apparatus, however great it may be, will also have to be examined and applied below in Book V. But now in this fourth book, although we start from those same sections of the circle, we shall not proceed to straight lines. Instead, we shall remain within the boundaries of the circle throughout the entire scope of the discussion. The reason was given in the preceding chapter, and will be stated more fully below in Chapter VI, where we will deal at greater length with both the kinship and the effect of this difference.

<margin>These harmonies belong to angles.</margin>
II. As for the terms of these harmonies or their perceptible subject: in Book III, these were sounds differing in pitch and depth <note>In historical music theory, 'acumen' and 'gravitas' refer to high and low pitches.</note>. Therefore, they were categorized under the genus of motion and were, in a way, shaped motions. In this fourth book, however, they are not voices, as stated in the preamble, nor are they certain motions among which one might recognize harmonies; but they reside in the angles which two planets, having emitted luminous rays, form at the Earth, insofar as such an angle [meets] with four right angles at a single point of concurrence...

<summary>Kepler explains that the mind recognizes external harmonies because it is accustomed to the internal vibrations of the human voice. He begins a comparison between the musical harmonies of Book III and the astronomical/angular harmonies of Book IV, noting that this book focuses strictly on circular geometry rather than linear proportions.</summary>

<margin>CHAPTER IV.</margin>
<margin>How [the proportions] of the arcs of the Zodiac</margin>
...can be compared to the surrounding [terms]. And here the reader requires a clear warning. For I am able to explain these terms quite clearly for the sake of understanding, but I cannot do so without the danger of confusion in sound philosophizing unless I carefully prepare the philosophic reader. For while the terms of a proportion must differ in quantity—and the quantity of angles, that is their measure, is an arc of a circle described from the point where the angles meet, as we are taught in Geometry—yet in the whole space of the world, which extends from here at the Earth even to the ends of things, we cannot anywhere describe or perceive a circle suitable for measuring the angles of the rays. The only exception is that same visible circle in the highest ether, expressed by the most crowded fixed stars, which gained the name "Zodiac" <note>The word Zodiac comes from the Greek *zodiakos*, meaning "circle of animals," because the constellations were identified with animal shapes.</note> from those stars being arranged into certain forms of animals. Indeed, it is beneath this very circle that the Planets always move, and each one seems to us to cover a single place in it by the positioning of their bodies; and at its center, the Earth, our dwelling place, seems to be hidden—not only by its own center, which is a point, but by the mass of its whole body, across the surface of which we humans are distributed. Therefore, nothing is easier to perceive than if we say (as in the preceding chapter) that the harmonic proportions we are to deal with in this book exist between the whole Zodiac circle and that arc of it which two planets seem to designate, terminate, or cut off by that visible positioning of their bodies.

<margin>Not truly celestial.</margin>
Even if this is so arranged, and is most excellently pronounced based on Geometric and Astronomical Reasoning, the philosophic reader must nevertheless take the utmost care not to assume in their mind that this harmony (the subject matter of the fourth book) exists in the heavens themselves, in the Zodiac circle, or even in the planets. Not in the least! For this harmony exists in the parts of the Zodiac not for their own sake—since the radiating planets stand at an immense distance below this circle—but because those parts measure the angles of the rays meeting on the Earth. Indeed, it is because the parts themselves do not perform the measuring in actuality, but in their place, an exact **Image** <note>original: "Icon"</note> of the celestial Zodiac in the **Sublunary Soul** <note>Kepler believed the Earth and its atmosphere had a "soul" or vital faculty that could sense and react to the geometric patterns formed by planetary light.</note> undergoes this duty of measuring. It exists in the rays of the planets not insofar as they individually descend from their planet or are the offspring of light (though not without this), but insofar as two rays from two planets, joined here on Earth, form a certain harmonic angle. On both counts, the subject of this harmony is **Terrestrial** (formally, and insofar as the rays become the Terms of the harmonic Proportion); it is by no means celestial, except only materially and with respect to its own **BEING**, without consideration of the Harmonies. That is to say, it is celestial only insofar as the luminous rays—a thing originating in heaven but now fallen to earth—form the angles made on earth, which are the proper subject of this harmony. Regarding truly celestial harmonies, we shall deal with them specifically in Book V. In short, the <term>Terms</term> <note>In a proportion, the "terms" are the two quantities being compared, such as the lengths of two strings or the sizes of two angles.</note> of the harmonies in Book III were the work of Man or of Art; in this **Book IV**, they will be the work of Nature; and finally, in **Book V**, they will be the work of God the Creator.
<margin>But Terrestrial.</margin>

III. As for the Rational cause, which grants these harmonies their **BEING**: there is no difference between the Third and Fourth books in general, but only in species. For in Book III, the harmonies flowed in by reason of...

<margin>CHAPTER IV.</margin>
...of their material subject (sounds) into the senses, they were received and judged by reason of their formal essence, by which they are harmonies (that is, they were formed) by an instinct co-created with the Mind, which participates in reason without the need for logical discourse. And thus far, the Harmonies were considered only in themselves.

Next, however, through a hidden but nonetheless acknowledged interaction between the faculties of the soul, the harmonies received within were poured into various affections of the heart through certain likenesses or images of themselves; they were also poured into the locomotive faculty, so that a human might express the form of harmony conceived in the mind not only with the voice, but also imitate it through the movement of the body. In this way, the Harmonies took on the role of a cause.

Similarly, it is necessary here to assume a Soul, into which this <term>criterion</term> <note>original: κριτήριον (*kriterion*); a standard or benchmark for judgment</note> of harmonic proportions has been instilled since the creation of things. This soul estimates for itself the angle of two radiating stars, in whatever way it is received within (whether that happens by some means analogous to the senses, or by a property of its own essence as a soul—a point discussed in the previous chapter and to be discussed further in those following). It compares the angle to four right angles <note>Kepler refers to the 360 degrees of a full circle</note>, distinguishes the harmonic from the non-harmonic, and thus provides to the harmony its intellectual **Being**, which these angles did not yet possess outside, beyond the thresholds of the mind.

<margin>These harmonies shine forth: 1. In the Soul of man.</margin>
If it is asked what kind of soul this is, or where or in what body it is located, I answer: first, that such are the souls of all human beings. But in the third book, we were dealing with the faculty that presides over hearing, and thus the senses; here, it is not the sensory faculty. For the eyes, whose objects are Light and luminous rays, provide no suitable evidence of the harmonic radiation of two planets. Nor is it the Reasoning faculty: for although reason finds and calculates which <term>aspects</term> <note>The specific angular relationships between planets, like a square (90°) or trine (120°)</note> exist at any given time from astronomical observations conducted through the eyes, it does not do this naturally—seeing as it is not found among all people indiscriminately, but voluntarily, among the few uniquely devoted to astronomy. But human souls are the subject of those harmonies, first by reason of natural instinct, insofar as souls are patterns of the Creator (as said in Chapter IV); secondly, by reason of the faculties—the Vital and the Natural—and the vital and natural movements, or in the Platonic manner, the Desiring and Spirited parts. They are subjects by reason of the former insofar as they are Harmonies; but by reason of the latter, insofar as the forms of the Harmonies are imprinted upon these faculties and become the driving and stimulating causes of the works of Nature, both in the mind and in the body.

<margin>2. In sublunary Nature, or the soul of the Earth.</margin>
Furthermore, the principal soul into which these Harmonies of radiations flow is that which is called <term>sublunary Nature</term> <note>The governing spirit of the Earth's physical realm, responsible for weather and biological growth</note> by philosophers, diffused through the entire body of the Earth, our foster-mother, and rooted in some specific part of it, no differently than the human soul is in the heart. From this center—as if from a hearth, fountain, or inner shrine—it goes out by its own likeness into the Ocean surrounding the Earth and the Air spread over both.

Just as one who listens to a musician singing sweetly testifies—by the joy on his face, his voice, and the clapping of hands or feet tempered to the measure of the melody—that he perceives and approves what is harmonic in the melody; in no other way does <term>sublunary Nature</term>, by a remarkable and mani[fest]...

He identifies two main subjects that respond to these harmonies: the human soul (through instinct and vital faculties) and the "sublunary nature" or soul of the Earth.</summary>

# HARMONICS BOOK IV.
### CHAPTER IV.

...evident in the bowels of the Earth, especially on those days when the wandering stars <note>the planets</note> are harmonically configured toward the Earth by their rays. This testifies to what we have already established: that the Earth, by a certain natural instinct, is no less capable of perceiving the harmonic proportions of angles than it is empowered by a natural faculty—similar to our own vital faculty—to heat and stir up the body of the Earth and the subterranean workshops in the mountains at specific harmonic times. It does this so that they exhale a great abundance of vapors and mists, from which, through the **opposition of the surrounding cold** <note>original: *Antiperistases*; a physical theory where one quality, like cold, intensifies another, like heat, by surrounding and compressing it</note> in the upper air, all kinds of weather phenomena are formed.

<margin>See Chapter VII.</margin>
For this soul must be placed within the body of the Earth, because the harmonic angles of the rays do not exist in any other part of the world except on the Earth; and the works of Nature which follow the configurations of the rays take their origin from the bowels of the Earth and the caverns of the mountains.

IV. The fourth distinction consists in the ways in which different harmonies exist within their subjects.

<margin>Dissimilarity of harmonies and music in their continuity.</margin>
<margin>They are momentary.</margin>
For in Book III, when harmonies were present in song, they were present in the whole of it—that is, during the entire time the song lasted. And although the intervals of the voices, like all things participating in quantity, allow for continuous division, the song did not transition from a lower sound through infinite intermediate points until it reached one that was first consonant or melodic; rather, all those intermediates were passed over with a leap and silence, and every vocal pause occurred on sounds that were melodic in relation to each other. In the same way, in a **Concert**, although infinite intervals lie between the **Octave** <note>original: *Diapason*</note> and the **Major Sixth** <note>original: *Dihex*</note>, the pitch of the voices was not increased continuously through all the intermediates until the Octave became a Sixth. Instead, the voices were carried by a leap from a pure Octave to a pure Sixth, with all intermediates passed over in silence. In organs, one leaped from one pipe to another; in stringed instruments, such as the **Lute** and **Harp**, from one string to another; or if multi-toned strings were used, as in the **Clavichord**, **Mandore**, **Lyre**, or **Cittern**, from one fret to another; and in the human throat, from one ring of the windpipe to another. This is not the case in Book IV. For the harmonies we consider here—as we began to say in the preceding chapter—do not always exist between the angle of two planetary rays and the four right angles <note>360 degrees</note>. Instead, there is a continuous separation of the planets (to whom this motion under the Zodiac circle is given) through all <term>unharmonic</term> <note>original: ἀνάρμοσα (*anarmosa*); intervals that do not form a geometric or musical harmony</note> intervals toward the harmonic ones, the furthest of which is two right angles (a semicircle or opposition); and from there, they return in a backward order through all the again-unmelodic and dissonant intervals back to a conjunction. No leap is made here from one harmonic angle to another—for example, from a **Trine** <note>original: *Trigonus*; a 120-degree aspect</note> to a **Square** <note>original: *Quadratum*; a 90-degree aspect</note>—but the transition from the former to the latter is continuous through all intermediates. Therefore, unmelodic configurations of rays occupy the entire time of the celestial motions, while harmonic configurations of two, or sometimes three or even four planets, mark out only specific moments, with the rest proceeding in incongruity. It is as if seven organ pipes were to emit as many dissonant sounds through a continuous alteration of tension, and by the mutual meeting of these tensions, it would happen that occasionally...

## ON THE CONFIGURATIONS

<margin>CHAPTER IV.</margin>
<margin>Their effect is not, however, instantaneous.</margin>
...two or three were in consonance, with the others being dissonant. Thus, to speak truly and properly, the harmonic configurations themselves do not exist within time, but are perfected in indivisible moments. Yet it is also equally true that the stirrings which arise in Souls from these harmonies are not momentary. For harmonic configurations move things insofar as they are "in the making" <note>original: *in fieri*; a philosophical term for something in the process of becoming</note>, and at the very moment they are perfected, their stimulus slackens again. However, the works of Nature, which are urged on by these stimuli, receive the measurements of their own duration from the conditions of matter; they often last far beyond the moment in which the radiation <note>the alignment of planetary rays</note> is perfected. Thus, a brass machine <note>original: *machina ænea*; likely referring to a cannon</note>, once discharged by the force of ignited gunpowder, grows hot, and does not immediately cool down from that heat once the fuel of the fire is consumed. So too the body of an animal—to provide a more fitting example—is tossed by a fit of fever; although the vital faculty of the soul, which is the author of the inflammation, may cease its effort once its duty is done and the feverish matter is either melted down or cast out from the inner parts toward the exterior, the body is not immediately freed from all heat. For that heat clings to the matter of the body—the flesh, bones, and nerves—for a long time, until it too expires in the course of time.

<margin>Fol. 124. They are mixed with ineffective, incongruous ones.</margin>
These Harmonies are therefore among the number of those which we said above in Chapter II are not subject to a free providence, but are mixed by the necessity of motions with infinite incongruities of their own kind. God ordained minds which, when these harmonies occur, would recognize them. Yet Sublunary Nature <note>the "soul" of the Earth and the environment below the moon</note> is far more successful in discerning these than the ears are in discerning song. For the sense of hearing is not greatly delighted by the Harmony of two voices if five other dissonant voices are shouting over them. Sublunary Nature, accustomed to perpetual incongruous configurations, treats them as nothing because it notices nothing new; but it is so intent upon a harmonic angle as if it were the only one present. Thus, when a Prognosticator <note>an astrologer or weather-forecaster</note> errs several thousand times, it is nevertheless ignored; but if he hits the mark even once, it is deemed worthy of memory and is celebrated in everyone’s conversation.

<margin>They are necessary, not deliberately produced.</margin>
From these things, then, it is given to be understood that Harmonies in voices are established by the will and design of the singer; but in the angles of the rays, they arise by no design of Sublunary Nature, but by pure geometric necessity of the motions. For because two Planets must be separated by the length of a whole semicircle, or 180 Degrees, it necessarily happens that at their certain moments, they are also distant by its harmonic parts—namely, 30, 60, 90, 120, etc. degrees. Therefore, the harmonies of song are sought from within by the singer, while the harmonies of the rays are expected from without by Sublunary Nature; they are observed when they occur, distinguished from the non-harmonic ones (and thus receive their **BEING** <note>original: *E S S E*</note> from it), and are received and applied. In short, the configurations lead the song, and Sublunary Nature dances to the laws of this tune.

<margin>Dissimilarity in the order of causes.</margin>
V. The fifth distinction is to be joined in some way to the first. For the Harmonies of this book and the preceding one differ not only in their breadth <note>referring to the "latitude" or range of the aspects</note>, but also in the order of different respects by which Geometric Figures produce both kinds of Harmonic proportions. For in the third book, the respect of Knowability <note>original: *Scibilitatis*; the capacity for a shape to be constructed and known by the mind</note> was more important, while in this fourth book, the respect of Congruence <note>the way shapes fit together</note> will be more important. But we shall deal with this fifth distinction expressly in Chapter V, in the explanation of the Axioms.

# CHAPTER V.
<margin>CHAPTER V.</margin>

## On the causes of effective Configurations;
### and on their Number and the order of their ranks.

# DEFINITION I.

**T**he term "Configuration" is used for that angle of two rays, each descending from its own planet, at which angle the rays meet here on Earth (which is considered as a mathematical point); or, what amounts to the same thing, it is used for the arc of a Great Circle described in the Zodiac, which arc is the measure of the said angle, or which arc the two planets seem to us Earth-dwellers to terminate and, as it were, mark off by the positions of their bodies.

*Regarding the name, it should first be noted that Ptolemy, in his Tetrabiblos <note>original: *Quadripartito*; Ptolemy's foundational work on astrology</note>, in his Great Work <note>the Almagest</note>, and in his Harmonics, calls this a <term>formation</term> <note>original: Σχηματισμὸς (Schēmatismos)</note>, which the Arabs translated as "Aspects" <note>from the Latin *aspectus*, meaning "look" or "appearance"</note>; as if the "Scheme" or "Formation" were the same as a look or a face. This is also found in our German tongue, which is accustomed to naming the face "das Angeſicht" or "Aspect," and the formations of masks—coverings for the face—as "Geſichter" <note>faces</note>, which the Italians call "Mascaras" <note>masks</note>. However, the term <term>gazes</term> <note>original: προσβλέψεις (prosblepseis)</note> is also found, which we translate as "Aspects" not only from the Arabic, but also which good Latin authors are accustomed to call "Intuitions" <note>original: *Intuitus*</note> and "Gazing Signs." But in this sense, the term applies not so much to the planets as to the signs or twelfth-parts <note>original: *Dodecatemoriis*; the 30-degree divisions of the Zodiac</note> of the Zodiac; for since these have length, they can be turned toward one another in these hollows to a greater or lesser degree. For adjacent signs cannot "gaze" at one another, because their "faces" are not turned toward each other, but are directed side-by-side toward the same region.*

*Next, note that at the same time two planets form an angle at the Earth, they also form other angles in other places in the universe; but nowhere is the angle so significant as on the arc of the circle drawn through their bodies and the Earth, or around the line that connects their bodies, as if rotated around an axis. Outside of these places, their radiations meet at far different angles—whether those be harmonic or incongruous—as they do throughout nearly the rest of the world. Note especially that no angle is formed at either of the planetary bodies themselves. For an angle requires two rays, but every ray is outside the body; no ray exists within the body itself. This must be noted because a physical effect on Earth follows the formation of an angle on Earth; at the time of these Aspects, the matter of rains and other atmospheric phenomena <note>original: *meteororum*; in Kepler's era, "meteors" referred to any weather event or phenomenon in the air</note> "expires" <note>is released or triggered</note>. Thus, we can argue concerning the seat of the cause that moves these weather events: that the cause is not in one planet or the other, nor in some other empty place in the world, but in the Earth itself.*

*Thirdly, the mention that the Earth is considered as a point was not added in vain. For from this it follows that even though there are countless living beings on Earth, and the rays from any planet to them and to the rest of the points on Earth are infinite, the angle of the rays coming from two planets at the same time is nevertheless, for all practical purposes, the same through all points of the Earth—whether at the center, on the surface, or in the caverns of the mountains. All those aspects, though infinite in number, are held as a single aspect; for they are all effectively equal to one another.*

<summary>Kepler defines a planetary "aspect" as the angle formed by two planetary rays meeting at the Earth and argues that the resulting meteorological effects occur on Earth because that is where the geometric harmony is perceived.</summary>

<margin>CHAPTER V.</margin>

## DEFINITION II.

**A** configuration is called **effective** when the rays of two planets form such an angle that it is suitable for stimulating <term>sublunary Nature</term> <note>The natural world below the moon, specifically the Earth and its atmosphere</note> and the lower faculties of living creatures, so that each becomes more active in its own work around the time of the configuration.

*Efficacy is attributed to a configuration, which is formally a <term>being of reason</term> <note>original: "Ens rationis"; an abstract concept or mental construct rather than a physical thing</note>, but this efficacy is not immediate upon the matter itself—as if rain and similar things actually fell from the sky itself, or from the configured planets, which is the foolish belief of the common people. Rather, the efficacy is mediated and objective. For just as objects move the senses—sound moving the hearing but not the eyes, and color moving the sight but not the hearing—so too here: a certain quality of this Relation, which is called a configuration, moves not the senses of the body, but the <term>animal faculty</term> <note>the instinctive part of the soul shared by humans and animals</note>, which is capable of perceiving Reason by instinct without the need for logical discourse. Therefore, the Configuration performs this by the power of the Soul, not by its own power; the Soul is said to be "acted upon," when in truth it is rather the Soul acting upon itself. Afterward, the soul or sublunary Nature, having been moved or stimulated by this influence and reminded of its own nature, rouses itself to draw out from the bowels of the earth the material for every kind of weather. If there were no Soul in the Earth—which we call sublunary Nature—the planets themselves could achieve nothing on Earth, neither by themselves nor through a favorable aspect. For it is an absurd thought, more like a poetic joke or play, to suggest that from the "harmonic intercourse" of two rays—as if from the mating of a male and female—a vapor is conceived as the material for wind or rain. As if, just as seed comes from the substance of parents, so moisture and the other things that expire from the earth could come from the substance of either Harmony (which is a relation), or an Angle (which is a qualitative quantity), or even Light itself (which is a quality and by no means a substance). Just as we say that "nothing comes from nothing" <note>original: "ex nihilo nihil fieri"</note>, so also nothing material can be naturally drawn out from something immaterial. See more on this in Chapter VII.*

## Axiom I.

**T**he arc of the circle of the Zodiac, which is cut off by the side of a congruent and knowable <term>figure</term> <note>a geometric polygon, such as a triangle or square</note> or star, measures the angle of an effective Configuration.

## Axiom II.

**T**he angle of a knowable and congruent figure or star is the measure of the angle of an effective Configuration.

*This whole business rests upon these two Axioms. I have made them into two because there are two probable ways by which Souls and sublunary Natures can come to notice the Configurations that exist at any given time.*

*For they perceive either that figure whose side cuts off an arc from the Zodiac circle (which is the measure of the Configuration or the radiant angle), or they perceive that figure whose basic element is that very angle of the configuration. What the difference is between these figures, and what their mutual relationship is, can be seen from these diagrams, following in order—*

Such circles are, in potential, the **souls** themselves, which are moved by the "aspects" <note>the geometric angles between planets</note>; they are circles, as it were, abstracted from quantity itself and reduced into the narrowness of a qualitative point capable of perceiving directions.

I have placed the two radiating stars outside this circle, one higher than the other, so that I might advise by this visual representation that it makes no difference to the Configuration on Earth whether a planet is high or low in the heavens; one can be many times higher than the other while the same Configuration remains on Earth.

Both are effective because of **Knowability** as well as **Congruence**, though not equally so. ## Proposition I.

The kinship of **Radiations** <note>the rays of influence or "aspects" between planets</note> with the **C**ircle and its arcs is greater than that of Consonances <note>musical harmonies</note>.

<margin>Figure III</margin>
*The foundations of this were laid out in Book III; it should now be rightfully taken into Book IV as an Axiom; however, it is proven thus: 1. Consonances belong to sounds; sounds consist of motions; and their high and low pitches, by which Consonances are expressed, arise from the speed and slowness of motions, as demonstrated in Book III. Yet fast and slow sounds are drawn from strings that have been stretched and struck, not only if the tension is circular, but also—and much more commonly—if it is in a straight line. Therefore, consonances do not immediately relate to the circle and its arcs because of its circular shape, but because of the length of the parts—that is, their mutual proportion. They possess what they possess from the circle even if the circle is broken and stretched out into a straight line. Aspects <note>the angular relationships between planets</note>, on the contrary, by Definition I, are angles measured by the circle and its arcs. They cannot exist otherwise unless the circle remains as it is: namely, insofar as it both has a circular shape and retains it as a whole.*

*2. Not all Consonances were derived from the circle and its parts with equal closeness. It is the opposite with Aspects: for regarding that which corresponds only to a circle, the measurements can in no way have a relationship to straightness.*

## **F**or the efficacy of configurations, the Congruence of figures has more power than Knowability.

In turn, a point has around itself a region for drawing a circle: so too in the **Soul** no operation exists without an imaginative impression; conversely, every internal reception or meditation exists for the sake of external motion; every interior faculty of the soul exists for the sake of those further outward. The very ruler and supreme faculty of the Soul, called the **Mind**, what is it but a **Center**? And the **Reasoning faculty**, what is it but a **Circle**? For just as the center is within and the circle is without, so the Mind remains within itself, while reasoning weaves a certain outer web: and just as the center is the basis of the circle, so the Mind is the basis, fountain, and origin of reasonings. Again, every such faculty of the Soul—both the <term>Intellect</term> <note>The faculty of direct understanding</note> and

<term>Discourse</term> <note>The step-by-step process of logical reasoning</note>, and finally even the <term>Sensitive faculty</term> <note>The ability to perceive through the senses</note>—are a certain **Center**; but the motive faculties of the Soul are the **Circle**: because just as the outer circle is placed around the center, so operation is directed outward, while knowledge and meditation are perfected within. And as the circle relates to the point, so in a certain way does external Action relate to internal Contemplation, and animal motion relate to <term>sensation</term> <note>The act of feeling or perceiving</note>. For the point, because it is everywhere opposite to the circumference, is naturally suited for representing the Passive subject; and the sensitive Soul (or here, the soul capable of perceiving <term>Radiations</term> <note>The geometric "rays" or influences emitted by planets</note>), what else does it do in sensing and perceiving than act as a passive subject? Namely, because it is moved by objects.

<margin>Figure XII.</margin>
By also comparing both comparisons: just as the **center** is the same on both sides, so too is the form of knowledge in some way the same—the ruling mental form and the sensitive form (or that which is analogous to it), which perceives the **Radiations**. Neither of these uses discourse within itself, insofar as it is such a faculty, but rather knows without it. Thus, this nature—I mean the sublunary <note>The world below the moon; the physical Earthly realm</note> or sensitive nature—is a certain thin image of the ruling human Mind: just as that discourse of reason is an image of these actions or operations of the soul; both are a circle.

Therefore, insofar as Souls perceive celestial radiations and are thus moved by them within themselves, let them be points to us; but insofar as they in turn move—that is, insofar as they transfer the perceived <term>harmonies</term> <note>The geometric ratios formed by planetary angles</note> of the radiations into their own works and are stimulated by them to act—they ought to be considered as a circle.

It follows, then, that in as much as the soul knows the **Harmonies** of the rays, it is occupied chiefly with the central figure; but in as much as it acts, stirring up meteors (and similar things in man), it accommodates itself to the circumferential figure. And indeed, in an aspect <note>The specific angle between planets</note>, our first concern is for its efficacy, rather than the manner in which it is perceived by the operating Soul; therefore, the consideration of the circumferential figure is prior to that of the central one.

## Proposition VII.

**In a circumferential figure, Congruity takes precedence over the Knowability of the side; conversely, in a central figure, the Knowability of the side takes precedence over the Congruity of the figure.**

*This proposition pertains to the completion of the matter begun in Proposition III. For although Congruity is more powerful in Book IV than in Book III, and <term>demonstrability</term> <note>The quality of being geometrically provable or "knowable" through construction</note> was more powerful in Book III, this latter quality must not be entirely separated from the constitution of the <term>Aspects</term> <note>The angular distances between planets that create astrological effects</note>. This is because no Congruity lacks its own scientific determination, and thus it depends upon that determination—both of the side and especially of the area enclosed by the sides of the figure; for it is from the angles, in which the aptitude for congruity resides, that the demonstration is summoned.*

*Regarding this proposition itself, the opposite might seem to be true in both cases. For concerning the central figure, its single angle is actually expressed by the rays [of the planets]; in the circumferential figure, no angle is expressed, but only the side to some extent. Since Congruity is a property of angles, it seems it should primarily be considered in the Central figure. For if the <term>sublunary nature</term> <note>The "soul" of the Earth or the guiding intelligence of the realm below the moon, which Kepler believed responded instinctively to planetary geometry</note> perceives the magnitude of the angle which the rays of two planets form at the Earth, it seems it should also be able to perceive the aptitude of that angle for fitting together with others.*

*Conversely, it seems evident that in the circumferential figure, the Knowability of the side should be considered rather than the Congruity of the figure. For the science by which a figure is known—as demonstrated in Book I—consists in equality: either of the side with an <term>effable</term> <note>original: "effabili"; meaning a length that can be expressed as a rational number or a square root relative to the diameter</note> part of the diameter; or of the square of the side with an effable part of the square of the diameter; or of the area of the figure with the same; or in another connection and determination of either the side, its square, or the area, to the diameter or its square. Therefore, granted that the sublunary Nature has a sense of the circle of the Zodiac—that sensible circle standing outside, which it examines against the idea of the abstract intellectual circle it has innate or co-created within itself—then it surely follows that, in the order of nature, it first feels how great an arc of the Zodiac is marked out by two planets, and how great a straight line is subtended by it. It perceives the quality of that line: whether it is effable in length, or only in the power of its square; or whether with some other line it makes an effable sum of squares and an effable rectangle (on which property the Effability of the area is founded). These things, I say, seem to become known to the sublunary Nature first in the order of nature, because the side exists before the figure described by the multiplication of that side. Only later, when the whole figure has been described in the circle of the Zodiac, do its angles become apparent, along with their magnitude, and whether they are among the "congruous" ones, and whether the figure concurs at all angles toward the same species of congruity, and whether the congruity is continuable. Briefly: congruity is an affection of the angles, knowability is an affection of the sides. Where, therefore, the angle of a figure becomes known before the side, there the parts of Congruity seem to be prior and more powerful than those of Knowability; where it becomes known later, they are secondary. But in a figure reaching to the center, the angle becomes known first; while in a figure described on the surface (formed, for instance, by only two planets), the side becomes known first. Therefore, it seems rightly done if in the central figure, more account is taken of congruity, and in the superficial figure, more account is taken of knowability.*

<margin>CHAPTER V.</margin>

*These arguments brought against our proposition must therefore be refuted; and by that same effort, the order of the properties—*Congruity* and *Knowability*—must be strengthened by true arguments.*

*First, although it is true that in a central figure <note>A "central figure" refers to an aspect where the angle is formed at the Earth, the center of the planetary system</note> a single angle is formed by the rays of two planets, it does not follow from this that the mind, in perceiving the size of the angle, perceives the *Congruity* of the figure to which that angle belongs as being prior in the order of nature. The reason is clear: Congruity, insofar as it belongs to a single angle and a certain number of its equals in a flat space, is too general. For there are infinite forms of angles that fit together in this way, and they are always more numerous as the individual angles are smaller. Therefore, this is not that *Congruity* which we discussed in Book II, which does not happen to angles in isolation, but to whole figures because of their angles—and not to single figures, but to several joined together.*

*Thus, the objection is not only dissolved but even turned back on itself. For what had been claimed regarding the Circumferential figure, we can with equal right claim regarding the Central figure: that the *Congruity* we have proposed here is posterior <note>Occurring later in the logical sequence</note> to *Knowability*. Consequently, by the opponent's own admission, the role of Knowability must be more important than that of Congruity. For a figure must first be formed before the whole can "congruat" <note>Original: "congruere," meaning to fit together or tile a surface</note>. Now, unless the side of a figure is "knowable" <note>In Kepler’s geometry, a "knowable" (scibile) side is one that can be constructed using only a straightedge and compass</note>, the figure cannot be formed. For even if it is true that, given one angle of a figure formed by the rays of two planets at the center, the total number of sides is given (and through them the aptitude of the whole figure for fitting together), and even if the nature of the side does not enter into this demonstration, that single angle of the figure is not actually "given"—that is, it is not recognized as the angle of a congruent figure—except through a knowable side. Therefore (in the order of nature), the Soul knows the side before it recognizes that a congruent angle has been given to it.*

<margin>Fol. 136. Figure IV. Figure III.</margin>

*But if we compare both figures here, the side or area of the central figure is actually less "given" by the act of radiation itself than the side of the circumferential figure. For the rays themselves always determine the latter, whereas they do not always determine the former, except in certain figures, such as in the <term>Trigon</term> <note>The astrological aspect of 120 degrees, forming an equilateral triangle</note>, because each of the sides of the circumferential <gloss>*</gloss> <note>The gloss asterisk likely clarifies that "circumferential" refers to the angle's placement on the circle's edge</note> angle subtends an arc equal to the intercepted arc. Thus, the central figure is further removed from the act of knowing than the circumferential one; consequently, the notification of *Congruity* is also more remote. The objection, however, relied on the opposite: as if Central Congruity were closer to knowledge than Circumferential Congruity.*

*Furthermore, if the size of the angle is perceived, why would it be perceived except by its own measure—that is, by the arc of that circle which is described from the point of the proposed angle (which is the Earth)? But it is not primarily perceived by that circle which is circumscribed around the central figure and passes through the Earth. Therefore, in perceiving the size of the angle of a central figure, the Soul must exert that power by which it is a circle, not that power by which it is a tiny point which the angle reaches. Yet, by that same pattern of its own circular essence, it also perceives the side of the circumferential figure and its arc, and it does so first. Only afterwards, by doubling this arc, does the arc of the smaller circle emerge (the one circumscribed around the central figure and drawn through the center of the first circle); this arc serves for the inscription of the central figure into a circle. For the same order that exists in reasoning also exists in instinct. Thus, it is demonstrated once again that the path toward perceiving the central figure is longer, and likewise for its *Congruity*. Therefore, the objection subverts itself, since it placed the advantage in prior perception.*

# ON THE HARMONICS, BOOK IV.

*...of two things, where one is the cause of the other, that which is the cause might also move a third thing even more strongly. For according to the capacity of the soul which is to be moved, the cause often has less power over it than the effect; as here, the sublunary soul <note>Kepler’s term for the vital spirit of the Earth, which he believed perceived and reacted to the geometric patterns of the planets.</note>, insofar as it is perceptive, is moved more by the **knowability** <term>scibilitas: the quality of a shape being constructible by a straightedge and compass</term> of the central figure; but insofar as it is operative <note>The "operative" faculty is the soul's power to act or create, rather than just perceive.</note>, it is moved more by the **congruity** <term>congruentia: the property of shapes to tile together perfectly to fill a plane</term> of the circumferential figure.*

<margin>Earlier, Proposition VI.</margin>
*Indeed, my own arguments for proving the proposition are these: for we have adopted the principle that the **center** is a certain idea of the Theoretical mind, or intellect; while the **circumference** belongs to the Practical or operative faculty. For just as the center of a circle is the basis and origin, so is meditation the basis of action. Therefore, a figure which extends its angle to the center—that is, to the Earth where the Soul sits—is a perceiving figure, extending itself as if for the purpose of knowing and judging, since the center represents the tribunal of knowledge. Therefore, in the central figure, knowledge <note>Referring to "Knowability" or the intellectual grasp of the shape's proportions.</note> ought rather to be considered; notwithstanding that it is prepared through the circle as an instrument, as was said a little earlier.*

*Conversely, a figure which arranges its angles on the circumference applies itself more to imitating and expressing itself in the work of the Soul, as if concurring with the "idea" <note>Kepler uses "idea" in the Platonic sense: a divine blueprint or archetype.</note> of works. And yet, congruity rather than knowability possesses the idea of sensible works and constructions; for it follows whole figures, whereas the side by which a figure is known is merely its element. For this reason, in the circumferential figure, congruity is rather to be respected than knowability.*

*The second argument for this second part rests on the same consideration of the Soul. That for which all other things exist is superior. But the configurations of the planets are perceived for the sake of the work of the sublunary Nature, and thus also the human Soul and the lower faculties; that is, they are perceived so that they may be expressed in work. Therefore, the dignity of the motor <note>The "motor faculty" is the part of the soul responsible for physical movement and change.</note> faculty is greater in this business. But the knowability of the circumferential figure serves perception, while Congruity serves operation, as shown so far: therefore, the congruity of the circumferential figure also excels its own knowability.*

# Proposition VIII.

**A**n arc of a circle which is formed by an **incongruent** figure <note>A shape that cannot tile a flat surface perfectly.</note> grants no **Effectiveness** to the radiations of the two planets that determine that arc.

*For if congruity is the most powerful cause of Effectiveness (per Propositions III, IV, and VII), then if this is lacking, the cause that is secondary in this context—knowability—will not be sufficient. For although knowability prevails over congruity in a **Central** figure (per the other part of Prop. VII), conversely, the **circumferential** figure is more powerful than the central one (per Prop. VI). And in that circumferential figure, congruity is more powerful (per the first part of Prop. VII). Therefore, the congruity of the circumferential figure still prevails over the knowability of the central figure.*

Behold the reason why, although "knowable" figures are infinite (though of different degrees), the **Aspects** <note>Astrological angles such as the square (90°), trine (120°), or sextile (60°).</note> are nevertheless few.

# AXIOM III.

**A**rcs of a circle whose figures possess more and more powerful degrees of congruity and knowability also receive more effective configurations.

<summary>Kepler argues that "Congruity" (the ability of shapes to tile) is the primary reason why only a few specific planetary angles (aspects) have any physical or astrological effect on the Earth's soul. He distinguishes between the "Theoretical" mind, which values how a shape is known, and the "Practical" soul, which values how shapes fit together to produce work.</summary>

<margin>CHAPTER V.</margin>
If the first two axioms are consistent with the truth, this one will be as well: because that which causes a thing to be what it is, when intensified, makes the thing even more so. <note>original: "propter quod unumquodque est tale; illo intenso, istud etiam magis erit tale." This is a standard scholastic axiom: the cause of a quality must possess that quality more intensely than the effect.</note> Understand it in this way: that in the circumferential figure <note>A shape whose vertices touch the circle's edge.</note>, the comparison of the degrees of **Congruity** <term>congruentia: the property of shapes to tile together perfectly to fill a plane</term> is primary; in the central figure <note>A shape whose angles meet at the center of the circle.</note>, the degrees of **Knowability** <term>scibilitas: the quality of a shape being constructible by a straightedge and compass</term> take precedence; and finally, the parts of the circumferential figure are more powerful.

## Proposition IX.

**E**ffective configurations <note>Often called "aspects" in astrology, these are specific angular distances between planets.</note> are those which intercept the following arcs of the Zodiac circle:
180 Degrees: Opposition ☍, from the Diameter of the circle: as in Figure I.
90 Degrees: Quadrature <note>Square</note> □, from the Tetragon <note>Square</note>: as in Figure II.
120 Degrees: Trine △ and 60 Degrees: Sextile ⚹, from the Triangle and Hexagon: as in Figures III and IV.
45 Degrees: Octile or Semisquare, and 135 Degrees: Trioctile or Sesquisquare ⚼ from the Octagon and its Star: as in Figures V and VI.
30 Degrees: Semisextile ⚺, and 150 Degrees: Quincunx, from the Dodecagon and its Star: as in Figures VII and VIII.
72 Degrees: Quintile <note>glyph: ☿-like</note>, and 108 Degrees: Tridecile or Sesquiquintile: from the Pentagon and the Decagon-star: as in Figures IX and X.
144 Degrees: Biquintile ⚝, and 36 Degrees: Semiquintile or Decile: from the Pentagon-star and the Decagon: as in Figures XI and XII.

*That these figures are **Knowable** and demonstrable was shown in Book I; and that they are **Congruous**, in Book II. That the configurations of arcs expressed by such figures are effective follows from the first two axioms previously stated.*

## Proposition X.

**T**he first and strongest degree of effectiveness of the Aspects is that of the Conjunction ☌ and the Opposition ☍.

<margin>Commonly used symbols.</margin>
*For in a Conjunction, two rays join into the same line and descend from the same direction; in an Opposition ☍, though they descend from different directions, they nonetheless become parts of a single continuous line. This is indeed the most perfect **Congruity** and the very principle of all congruity. Thus, since a point marked on the circumference of a circle represents a conjunction, and the Diameter represents the opposition, these are certainly the principles and the measures of all knowledge in this branch of science; for every straight line in a circle is contained within knowledge by demonstrative determination through either the length or the power <note>Likely referring to the geometric "power" or square of the line.</note> of the Diameter: as in Book...*

<summary>Kepler defines the specific angular distances (aspects) between planets that create "harmonies," basing their effectiveness on the geometric shapes (like squares and triangles) they represent. He identifies the Conjunction and Opposition as the most powerful because they align planets along a single straight line.</summary>

## Proposition XI.
<margin>CHAPTER V.</margin>

**T**he second degree in the Efficacy of Aspects is the Square □.
Indeed, in the Square many prerogatives coincide. The first is that the central figure <note>A figure formed by the positions of the planets relative to the center of the Earth.</note> is similar to the circumferential figure <note>The shape inscribed within the circle of the Zodiac.</note>: therefore, whatever degrees of **Congruity** <term>congruentia: the ability of a shape to tile a surface without gaps</term> and **Knowability** <term>scibilitas: the quality of being constructible with a straightedge and compass</term> it possesses, they are understood to be somehow doubled compared to the other Aspects. For just as the Square is the first figure after the Opposition <note>The 180-degree line.</note> to expand from the thinness of a line into a certain width or surface area, so the other Aspects depart from the identity of the Square's figures into a different form. Since, therefore, in physical matters a "united power" <note>original: "unita virtus." A common philosophical idea that concentrated or unified forces are stronger.</note> is more powerful, there will also be a greater degree of strength in this ideal and objective impression where the figures in distinct places—namely, one central and one circumferential—are of the same species.

Secondly, as for Congruity, it is most perfect and all-encompassing in the Square (or Tetragon). For this figure is congruent with itself in a solid to form the **Cube**, which is the measure of all solidity. It is congruent in the simplest way, requiring only three angles to meet <note>at a vertex in 3D</note>. It is also congruent with itself in a plane, with four angles meeting <note>to fill 360 degrees</note>. Furthermore, it is congruent in a solid with the Triangle, Pentagon, Hexagon, Octagon, and Decagon in various ways to form solid figures <note>the Platonic and Archimedean solids</term>. It is congruent with all of these, and additionally with the Dodecagon and Icosigon <note>20-sided figure</note> to some extent, in paving a plane. In this property of congruity, the Square is surpassed by no other shape.

Thirdly, the area of the Square is **expressible** <note>original: "effabilis." Meaning it has a rational relationship to the circle's diameter.</note>, which is a principle of a certain singular and distinguished Congruity in the plane; so that a certain number of the areas of this figure equals a certain number of the squares of the diameter. Thus, the figures are not only congruent among themselves by their angles and sides, but also, through their specific lines, with the sides of the square of the diameter. In this property, the Square aspect has only the Semisextile <note>30 degrees</note> as a partial partner. See Book II.

Fourthly, the degree of "knowledge of the side" is not ignoble, as it is **expressible in power** <note>original: "effabile potentiâ." A Greek mathematical term (dynamis) meaning that while the side itself might be an irrational number, its square is a rational number.</note>. In this degree, it excels all other figures except the Hexagon. Yet, it does not yield its place to the Hexagon for that reason, since Knowability is not to be compared to Congruity, as was explained above; and indeed, the accumulation of prerogatives serves to increase Efficacy, according to Axiom III of this book.
