## Proposition XIII.

The **f**ourth Degree in the Efficacy of Configurations consists of the Quintile <note>An aspect of 72°, or 1/5 of the circle.</note>, the Bi-quintile <note>An aspect of 144°, or 2/5 of the circle.</note>, and the Quincunx <note>Usually 150° (5/12), but here discussed in relation to the dodecagonal or 12-sided star systems.</note>.

*For these share a common <term>congruence</term> <note>The ability of geometric shapes to fit together to fill a plane or form a solid without gaps.</note> of the primary figures alone in a plane, though not of each individual species with itself; rather, the first two species are congruent with each other mutually, and the last with others related to it. The first two aspects excel because their figures—the Pentagon and its star <note>The pentagram.</note>—congru even in the solid state, forming two regular solid figures <note>The Dodecahedron and the Icosahedron.</note>; by this nobility, they almost join their aspects to the Trine and the Square. The Dodecagonal star <note>A 12-pointed star polygon.</note> does not congru in the solid state. But in turn, the Dodecagonal figure excels in plane congruence, which it can continue into infinity; whereas the others cannot be continued far without an irregular mixture. See all these matters in Book II.*

*As far as the <term>knowability</term> <note>original: "scibilitas." In Kepler's geometry, this refers to whether a polygon's side can be constructed using only a compass and straightedge (Euclidean constructability).</note> of the sides in central figures is concerned: here also the sides of the Decagon <note>10-sided polygon.</note>, the Tridecile <note>Likely referring to the 3/10 division or 108°.</note>, and the Dodecagon <note>12-sided polygon.</note> stand in a middle position. In this class, they are central between the side of the preceding Triangle and the sides of the Pentagon and the Pentagonal star, which are the central figures in the following class. For it was demonstrated in Book I that, in the hierarchy of knowledge, the Decagonal side is prior to the Pentagonal side, and the Tridecile side is prior to the Pentagonal star side. Therefore, Knowability leads to the same conclusion as Congruence, through Proposition VII; which was specifically brought forward for the sake of this demonstration, so that the Decile or Tridecile would not be preferred over the Quintile and Biquintile. If, however, someone wishes to seek Knowability in the circumference rather than the central figure, no less than Congruence: although it must be confessed that in this way the Decile would be preferred to the Quintile, and the Tridecile to the Biquintile; yet let him remember that the primary roles belong to Congruence, as...*

# Proposition XIV.

**T**he fifth, last, and weakest Degree of aspects is the Decile and Tridecile, the Octile and Trioctile.

I have made the fifth place for the Decile <note>36°, or 1/10 of a circle.</note> and Tridecile <note>108°, or 3/10 of a circle.</note> (**Maestlin** <note>Michael Maestlin (1550–1631), Kepler's astronomy professor.</note> **calls them the Semiquintile and Sesquiquintile**), which I have omitted from the Ephemerides until now. With these I have associated the Octile <note>45°, or 1/8 of a circle.</note> and Trioctile <note>135°, or 3/8 of a circle.</note> (also called the Semi-square and Sesqui-square); which the calendar-makers have snatched up from my own suggestion and some authority of Ptolemy, but too hotly and without enough consideration. Both must therefore be proven: first, that these four are weaker than the Quintile and Biquintile; second, that the Decile and Tridecile are only very slightly stronger than the Octile and Trioctile.

Since, therefore, our Propositions place the chief momentum of Efficacy in the <term>congruence</term> <note>The ability of shapes to fit together perfectly.</note> of the primary figure—that is, the figure on the circumference—it is manifest that the Pentagon and its star congru with the other figures of their own species to form a perfect solid, as was just said; they also congru beautifully with each other to pave a plane. Conversely, the Decagon and Octagon with their stars cannot congru in a solid, each with others of its own species. To be sure, the Decagon and Octagon do congru, but not with all others of their own kind; their stars, however, begin a certain congruence in a solid but do not complete it. Even in a plane their congruence is less noble, because they do not perform mutual services—any figure with its own solitary star, as the Pentagon does with its own—but the Octagon comes into partnership with the Tetragon <note>A square.</note> and with those stars of its, a congruence...

*I have examined all the cases to ensure my arguments were sound; lest the number of aspects becomes too great, which would create confusion in practical experience. Therefore, one must stop at the Square, the Quintile, and the Biquintile <note>These are astrological "aspects" or angles between planets: 90°, 72°, and 144° respectively.</note>, and not proceed to their four derivatives of the lowest degree, which are extremely weak; although the first proposition would technically allow them. If, however, these do not satisfy, and if the dignity of the first Proposition is so great that all objections are removed: well then, let everyone be free as far as I am concerned to consider these Aspects also, especially at those times when all the others are missing. For it is only right that experience be heard testifying on these as well; for it was experience that first gave credit to the others, even before the underlying reasons were known.*

## Proposition XV.

**T**here are certain configurations that are ambiguous, hovering between effective and ineffective: namely, the Arc of 24 Degrees derived from the <term>Fifteen-sided polygon</term> <note>original: "Pentekædecagono."</note>, and the Arc of 18 Degrees from the <term>Twenty-sided polygon</term> <note>original: "Icosigono."</note>.

For these figures are "knowable" <note>In Kepler's terms, "knowable" means they can be constructed using a compass and straightedge according to Euclidean geometry.</note>, but the former is so only improperly, and the latter at a remote degree, as was demonstrated in Book I. They are also congruent <note>Capable of tiling or fitting together without gaps.</note>, but the former does not fit at all angles equally in the same form of <term>Congruence</term>; the latter fits at all angles, but in a <term>Congruence</term> that plainly cannot be continued to fill a plane, as shown in Book II. Therefore, there is a certain <term>Rudiment</term> of <term>Effectiveness</term>—a sort of attempt at influence—but the actual effect is either non-existent or imperfect.

These figures contain many stars; the former has five, whose sides span these arcs of the circle: 48°, 96°, 112°, 156°, and 168°. The latter has four, whose sides span arcs of 54°, 126°, 162°, and 171°. But since these stars have hollow [re-entrant] angles into which other congruent angles cannot be received (in the way that the hollow angles of the <term>Pentagonal</term> and <term>Decagonal</term> stars receive <term>Pentagonal</term> angles, or the <term>Octagonal</term> star receives the angle of a <term>Square</term>, and the <term>Twelve-sided</term> star receives the angle of a <term>Triangle</term>), there remains for them only the <term>Congruence</term> of the acute points, which we call <term>Rays</term>. They are therefore of less value than their own parent figures.

The title of one was *Response to the Objections of Röslin*, and the other was *The Third Man in the Middle* <note>original: "Tertius interveniens"; in this famous work, Kepler argued for a "middle way" between total belief in and total rejection of astrology.</note>. In the latter, I defended the truth of the **Aspects** <term>Aspects</term> <note>The specific angular relationships (like 60°, 90°, etc.) between planets that were believed to exert physical influence on Earth.</note>, and in the former, I asserted the manner of the cause by which the **Aspects** are effective. And so, learned men have testified in letters written to me that, at last, astrologers are being taught a purer philosophy by me.

In all these booklets, I mentioned the kinship that exists between musical consonances and the **Aspects**. However, in the first one, I was still stuck regarding the number of **Aspects**—observing some as "spurious" or certainly weak among the principal ones, and completely neglecting others that were stronger. But in the German works, I began to uncover these defects in my speculation; I recently decided to repeat this with a somewhat fuller declaration, as the topic required, in the *Introduction to the Ephemerides* <note>original: "Prolegomenis Ephemeridum"; "Ephemerides" are tables of predicted planetary positions.</note>, on pages 33, 34, 35, and 36. Those things which could not be explained more expansively there due to the required brevity, I will now supply here, as the order of the work demands.

The axiom which I used in the year 1606, and which I took up to examine and refute in the cited passage of the *Ephemerides*, was this: *God the Creator either took the laws for ordering the Aspects from the harmonies of song below the Octave, described in Book III; or He tempered the human ear, the judge of those harmonies, to match the celestial **Aspects**.* If this axiom were true in every respect, there would have to be exactly as many aspects in number as there are harmonies up to the **Octave** <note>original: "Diapason"</note>. For the **Sextile** corresponds to the **Minor Third**, the **Quintile** to the **Major Third**, the **Square** to the **Fourth** <note>original: "Diatessaron"</note>, the **Trine** to the **Fifth** <note>original: "Diapente"</note>, the **Sesquiquadrate** to the **Minor Sixth**, the **Biquintile** to the **Major Sixth**, and the **Opposition** to the **Octave**. This is because if you take away from a whole string a portion equal to the portion of the circle that any aspect takes away, the remainder of the string creates with the whole that specific Consonance which is assigned to each Aspect here.

Since, therefore, this seven-fold number of harmonies—or rather of harmonic divisions, which each harmony follows below the Octave—is certain and demonstrative (no less than the five-fold number of **Regular Solids** <note>The five Platonic Solids</note> is in Geometry, as was shown in Book III, Chapter II), the method for demonstrating the number of **Aspects** would therefore have been easy and ready through this adopted Axiom. There would have been no need for the laborious apparatus of new axioms in this fourth book.

And indeed, if meteorological observations had supported this set of seven Aspects exactly, I would have rested content with the axiom stated above, nor would I have been very concerned about those objections that could be raised from the origin of harmonic ratios or from the consideration of metaphysical causes. But because it has frequently been discovered that sublunary nature <note>The Earth and its atmosphere.</note> is also stimulated by the **Semisextile** <note>original: "Semisexto"; an angle of 30°.</note>, which intercepts a twelfth part of the circle, even though when a twelfth part is taken away from a string, the remainder—of eleven parts...

<margin>1. In forming a concordance, the Remainder of the circle counts; it does not count in forming an Aspect.</margin>
> *The cause, therefore, why there are not as many Aspects as there are Harmonic sections in Music—as I had believed up until the year 1608—is this: because Music draws some of its septenary principles <note>Principles related to the number seven.</note> from the very straightness of the string; whereas the circle, in which we mark the Aspects, returns into itself; nor can another circle be made from the Remainder of the Zodiac, as can be done from the remainder of a string.*

These are the words of the said *Introduction* on page 35, which are to be explained as follows. For as was said in Chapter IV of this book, Harmonic sections arise in one way, and **Aspects** in another, even though both arise from the same circle. For in Book III, the Axioms were so arranged that any string, or part of a string—whether long or short—could again be compared to the whole circle, no less than the whole or longest string was compared to that same circle. But in this fourth book, an arc of a circle (whether larger or smaller than a semicircle) could not be compared to the whole.

I shall speak more clearly: in whatever ways a circle is divided demonstratively <note>Through geometric proof.</note>, all those ways can be transferred to a straight line—that is, a string—and any part of it. But the demonstrative division of the whole circle (for example, into three or five parts) cannot therefore also be transferred to any arc of it: which is sufficiently demonstrated in the final propositions of the first book. The cause lies in the figure; for a straight line remains a straight line, whether it is cut short or lengthened; but a truncated circle does not remain a circle. Therefore, a proportional section exists for any two straight lines, and it exists for any two circles, but it does not exist for any two arcs of a single circle. 

These things are applied to the proposal in this way: If a string is divided into eight parts by the demonstrative division of the circle, one-eighth harmonizes with the whole, and three-eighths also harmonize, because one-eighth of a circle can be demonstratively cut off, as can three-eighths. The same demonstrative determination is also among the causes why the **Octile** <term>Octile</term> <note>A 45-degree aspect (1/8 of a circle).</note> and **Trioctile** <term>Trioctile</term> <note>A 135-degree aspect (3/8 of a circle).</note> are effective. But this is the distinction: in the former case, a harmonic <term>SECTION</term> is not yet established unless the Remainder—the seven-eighths and five-eighths—also harmonize both with the whole of eight parts, and with the cut parts (7 with 1, and 5 with 3). And yet, the demonstrative determination of part 1 and part 3 does not grant to their remainders (7 and 5) that they themselves should be consonant: for 5 is indeed consonant, but 7 is dissonant. Therefore, the section of the whole 8 into 5 and 3 is harmonic, but in 7 and 1 it is not harmonic. From where, then, does the Remainder 5 get its consonance with the whole 8, and the Remainder 7 its dissonance from it? Surely from this: because a circle divided into 5 has a subtended line <note>A chord connecting two points on the circle.</note> for two-fifths that is demonstrative; hence it is that a string divided into five (as in this proposed part of a string of 8) harmonizes with the part that is 2 portions long; and therefore also with...

In contrast, a circle divided into 7 does not produce a chord demonstrative of a single seventh part; therefore, that Remainder of the chord which has 7 is dissonant with 1, and likewise with 2, 4, and 8. Observe how the harmonic section of the whole 8 into 3 and 5 has only one consonance from the Octagon <note>The 8-sided figure</note>, while the other comes from the Pentagon <note>The 5-sided figure</note>. Indeed, it even has a third consonance from another figure, namely from the Decagon <note>The 10-sided figure</note>. For Part 3 would not harmonize with the Remainder 5, unless it first harmonized with its double, 10; and this is because, in a circle divided into 10, the line subtending three-tenths is demonstrative <note>original: "demonstrativa"; meaning it can be geometrically constructed using only a compass and straightedge.</note>. This coupling of multiple figures, however, has no place in the circle and its parts. For if you first inscribed a regular Octagon in the whole circle, and then supposed you could divide the arc that contains three-eighths into five parts (although it is impossible to do so demonstratively), certainly a Pentagon could not be inscribed according to those divisions; it would become highly irregular, more like a hexagon, since an arc has two boundaries before its division. Since, therefore, there is a vast difference in Remainders between the chord on one hand and the circle on the other, it is clear that unless we proceed from the circle to the straight line as well, no account can be taken of the Remainder.

Yet an Aspect is an angle, the measure of which is not any straight line, but an arc of the circle described from the point where the rays meet. Therefore, the circle does not measure the Aspect, nor form it, nor render it effective by reason of the Remainder, but only by reason of the arc intercepted by the aspect. If it is not by reason of the Remainder, then it is not by reason of the harmonic section of the chord arising from that division of the circle—because a harmonic section cannot be defined without a Remainder. And thus, that axiom is overthrown: that the harmonic proportions of song are the causes of the Aspects. Nor does it follow that because the **Sesquiquadrate** <term>Sesquiquadrate</term> <note>An aspect of 135 degrees, or three-eighths of a circle. Kepler also calls it the "Trioctile."</note> corresponds to the harmonic section that generates the "soft third" <note>The minor third in music.</note> and is effective, that its effectiveness comes from the harmonic section of the circle as such.

But this much is true, as the Introduction states: *There is a great kinship between Harmonies and Aspects; both genres have the same origin from the noble figures that can be inscribed in a circle.* That is to say, the "knowability" <term>Knowability</term> <note>original: "scibilitas"; the property of being geometrically constructible.</note> of the line subtending three-eighths of the circle is among the elements from which both the harmonic section in Music and the effective Aspect in Physics are constituted. I speak here on the hypothesis that the mere "knowability" of a figure would suffice for effectiveness, just as it suffices for the simple consonance of a Part with the Whole. For if we are to be precise, there is also this distinction: in Consonances, "Knowability" carries the most weight; but in Aspects, the **Congruence** <term>Congruence</term> <note>original: "Congruentia"; the ability of geometric shapes to fit together perfectly to fill a space or form a solid.</note> of figures excels. The **Semisquare** <note>45 degrees</note> and **Sesquiquadrate** <note>135 degrees</note> are effective not only because the side of the Octagon and its star-form are "knowable," but also, and most importantly, because the Octagon and its star are congruent figures.

It is because Music does not form the Aspects; rather, **Geometry** forms both kinds, though by different laws for each. In Music, anything derived from a "noble" figure <note>A "noble" figure is a regular polygon that can be constructed with a compass and straightedge.</note> (which possesses singular privileges in Geometry) is harmonic, and in Meteorology <note>Kepler uses "meteorology" to refer to the effects of planets on Earth's weather and sublunary nature.</note>, it is effective. 

But Meteorology and Music are like different nations originating from the same homeland of Geometry. One of these—the Harmonic proportions discussed in Book III—acknowledged the circle as its homeland and credited it with its origin, no less than the Aspects do here. Yet, having departed as if from the circle, they led away their own colony and propagated themselves living by their own laws. The Aspects, remaining within the circle of their homeland, use no laws other than those which the roundness of the circle prescribes for them, taken from the **Regular Congruent plane figures** inscribed in the circle.

# ON THE HARMONIES, BOOK IV

<margin>CHAPTER VI.</margin>

...regarding the fourths: through musical generation <note>The process of creating new intervals by adding or subtracting existing ones.</note> (by the addition of one **Octave** <term>Diapason</term>), a "Part" is born: the three-eighths. With all due respect to the senatorial class <note>Kepler uses social ranks to describe the hierarchy of geometric shapes.</note>, this part is permitted to marry a commoner named "five-eighths." The conditions of its birth are the same: its mother is the Remainder (namely, four-fifths), and its father is a patrician, the one-fifth, whose geometric nobility comes from the **Pentagon** <term>Quinquangulum</term>.

The twelfth part of the circle, however, holds the right of citizenship in Music. Its subtended line <note>The straight line connecting two points on a circle; the "chord" of the arc.</note> possesses a primary nobility in Geometry, earned both by its own merit (because of its **Congruence** <note>The ability of a shape to tile a plane perfectly, like tiles on a floor.</note>) and inherited from its parents. These parents are the noble figures of the Hexagon and the Triangle; by doubling their sides, the **Dodecagon** <term>Dodecagonus</term> is created. The Dodecagon is even more excellent than its parents because its area can be expressed as a rational number. Yet, because this twelfth part has a wife—the Remainder of eleven-twelfths—who is of "foreign" origin in Music and Geometry alike, she traces her lineage to the **Hendecagon** <term>Undecangulum</term> <note>An 11-sided figure.</note>. This is a figure that cannot be constructed by ruler and compass, and therefore it cannot obtain the right of citizenship. Consequently, the husband has no right to sit on the "Council of Seven" <note>The seven primary harmonic divisions of the string.</note> in Music to establish the number of divisions on the **monochord** <term>monochordum</term> <note>A one-stringed instrument used for measuring musical ratios.</note>.

By contrast, in **Meteorology** <term>Meteorologia</term> <note>For Kepler, this refers to the study of how planetary aspects influence Earth's atmosphere and weather.</note>, the custom is different. Here, whoever is noble either by birth or by merit (namely, by "Knowability" or **Congruence**) carries the most authority; the others flit about like shadows. No account is taken of the "wives" <note>The "remainder" of the circle is ignored in astrology, whereas in music, both the interval and the remaining part of the string must be "noble."</note>.

In this context, therefore, the **Octile** <term>Octilis</term> <note>A 45-degree aspect.</note>, the **Semi-square** <term>Sequadrus</term>, and the **Sesqui-square** <term>Sesquadrus</term> <note>A 135-degree aspect.</note>, having set aside their rights in Music (because they have "ignoble" subtended lines), are considered part of the common people. They have no power unless the magistrates are absent and the burden of business is pressing. That is to say: if for a long time there were no primary **Aspects** <term>Aspectus</term>, these minor Aspects might perhaps do something—especially if the Earth is full of moisture. In such a case, the Earth sometimes relieves itself without any stimulus from the planetary configurations. But because the primary aspects are usually present, the "sublunary nature" <note>The Earthly realm, which Kepler believes responds to the stars.</note> is so occupied by them that it does not feel these minor stimuli.

The **Decile** <term>Decilis</term> <note>A 36-degree aspect.</note> and **Tridecile** <term>Tridecilis</term> <note>A 108-degree aspect.</note> certainly come from an illustrious family—the tenfold division of the circle, which employs the "Divine Proportion" <note>The Golden Ratio.</note>. However, they have not made their lineage famous through their deeds (because they do not fit together perfectly in three dimensions). Nor are they the heads of their family. Even if they have some power (since they fit together to some extent in a flat plane, and even with others in three dimensions), all that power is snatched away from them by the "aristocrats" of other families, or their glory is dimmed by a greater splendor. For if Nature has been sufficiently stirred by an **Aspect** <term>Aspectus</term> of 30 degrees, and the Earth is sufficiently exhausted by it, very little work is left for a neighboring, weaker aspect of 36 degrees to perform.

Finally, the **Semisextile** <term>Semisextus</term> of 30 degrees possesses an excelling nobility from the **Dodecagon** <term>Dodecagonus</term>; it is both eminently "Knowable" and **Congruent**. The "foreign marriage" which previously blocked its path to honors in Music does not hinder it in any way in Meteorology. After this Dodecagon, the figures that follow—whether in the three "secret" families (Square, Triangle, and Pentagon) or in the fifteen-sided mixture—are all of inferior nobility. Furthermore, they have absolutely no merits of their own (in terms of **Congruence**). Therefore, by the inviolable law of the state, they are barred from the honors and the power of establishing **Aspects** <term>Aspectus</term>.

<summary>Kepler uses a social hierarchy metaphor to explain why certain geometric divisions of a circle function as astrological aspects (influencing weather) but not as musical harmonies. He concludes that while music requires both parts of a divided string to be "noble" (constructible), astrology only requires the aspect itself to be noble.</summary>

<keywords>harmony, geometry, astrology, dodecagon, pentagon, musical intervals, planetary aspects, meteorology, congruence, divine proportion</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Kepler’s complex ranking of astrological "Aspects" (the angles between planets). He is explaining the geometric reasons why some angles, like the Sextile or Square, are more "powerful" or "noble" than others. He uses the concepts of "Congruence" (how shapes tile together) and "Effability" (whether a shape's dimensions can be expressed as a rational number) to justify these hierarchies.</meta>

# ON THE CONFIGURATIONS

<margin>CHAPTER VI.</margin>

From these things it appears what I said in the Introduction to the *Ephemerides*: that in the establishment of the **Aspects** <term>Aspectus</term> <note>The specific angular distances between planets that astrologers believe create an influence.</note>, diverse causes are at work, as is their coincidence. Furthermore: "*Nature possesses a choice of those who are provided with more prerogatives*" and the **Semi-sextile** <note>An angle of 30 degrees.</note> has certain rights in common with the **Square** <note>An angle of 90 degrees.</note>; namely, the **Expressibility** <term>Effabilitas</term> <note>The ability of a geometric value (like area or side length) to be expressed as a rational proportion of the whole circle.</note> of the area within the figure. It also shares certain rights with the **Sextile** <note>An angle of 60 degrees.</note>, specifically the multi-faceted **Congruence** <term>Congruentia</term> <note>The ability of a shape to tile a flat surface perfectly without gaps.</note> in a plane. With these forces joined, the semi-sextile turns out to be in some way more powerful than the sextile itself, insofar as the expressibility of the **Dodecagonal** <note>12-sided figure.</note> area is superior to the expressibility of the **Hexagonal** <note>6-sided figure.</note> side; this is because a more perfect congruence in the plane follows from the former. Although in this Book IV, I have ordered the **Semi-sextile** to follow the **Sextile**, it remains within the same rank.

The Introduction to the *Ephemerides* also makes the **Trine** <note>120 degrees.</note>, the **Square**, the **Quintile** <note>72 degrees.</note>, and the **Biquintile** <note>144 degrees.</note> equal in the first and strongest cause—namely, pure congruence in a solid <note>This refers to the three-dimensional Platonic solids.</note> for the purpose of forming regular solid figures. I said the **Trine** and **Square** add a second cause, not much lighter: understand this as the pure congruence of figures in a plane <note>Two-dimensional tiling, like floor tiles.</note>. This cause is indeed also common to the **Sextile**; however, the Sextile does not add it to the first cause, but possesses it separately from it. Just as the **Square** is said to *add even a third cause*, namely the expressibility of the plane—not because the Semi-sextile does not also participate in it, but because those qualities which are found individually in others are accumulated in the Square, so that it becomes the most powerful of all.

Thus, in gathering the votes for the **Sextile**, *I said it shares some nobility with the **Opposition*** <note>180 degrees.</note>, hinting at the expressibility of the figure's side, because it is half the diameter of the circle. Again, it shares *some nobility with the **Trine** and **Square***: namely, the pure congruence in a plane mentioned earlier. For only *a certain particle* of this congruence—that is, congruence with figures of other species—belongs to the **Semi-sextile and other more ignoble aspects**. In this particle of congruence, the **Semi-sextile** and **Octile** <note>45 degrees, or 1/8th of a circle.</note> figures hold the *first rank*. To this, even the "star" of the semi-sextile could be associated, because the congruence they begin is continuable without a mixture of different shapes. The **Quintile** and **Biquintile** hold the *second rank*, except that they have a nobler congruence in the solid. Likewise the **Tri-octile** <note>135 degrees.</note>, **Decile** <note>36 degrees.</note>, and **Tri-decile** <note>108 degrees.</note> belong here, because their figures do continue the congruence, but not without a mixture of different shapes. All these agree to some extent even in the solid, more or less, with the exception of the **Quincunx** <note>150 degrees.</note> of the Dodecagonal star; it is therefore relegated to the *third rank*. To this, even the **Sesquadrate** <note>135 degrees, derived from the octagon.</note>, or the star of the Octagon, can be added, due to the obscurity of knowledge.

I have indeed extended the ranks even further, to the **Vigintile** <note>18 degrees.</note> and **Quindecile** <note>24 degrees.</note>—that is, to figures of fifteen and twenty angles—to which I gave the *fourth rank* (based on that single particle of congruence alone); the reason for this is contained in Proposition 3 of this book. A *fifth rank* was assigned to their **Stars** <note>Star-polygons or "Stellated" versions of these shapes.</note>, because they are equal to their primary figures in **Knowability** <term>Scibilitas</term> <note>The geometric property of being constructible with a compass and straightedge.</note>, but are far inferior in congruence, as they only relate to their individual angles. But it was not necessary for me to do that, since not even up to the third rank are clearly beyond-doubt aspects produced. We can plausibly fix a boundary for the sprouting Aspects in the congruence of the solid and in the perfect expressibility of the side or the plane. Therefore, let the ranks of nobility of the Figures rather be sought from the ends of Books I and II, from which the ranks of the Aspects have been distinguished in this book.

<summary>Kepler establishes a hierarchy of astrological aspects based on their geometric properties, specifically how well their corresponding shapes tile a surface or form 3D solids. He argues that the Square is the most powerful aspect because it combines multiple geometric "prerogatives" or "nobilities."</summary>

# ON THE HARMONICS, BOOK IV.
## CHAPTER VII.

### Epilogue: On Sublunary Nature and the Lower Faculties of the Soul, Especially Those Upon Which Astrology is Based.

<note>Kepler uses the term "sublunary" to refer to the Earthly realm—the region "below the moon"—which was traditionally thought to be subject to change and decay, unlike the "perfect" heavens.</note>

**M**any things have been said about this contemplation in the second chapter, many throughout this whole Fourth Book, and some also in Book III. I also discussed this a year ago in the *Introduction to the Ephemerides*, and in Book I of the *Epitome of Copernican Astronomy* (page 125); again in the year 1610, in *The Third Man Intervening* <note>original: "Tertio interveniente"—Kepler’s work where he acted as a "third party" mediator in a dispute over astrology</note>, in Numbers 40 to 43, and from 59 to 72, and 113, etc.; and in the *Response to the Objections of Roeslin*; and in the year 1606, in the book *On the New Star*, chapters VIII, IX, X, and XXIV, XXVIII, especially from page 171 to 175; and in the year 1604, in *The Optical Part of Astronomy*, pages 26, 27, and page 224. For I deliberately pass over the forecasts in which I have, from time to time, either prefaced or interjected remarks concerning the more certain foundations of astrology, as those are not widely scattered.

Since, however, I have appeared to some very famous Professors of Philosophy and Medicine to be establishing a new philosophy—and a very true one at that—this tender little plant (as all new things are) must be nurtured and raised with every care, so that it may take root in the minds of those practicing philosophy. It must not be suffocated by an excess of vain sophistries, nor washed away by the torrents of common opinions, nor grow stiff in the cold of public neglect. If it falls to me to guard against these things, I fear nothing from the winds of calumny <note>Malicious false statements</note> that might break it, nor from the Sun of solid censure that might wither it.

Therefore, since in Chapter I, I touched upon the essence of the **Soul**, but only for the sake of the **Harmonies**; and since the second Chapter was not expressly about the Soul, but about the Harmonies for the sake of the Soul: it is now pleasing in this chapter to discourse upon the Soul for its own sake, a little more generally. I wish to make a collection <note>original: "Syllogum"</note> in this Epilogue of everything that pertains to the present matter. Things that were said scatteringly, or in passing, or hidden away, I here bring under a single view, explaining the whole nature of the matter in a continuous thread of discourse.

<margin>Pages 115, 117.</margin>
That there is some **Soul of the entire universe**, presiding over the motions of the stars, the generation of the elements, the conservation of living things and plants, and finally the mutual sympathy of things above and below, was defended by Timaeus of Locri <note>A Pythagorean philosopher appearing in Plato's dialogues</note> based on Pythagorean teachings in Plato; and Proclus established this, both elsewhere and especially in the words transcribed in Chapter I of this Fourth Book. They made this Soul distinct from the **Mind** <term>Mens</term>; both because the Mind is simple, while that Soul is multiple in its faculties; and because the **Ideas** <note>The perfect "blueprints" of things</note> of all sensible things exist in the Mind primarily and by themselves, pure and identical; but in the Soul secondarily, because of the Mind and received from it, inclining more toward matter. For this reason, they used a distinction of names, calling the Intellectual or Mental ideas **PARADIGMS** <term>PARADIGMATA</term> <note>original Greek: patterns or models</note>, but the Animal ideas <note>Meaning "of the soul"</note> the **ICONS** <term>ICONES</term> <note>original Greek: images or representations</note> of those Paradigms. The sum of it comes to this: a Christian can very easily understand God the Creator in place of the Platonic "Mind," and the **Nature of things** in place of the "Soul."

# ON CONFIGURATIONS

<margin>CHAPTER VII.</margin> By what specific winds of contemplation they were driven to arrive at these doctrines must be examined by others; I shall speak of myself. And first, concerning the Soul of the whole universe <note>The *Anima Mundi*, a concept that the entire universe is a living being.</note>, although I do not reject the idea, I will say nothing of it in this fourth book. For it seems (if any such soul exists) to reside in the center of the World—which for me is the Sun—and from there to be spread throughout its whole extent <margin>See the Epilogue of Book V.</margin> by the exchange of light rays, which act in the place of Spirits in an animal body.

But concerning that Nature which presides over the elements, and which I call by the common epithet "sublunary," I began to establish similar views twenty years ago. I was moved to this not by reading or admiration of the Platonists, but solely and uniquely by the observation of the weather and the contemplation of the Aspects by which weather patterns are stirred.

<margin>See above, pages 123, 125, 130, 131, 132, 140, 143.</margin> For I have seen, with great consistency, that the state of the air is disturbed whenever the planets are either in conjunction or configured in those Aspects commonly celebrated by astrologers. I have seen that there is usually tranquility in the air if no Aspects, or only a few, occur, or if they are completed and passed quickly. <margin>The laziness of Astrologers.</margin> However, I decided that this business should not be considered as lightly as the common crowd of prognosticators <note>Astrologers who focus on predicting specific events or weather without physical reasoning.</note> does; they describe the effects of the stars as if they were certain Gods, powerful over heaven and earth, doing everything by their own will. They are entirely unconcerned by what means the stars accomplish each thing here among us on earth, since the stars themselves remain in the heavens and send nothing down to us that is perceptible to the senses except for rays of light. This is the primary source of the foulest astrological superstitions.

But I do not wonder much at the prognosticators, a class of men for the most part vulgar, childish, and dreamers; rather, the famous professors of Philosophy seem more deserving of rebuke. For while they accept from their master Aristotle that the life of living things and plants is nourished by the power of the Sun, <margin>And of the Philosophers.</margin> they do not consider that this power of the Sun must therefore be *perceived* by those creatures. It is a completely sluggish and drowsy philosophy that allows the Sun to act upon these lower things just as a sculptor acts upon lifeless matter—even though the Sun lacks chisels, graving tools, and all bodily instruments. How much more vigilant than these philosophers was the poet Virgil, and how much wiser? He does not attribute everything even to the rains (which are themselves merely part of matter), but compares the depths of the Earth to the *lap of a Spouse—and a joyful one at that*—that is, one who perceives what is happening to her with pleasure, and helps her husband with appropriate movement. All of these are signs of **LIFE**, and they presuppose a Soul in the body that is receiving the action. For it would not be easy for the Sun, lacking suitable soldiers, to invade this fortress of the earth’s guts, unless some kind of soul, sitting within, conspired with the "enemy" and opened the gates for him.

<margin>The mastery of the influence of the heavens lies with the sublunary Soul.</margin> You can see that most people who attribute even the slightest bit to astrology suffer from a neglect of this consideration, as if from some kind of lethargy. So much so, that when I emerged to demonstrate the way in which a change in the weather followed from an Aspect, a famous man came forward to refute me, contending with great assertiveness that the material of rain (which we also mocked among the common folk above on page 134) was celestial. <margin>The material of rains comes from the Earth.</margin> Nor, even so, did he teach how it happens that, since the rays of the planets always meet on Earth, rain falls precisely when the rays of two pla-

<margin>CHAPTER VII.</margin>
<margin>* Beware of ambiguity: <term>Aspects</term> <note>The angular relationships between planets, such as 60 or 90 degrees.</note> generally contribute to <term>Meteorological</term> <note>In the 17th century, "meteors" referred to any atmospheric phenomena, including rain, wind, and lightning.</note> effects among the causes; however, daily Aspects do not cause the continuous and general quality of a long part of the year, but rather act only upon the specific days on which they fall. See below.</margin>
Indeed, before all else, I decided that the twelve books of *Giovanni Pico della Mirandola* <note>A 15th-century Italian philosopher whose work *Disputationes adversus astrologiam divinatricem* was a massive critique of astrology.</note> against Astrology ought to be read by me, and the arguments he brought against each point examined. By this exercise, it happened that I was not only confirmed in my condemnation of many superstitions, but a certain new light also arose for me in certain matters. While I was shaking out the force of his objections through an intense struggle of the mind, I began to see into the heart of the matter more deeply. Finally, by refuting some points, that book caused me to place faith in those very things which the astrologers, by their weak defenses, had previously caused me to doubt. This was the case with the **Aspects**. For on one hand, I looked at very constant experience—not indeed gaping after snow, or winds, or thunders, and other things which astrologers are accustomed to predict in that specific way; but \* observing generally that the state of the air was stirred up in whatever way whenever there were aspects (for example, if *Mars and Jupiter* were in conjunction), and remained quiet if there were none. On the other hand, I heard *Mirandola* asking: why should one believe that *Jupiter and Mars*, when they are seen together, do more than when they are separate? For he argued that their light is not increased by conjunction, since they bring as much light into the meeting as they possessed when separate; and if planets of different qualities were to meet, they would seem to hinder rather than help each other. Here, I say, while seeking an answer so that I might defend the Aspects—to which I saw the <term>Meteors</term> <note>Weather events.</note> following—I began to consider the Aspects more diligently as a cause, and the weather as an effect. For the "form" of an Aspect, which makes an Aspect out of a random configuration or angling, was a qualitative quantity; or rather, it was a Relation of such quantities, namely a <term>being of reason</term> <note>Latin: *ens rationis*; a concept that exists in the mind rather than as a physical object.</note>. Therefore, for it to move the air, it was necessary for it first to move some **Reason** (a Mind or Soul) which has power over either the air or that by which the air is disturbed.

<margin>Consideration of the cause of Storms.</margin>
At the same time, the comparison of Aspects with **Musical Concords** was before my eyes—a comparison handed down by *Ptolemy*, explained by *Cardano*, but too rashly exploded by *Mirandola*. I was greatly helped by this analogy in the investigation of causes. For I saw that most of the things *Mirandola* opposed to the aspects could also be opposed to the contemplation of two voices in music. Surely the triple proportion (3:1) or the sesquialter (3:2) of two sounds effects nothing purely by the cause of their pitch; and yet the sounds are pleasing if they are in a triple or sesquialter ratio, while conversely they are abhorred if they are in a septuple (7:1) or sesquisixth (7:6) ratio. Since, therefore, it must be a **Rational** thing that distinguishes the triple from the septuple—namely, a **Soul** set over the sense of hearing—it must also be that in the matter of planetary Radiations, there is a **Rational creature** which discerns between chords of 60 degrees and those of 59 or 61. This creature might use logic for this, like a human understanding Geometry, or it might have this ability from a single concreated instinct, like the forms of plants, which guard a certain number of leaves entrusted to them from the origin of things and always build according to that architecture. There is no force of physical "mixing" here, as in medical measurements; the sounds do not delight, nor do the rays animate, because they are so tempered as when cold things are mixed with hot until a quality results suitable for a body taking a bath. For in such mixtures, there is usually only one optimal temperature, and all others approach it by degrees of "more" or "less." But among configurations...

<margin>
CHAPTER VII.

They are not physical.
</margin>
Among the intervals of sounds, there are several boundary marks, and it is only at these marks that the logic of **Consonances** exists on one hand, and **Aspects** on the other; if you depart even a little from these marks, the logic immediately perishes entirely. For as soon as the Sun, for example, has passed the **square** <note>original: *quadratum*; a 90-degree angle</note> of Saturn, all the stimulation of Nature cools down, and it ceases for thirty whole days (at least regarding the rays of Saturn and the Sun) until the Sun reaches the **Trine** <note>original: *Trinum*; a 120-degree angle</note> of Saturn; then once again, storms are incited for a single day, and they cease again once that day has passed. Such are not the alterations of physical bodies: for those occupy all the time from start to finish, never pausing, but growing with the increase of the cause and with time, and lessening again once the cause is diminished. In a word, just as a line relates to a Number, so the commonly known physical movements relate to these stimuli of the configurations.

<margin>But rather, they belong to the Soul.</margin>
If anyone considers these things carefully, he will be able to conclude with no difficulty that, just like Number, these momentary commotions—proceeding from an **Aspect**, which is an Entity of Reason—do not belong to the body but to the **Animal faculties** <note>The "anima" or soul-like powers that govern movement and perception in living beings.</note>. Therefore, it must be that there is a **Soul** which, being warned and as if awakened by the Aspect, stirs up meteors and storms.

The Soul is in the Earth.

What this Soul might be, or of what kind, I have been able to gather chiefly from its seat in the world. For since the Aspects to which the storms respond are the angles of two rays—not the rays that exist in one or another of the planets looking at each other, nor those in the Sun (which is of a vastly different scale), but those which are formed **here on Earth**—and since the planets themselves have no knowledge of the angles that their rays form here on Earth (unless we make them into Astronomers), it follows therefore that the Soul, which stirs up the air according to the prescription of the Aspects, is here on the Earth. And since that force accompanying the Aspects is felt throughout the entire globe of the Earth, that soul must be equally widely diffused. And since the matter of rains, winds, mists, <margin>The matter of storms rises from the Earth.</margin> thunders, and chasms <note>original: *chasmatum*; likely referring to atmospheric "gaps" or rifts seen during auroras or strange weather.</note> which are drawn out at the time of the Aspects is a moist vapor or spirit—at other times dry and fiery, bubbling up and exhaling from the earth (For why should a Philosopher listen only to **Aristotle** here, while scorning **Rodolphus Agricola** <note>A 15th-century Dutch humanist who wrote on the nature of things</note>, and indeed all farmers, and even his own very senses, <margin>Fol. 133.</margin> when he sees every day, as rains approach, the peaks of mountains "vomit" a great force of mists?): therefore, that soul will be not only on the surface of the earth, but also inside in the subterranean caverns and in the passages of the mountains. Finally, the globe of the Earth will be such a body as that of <margin>The Earth is a living creature.</margin> some animal; and what its own Soul is to an animal, this **sublunary Nature** <note>The realm of the Earth and atmosphere, traditionally everything below the moon's orbit.</note>—which moves storms at the presence of the Aspects—will be to the Earth.

Aspects are often ineffective.

In this, I was greatly confirmed by the very thing that might have deterred someone else: namely, that the commotions of storms do not always respond perfectly to the Aspects. Instead, the Earth occasionally seems sluggish and stubborn; at another time (namely after heavy and long-lasting configurations), having been "exacerbated," it indulges in evaporations even without the continuation of Aspects. To be sure, the Earth is not an animal such as a Dog, ready at every nod; but such as an **Ox** or an **Elephant**, slow to anger, and so much the more violent once it has been incensed.

<margin>
CHAPTER VII.

The works of the Earthly Soul.
</margin>
I was inquiring, also comparing the bodies of living things with the body of the Earth: I saw that almost everything that comes from the body of a living thing, testifying that a soul is within it, also comes from the body of the Earth. For just as the body produces hair on the surface of the skin, so the Earth brings forth plants and trees; and just as lice are born there, here caterpillars, cicadas, and various insects and sea monsters are born. And as the body produces tears, mucus <note>original: *blennam*</note>, and the waste-products of the ears, and sometimes even gum from facial pustules, so the Earth produces amber and bitumen. As the bladder pours out urine, so mountains pour out rivers; and as the body produces excrement of a sulfurous odor and intestinal rumblings <note>original: *crepitus*; gas or flatulence</note> which can even be ignited, so the Earth produces sulfur, subterranean fires, thunder, and lightning. And as blood is generated in the veins of a living thing, and with it sweat, which is ejected outside the body, so in the veins of the Earth are produced metals and fossils, and the rainy vapor.

<margin>
The Earth’s nourishment.
</margin>
It is necessary, therefore, that just as other living things draw in food and drink, so also the Earth, through certain channels, draws in some matter from which it concocts such diverse things—for nothing comes from nothing. It draws in and swallows seawater; this is the reason why the sea never overflows, despite the eternal pouring in of so many rivers. From the aforementioned things, you can gather how absurd those people are who attribute metals to the operation of the Sun alone, without the work of the Earth.

<margin>
What kind of Soul the Earth possesses.
</margin>
In my book on the New Star <note>Kepler's *De Stella Nova* (1606), discussing a supernova</note>, I also responded to that common objection: that if the Earth had a soul, it would also seem that it ought to grow and have limbs suited for movement. For as the body is, so the soul and its faculties correspond to it; since this soul exists for the sake of the Earth's body, and not this body for the sake of the Soul—just as the human body exists for the sake of the Mind, the chief faculty of the Soul. If, therefore, the Earth had needed growth, or if it had needed nourishment other than what I have described (as if from hunting), then those duties would have been entrusted to this Soul, and suitable instruments would have been given. This was the philosophy of the dying Socrates in the *Phaedo* <note>Plato’s dialogue on the immortality of the soul</note>, attributing everything to a governing Mind and to deliberation about what is best. Therefore, if anyone argues that there are only four faculties of the Soul <note>Usually referring to the vegetative, sensitive, appetitive, and motive powers</note>, none of which fit this Earthly Soul, and that there is therefore no soul in the Earth, I shall bid him add this fifth one to the number, following the same example and the same laws of reasoning by which those four were found in man.

<margin>
The imagination of the Earth's Soul.
</margin>
Moreover, so that I might attribute a Soul to the Earth even more confidently, I was moved by other things which I have hammered home here and there throughout my other books and collected in a bundle in the *Epitome of Copernican Astronomy*, page 125: chiefly this, that there is a formative faculty <term>formatrix facultas</term> <note>A power within nature capable of shaping matter into specific forms</note> in the bowels of the Earth which, in the manner of a pregnant woman, expresses the human things it encounters outside—as if it saw them—in fissile stones. Examples include the shapes of soldiers, monks, popes, kings, and whatever else is in the talk of men: new and unusual fashions. 
<margin>
Geometry in gems.
</margin>
This indeed happens rarely; but the following happens perpetually: that in gems and fossils it expresses the five regular geometric solids <note>The Platonic solids: tetrahedron, cube, octahedron, dodecahedron, and icosahedron</note>. For the work testifies to the craftsman. 
<margin>
Movement of its own body.
</margin>
To these things, let him who follows Copernicus add the daily rotation of the globe of the Earth, perpetual and most uniform; which he will most rightly reckon among the duties of this Soul.

<margin>Chapter VII.</margin>

<margin>In the Earth, the sense of touch.</margin>
What of the fact that a certain sense of either touch or hearing seems to reside in the globe of the Earth? This is confirmed by the constant tradition of many provinces: it is said that if someone climbs to the peaks of the highest mountains and casts a small stone into those deepest chasms they possess, a sound is usually stirred up from within; or if a stone is thrown into a mountain lake (which, without a doubt, lacks a bottom), storms are immediately provoked. In the same way, animals—if someone inserts something tickling into the tender passages of their ears or nostrils—are seized with a shudder, shake their heads, or rush into a gallop.

<margin>The Earth’s diseases.</margin>
There are also "languors" <note>original: *languores*; meaning illnesses or a lack of vitality</note> in certain regions of the Earth, and internal changes in its "innards." For sometimes they abound with too much fluid; at other times they suffer from <term>crudity</term> <note>original: *cruditate*; in Galenic medicine, this refers to undigested food or "raw" humors that cause illness</note> or imperfect digestion, as when dry winds emerge instead of timely rains. At other times, as if seized by a burning fever, the Earth produces no moisture, but instead exudes sulfurous breaths or pestilential vapors. Therefore, I was right to advise in my book on the *New Star* <note>Kepler’s *De Stella Nova* (1606)</note>, on page 173, that all the faculties of digestion—the <term>Attractive, Retentive, and Expulsive</term> <note>These are the three Galenic powers of the soul: the ability to draw in nutrients, keep them, and expel waste</note>—should be sought within the Earth, since those "diseases" are actually disturbances of these faculties.

<margin>The Earth’s breathing.</margin>
Indeed, what is more like the breathing of land animals—and especially that back-and-forth movement in fish, where they swallow water with their mouths and squeeze it back out through their gills—than that marvelous twice-daily ebb and flow of the Ocean? It is true that this motion adjusts itself to the movements of the Moon, so much so that it seemed probable to me in the Preface to my *Commentaries on Mars* <note>The *Astronomia Nova* (1609), where Kepler famously proposed that the Moon attracts the oceans like a magnet</note> that the waves are pulled by the Moon as iron is by a magnet, through a physical power of the union of bodies. <margin>From where comes the ebb and flow of the Ocean?</margin> This is a point I recently repeated in the introduction to my *Ephemerides* <note>astronomical tables</note>, where I examined the opinion of David Fabricius <note>A German astronomer and correspondent of Kepler</note>. Nevertheless, if someone were to argue that the Earth adjusts its own "respiration" to the motion of the Sun and Moon—just as animals have cycles of sleep and wakefulness that match day and night—I believe such a person should not be ignored in the study of philosophy. This is especially true if some evidence were found of flexible parts deep within the Earth that could serve the purpose of lungs or gills. For if their nature is like that of our air—capable of being compressed and expanded—then this "breathing" would not require the surface of the Earth to move like the diaphragm muscles in a breathing human body.

What better reason could there be for the Earth to receive seawater into its "kitchen of metals" <note>Kepler imagines the Earth's interior as a laboratory or kitchen where minerals are "cooked" and formed</note> than through these perpetual, twice-daily <term>Euripi</term> <note>original: *Euripos*; a term for narrow straits with violent currents, used here to describe the tidal channels</note>? What else does that strange event lead us to suspect when, a few years before the busy trade moved to Antwerp, the ebb and flow deserted the Ocean for a day (terrifying the city significantly), yet the Moon did not desert its course? Surely the Earth itself, possessing this back-and-forth motion, though it shares in the Moon’s natural motion, "held its breath" for that one day; just as living creatures sometimes hold their breath, even though the movement of the diaphragm is itself partly natural.

However, we shall perhaps more rightly prove that the Earth needs to breathe because of the presence of a Soul, rather than proving the Soul exists because of the breathing.

CHAPTER VII.
The Soul of the Earth is like a flame.

Now that we proceed to the contemplation of its essence, as if the fact that there is a soul in the Earth were a settled matter: it is indeed not merely a kind of light, like that of fires and fireflies, depending on itself rather than illumination from the sun; the proof for this being that it somehow senses the bright rays of the planets. Instead, it clearly seems to be a certain flame (to be nourished, of course, by "breathing" or "swallowing" <note>This refers to the tides and the intake of air or water into the Earth’s interior.</note>), the proof being the perpetual and sensible subterranean heat. <margin>Whence subterranean heat comes.</margin> The likes of which, without a soul, never persists as an actuality in plain matter; nor is it even present as a potential in things originating from the substance of animals and plants, unless produced by the Soul and its Forms, which are something fiery. See my *Optics*, pages 25, 26, 27.

<margin>
pages 115, 119, 121.
The Soul of the Earth is a kind of Zodiac.
</margin>

We shall assign this <note>the fiery subterranean heat</note> as the material, as it were, of the Earth’s Soul; upon which is now imprinted, in the place of a "form," the image of the divine countenance, with the Ideas of both the Circle and all its ratios, as well as of its own sensible body over which it has been set to rule, and even of the whole World in which its body was to be. For God has within Himself not only geometric patterns but also the concepts of all sensible things to be created; all of which pass simultaneously into Souls, which are the patterns of God, according to the capacity or use of each. Therefore, in the Soul of the Earth, there shines back a certain image of the sensible circle of the <margin>Pgs. 139, 141. The cause of the sympathy between heaven and Earth. Pgs. 122, 123. The Soul is energy.</margin> Zodiac, and indeed of the entire firmament, forming the bond of sympathy between celestial and earthly things. There shine back most especially in that Soul the *Archetypes* <note>the original patterns or "blueprints" in the mind of God</note> of all its own duties and all the movements by which it moves its body in any sense: which others might call *dynamis* <note>original: δύναμιν; power or potential</note>, but I would more gladly name *energeia* <note>original: ἐνέργειαν; activity or actualized energy</note>. For this is the essence of souls; it is, as it were, the *physis* <note>original: φύσις; nature or the principle of growth</note> of this flame, because the Souls themselves are always so prepared within as if they were performing that for which they were made, whether they actually possess the instruments of the body or are hindered. For God <margin>pg. 123.</margin> is substantial Energy, and exists by this very energy (to stammer about divine things in a human way): and therefore the essence of the divine image consists *in acting* <note>original: ἐν τῷ ἐνεργεῖν</note>, just as that of a flame consists *in being produced* <note>original: ἐν τῷ φύειν; literally "in growing" or "in natural arising"</note>; so that unless God sustained it eternally by irradiating its "matter," as it were, it would suddenly cease and be extinguished.

...for the sake of each, that [soul] is like a certain operational circle); it is always carried along in those works of its own. It acts more remarkably, however, when these three circles concur and conspire into one—that is, if the soul, alerted by the **Aspects** <note>Harmonious angles between planets that Kepler believes the Earth's soul "perceives."</note> of its very self, persists in its work with a certain excess. Indeed, that soul never ceases from "cooking," <note>Kepler uses the metaphor of "cooking" or "digestion" to describe the internal heat processes of the Earth.</note> nor is this cooking ever without smoke and vapor. From the smoke, fossils <note>In the 17th century, "fossil" referred to anything dug out of the ground, including minerals and ores.</note> are made (just as <term>Arsenic</term> <note>original: *Arsenicum*; here referring to the sublimation of minerals in metallic furnaces</note> consists of the smoke of metallic furnaces). From the warm vapor, however—cooled within the stony crusts of the Earth and gathered into drops—rivers trickle down to their sources. From that same vapor breathing out upon the surface of the Earth, the breathable air is daily renewed, which had fallen during the night by condensing into dew. Although this work of the <term>Soul of the Earth</term> is perpetual, there was nevertheless a need for certain "excesses" in its evaporating; these are not continuous for the whole time, but restricted to certain days. <margin>Why excesses occur through Aspects.</margin> This is so that, from the abundance of vapors sent abroad, timely rains might be supplied—interspersed with periods of Sun—for the sake of refreshing and moistening the Earth's surface, so that crops and fodder might grow for living creatures.

<margin>The Sun also rouses vapors outside of Aspects.</margin>
Someone might object to me regarding the innermost parts of Africa and Peru, situated under the equinoctial line <note>The Equator.</note>, where continuous rains fall throughout the entire summer. Where, then, is this distinction between <term>Aspects</term> and ineffective <term>configurations</term>? Where are the alternations of Sun and rain? And does not the course of the Sun—a solitary planet—alone do everything, without regard for its configuration with others? And does it not do this as a natural cause, rather than a <term>Rational being</term> <note>original: *Ens rationis*; a philosophical term for something that exists only in the mind or through logic</note>, insofar as it intensifies heat and warmth in those parts so that a thinned moisture expires from the bowels of the earth toward the parts so "toasted"? I respond that this natural action should not be denied to the Sun; but it is not unique to the <term>Torrid Zone</term>, but can also be observed among us. For when the Sun is present in our <term>Hemisphere</term> during the summer, more copious rains usually fall than any snow that usually falls in winter when the Sun is absent. As for the fact that our rivers are increased by melting snows—which do not seem to increase as much when rains fall, or certainly not with such long-lasting growth—that happens partly because the individual layers of snow falling bit by bit are piled up and preserved in a storehouse for many months by the power of the cold. <margin>So that rivers may increase.</margin> Meanwhile, the parched earth immediately drinks up the greatest part of summer rains, even the heaviest ones. It also happens because the snow in the Alps cannot be dissolved except by very heavy summer rains falling; thus, those continuous increases of the rivers are not from the snows alone, but also from the joined rains. Therefore, if you weigh everything, a greater abundance of moisture usually exudes even among us during the summer than during the winter. This objection, therefore, achieves this much: that there is a confluence of celestial causes, of which one is natural (the heat of the Sun) and the other rational (the **Aspect**). There is also a confluence of sublunary causes, so that not only does one Zone have more moisture than another, but even within the same climate, one region has more than another for its own reasons. Meanwhile, even in the Torrid Zone, it can rain more during the time of the Aspects than on days free from Aspects.

This "characterization" of the <term>Earthly Soul</term>—which I mentioned in the second place—is created by the sensible Zodiac and the entire sphere of the fixed stars; that also...

<margin>Chapter VII.</margin>
This is also confirmed by the great consensus of all ages: that if anything new appears in the sky—whether according to the ordinary course of the heavens, such as the rarer gatherings of several planets or notable eclipses of the sun and moon, or whether contrary to common nature, such as comets or new fixed stars—the sublunary Nature <note>Kepler refers to the "sublunary" realm, which is the Earth and its atmosphere, traditionally thought to be subject to change and decay unlike the "perfect" heavens.</note> is simultaneously disturbed by unusual passions. These include massive and continuous rains beyond the normal measure of the **Aspects**, <note>Harmonious angles between planets.</note> or the opposite—droughts and filth, accompanied by earthquakes. Finally, there are unusual dampness in the air, which brings on pestilential catarrhs and other epidemic plagues, especially in those places where they breathe out with greater force or where they are carried by more frequent winds.
<margin>The source of the effects of Comets and Eclipses.</margin>

Furthermore, I advised in my book on the New Star (*De Stella Nova*), Chapter X, page 44, that something similar to the **Memory of Animals** exists within this Soul. For this is the nature of all things related to light: when excited by the light of the Sun, or at least by the day, they conceive a certain impression that lasts for a fixed time. Thus, in the eyes, the <term>Visual Spirits</term> <note>original: *Spiritus visorij*; an early physiological theory that a "spirit" or fluid in the nerves allowed for sight.</note>—which are the offspring of light—when imbued by an improvident glance at the Sun, carry and bear this image around even against one's will, no matter where the eyes are turned. So too, among the secrets of the Chemists, there is this wonderful and especially noteworthy experiment: they prepare "gems" (as I recently learned from an <term>eyewitness</term>) <note>original: *αὐτοπτη* (autoptē)</note> which, although they stay dark like other things warmed by light, if someone exposes them to the light of day alone, they are "ignited" by it like candles. They carry this splendor with them even into the darkness, glowing like the eyes of cats, though the light is extinguished after a short time.
<margin>Pages 110, 111.</margin>
<margin>A stone ignited by the day.</margin>

Something similar happens to this Soul—which I have said is related to light and fire—so that in that region (for the Soul is a point distinguished by regions, or a potential Zodiac circle) in which the higher planets have met or an eclipse has appeared, it conceives a lasting **character** <note>A "character" here is a formal imprint or geometric mark left by the planetary alignment in the Earth's "mind."</note> of that conjunction for some time. Therefore, as often as any of the planets, especially the Sun or the Moon, passes over that place, the Soul exerts its power, just as it would at the very stimulation of the conjunction itself.
<margin>Source of the efficacy of the place of conjunction.</margin>

This whole business, I say, is similar to the memory of animals. For I carry the image of a man once seen in my mind, yet I do not always have him present in my thoughts; but when he or someone similar appears again, that former image is drawn out anew through remembrance and is established in the act of thinking. Even though human memory is nobler in this regard—because I am not only reminded of the thing remembered by an external encounter, but I can also remind myself whenever I wish—this is surely because the faculty of reasoning is present in man, which is absent in this Soul. Truly, these things will be more evident in the contemplation of the human Soul.
<margin>The Memory of the Earth's Soul.</margin>

Now one difficulty, touched upon above but only lightly, must be resolved regarding the manner and means of reception. For us humans, receiving the images of sensible things inward into the Soul seems a straightforward and plain matter: the openings of the pupils are in plain sight, through which they enter; there is the eye, the former of the image; there is the <term>crystalline humor</term>, <note>The lens of the eye.</note> the temperer of the radiant brush; there is the <term>retiform tunic</term> <note>The retina; literally the "net-like cloak."</note> of the optic nerve, the receiver of the picture of external things. Nothing of the sort appears in the body of the earth: no eye is here by which the Earth’s Soul might see the radiations of the Planets and their angles. How then shall it feel light without vision? How shall it perceive...

The mode of seeing the truth.

...perceive or receive the angles without an instrument? There is some difficulty here, I confess; but if you look more deeply into the matter, that difficulty is common both here and there <note>Meaning both in the Earth's perception and in human sight.</note>. In my *Optical Part of Astronomy*, page 169, you will see the ancient complaint even regarding human sight. For although in that place, the mode of seeing was finally demonstrated most solidly by me after so many fruitless attempts by others—as the more diligent Opticians and Anatomical Physicians admit—nevertheless, that mode of seeing does not extend beyond the <term>retiform tunic</term> <note>original: "retiformem tunicam"; the retina, which Kepler was the first to correctly identify as the surface where the image is formed</note>, through which the humors of the eye are transparent. 

<margin>
François d’Aguilon.
</margin>

(Although *François d’Aguilon*, whose great work on Optics appeared four years ago, did not see my book, and thus, remaining in the ancient error regarding the mode of vision, built a new and truly beautiful but futile extension upon it.) There remains yet a question, not yet discussed by the *Physicists* whom I have challenged: how the picture of the thing to be seen, formed by me on the retina, is then carried further inward through the opaque parts of the body to the inner chambers of the *Soul*? Or does the soul go forth to meet it? And other related matters. And, to confess frankly, I am more stuck on the nature of vision than on this perception of the angle of the rays—about which I feel I can stammer something not entirely foolish, whereas on the former I am completely silent.

I could indeed, without compromising the core of the matter, evade the labor of speculation and answer the one asking, "With what eyes does the soul of the *Earth* see the rays of the stars?" by saying: "With the same eyes by which it saw the soldier with ragged boots, whose image it planted in a piece of fissile stone." <note>Kepler refers to "figured stones" or fossils/mineral patterns that look like human artifacts, which he attributed to the Earth's formative soul.</note> But laziness is the death of philosophy: let us live and exercise ourselves.

First, the soul has obtained the character of a point in actuality (at least by reason of its connection to its body), and the figure of a circle in potentiality. Since the soul is <term>Energy</term> <note>original: "Energia"; used here in the Aristotelian sense of an active, vital force</note>, it spreads itself from that seat in the point out into a circle. For whether it must sense external things, which surround it in a spherical manner, or whether it must

govern a body, it also has a body cast around it; it lies hidden within, rooted in a certain point of that body, from which it goes out by its own <term>species</term> <note>original: "speciem"; in 17th-century optics, this refers to the radiating form or likeness of a thing transmitted through space</note> into the rest of the body. But how should it go out, except through straight lines? For this is truly to "go out." How could it have any other manner of going out—it being both light and flame—than how other lights go out from their sources: namely, in straight lines? It goes out, therefore, toward the outer parts of the body by the same laws as the surrounding lights of the firmament enter toward it where it resides in the point. 

Moreover, since the entire surface of the half-globe of the Earth—and indeed all points of the surface of the air with which it is clothed—is irradiated by infinite rays from one and the same *Planet*, among all these rays, only one single ray tends toward that point which is the seat of the soul. And in turn, when the *Soul* goes out in infinite lines to all points of the surface of its body (just like the rays of the *Sun*, because it is also a kind of light; and the <term>spirits</term> <note>Vital fluids or subtle substances thought to move through the nerves.</note> commonly celebrated seem to be nothing other than these rectilinear rays and these species of the soul), there is nevertheless only one line among them all which tends from the center to that point on the surface which is struck by that unique ray of the *Planet* that tends toward the seat of the *Soul*. 

Let us suppose, then, that the perception of the rays of a single planet consists in this: when the in-rushing of the one and the out-going of the other coincide in one straight geometric line. This is very similar to the example of vision, which is perfect and accurate only in the single perpendicular ray in the center of the entire eye. CHAPTER VII;
What it is to perceive, and how it occurs.
