...external things, except insofar as the sensory instrument is affected by that thing. For the Soul, through those outpourings of its own <term>forms</term> <note>original: "specierum"; in the philosophy of the time, "species" were the mental or immaterial images of objects transmitted to the mind</note>, has a faithful knowledge of all the members of its own body, and of those things which occur as new in each of them at any time. Given these facts, it follows that if such an impression is made by a Planet upon some point of the air which does not tend toward the seat of the soul, but passes it by on the side, the soul indeed receives the <term>form</term> of that affected point through the return of its own form; but it disregards it as a thing of no value. But if such an impression is made on some point of the surface of the air that it tends toward the seat of the Soul, this point thus affected is also announced to the Soul, and this perception is valued as pertaining to the Soul and is distinguished from the rest; and thus, in that point alone, the Soul imagines the star for itself, but not at all in the others already mentioned. For the ray of the Soul is <term>actuated</term> <note>original: "actuatur"; made active or brought into reality</note> and, as it were, illuminated by the ray of the star falling upon the same straight line; just as the color of visible things is actuated by the arrival of light; and just as vision is actuated when we gather and weigh the fact that we see. Since this is the case not only in one planet, but also in two, the soul will also find two signs in two parts of its body. Whether its body is now round, or uneven and rough, the Soul has it surrounding itself (sitting in a single point) in the manner of a sphere; and by its rays, or forms of its immaterial self—or as others say, by <term>secondary acts</term> <note>original: "actib⁹ secundis"; a technical term in Scholastic philosophy referring to the operation or exercise of a faculty</note> sent out from itself—it breathes out, as it were, a perfect sphere as far as its body extends. Therefore, it examines that body according to the idea of a circle—and indeed the circle of the Zodiac—described around its own seat as a center, and measures its distinct parts. Thus, there is no need to grant that the Earth is transparent all the way to the center, nor for the soul to go out as far as the stars; nevertheless, the way is clear by which the angles of the configurations may be perceived by the Soul.

<margin>
Optical illusions apply to the Soul of the Earth and its works.
</margin>
By this supposition, all the arguments are dissolved which <term>Pico della Mirandola</term> <note>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola (1463–1494), a famous Renaissance philosopher who wrote a massive critique of astrology</note> brought forward to overthrow the doctrine of Great Conjunctions and aspects. For because the Soul arranges all the bodies of the world around the point of its seat (by imagining them) into the form of a sphere, and all the planets into the form of a circle—and this by the law of straight lines drawn from a single point—it therefore matters nothing whether a star be great or small, whether it completes a large or small journey in the heavens, or whether it is high or near to the Earth. For all these things move the Soul just as they are perceived; and they are perceived by the same laws by which they are also seen by us: namely, all as if at the same height, and as if lacking a <term>secondary motion</term> <note>original: "motu secundo"; the individual orbital motion of a planet</note>, but as if equally swift in the <term>first daily motion</term> <note>original: "motu verò primo diurno"; the apparent rotation of the sky caused by the Earth's rotation</note>, and without a great difference in visible size. For other things which can be answered to Pico's arguments, seek them in the often-cited place in my book *On the New Star*. Enough for now regarding the Soul of the Earth, which they call the Sublunary Nature.

<margin>
On the human Soul.
</margin>
Whatever has been said so far regarding the Soul of the Earth can likewise be applied to the faculties of the human Soul: most things in these, however, are more evident, and as much more manifold as these faculties are set over more duties than that one.

<margin>
On the Mind: pages 140, 143, 139, 120, 121, 135, 124, 115, 117.

Concerning the chief faculty of the soul, which is called the Mind, besides those things which I brought forward above in Chapter I from <term>Proclus</term> <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher whom Kepler frequently cites as an authority on the mathematical nature of the soul</note>, the business of Radiations suggests nothing further for me to say. It is a point, as the Mind; it is a circle, as Reasoning; it is an image of the divine countenance; it is Harmony, insofar as it is a single energy; within it are the mathematical Ideas and forms, through the circle; it gives...

<margin>
CHAPTER VII.

How Mathematical Genera exist differently in the mind.
</margin>
...to these, and to the Harmonies, it gives their intellectual BEING. Let the reader seek all these things from the previous sections: there is no need for more here. I advise this one thing concerning the argument of **Proclus** <note>Proclus (412–485 AD) was a Neoplatonist philosopher who argued that mathematical truths are innate to the soul.</note>; It does not seem to rely on good examples when he insists that lines, surfaces, and points must be established in the soul because in sensible <note>Meaning "physical" or "perceptible by the senses."</note> things no pure and separate surfaces, lines, or points exist. And yet, neither in the Soul is there a pure line existing by itself; rather, it exists within a mental surface of which it is the extremity, no less than in sensible corporeal quantities a mere surface exists at the extremity of a body, a mere line at the extremity of a surface, and a mere point at the end of a line: for the BEING of imperfect quantities is to be INHERENT IN THE PERFECT.

<margin>Species and the Circle are different.</margin>
Indeed, mathematical GENERA <note>General categories of mathematics.</note> are not in the Soul differently from other universals and various concepts abstracted from sensible things. But among the mathematical SPECIES <note>Specific types or forms.</note>, that which is called the **Circle** exists in the Soul in a far different way—not only as an Idea of external things, but even as a certain form of the Soul itself; finally, as a unique storehouse of all geometrical and arithmetical science. Of these, the former [geometry] is most evident in the doctrine of Sines, the latter [arithmetic] in the wonderful business of **Logarithms**; for in these, having arisen from the circle, there is a kind of counting-board of all multiplications and divisions that can ever be made, as if already completed. But enough regarding the Sovereign faculty of the Soul; let us come now to the lower ones.
<margin>Use of the Logarithm by John Napier <note>original: "L. B. Neperi"; Referring to John Napier, the Baron of Merchiston, who invented logarithms which Kepler used extensively for his planetary tables.</note></margin>

<margin>On the Vital faculty.</margin>
Therefore, the **vital faculty** <note>In Kepler’s biology, this is the subconscious part of the soul that governs growth, health, and instinctive reactions.</note> in Man possesses within itself not only Harmonies involved with luminous rays, but also Harmonies encrusted with the <term>species</term> <note>original: "speciebus"; mental images or patterns transmitted to the mind.</note> of sounds. And indeed, it drinks in sounds with the ears as its proper object; but it admits the rays of the stars—not as if with eyes, but in that same obscure mode of perception explained a little above—and examines them against the innate Ideas of Harmony. For those things seen with the eyes serve <term>discursive reasoning</term> <note>The step-by-step process of logical thought.</note>; the recognition of Harmonies is without discourse. **J. C. Scaliger** <note>Julius Caesar Scaliger (1484–1558), a famous scholar and physician.</note> asks if the idea of a kite <note>A predatory bird.</note> is thus innate to a chicken; not indeed as a simple idea, but with a note of destruction to be avoided.
<margin>Scaliger on Ideas.</margin>

<margin>What the stars can do to the vital faculty.</margin>
From this, therefore, human Souls have the trait that at the time of celestial <term>aspects</term> <note>The specific angles formed between planets in the sky.</note> they catch their chief impulses for carrying out the business they have at hand. For what the goad is to the ox, the spur or command to the horse, the drum and trumpet to the soldier, the stirring speech to the audience, the piping or bagpipes and panpipes to the crowd of peasants; this to all people—and especially to those gathered together—is the celestial configuration of suitable Planets; so that individuals are incited in their meditations and works, and everyone becomes more ready for conspiring together and joining hands. Therefore, in warfare you see battles, fights, invasions, assaults, conquests, riots, and panic terrors mostly occurring at the times of Aspects of **Mars and Mercury**, **Jupiter and Mars**, **Sun and Mars**, **Saturn and Mars**, etc. In epidemic diseases, more people take to their beds at the time of strong Aspects, are more severely tormented, or even die; namely, as Nature fails in the struggle with the disease—to which struggle (but not to death) it is incited by the Aspect. All these things the heaven itself does not do without a medium, but the vital faculty of the Soul, associating its own works with celestial Harmonies, holds the mastery in this so-called "influence of the heaven." To be sure, this word **Influence** has fascinated some philosophers, so that...

<margin>CHAPTER VI</margin>
...they would rather be mad with the foolish mob than be wise with me. Their chain of reasoning is indeed weak: that the Stars act upon the air, the air upon the temperament of the body, and this in turn upon the Soul. Let this be so in some cases, but what does this have to do with an **Aspect**, which is a conceptual entity <note>original: "ens rationis"; a thing that exists in the mind rather than as a physical object</note>? How will the element of air receive this aspect, and how will the body? It cannot, unless each is governed by its own soul, which perceives the aspect primarily through itself, in the manner I have just described.

<margin>The vital faculty is a flame.</margin>
That this vital faculty is a kind of flame, ignited in the heart (and for that reason it dies when its fuel is consumed, while the Mind endures), I proved in the optical part of my *Astronomy* <note>Referring to his 1604 work *Ad Vitellionem paralipomena, quibus astronomiae pars optica traditur*</note>, on page 26. I did so through a brilliant comparison of the heart and its reciprocal motions—**Systole** and **Diastole** <note>The contraction and expansion of the heart</note>—with a closed lamp in which a flame must be nourished by oil, ventilation, and the clearing away of smoke.

<margin>How each birth governs its own affairs, and on what foundation.</margin>
This admirable business of horoscopes <note>original: "negocium genethliacum," referring to the calculation of birth charts</note> rests primarily on this property of its essence. For since the vital faculty, ignited in the heart and burning as long as life remains, is a certain <term>Zodiacal</term> <note>original: "Zodiacus"</note> circle; and since its essence consists in energy and a kind of flaming flux: it follows that the figure of the entire perceptible <term>Zodiac</term> flows into that faculty when it is newly ignited at birth. It grows deep within it (even though the sky moves on and is transformed into entirely different configurations after the moment of birth). In this "animal idea" of the <term>Zodiacal</term> circle, the soul marks all the positions that the Planets held under the fixed stars, as well as the points of rising, setting, or the mid-heaven.

<margin>pages 120, 124</margin>
<margin>Why it is the chart of birth rather than of conception.</margin>
But above all other astronomical matters, a far greater necessity exists for the radiant Harmonies during the first rising and formation of this vital faculty in man. For we have said that any faculty of the Soul is a circle in respect of its essence; but when it acts upon itself by instinct—that is, when it compares its circle with its parts—these are archetypal Harmonies. Now, the vital faculty begins to act and is brought into actual being when it is inflamed within the lamp of the heart through birth, such that it thereafter requires respiration to nourish the flame of life. Therefore, when it begins to be what it is at that moment, it "architects" the Harmonies: then the perceptible radiant Harmony of the Planets flows into it most strongly.

<margin>What Aspects can do in a Birth.</margin>
This is the very reason why those who are born during a time of many **Aspects** <note>Geometrical angles between planets</note> between the planets usually turn out to be both hardworking and industrious—whether they grow accustomed to accumulating wealth from childhood, or are born or chosen as governors of public affairs, or finally apply themselves to study. If I seem to anyone to be an example of this kind of life, I have not begrudged them the knowledge of my own birth <note>original: "genesis"</note> in my book *On the New Star* <note>Kepler's *De Stella Nova* (1606)</note>, page 43; it is convenient to explain it again on this occasion. I do not care about the charge of boasting; let them make accusations if they wish—those who condemn this whole kind of writing as folly, whether in their speech or their way of life: the ignorant, the half-learned, the peddlers of titles and trappings meant to deceive the people, and even "plebeian theologians," as **Pico** <note>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola (1463–1494), who wrote famously against astrology</note> calls them. Among true lovers of wisdom of whatever rank, I easily wash away this charge for the benefit of my reader; for I have explored the birth and internal disposition of no one's mind as certainly as my own. Jupiter, therefore, being very close to a ninety-degree angle, had surpassed by four degrees...

...the trine <note>A 120-degree angle between planets, considered harmonious</note> of Saturn was passing; the Sun and Venus were joined and moving away from that position, while applying themselves toward a sextile <note>A 60-degree angle</note> from both sides. They were also moving away from a square <note>A 90-degree angle, often considered tense</note> with Mars, toward which Mercury was moving very closely. The Moon was moving toward a trine with Mars, very near the "Eye of the Bull" <note>The star Aldebaran</note>, even in latitude. Meanwhile, 25 degrees of Gemini was rising, and 22 degrees of Aquarius was culminating <note>At the highest point in the sky</note>. The change in the atmosphere revealed a triple configuration occurring on that day: a partile <note>Exact to the degree</note> sextile of Saturn and the Sun, a sextile of Jupiter and Venus, and a square of Mercury and Mars. For after several days of frost, on that very day a warmth arose, melted the ice, and brought rain.

<margin>
An exception against Astrology.
</margin>
<margin>
Things produced by the circumstances of earthly matters are not to be ascribed to the stars.
</margin>
However, I do not wish to defend and confirm all the aphorisms of the astrologers by this single example; nor do I hand over the steering oars of human affairs to the heavens. This philosophical observation of mine is still a vast distance away from that folly—or better yet, madness. For to follow the traces of this very example: I know a woman born under almost the same aspects, possessing a truly restless disposition. However, through this disposition, she not only fails to profit in letters (which is not surprising in a woman <note>Kepler reflects the social views of the 1600s here, though he often engaged with female intellectuals like his mother</note>), but she also throws her whole town into turmoil and is the author of her own deplorable misery. 

Therefore, several factors were added to the aspects of the planets in my case: first, the long-lasting imagination of my pregnant mother, who greatly admired her mother-in-law (my grandmother), a student of folk medicine which was also practiced by my father. Second, there is the fact that I was born a man and not a woman—a distinction of sex that astrologers seek in the heavens in vain. Third, I derive a temperament of body from my mother that is more suited to studies than to other ways of life. Fourth, my parents' wealth was not great; there was no "clod of earth" <note>Meaning inherited land or an estate</note> for me to be born into or to cling to. Fifth, schools were available, as were examples of the generosity of the Magistrates toward boys suited for study.

<margin>
Qualities of the soul agree most with the qualities of the planets.
</margin>
<margin>
* Here is a little gift for our Satirists. For, as it appears, poverty presses upon those very people who have already ruminated several times within a twelve-year cycle on a single joke of mine similar to this one from my book on the New Star.
</margin>
At this point, I shall introduce again from the beginning <note>original: "ex Genesi"; likely referring to the "genesis" or origin of the soul's character</note> the distinctions of the planets in their qualities. For if the Soul is a kind of light, it will distinguish the redness of Mars from the brilliance of Jupiter and the lividness <note>A leaden or bluish-grey color</note> of Saturn. Thus, it must be admitted that great help comes from Mars—not only for industry, as mentioned before, but also for the sharpness of the mind, which consists of a fiery power. You may see the most distinguished experts in natural philosophy and medicine born under suitable aspects of Mars with the Sun and Mercury. This is because, clearly, a greater sharpness and greater skill are required to unearth the secrets of Nature than for the remaining business of life and the studies that serve them. 

I will even grant something more: it is because of Jupiter being elevated in the Midheaven <note>The highest point of the astrological chart</note> that I am more delighted by Geometry expressed in physical things than by that abstract Geometry which shows the dryness of Saturn. I am more delighted, I say, by Physics than by Geometry. And because the gibbous <note>More than half but not fully illuminated</note> Moon in the bright constellation of the Bull's forehead fills the "Fantastic faculty" <note>The faculty of imagination or forming mental images</note> of my soul with images; many of these I have found in reality to be in harmony with the nature of things, as if they had fallen from the *Paradigms* of Proclus <note>A 5th-century Neoplatonist philosopher who influenced Kepler's ideas on mathematical forms</note>. 

But if I speak now of the outcome of my studies, what, I ask, do I find further in the heavens that alludes to it even slightly? Experts admit that parts of philosophy have been either unearthed anew, corrected, or clearly perfected by me through no small effort. But here, my "stars" were not Mercury rising in the corner of the seventh house in a square with Mars; rather, they were Copernicus and Tycho Brahe. Without Tycho’s books of observations, everything that has now been placed in the clearest light by me would lie buried in darkness. My "lords" were not Saturn, the master of Mercury, but the August Emperors Rudolph and Matthias. My home was not the "house" of the planets, like Saturn's Capricorn, but Upper Austria, the house of the Emperor...

<margin>
No individual events come from the stars.

...and finally, when I sought it from the Nobles, a prompt generosity of a kind not commonly seen. This is that corner—not the setting <term>Angle</term><note>In astrology, an "angle" refers to one of the four cardinal points of a horoscope (the houses). Kepler is punning on his physical location versus his birth chart.</note> of a birth chart, but a corner of the Earth—into which, by the permission of my Lord the Emperor, I have withdrawn from a far too restless court. It is here that I struggle through these years, now verging toward the sunset of my life, on these *Harmonics* and whatever other works I have on hand. An astrologer would search in vain in my <term>birth chart</term><note>original: "Themate Genethliaco"</note> for the causes of the proportions between the celestial spheres discovered by me in the year 1596 <note>His first major work, *Mysterium Cosmographicum*</note>; for the mode of seeing discovered in 1604 <note>His work on optics, *Astronomiae Pars Optica*</note>; for the causes, found this year 1618, why such a great <term>eccentricity</term><note>The deviation of a planet's orbit from a perfect circle.</note>—no more and no less—falls to any planet; for the physical proofs of the heavens and the ways the planets are moved demonstrated in the intervening years, as well as their true motions; and finally, for the metaphysical foundations of celestial influence upon these lower realms. Those things did not flow in with the "character" of the sky into that little flame of the <term>vital faculty</term><note>The soul's animating power</note> when it was recently lit and brought into action. Rather, they lay hidden deep within the very essence of the Soul, according to the Platonic doctrine cited above from Proclus.

<margin>
Fol. 117.
General effect of the stars.
</margin>
Partly they were received inward by another way, namely through the eyes. The only and unique work of the birth chart was this: that it **trimmed those little sparks of wit and judgment**, and it spurred the mind toward untiring labor, and it increased the desire for knowledge. In short, it did not inspire the mind, nor any of the faculties mentioned here, but it awakened them.

<margin>
Vain topics of Astrology.
</margin>
From this example, it is easily apparent to anyone how far Astrology is from being able to give exact answers from a single birth chart regarding those topics commonly proposed: concerning Parents, Sex, Wealth, Children, number of Wives, Religion, Profession, Friends, Enemies, Inheritances, Family, Regions, and infinite others.

Regarding the length of life, insofar as an astrologer might pronounce upon it—that is, what the power of the <term>directions</term><note>A predictive technique in astrology where one degree of planetary movement is equated to one year of life.</note> may be—I shall speak a little later. But concerning the **Fortune** of the one born, I see I must now say something separately, in agreement with what was said above.

<margin>
By what means does human fortune depend to some extent on the stars?
</margin>
There are three things upon which a man's fortune seems to lean, as far as natural things are concerned: the **Mind**, the **Physiognomy** of the body, and the **Guardian Genius**. Concerning the first, no one doubts it; the second is more hidden and not so well known to the common people; concerning the third, I can offer nothing but conjectures. We have dealt with the first until now—namely the Mind—from which Manners and Character depend. About these, there is a well-worn common proverb: *Everyone is the architect of their own fortune.* In this saying is contained the sum of this entire part of philosophy.

<margin>
Character is the architect of fortune.
</margin>
Consider for a moment one kind of action and character (having touched upon the example of the woman earlier) and let us set it before our eyes as a representative of all. Human affairs are so arranged that there is always a great abundance of "thick" and "popularly wise" men, not only among the common folk, but even among Magistrates and in the sacred orders. To these men, the discerning, the critical, and the reformers are annoying, and are looked upon as mere troublemakers. Therefore, for someone to enjoy **prosperous fortune**—I mean that which comes from the company of men—even if they have a right judgment of morals and industry in their own private affairs away from the crowd, it is nevertheless necessary for there to be a bit of "fatness" <note>Kepler uses "fatness" (pinguedinis) here to mean a lack of over-refinement or a "common touch" that allows one to get along with simpler people.</note> mixed into the mind. Their manners must be popular and their way of acting must be such as pleases the "thick" common people. Minds that are too subtle and restless, unless they withdraw into some seclusion of study (and by that very act are looked down upon and despised), usually create misfortunes for themselves.

The charm of the face.

Folio 117.
The birth chart expressed in the face.

Folio 122.

For, to summon another foundation of human fortune from higher things—namely, the dignity of the face—the imagination of mothers contributes a great deal to the fetus throughout the entire time of gestation. Thus, the face, manners, and a similar fortune resting on those foundations are often transferred to the fetus from unhappy parents (and even from other men or animals frequently and emphatically appearing before the pregnant woman). Yet, just as the mental paradigms of <note>Proclus (412–485 AD) was a Neoplatonist philosopher who influenced Kepler’s views on geometry and the soul.</note> **Proclus** mentioned above were multiplied into living, mobile, and complex animals—namely, by the ideas of life and motion—so too here the celestial character of the birth is immersed into the appearance of the face by the hidden power of the **formative faculty**. It is recognized from the face of the newborn by a still more hidden instinct in those who behold it. You may see that those born under the conjunction of several planets before the Sun (which astrologers call <term>spear-bearing</term><note>original: "δορυφορίας" (doryphorias). An example of this matter, commended to the memory of all posterity, can be seen in **Hieronymus Cardanus** <note>Girolamo Cardano (1501–1576), a famous Italian polymath and astrologer.</note> in his birth chart of **Luther**; although many causes of public upheaval concurred there. Those who are born thus (although one certain form cannot be prescribed) prevail greatly in authority among the people, in votes in council, and in favor with the Princes of the Republic, whose nature indeed corresponds to them. Thus, fortune often stands on the side of the undeserving, even those not endowed with other suitable virtues of the mind. Refer here to the rest of what I said above regarding **Physiognomy**, and what more could be said.

<margin>
The guardianship of the Spirits.
Job 33.
Matthew 18.
Luke 15.

Whether clearly accidental evils depend on the stars?
</margin>
The divine oracles testify concerning the **Guardian Spirit**, stating that to each individual a guardianship is assigned, and that both admonition and intercession are given at the tribunal of God’s providence. Here, the nature of sensible things has no possession. If, however, astrologers are able to predict from the natal theme events that are clearly accidental (speaking naturally)—that is, such as did not happen because of a man’s bad character, or from recklessness, or from intemperance of anger or lust, nor depend on the designation of the face (which are the two foundations of fortune explained thus far)—such as a tile falling from a roof striking a passerby, or an unforeseen bullet or arrow striking one creeping in the woods; or that a sunken ship exposes wretched travelers to the midst of the waves; or that one is cut off and extinguished by flames, while another is crushed by the ruin of a house or a mountain; and conversely, that one comes into an unexpected inheritance, while another finds a treasure by chance: if, I say, the birth chart contains indications of these occurrences, which belong beyond controversy to the duties of the **Guardian Angel**, it must be that impediments and contrary promotions arise for this guardianship from the natal star. Whether this contains an impious sentiment within it, let the Theologians see—especially those who write birth charts and prognostications in great numbers. I myself have an experience (of what kind, I know not how to say) of two men who, although they were born under the most violent constellations and followed manners that were not dissimilar, so much so that for one of them the game...

...to be carried by a leap through <note>The OCR "p" is an abbreviation for the Latin *per*, meaning "through."</note> precipices, and to catch a rope in mid-flight; if they had missed it, their lives would already have been over. Yet it did not seem that they brought destruction upon themselves by their own recklessness: for one was struck by lightning, the other by a lead bullet from a hunter, who, lying in wait for wild beasts, had erred in sight and hearing. Nor do I see how the heavens could do such things to a man, without the intervention of <term>Genii</term><note>In this context, Kepler refers to "Genii" as guardian spirits or personal guiding intelligences that mediate between the celestial influence and human experience.</note>, since everything else it can do is found to be possible through the human Soul or body (in which there is no inherent power for such things). <margin>Often sins are the causes of chance occurrences.</margin> It has happened to me more than once that after I had tormented myself for a long time with pity for certain people perishing by chance, who seemed most innocent to me, I finally learned from trustworthy sources that their lives had been such—more so than others—that a good angel might easily be driven away, just as bees are driven off by smoke. Thus, a man is usually left to blind accidents, like a chariot without a driver, as if emancipated from the paternal power of God his creator, and left to his own judgment, or rather to the tyranny of Satan. Whether something of this sort should also be determined regarding the examples previously set down, and those accidents attributed to divine <term>Nemesis</term><note>The Greek goddess of retribution and vengeance.</note>; He alone knows who searches hearts: who visits the iniquity of the fathers upon the children, unto the third and fourth generation.

But far be it from me to pass the same judgment on all who perish by accident. For "conjectors" <note>astrologers</note> from the stars cannot see such impiety of life; for divine aids are not described in the figure of the heavens against the crooked inclinations of minds, into which the influence of the heavens degenerates after the Fall—not corrupting the mind, but inciting a mind already corrupted. Much less are the kinds of punishments due for individual sins inscribed in the lividness of <term>Saturn</term> or the redness of <term>Mars</term>, as if in the <term>Pandects</term><note>The *Pandects* or *Digest* was a vast compendium of Roman Law; Kepler is saying the laws of punishment aren't written in the planets.</note>. <margin>Human deeds do not come from the sky.</margin>

<margin>Does the guardian spirit have business with the client's birth chart?</margin>
Therefore, since there is no immediate natural connection of these things with the heavens, I have now, once and again over these twenty years, offered this for public consideration: Whether, just as those spiritual overseers of Provinces and peoples complain in <term>Chapter IX of Daniel</term> that they are hindered by waylaying spirits, so also the <term>Genii</term> of individual men are naturally hindered by the stars? This would mean they are less able to conveniently resist the powers of the air that waylay us <term>collectively</term><note>original Greek: "πανδημεί" (pandemei), meaning "en masse" or "publicly."</note>, and those impediments might be foreseen from the chart of the Birth; which perhaps also flowed into the Genius, no less than into the mind of the one being born. From this follows some general unhappiness of the person born, from which the proverb arose, *Misery loves company* <note>original Latin: "Nulla calamitas sola," literally "No calamity comes alone."</note>. Indeed, God does not frequently hinder this course of the nature of invisible things, because He knows how to procure some good even from that hindrance of protection, which may turn out for the good of the person in danger, if he is pleasing to God, or if he is displeasing, may fulfill the measure of just vengeance. <margin>Warnings of the guardian spirits</margin> Surely, if the guardian Angel cannot prevent an imminent evil, he at least warns in hidden ways, so as not to let his client perish unprepared. Such omens and warnings even preceded that recent mountain collapse among the <term>Rhaetians</term><note>Referring to the 1618 landslide in Pleurs (Piuro), in the Rhaetian Alps, which buried the town and killed thousands.</note>.

Let this, therefore, be the third foundation of a man's fortune, at least a conjectural one, for I affirm nothing. We must now return to the consideration of the Essence of the <term>Vital Soul</term><note>Kepler distinguishes the "vital soul" (the biological life force) from the "rational soul" (the intellect).</note> faculty. <margin>What is the principle of human life in the womb and of what kind?</margin> For it can be asked, if the character of the heavens only flows in at the exact point of Birth, does the fetus then only conceive the vital faculty of the soul at birth, and should I call it soulless before birth? It only actually conceives its own proper energetic vital faculty when it is separated from its mother; before then, it was illuminated by the rays of the mother's vital flame through the umbilical vein and artery, which artery in...

<page-num>174</page-num>
<header>ON CONFIGURATIONS</header>

<margin>CHAPTER VII.</margin>

<margin>How does the fetus live before birth?</margin>
...the artery is inserted into the heart of the fetus, with a passage separate from those two by which it later nourishes the flame of its own life within, drawing blood from one side and air from the lungs on the other. This separate passage of the heart collapses on the first day of life and disappears entirely; as was shown to me in Prague in a recently born piglet by **Georgius Horstius** <note>Georg Horst (1578–1636), a prominent physician to the Landgrave of Hesse and a correspondent of Kepler.</note>, a physician most learned in all of nature. From this, I draw arguments that the heart of the fetus, while it is in the womb, lacks that motion of **systole** <term>systole</term><note>The phase of the heartbeat when the heart muscle contracts and pumps blood from the chambers into the arteries.</note> and **diastole** <term>diastole</term><note>The phase of the heartbeat when the heart muscle relaxes and allows the chambers to fill with blood.</note> no less than it lacks respiration, and therefore the flame of its own life is not yet kindled in it. And to insist more firmly on a most faithful analogy: as the smoke of a wooden roof, toasted by fire, relates to the flame that suddenly seizes it: so does that which precedes in the fetus relate to the vital faculty, kindled at the birth itself, or a little before.

<margin>Whence comes the power of planetary transits through the positions of the birth?</margin>
In this vital faculty of Man, thus kindled at birth, there shines out especially that likeness of **Memory**, which I also showed above in the **Soul of the Earth** <note>Kepler believed the Earth was a living being with a soul (*Anima Terrae*) that perceives and reacts to the harmonious angles of the planets.</note>: since there is such constancy in the celestial character, and in all parts of the **Birth Theme** <note>original: *Thematis Genethliaci*; referring to the horoscope or birth chart.</note>, and such durability of it in the Soul, that it is not set aside before the end of life; since this faculty moves itself at every transit of the planets through the primary positions of the theme, exactly as if those positions were not mere naked images surviving in the soul of things that passed long ago, but were true stars. Thus, for example, there would not be one, but two Suns in the heavens, meeting in one; and by that meeting, the nature of the vital faculty would be moved in the manner described above.

<margin>Why are the births of parents and children related?</margin>
The clearest testimony of this matter, beyond all exception, is found in the kinship of the births <note>original: *geneseon*</note> under which parents are born and those under which their children are born. For when the fetus is mature, the formative faculty of the soul, which is in charge of generation, then especially prepares itself to extrude the fetus, and by that extrusion to kindle the new vital faculty of the soul; this happens when the stars have returned to the seats of the maternal or paternal birth, or into the same configurations, reminding the Soul of itself and of its own celestial character. See the book on the *New Star*, page 43.

<margin>Note the natural foundation of Directions.</margin>
What of the fact that this faculty observes not only the true transits of the planets through the positions of the native theme; but also the successions of the parts of heaven (which held planets at the Birth) into the primary positions of the themes which are established when whole days have passed from the birth? It observes the proportion of a day to a Year (as the revolution of both is attributed to the Earth by **Copernicus** <note>Nicolaus Copernicus (1473–1543). Kepler uses the Copernican ratio of a day's rotation to a year's orbit to justify the "Day for a Year" system of astrological progressions.</note>); and by that proportion, it dispenses its works throughout the entire life of a Man. Thus, as much longer as the Year is than the Day, so much later does the Effect follow its Sign in the **direction** <term>direction</term><note>An astrological technique (now often called "primary directions") where one degree of the sky's rotation after birth is equated to one year of life.</note>, as the Sign in the direction follows the birth. In this way, this celestial impression does not merely endure while resting, but also by enduring, it propagates itself by a motion of extension into the longer times of life. Truly, this faculty is not only a circle, but an ideal circular motion, and a twin one at that; it is, finally, through motion, also an ideal Time. See the words of **Proclus** <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 412–485 AD) whose work deeply influenced Kepler's views on geometry and the soul.</note> above on page 117. We can again seek an example of this thing from **Memory**, which is a slightly higher faculty. For on a tablet, indeed, things are painted only with the circumstance of place: but in the memory, things done are preserved, even with the character of time: finally, in this business of **Directions**, the character of positions and motions of time...

<summary>Kepler argues that a child's independent life begins at birth, not in the womb, and that the soul "remembers" the planetary configuration of that moment throughout life. He uses this "celestial memory" to explain why planetary transits and "directions" (the day-for-a-year system) affect human fate.</summary>

<margin>CHAPTER VII.</margin>
...once the body has been traversed, it is multiplied into operations, observing the sensible mundane proportion of the daily revolution to the annual movement through the **Zodiac**; so that these operations are now extended by a ratio of time from their original stimuli. You might say that as the body of the newborn grows, so does the timeframe for the <term>Genethliacal character</term> <note>The "genethliacal character" refers to the specific configuration of the stars at the moment of birth (the "nativity").</note> of its motions.

<margin>Whether the length of life or the year of death can be predicted from the stars.</margin>
<margin>What a "direction" is, physically.</margin>
<margin>The genuine causes of death</margin>
Therefore, whatever astrologers presume to predict about the length of life from a birth chart is all condensed into this chapter: the preliminaries of <term>Directions</term> <note>A technique where the movement of stars in the hours or days after birth is used to predict events in later years (e.g., "a day for a year").</note>, acting as if from the pulpit of the birth chart, inform the vital faculty in which particular year of life one or another redundant **humor** <note>The four "humors" (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) were believed to govern health and personality in traditional medicine.</note> ought to be expelled from the body or stirred up. This is a stimulus of Nature to perform its extraordinary work, which results in the prolongation of life. There is no "death" in the stars or in the birth chart, nor in the "Direction," let alone various forms of death. It is the matter of the body that either overwhelms the flame of life by flooding it or deserts it by failing; it is the body that hinders Nature's efforts and twists them toward destruction. It is **sin** that once deprived the human race of the granted remedy of immortality; it is sin that even now drives away, hinders, and repels the Guardian Angel from protecting life against the assaults of demons, men, and the elements. But this matter should be discussed at greater length in a work on Astrology, and I have discussed it quite concisely in my book *On the New Star* <note>original: "de stella," referring to Kepler's 1606 work *De Stella Nova*.</note> on page 43, and in the *Third Intervener* <note>original: "Tertio interveniente," Kepler's 1610 work where he mediates between superstitious astrology and total skepticism.</note> at number 65 and following. Perhaps it will come to pass that I publish the books of **Giovanni Pico della Mirandola** <note>A 15th-century philosopher who wrote a famous critique of astrology; Kepler intended to provide a commentary on it.</note> with a commentary, if I see that I would be doing something pleasing to students of Philosophy, provided I am not lacking the necessary resources.

<margin>The reason and power of the Horoscope, or the degree of the Ascendant, in the Birth.</margin>
<margin>The Genesis of the World.</margin>
Now, because I am hurrying toward the end, I will add a comparison between the vital faculty in man and the **Soul of the Earth** <term>Anima Telluris</term> <note>Kepler's theory that the Earth itself is a living organism that reacts to planetary harmonies.</note> regarding the influence of the heavens. It seems to be this: the Soul of the Earth is like a circle that has no beginning or end, and is not bound at any part of itself. But the vital faculty of man is compared to a circle bound as if by several points. The reason is that the Soul of the Earth has no "Birth Character," since it always remains the same and is never "born" or "kindled." However, the birth of a man—being recent and close to death—receives a character of its own origin, which marks the Zodiac with certain points of beginning and end. And even if you assign a "Birth Character" to the Earth from the first day of Creation, the entire space of the sky is always open to it; nothing in it has the status of a beginning or end, or a rising or setting. For a human, the surface of the Earth hides half the sky and distinguishes the signs of rising and setting. Thus the reason for the comparison is clear.

<margin>The foundation of Crises.</margin>
<margin>What a disease is.</margin>
This comparison—of the vital faculty established in action to a circle bound by certain points—is so true that even at the onset of a **disease** (which is like a "new life," namely a new energy of the vital faculty, or its extraordinary action, natural yet outside the usual state of the constitution, striving to expel harmful humors from the body), the place the Moon occupied then flows into the Soul. It conceives a power like that of a "true Moon," but immobile in that specific degree. If the actual Moon in the sky reaches the square or opposite positions of that point, the nature of the man is stimulated to struggle with the disease. On this matter rests the doctrine of **Crises** <note>In traditional medicine, a "crisis" was a critical turning point in a disease where the patient either begins to recover or declines toward death.</note>, which I have treated accurately enough in the *Third Intervener*, number 70 and following.

<summary>Kepler argues that astrological "directions" do not cause death but signal when the body's vital faculty reacts to physical humors. He distinguishes the human soul, which is fixed to a birth moment and a horizon, from the Soul of the Earth, which perceives the entire cosmos continuously.</summary>

<margin>CHAPTER VII.</margin>
Let enough have been said for the present regarding the lower faculty <note>The "lower faculty" refers to the irrational or vegetative part of the soul that regulates biological life and responds to celestial patterns.</note> of the human Soul as well, and about this entire subject matter.

Furthermore, I have discussed these things regarding the Soul up to this point, not indeed with the intention of completely turning students of divine philosophy away from reading Metaphysical authors; nor to "pluck out the eyes" <note>A metaphorical way of saying he does not wish to blind readers to, or harshly criticize, the established authorities.</note> of so many interpreters of Plato and Aristotle—those of the deepest investigation among the Greeks, Arabs, and Latins: Plotinus, Themistius, Simplicius, Porphyry, Alexander <note>Alexander of Aphrodisias, a famous commentator on Aristotle.</note>, Averroes (and those not few of his own nation whom he cites), as well as Boethius, and the most recent and subtle Julius Caesar Scaliger <note>Scaliger (1484–1558) was a prominent humanist scholar whose work on the nature of the soul Kepler held in high regard.</note>, when they dispute concerning the Soul and the Intelligences. From these additions, those who after me will devote themselves to this Metaphysical contemplation and read the aforementioned authors, may compare these experiments of ours with their reasonings. They shall examine both according to the "file" of the most free judgment of reason <note>To "examine with a file" is a classical metaphor for refining or perfecting a work through careful critique.</note> (which I confess has been done by me very little on this occasion), so that this part of Metaphysical science may finally be established as more illustrious, richer, and more complete in all its parts. That this may yield to the glory of the most blessed Name of God, the Creator of things Visible and Invisible, and to the increase of holiness and innocence of life in those who contemplate these things, and finally to the eternal salvation of many Souls, I humbly pray to that very

# ON THE MOVEMENTS OF THE PLANETS

## Preface.

**W**hat twenty-two years ago I first suspected, when I discovered the <term>five solid figures</term> <note>Also known as the Platonic solids: the cube, tetrahedron, octahedron, dodecahedron, and icosahedron. Kepler famously proposed they nested between the planetary spheres.</note> between the celestial spheres; what I firmly persuaded myself of in my mind even before I had seen Ptolemy’s *Harmonics*; what I promised to my friends in the very title of this fifth book before I was certain of the matter itself; what sixteen years ago I urged should be sought in a published writing; for the sake of which I spent the best part of my life in astronomical contemplations, met with Tycho Brahe, and chose Prague as my home: that at last, by the grace of God the Best and Greatest—who inspired my mind, excited this great desire, and also prolonged my life and the strength of my intellect, while providing other means through the generosity of two Emperors and the Nobles of this province of <term>Upper Austria</term> <note>Latin: "Austria Supr-Anisana," referring to the region of Austria "above the river Enns."</note>—I have finally, after completing my astronomical duties as much as was sufficient, brought into the light. And I have found it to be truer than I ever dared to hope: that the entire nature of Harmony, in all its magnitude and with all its parts as explained in Book III, is found among the celestial movements. This was found not indeed in the way I had first conceived in my mind (and this is not the least part of my joy), but in a very different, and at the same time most excellent and perfect way. In this intervening time, while the most laborious restoration of the Movements held me in suspense, there came a principal increase to my desire and an incentive to my purpose: the reading of Ptolemy’s *Harmonics*. This manuscript was sent to me by that extraordinary man, born to promote philosophy and every kind of erudition, Johannes Georgius Herwart von Hohenburg, the Chancellor of Bavaria. There, beyond expectation and with the greatest admiration, I found that nearly his entire third book was occupied with the same contemplation of celestial harmony, fifteen hundred years ago. But at that age, much was still lacking in Astronomy; and Ptolemy, having attempted the matter unsuccessfully, might have caused others to despair—looking more like someone reciting a sweet Pythagorean dream in the manner of Cicero’s Scipio than someone aiding philosophy. Yet, both that rudeness of ancient Astronomy and this very agreement of our meditations (exactly precise despite an interval of fifteen centuries) vehemently confirmed me in pursuing my goal. For why do we need many words? Nature herself was going to betray herself to men through different interpreters separated by centuries; it was the <term>finger of God</term> <note>A biblical idiom (Exodus 8:19, Luke 11:20) signifying direct divine intervention or revelation.</note>—to speak with the Hebrews—this same concept of the conformation of the World in the minds of two men who had devoted themselves entirely to the contemplation of Nature, though neither had been a leader to the other in entering this path. Now, since eighteen months ago the first light dawned; since three months ago, the full day; and since indeed a very few days ago, the pure Sun of this most admirable contemplation has shone forth: nothing holds me back. It is my pleasure to indulge in <term>sacred fury</term> <note>A state of divine inspiration or poetic madness (Latin: "sacro furori").</note>; it is my pleasure to taunt mortals with the candid confession: that I [have stolen] the golden vessels... <note>Kepler is alluding to the Israelites taking the "vessels of gold" from the Egyptians (Exodus 12:35) to furnish the Tabernacle; he views his use of "pagan" geometry to explain God's heavens in the same light. The sentence continues on the next page.</note>

<summary>Kepler recounts his long journey to discover the mathematical harmonies of the planets, crediting divine inspiration and noting his surprise at finding similar attempts in the work of the ancient astronomer Ptolemy. He describes his "Eureka" moment, claiming the laws of harmony perfectly describe planetary motion.</summary>

...to steal the golden vessels of the Egyptians, so that I may build from them a Tabernacle for my God, far away from the borders of Egypt. <note>Kepler is using a biblical metaphor from Exodus (12:35-36). He means he is taking "pagan" or secular mathematical and astronomical knowledge to use for the sacred purpose of explaining God's creation.</note> If you forgive me, I shall rejoice; if you are angry, I shall bear it. ## The chapters of this book are as follows:

I. *On the five regular solid figures.* <note>The Platonic solids: tetrahedron, cube, octahedron, dodecahedron, and icosahedron.</note>
II. *On the relationship between these and harmonic proportions.*
III. *A summary of the astronomical doctrine necessary for the contemplation of celestial harmonies.*
IV. *In which matters pertaining to the motions of the planets simple harmonies are expressed, and that all those found in song are present in the Heavens.*
V. *That the keys of the musical scale, or the positions of the system, and the types of harmony—<term>Major and Minor</term> <note>original: "Durum & Molle," literally "Hard and Soft," the terms used in Kepler's time for major and minor scales.</note>—are expressed by certain motions.*
VI. *That the individual musical tones or modes are expressed, in a way, by the individual planets.*
VII. *That universal counterpoints or harmonies of all the planets can exist, and that they are diverse, one arising from another.*
VIII. *That the natures of the four voices—Soprano, Alto, Tenor, and Bass—are expressed in the planets.*
IX. *A demonstration that, to obtain this harmonic arrangement, those very eccentricities of the planets which each has for itself, and no others, had to be established.*
X. *Epilogue on the Sun, from most pregnant conjectures.*

*The Appendix contains: I. A translation of the third book of Ptolemy's Harmonics from Chapter III, which treats the same subject.*
*II. A supplement to Ptolemy’s text for the last three chapters, for which Ptolemy provided only the headings.*
*III. Notes to this part of the Harmonics, in which I explain and refute the author, and compare either his discoveries or his attempts with my own.*

As I begin to treat these matters, I wish to impress upon my readers the most holy exhortation of Timaeus, a <term>Gentile</term> <note>non-Christian or pagan</note> philosopher, who began his discussion of these same things in a way that Christians should acknowledge with the highest admiration and even shame if they do not imitate it. It is as follows: <note>Kepler here quotes Plato’s *Timaeus* (27c) in Greek.</note> "But, O Socrates, all those who possess even a small measure of wisdom always call upon God at the beginning of every undertaking, whether small or great; and since we are about to speak concerning the UNIVERSE..." <note>original Greek: 'Αλλ’ ὦ Σώκρατες, Τοῦτό γε δὴ πάντες... περὶ ΠΑΝΤΟΣ λόγους ποιεῖσθαι</note>

Therefore, from the *Mysterium Cosmographicum* <note>Kepler’s first major work (1596), "The Secret of the Universe," where he first proposed that the orbits of the planets were determined by the five Platonic solids nested within one another.</note> I briefly repeat here the order of the five figures in the World, of which three are primary and two are secondary. The **Icosahedron (4)** follows this because of its similarity, being the last of the secondary figures, which uses a multilinear solid angle <note>A vertex where many lines meet.</note>. The innermost is the **Octahedron (5)**, which is similar to the Cube and is the first figure of the secondary class; for that reason, the first place among the interior figures is due to it, since it is "inscribable" <term>inscriptilis: a shape that fits inside another so its vertices touch the other's faces</term>, just as the first place among the exterior figures belongs to the "circumscribable" cube.

There are, however, two notable "marriages," as it were, of these figures, combined from different classes: the **Males**, the Cube and the Dodecahedron from the primary class; and the **Females**, the Octahedron and the Icosahedron from the secondary class. To these is added one that is, so to speak, celibate or **Androgynous**, the Tetrahedron; this is because it is inscribed within itself <note>The tetrahedron is "self-dual": if you place a point at the center of each face and connect them, you get another tetrahedron.</note>, whereas those "little females" are inscribed within the males and are, as it were, subjected to them. They also possess feminine signs of sex opposite to the masculine ones—namely, they have angles where the males have planes.

<margin>
In the first figure, the Tetrahedron ACDE appears hidden within the Cube, such that any plane of the Tetrahedron (like ACD) is covered by one angle of the Cube (ACDE).

In the second figure, the Cube AED appears hidden inside the Dodecahedron, such that any plane of the Cube (like AED) is covered by two angles of the Dodecahedron, or by the Pentagon ABCDE, which is divisible into three dissimilar tetrahedra by two planes, DCA and ABD.

Here you see the Octahedron inscribed in the Cube; the Icosahedron in the Dodecahedron; and the Tetrahedron in the Tetrahedron.
</margin>

Furthermore, just as the Tetrahedron is the element, the internal organs, and as it were the "rib" of the male Cube; so the female Octahedron is the element and part of the Tetrahedron, by another ratio. Thus, the Tetrahedron acts as a mediator in this marriage.

The principal difference between these "weddings" or families consists in this: the proportion of the Cubic marriage is indeed **Expressible** <term>Effabilis: a ratio that can be expressed as a whole number or simple fraction (rational)</term>; for the Tetrahedron is a third of the Cubic body, and the Octahedron is half of the Tetrahedral body, making it a sixth part of the Cube. But the proportion of the Dodecahedral marriage is **Inexpressible** <term>Ineffabilis: an irrational ratio, specifically the Golden Ratio</term>, yet it is **Divine**.

The coupling of these two words <note>"Inexpressible" and "Divine."</note> warns the reader to be careful about their meaning. For the word *Inexpressible* here does not by itself denote some kind of nobility, as it usually does in theology and divine matters; but it denotes a condition...

[...no] worse condition: for in Geometry, as stated in the first book, there are many ineffable <note>original: "ineffabilia," meaning irrational numbers that cannot be expressed as a simple ratio of whole numbers, such as the square root of 2.</note> things, which do not therefore participate in the divine proportion. What the divine proportion <term>divina proportio: the Golden Ratio, a mathematical ratio found in nature and art where the ratio of the whole to the larger part is the same as the larger part to the smaller.</term> (which should rather be called "sectoral") is must be sought from the first book. For while other proportions are supplied by their own four terms, and *Continuous* ones by three, the divine proportion also requires a singular relationship of terms, beyond the proportion itself: namely, that the two smaller terms, as parts, constitute the larger, as the *whole*.

Therefore, as much as this Dodecahedric Marriage <note>The pairing of the Dodecahedron and the Icosahedron.</note> loses because it employs an ineffable proportion; it gains just as much in return because that ineffable quality advances into the *divine*.

This marriage also possesses a solid star <note>original: "stellam solidam"; this refers to the Great Stellated Dodecahedron, one of the "Kepler-Poinsot" solids first described by Kepler.</note>, the origin of which is from the continuation of the five planes of the Dodecahedron until they all meet at a single point: see its origin in Book II.

Lastly, the proportion of the Orbs <note>The spheres supposed to carry the planets in the Copernican/Keplerian model.</note> Circumscribed around them to those Inscribed within them should be noted:
*   In the **Tetrahedron**, it is expressible <note>Rational or whole-numbered.</note>, as 100,000 to 33,333, or as 3 to 1.
*   In the **Cubic** marriage, it is ineffable <note>Irrational.</note>; yet the semi-diameter of the inscribed orb is expressible in power <note>original: "potentiâ effabilis"; meaning the square of the number is rational.</note>, being the root of the third part of the diameter's power, namely as 100,000 to 57,735.
*   In the **Dodecahedric** marriage, it is plainly ineffable, as 100,000 to 79,465.
*   In the **star**, as 100,000 to 52,573—the half-side of the Icosahedron, or half the distance of two radii.

## On the kinship of Harmonic Proportions

### with the five

->Regular Figures.<-

**V**arious and manifold is this kinship: there are, however, four primary degrees. For either the indication of kinship is taken from the external appearance alone which the figures have; or the same proportions that are harmonic are born with the very construction of the side; or they result from figures already constructed, individually or joined; or finally, they are either equal to or close to the proportions of the orbs of the Figure.

In the first degree, Proportions whose character or larger term is 3 have a familiarity with the Triangular plane of the Tetrahedron, Octahedron, and Icosahedron; those whose larger term is 4, with the Square plane of the Cube; and those of 5, with the Pentagonal plane of the Dodecahedron.

This similarity of the plane can even be extended to the smaller term of the proportion; so that wherever a "three" is found next to one of the continuous doubles <note>Numbers in the series 1, 2, 4, 8, etc.</note>, that proportion is held to be familiar to the three figures first named.

The second degree of kinship, which consists in the origin, is to be understood thus. First, there are some harmonic ratios of numbers familiar to one marriage or family: specifically, the individual perfect proportions belong to the Cubic family. Conversely, there is a proportion that is never expressed in whole numbers, nor otherwise demonstrated through numbers except by a long series of them gradually approaching it: *which is called the <term>Divine Proportion: the Golden Ratio, approximately 1.618.</term>* when it is perfect. It reigns variously through the Dodecahedral marriage; therefore, those harmonies 1:2, 2:3, 3:5, and 5:8 begin to foreshadow that proportion. For it is most imperfectly in 1:2, and most perfectly in 5:8—becoming even more perfect if we place 8 over the sum of 5 and 8 (which is 13), unless this would then cease to be harmonic.

Furthermore, to establish the side of a figure, the diameter of the sphere must be cut: and the Octahedron requires its bisection <note>division into two</note>, the Cube and Tetrahedron its trisection <note>division into three</note>, and the Dodecahedral marriage its <note>original: "Quinisectionem"</note> quinisection <note>division into five</note>. Proportions are therefore distributed among the figures according to these numbers which express them. Truly, the square of the diameter is also cut, or rather, the square of the figure's side is formed from a certain part of it. And then the squares of the sides are compared with the square of the diameter, and thus they constitute proportions: Cubic 1:3, Tetrahedral 2:3, Octahedral 1:2. Wherefore, when joined in pairs, the Cubic and Tetrahedral make 1:2, the Cubic and Octahedral 2:3, and the Octahedral and Tetrahedral 3:4. The sides of the Dodecahedral marriage are <note>original: "ineffabilia," meaning irrational numbers that cannot be represented as simple fractions.</note> ineffable.

# ON THE HARMONIES, BOOK V

<margin>CHAPTER III.</margin>
...must be removed from this consideration and cast out from the mind; for they do not present the true arrangement of the bodies of the world, nor the <term>Governance of Motions: the orderly rules and patterns that guide planetary movement.</term>.

<margin>The Hypotheses of Copernicus.</margin>
<margin>The Hypotheses of Tycho Brahe.</margin>
<margin>Comparison of both.</margin>
<margin>The Harmonic contemplation holds true in the Hypotheses of Brahe.</margin>
In their place—although I cannot do otherwise than substitute Copernicus's view of the world as the only one and, if it were possible, persuade everyone of it—it must be acknowledged that this matter is still new to the common crowd of scholars. To most, the <term>dogma: an established principle or set of beliefs.</term> that the Earth is one of the Planets and is carried among the stars around an unmoving Sun sounds utterly absurd. Therefore, let those who are offended by the strangeness of this opinion know: these harmonic speculations hold their place even within the <term>Hypotheses of Tycho Brahe: a "geo-heliocentric" model where the Sun orbits the Earth, but the planets orbit the Sun.</term>. This is because that Author <note>Tycho Brahe</note> shares everything else with Copernicus concerning the arrangement of bodies and the proportioning of motions. Tycho simply transfers the Copernican annual motion of the Earth to the whole system of planetary <term>Orbs: the celestial spheres or paths of the planets.</term> and to the Sun, which occupies the center of that system by the agreement of both authors. For from this transfer of motion, it nevertheless follows that the Earth—if not in that vast and immense space of the sphere of fixed stars, then at least in the system of the planetary world—occupies the same place at any given time in Tycho's model as Copernicus gives it. 

Just as one who writes a circle on paper moves the writing leg of the compass around; but one who attaches the paper or tablet to a spinning <term>lathe: a machine tool used for shaping wood or metal by rotating the workpiece.</term> describes that same circle with a stationary compass leg or stylus as the tablet runs beneath it; so it is here. For Copernicus, the Earth measures out a circle by the real motion of its body, traveling between the outer circle of Mars and the inner circle of Venus. But for Tycho Brahe, the whole planetary system (in which, among others, are the circles of Mars and Venus) is turned like a tablet on a lathe, applying the space between the circles of Mars and Venus to the immobile Earth, as if to the turner’s stylus. By this motion of the system, it happens that the Earth marks out the same circle around the Sun—intermediate between Mars and Venus—while remaining immobile itself, as it marks out in the Copernican system by the motion of its own body while the system remains at rest. 

Since, therefore, Harmonic contemplation considers the <term>eccentric motions: planetary paths that are not perfectly centered on the Sun/Earth, resulting in varying speeds.</term> of the planets as if seen from the Sun, it is easily understood that if a spectator were in the Sun (however much it might move), the Earth (even if granted to be stationary, as Tycho would have it) would nevertheless be seen to travel that annual circle between the Planets in the same span of time. Therefore, even if a man is of weak faith and cannot grasp the motion of the Earth among the stars, he can nonetheless enjoy the most excellent contemplation of this most divine machine; provided that whatever he hears about the daily motions of the Earth in its eccentric path, he applies to their appearance from the Sun—an appearance which Tycho Brahe also exhibits while the Earth remains still.

<margin>It holds much more strongly for the Copernicans.</margin>
Yet the cultivators of the true <term>Samian philosophy: the Pythagorean school of thought, which famously originated in Samos and proposed that the Earth moves.</term> have no just cause to begrudge such people the sharing of this most delightful speculation. Their own joy will be many times more perfect, arising from the absolute perfection of the speculation, if they also accept the immobility of the Sun and the motion of the Earth.

# ON THE MOTIONS OF THE PLANETS

<margin>
CHAPTER III.
I. Which bodies' revolutions establish the Harmonies.
</margin>
First, therefore, let readers hold this as a most certain fact among all astronomers today: that all Planets circle the Sun, except for the Moon, which alone has the Earth for its center. The size of the Moon's orbit or <term>curriculum: a path or course of running.</term> is not so great that it can be drawn on this page in just proportion to the others. To the five remaining planets, a sixth is added—the Earth—which, whether by its own motion while the Sun stands still, or being itself unmoved while the whole planetary system is turned, also describes a sixth circle around the Sun.

<margin>
II. What diversity exists in the intervals of those bodies.
</margin>
Second, it is also certain that all Planets are <term>eccentric: having an orbit that is not a perfect circle centered on the Sun, causing the distance to vary.</term>; that is, they change their distances from the Sun, so that in one part of the circle they are most remote from the Sun, and in the opposite part they come nearest to the Sun. <margin>Refer here to the diagram of ♄ ♃ ♂ ☉ ♀ ☿ <note>Symbols for Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, Sun, Venus, and Mercury.</note></margin> In the attached diagram, three circles are drawn for each planet. None of these indicates the actual eccentric path of the Planet. Instead, the middle one (as in Mars, labeled BE) is equal to the <term>eccentric Orbit: the actual elliptical-like path the planet takes.</term> in terms of its longer diameter. The Orbit itself, however, like AD, touches the upper of the three circles, AF, at one side A, and the lower circle, CD, at the opposite side D. The circle GH, shaded with dots and described through the center of the Sun, indicates the path of the Sun according to Tycho Brahe. If the Sun moves along this path, then every single point of the entire planetary system depicted here moves along an equal path, each according to its own. When one point—namely the center of the Sun—stands in one part of its circle (as here at the bottom), every single point of the System will stand in the lowest parts of their respective circles. Also, the three circles of Venus have merged into one due to the narrowness of the space, contrary to my intention.

<margin>
III. What cause the number of bodies making the Harmonies has.
</margin>
Third, let the reader recall from my *Cosmographic Mystery* <note>original: "Mysterio meo Cosmographico", Kepler's first major work (1596).</note>, which I published 22 years ago: the number of Planets or courses around the Sun was chosen by the most wise Creator from the five <term>regular solid figures: the Platonic Solids (tetrahedron, cube, octahedron, dodecahedron, and icosahedron).</term>. Euclid wrote a book about these so many centuries ago, which is called the *Elements*, because it is constructed from a series of Propositions. Furthermore, that there cannot be more regular bodies—that is, that regular plane figures cannot fit together to form a solid more than five times—was made clear in the second book of this work.

<margin>
IV. What cause the magnitude of the Spheres, which those bodies permeate, has?
</margin>
Fourth, as regards the proportion of the Planetary Orbits: the distance between two neighboring Orbits is always so great that it easily appears that each of them approaches the unique proportion of the spheres of one of the five solid figures—specifically, the proportion of the <term>Circumscribed Sphere: a sphere touching all the corners of a solid.</term> to the <term>Inscribed Sphere: a sphere tucked inside the solid, touching the centers of its faces.</term>. Yet the proportion is not entirely equal, as I once dared to promise for a perfected astronomy. For after the complete demonstration of the intervals based on the observations of Brahe <note>Tycho Brahe, the Danish astronomer whose data Kepler used.</note>, I discovered this: the corners of the Cube, when applied to the innermost circle of Saturn, almost touch the centers of the faces of the middle circle of Jupiter; and the corners of the Tetrahedron, resting on the innermost circle of Jupiter, almost touch the outermost circle of Mars. Likewise, the corners of the Octahedron, rising from any of the circles of Venus (for all three are reduced to a very narrow interval), the centers of the Octahedral faces penetrate and descend deeper below the circle of Mercury...

From which thing it is clear that the very proportions of the Planetary intervals from the Sun are not taken from the Regular figures alone; for the Creator, the very source of Geometry, does not wander from his own Archetype, and, as <term>Plato</term> wrote, *practicing eternal Geometry*. And indeed this very thing could be gathered even from the fact that all <term>Planets</term> <note>original: Planetae</note> change their intervals through certain periods of time: so that each one has two notable intervals from the <term>Sun</term> <note>original: Sol</note>, **Maximum** and **Minimum**; and between every two Planets, a fourfold comparison of intervals from the Sun is given: either of the maximums, or the minimums, or the opposites farthest from each other, or the closest: thus there are twenty comparisons of pairs of neighboring planets in number: when on the contrary, there are only five solid figures. But indeed it is consistent that the Creator, if he had a care for the proportion of the Orbs in general, also had a care for the proportion which exists between the varying intervals of each in particular; and that care is the same on both sides, and the one is linked from the other: which having been considered, we will surely obtain this as well, that to establish both the diameters and the <term>Eccentricities</term> <note>original: Eccentricitates; a measurement of how much an elliptical orbit departs from a perfect circle</note> of the Orbs jointly, there is need for more principles besides the five regular bodies.

<margin>V. Astronomical axioms of true motions.</margin>

# ON THE MOTIONS OF THE PLANETS

<margin>2.</margin>
Assuming equal times—for instance, one natural day—the *true daily arcs of a single eccentric orbit corresponding to those times have a proportion to each other that is the inverse of the proportion of the two distances from the Sun.* <note>This is a precursor to Kepler's Second Law, describing how a planet moves faster when closer to the Sun.</note> At the same time, it has been demonstrated by me that *the orbit of a planet is elliptical, and the Sun, the source of motion, is at one of the foci of this ellipse;* <note>Kepler’s First Law: planets move in ellipses with the Sun at one focus.</note> thus it happens that when a planet has completed a quadrant <note>90 degrees or one quarter</note> of its total circuit from its aphelion, it is at precisely the <margin>3. 4. 5.</margin> *mean distance from the Sun,* between the maximum distance at aphelion <note>the point furthest from the Sun</note> and the minimum at perihelion <note>the point closest to the Sun</note>. <margin>6.</margin> From these two axioms it is established that *the daily mean motion of a planet in the eccentric is the same as its true daily arc of that eccentric* at those moments when the planet is *at the end of the quadrant of the eccentric* calculated from aphelion, even though that true quadrant may still appear smaller than a <margin>7.</margin> proper quadrant. It follows further that *any two true daily arcs of the eccentric, being truly equidistant—one from the aphelion and the other from the perihelion—when joined together, equal two daily mean motions:* and consequently, since the proportion of circles is the <margin>8.</margin> same as that of their diameters, *the proportion of one daily mean motion to all the joined mean motions (which are equal to each other) throughout the entire circuit, is the same as the proportion of the daily mean to all the joined true eccentric arcs,* which are equal in number but unequal to each other. These things regarding the true daily arcs of the eccentric and the true motions must be understood beforehand, so that we may now understand from them the apparent motions, assuming the eye is placed in the Sun.

<margin>VI. Astronomical Axioms of the motions as they appear from the Sun, or the angles which the daily lines encompass at the center of the Sun.</margin>

Sixth, as far as concerns the arcs appearing as if from the Sun: it is known even from ancient astronomy that regarding true motions—even those equal to each other—that which has receded further from the center of the world (such as a planet at aphelion) appears smaller to an observer at that center; while that which becomes closer, such as at perihelion, appears larger. Since, moreover, the true daily arcs are even larger when nearby because of the faster motion, and smaller at the remote aphelion because of the slowness of motion: hence I have demonstrated in my *Work on Mars* <note>original: "Martialibus," referring to his book *Astronomia Nova* (1609), which focused on the orbit of Mars</note> that *the proportion of the apparent daily arcs of a single eccentric is, quite precisely, the inverse square of the proportion of their distances from the Sun.* <margin>2.</margin> For example, if a planet in one of its days, when it is at aphelion, were distant from the Sun by 10 units of any measure, and on the opposite day, when it is at perihelion, by 9 such units: it is certain that its apparent advancement from the Sun at aphelion will be to the apparent advancement at perihelion as 81 is to 100. <note>Kepler is explaining that apparent speed changes more drastically than actual speed because of the changing distance.</note>

However, this is true with these cautions: first, that the *arcs of the eccentric are not large,* lest they involve different distances that <margin>3.</margin> differ greatly—that is, lest they cause a sensible variation in the distance of <margin>4.</margin> their endpoints from the Apsides <note>the points of least or greatest distance</note>; second, that the *eccentricity is not very large:* for the greater the eccentricity (that is, the larger the arc), the more the angle of its appearance increases beyond the measure of its <margin>5.</margin> approach to the Sun, according to *Theorem 8 of Euclid’s Optics:* <note>Euclid's Theorem 8 states that equal lengths on a line appear unequal when viewed from different distances.</note> which, however, in small arcs and great distance is of no importance, as I warned in my *Optics,* <margin>6.</margin> Chapter XI. But there is another reason why I mention this. For *eccentric arcs near the Mean Anomalies are viewed obliquely* from the center of the Sun, and this obliquity diminishes the magnitude of the appearance; whereas, conversely, *arcs near the Apsides* <margin>7.</margin> *are presented directly to the view* as if placed in the Sun. Therefore, when the eccentricity is very large, the proportion of the motion is sensibly harmed...
