# HARMONICS BOOK V.

...your <note>Kepler is addressing the reader, continuing from the previous page's discussion on calculating motion</note>, if we apply the mean daily motion without reduction to the mean distance, it appears as great as it truly is from that mean distance: as will appear below in the case of Mercury. All these matters are treated more at length in Book V of the *Epitome of Copernican Astronomy*; however, they had to be mentioned here as well, because they pertain to the very terms of the celestial harmonies, when each is considered separately on its own.

<margin>VII. Rejection of the motions that appear to those looking from the Earth.</margin>
**Seventhly**, if anyone should happen to encounter those daily motions which do not appear as if from the Sun, but from the perspective of those looking from the Earth (about which Book VI of the *Epitome of Copernican Astronomy* treats), he should know that no account of them is taken in this business. Indeed, it should not be, since the Earth is not the source of their motion; nor can it be, since those motions degenerate not only into mere rest or an apparent stationary point, but clearly into a "retrogradation" <note>the optical illusion where a planet appears to move backward in the sky</note> according to deceptive appearance. By this reasoning, an infinity of proportions would be attributed to all planets simultaneously and equally. Therefore, to ensure we have certain knowledge of what proper proportions the daily motions of each true eccentric orbit constitute (even though they themselves are still "apparent" as if to one looking from the Sun, the source of motion), we must first remove from those proper motions this "fantasy"—common to all five planets—of the annual adventitious motion <note>original: *motus annui adventitij*; this refers to the apparent motion caused by the Earth's own yearly orbit</note>. Whether that arises from the motion of the Earth itself, according to Copernicus, or from the annual motion of the whole system, according to Tycho Brahe, the motions proper to each planet must be unshelled and placed before our view.

<margin>VIII. What is the proportion of the periodic Times to the intervals of any two from the Sun? 2. 3. 4.</margin>
**Eighthly**, so far we have dealt with the diverse delays or arcs of one and the same planet. Now we must also deal with the motions of two planets compared with each other. Here, note the definition of terms which will be necessary for us. We shall call the nearest <term>Apsides</term> <note>the points in an orbit closest or farthest from the center of motion</note> of two planets the <term>Perihelion</term> <note>point closest to the sun</note> of the higher one and the <term>Aphelion</term> <note>point farthest from the sun</note> of the lower one, notwithstanding that they may face toward different, and perhaps opposite, regions of the world. By *extreme motions*, understand the slowest and the fastest of the whole planetary circuit. <term>Convergent</term> or *conversed* extremes are those at the nearest Apsides of two planets—namely, at the Perihelion of the higher and the Aphelion of the lower. <term>Divergent</term> or *diverse* extremes are those at the opposite Apsides—namely, the Aphelion of the higher and the Perihelion of the lower. Here again, therefore, some part of my <term>Cosmographic Mystery</term> <note>Kepler’s first book, *Mysterium Cosmographicum*, published 22 years earlier</note>, suspended twenty-two years ago because it was not yet clear, must be completed and inserted here. For after the true intervals of the orbits were found through Brahe’s observations by the continuous labor of a very long time, at last, at last, the genuine proportion of the periodic Times to the proportion of the Orbits—*Late indeed, she looked back upon the sluggish one,* 

->*Yet she looked back and came after a long time;*<-
<note>Kepler is quoting Virgil’s *Eclogues* to describe his long-awaited discovery of the Third Law.</note>

And if you ask for the exact moment of time, it was conceived in my mind on the 8th of March of this year, one thousand six hundred and eighteen, but submitted to calculation unluckily, and therefore rejected as false. Finally, returning on the 15th of May, and taking a new start, it conquered the darkness of my mind by such a great proof, through the convergence of my seventeen years of labor on Brahe’s observations and this present meditation, that I first believed I was dreaming and assuming the very thing I was seeking among my first principles. But the matter is most certain and most exact: *the proportion which exists between the periodic times of any two planets is precisely the sesquialterate proportion of the mean distances* <note>original: *sesquialtera proportionis*; this is Kepler's Third Law: the square of the orbital period ($T^2$) is proportional to the cube of the mean distance ($r^3$)</note>, that

CHAPTER III.
For in the *Commentaries on Mars* <note>original: *Commentarijs Martis*, referring to Kepler’s 1609 work, *Astronomia Nova*</note> chapter 48, folio 232, I proved that *this arithmetic mean is either the diameter of the circle which equals the elliptical orbit in length, or is very nearly less than it.*
</margin>
...is of the Orbs themselves; noting however this, that *the arithmetic mean <note>the average value</note> between both diameters of an elliptical orbit is slightly less than the longer diameter.* Thus if anyone, from the period of the Earth (for example), which is one year, and from the period of Saturn, thirty years, takes the third part of the proportion—that is, the cube roots—and squares those roots, he will have in the resulting numbers a *most accurate proportion* of the *mean* distances of the Earth and Saturn from the Sun. For the cube root of 1 is 1, and its square is 1. And the cube root of 30 is greater than 3; its square is therefore greater than 9. And Saturn, at its average distance from the Sun, is a little higher than nine times the average distance of the Earth from the Sun. The use of this Theorem will be necessary below in Chapter IX for the demonstration of eccentricities <note>the measure of how much an orbit deviates from a perfect circle</note>.

<margin>
IX. How much space any planet traverses with respect to another in any given time.
</margin>
Ninthly, if you wish to measure the very truest daily paths of each planet through the ethereal air <note>the vacuum of space, which 17th-century scientists believed was filled with a subtle fluid</note> as if with the same ten-foot rod <note>original: *decempeda*, a standard Roman measuring rod</note>; two proportions must be joined: one of the true (not apparent) daily arcs of the Eccentric, and the other of the mean distances of each from the Sun, because this is also the proportion of the size of the orbits. *That is, the true daily arc of each planet must be multiplied by the semi-diameter of its orbit:* when this is done, numbers suitable for investigating whether those paths form <term>Harmonic proportions</term> <note>ratios that correspond to musical intervals, which Kepler believed governed the structure of the universe</note> will result.

<margin>
X. How, from the true paths and true distances of the planets from the Sun, the apparent motion from the Sun is obtained—the subject of celestial Harmony.
</margin>
Tenthly, to find how great an appearance any of these daily paths makes as if to an eye placed in the Sun; although this same thing can be sought directly from Astronomy, it will nevertheless be clear if you add to the proportion of the paths the inverse proportion of the distances—not the mean distances, but the true ones at any point on the eccentrics: *by multiplying the path of the higher planet by the distance of the lower from the Sun, and conversely the path of the lower by the distance of the higher from the Sun.*

<margin>
XI. How, from the apparent daily motions (as seen from the Sun), the distances of the planets from the Sun are elicited.
</margin>
Eleventhly, no less also from given apparent motions—the <term>Aphelion</term> <note>the point in an orbit furthest from the Sun</note> of one and the <term>Perihelion</term> <note>the point in an orbit closest to the Sun</note> of another, or vice versa or alternately—the proportions of the distances are elicited: of the Aphelion of one to the Perihelion of the other. Here, however, the mean motions must be known beforehand: namely, the inverse proportion of the periodic times, from which the proportion of the Orbs is elicited through Number VIII above. Then, *having taken the mean proportional between either apparent motion and its own mean, it follows that as this mean proportional is to the semi-diameter of the orbit now revealed, so is the mean motion to the sought-after distance.* Let the periodic times of two planets be 27 and 8. Therefore, the daily mean motions of the former to the latter are as 8 to 27. Wherefore the semi-diameters of the orbits will be as 9 to 4. For the cube root of 27 is 3, and of 8 is 2; the squares of these roots, 3 and 2, are 9 and 4. Now let the apparent motions be: the Aphelion of one, 2, and the Perihelion of the other, 33 1/3 <note>original: *3 1/3 cum tertiâ parte*, which in this mathematical context implies 33 and one-third</note>. The mean proportionals between the mean motions (8 and 27) and these apparent ones will be 4 and 30 <note>Since $\sqrt{8 \times 2} = 4$ and $\sqrt{27 \times 33.33} = 30$</note>. If therefore the mean 4 gives a mean distance of the planet of 9, then the mean motion 8 gives an aphelion distance of 18, corresponding to the apparent motion 2. And if the other mean 30 gives a mean distance of the other planet of 4, then the mean motion 27 gives a perihelion distance for it of 3 and 3/5 <note>3.6</note>. I say therefore, the aphelion distance of the former is to the perihelion of the latter as 18 is to 3 and 3/5. From which it is clear that...

# BOOK V OF THE HARMONIES
## CHAPTER III

...[from] harmonies, between the extreme motions of two [planets], and with the periodic times prescribed to each, the extreme and middle intervals—and therefore also the <term>eccentricities</term> <note>the measure of how much an orbit deviates from a perfect circle</note>—are necessitated.

<margin>XII. What the proportion of the Mean Motion is to the extreme motions.</margin>

Twelfthly, from the various extreme motions of one and the same planet, it is also possible to find the *mean motion* <note>the average orbital speed</note>. For this is not precisely the *arithmetic mean* <note>the simple average</note> *between the extreme motions, nor precisely the geometric mean; but it is as much smaller than the geometric mean as the geometric mean is smaller than the average between both.* Let there be two extreme motions, 8 and 10. The mean motion will be less than 9, and also less than the square root of 80 <note>approx. 8.94</note>, by half of that which is between the two, [namely] 9 and the square root of 80. Likewise, if the <term>aphelion</term> <note>the point in orbit furthest from the sun</note> is 20 and the <term>perihelion</term> <note>the point in orbit closest to the sun</note> is 24, the mean motion will be less than 22, and also less than the square root of 480 <note>approx. 21.9</note>, by half of that which is between this root and 22. The use of this theorem is in the following.

<margin>XIII. The relationship of the proportion of the intervals between two planets and the Sun to the proportion of the apparent motions of both.</margin>

Thirteenthly, from the premises, this PROPOSITION is demonstrated—which will be very necessary for us in the future—that just as the proportion of the mean motions in two planets is the inverse <term>sesquialtera</term> <note>The "sesquialtera" or 3:2 ratio is central to Kepler's Third Law: the square of the orbital period is proportional to the cube of the distance. "Inverse sesquialtera" here refers to the relationship where speed decreases as distance increases.</note> of the proportion of the orbits; *so the proportion of the two convergent extreme apparent motions always falls short of the sesquialtera proportion of the intervals corresponding to those extreme motions:* and *as long as the two proportions of the two corresponding intervals, joined to the two middle intervals or to the semi-diameters of the two orbits, make less than half of the proportion of the orbits, so long is the proportion of the two extreme convergent motions greater than the proportion of the corresponding intervals; but if that sum exceeds half of the proportion of the orbits, then the proportion of the convergent motions would become less than the proportion of their intervals.*

Let the proportion of the Orbs be DH to AE, and the proportion of the mean motions be HI to EM, the inverse sesquialtera of the former. Let the interval there be the minimum of its orb, namely CG, and here the maximum of its own, namely BF; and let the joined proportions DH to CG and BF to AE be first smaller than half of DH to AE. And let the apparent motion of the upper perihelion be GK, and of the lower aphelion be FL, so that they are the "convergent extremes" <note>the closest values between the speeds of two neighboring planets</note>. I say that the proportion of GK to FL is greater than the inverse proportion of CG to BF, yet less than its sesquialtera. For the proportion of HI to GK is double the proportion of CG to DH, and the proportion of FL to EM is double the proportion of AE to BF. Therefore, the two joined proportions, HI to GK and FL to EM, produce double the joined proportions of CG to DH and AE to BF. But the joined [proportions] CG to DH and AE to BF are less than half of the proportion AE to DH, by a certain deficit, as is in the suppositions; therefore, the joined HI to GK and FL to EM are less than double the half—that is, less than the whole proportion AE to DH—by double the previous deficit. But HI to EM is the sesquialtera of the proportion AE to DH, by the eighth [proposition] premised. Therefore, less than the whole doubled deficit, subtracted from the sesquialtera—namely the proportions HI to GK and FL to EM from the proportion **HI to EM**—leaves more than half of the proportion AE to DH, by the doubled excess: they leave, in fact, the proportion GK to FL. Therefore, the proportion GK to FL is more than half the proportion AE to DH, by the doubled excess. But the proportion AE to DH is composed of three: from AE to BF, from BF to CG, and from CG to DH. <margin>CHAPTER III</margin> [the ratio of the motions] is less than half of AE to DH, by a single deficit. Therefore, the ratio of BF to CG is more than half of AE to DH, by a single excess. But the proportion of GK to FL was also more than half of that same AE to DH, yet by a double excess. Truly, a double excess is greater than a single one. Therefore, the proportion of the motions GK to FL is greater than the proportion of the corresponding intervals, BF to CG.

In exactly the same way, the opposite is demonstrated: if the planets approach each other at G and F, beyond the mean distances at H and E, so that the proportion of the mean distances DH to AE loses more than half; then the proportion of the motions GK to FL becomes less than the proportion of their intervals BF to CG. For nothing further needs to be done than to change the words *Greater* to *Lesser*, *Plus* to *Minus*, *Excess* to *Deficit*, and vice versa.

In the assigned numbers, because half of 4 to 9 is 2 to 3; and 5 to 8 is still greater than 2 to 3 by the amount of the excess 15 to 16; and indeed, the double of the proportion 8 to 9 is made the proportion 1600 to 2025, that is 64 to 81; and the double of the proportion 4 to 5 is made the proportion 3456 to 5400, that is 16 to 25. Finally, the <term>sesquialter</term> <note>a ratio of 3:2, or 1.5. This is the mathematical basis for Kepler's Third Law, where the square of the period is proportional to the cube of the distance</note> of the proportion 4 to 9 is made the proportion 1600 to 5400, that is 8 to 27: therefore, the proportion 2025 to 3456, which is 75 to 128, is also greater than 5 to 8, which is 75 to 120, by the amount of the excess likewise (120 to 128, which is) 15 to 16. Thus, *the proportion of the Convergent motions 2025 to 3456 exceeds the inverted proportion of the corresponding intervals 5 to 8 by as much as this exceeds half the proportion of the Orbits 4 to 9.* Or, what comes to the same thing, *the proportion of two convergent intervals is the geometric mean between half the Proportion of the Orbits and the inverted proportion of the corresponding Motions.*

Furthermore, from this it is given to be understood that *the proportion of divergent motions is much greater than the sesquialter proportion of the orbits*; since the doubles of the proportions of the <term>aphelion</term> <note>the point furthest from the Sun</note> interval to the mean interval, and of the mean to the <term>perihelion</term> <note>the point closest to the Sun</note>, approach the sesquialter.

# CHAPTER IV.

## In which things pertaining to the motions of the Planets have Harmonic proportions been expressed by the Creator, and in what way?

**T**herefore, the illusion of <term>retrogradations</term> <note>the apparent backward motion of planets as seen from Earth</note> and stations having been removed, and the planets' own motions in their genuine <term>eccentric orbits</term> <note>orbits that are not perfect circles centered on the Sun</note> having been laid bare, these distinct things still remain in the planets: 1. Intervals from the Sun. 2. Periodic times. 3. Daily eccentric arcs. 4. Daily delays in those arcs. 5. Angles at the Sun, or apparent daily arcs as if seen from the Sun. And again, all these (except for the Periodic times) are variable throughout the whole circuit—most variable at the mean longitudes, and least at the extremities,

# THE HARMONICS, BOOK V.

<margin>CHAPTER IV.</margin>
When a transition is made from one of these <note>the extremes of planetary distance and speed</note>, they return to the opposite; as when a Planet is at its lowest point and closest to the Sun <note>original: "pihelio," a typo for "perihelio"</note>, it remains in a single degree of the **Eccentric** <note>the off-center circular path of a planet's orbit</note> for the shortest possible time, and conversely, in one day it completes the greatest arc of the **Eccentric**, appearing at its swiftest from the Sun. Then its motion remains for some time in this strength, without any perceptible variation, until, having passed the perihelion, the planet begins to gradually move further away from the Sun in a straight line. Then, simultaneously, it remains longer in the degrees of the **Eccentric**; or, if you consider the motion of a single day, it makes less progress on the following day, and appears much slower from the Sun, until it approaches the **highest Apside** <note>the aphelion, or the point in the orbit farthest from the Sun</note>, making its interval from the Sun the greatest. For then it remains the longest of all in one degree of the **Eccentric**; or conversely, in one day it completes its smallest arc, and produces the smallest appearance of its entire circuit.

Finally, all these things occur either within a single Planet through different times, or they occur among different planets; so that, assuming an infinity of time, all the characteristics of one planet's circuit can coincide and be compared with all the characteristics of another planet's circuit at the same moment of time. And then, the entire **Eccentrics**, compared among themselves, have the same proportion as their semi-diameters, or their mean intervals. Truly, the arcs of two **Eccentrics**, even if they are named by the same number of degrees, nevertheless have unequal true lengths in proportion to the whole **Eccentrics**. For example, one degree in the Sphere of Saturn is almost twice as large as one degree in the Sphere of Jupiter. And conversely, the daily arcs of the **Eccentrics** expressed in astronomical numbers do not show the proportion of the true journeys which the globes complete in one day through the ethereal breeze, because individual units denote a larger part of the journey in the wider circle of a superior Planet, but a smaller part in the narrower circle of an inferior one. Thus, this sixth part of our consideration now approaches: concerning the daily Journeys of pairs of Planets.

First, therefore, let us take what follows from what has been set forth: namely, the **periodic Times** of the Planets. These contain the total sums collected from all the "Stays" <note>the time spent traversing</note> of all the Degrees of the entire circuit—the long, the medium, and the short. And it has been discovered from ancient times down to our own, that the Planets complete their returns around the sun as follows in the Table.

In these periodic times, therefore, there are no harmonic proportions, as is easily apparent if the longer periods are continually halved and the shorter ones continually doubled, so that—ignoring the intervals of the Octave <note>original: "Diapason"</note>—we can seek those ratios which exist within the span of a single Octave.

<note>Kepler is mathematically "folding" the planetary years into a single musical octave to see if they create chords. For example, he halves Saturn's long year several times to compare it to Mercury's year, which he doubles.</note>

All the final results, as you see, shrink away from harmonic proportions and seem similar to irrational numbers. For if the number of days for Mars, 687, takes the measure of 120—which is the standard division of a String <note>referring to the monochord, a tool used to measure musical intervals</note>—then in this same measure, Saturn would be assigned (for its sixteenth part) a little more than 117; Jupiter (for its eighth part) less than 95; Earth less than 64; Venus (for its double) more than 78; and Mercury (for its quadruple) more than 61. And yet these numbers do not form any harmonic proportion with 120; rather, it is their neighbors—60, 75, 80, 96—that do so. Likewise, in a system where Saturn has 120, Jupiter has nearly 97, Earth over 65, Venus more than 80, and Mercury less than 63. And where Jupiter has 120, Earth has less than 81, Venus less than 100, and Mercury less than 78. Again, where Venus has 120, Earth has less than 95 and Mercury more than 94. Finally, where Earth has 120, Mercury has less than 116. If a free choice of proportions had prevailed here, the harmonies would have been altogether perfect, rather than these "exceeding" and "falling short" values. It is therefore not found that God the Creator intended to introduce harmonic proportions among these total sums of durations collected into periodic Times.

<margin>The proportion of the planetary globes to one another.</margin>

And since it is a most probable conjecture (relying as it does on Geometric demonstrations and the doctrine of the causes of planetary motions handed down in the *Commentaries on Mars* <note>A reference to Kepler's 1609 work, *Astronomia Nova*</note>) that the physical masses of the planetary bodies are in proportion to their periodic Times, such that the globe of Saturn is about thirty times larger than the globe of Earth, Jupiter twelve times larger, Mars less than double, Earth one-and-a-half times larger than the globe of Venus, and four times larger than the globe of Mercury: it follows that these proportions of the bodies will not be harmonic either.

However, since God has established nothing without Geometric beauty—unless it was bound by some law of necessity to something prior—we easily gather that the periodic times receive their specific lengths, and the moving bodies their specific masses, from something that is prior in the Archetype <note>The divine blueprint or original "Idea" of the world in the mind of God</note>. To express that Archetype, these seemingly disproportionate masses and periods were fitted into this current scale. But I have said that these Periods are gathered from "delays" <note>the time spent in specific parts of the orbit</note>—the longest, the middling, and the slowest. Therefore, it must be either in these delays, or in something even more fundamental in the mind of the Architect, that the Geometric concords are to be found. Indeed, the proportions of the delays are bound together by the daily arcs— <note>The text cuts off mid-sentence; the catchword indicates the next word is "diurnal" or "daily."</note>

<margin>By what steps the true celestial harmonies were reached.</margin>
<margin>
The same analogy exists between the convex sphere and a circular line as between solid figures and harmonies: the same also exists between a body and the motion of a body.
</margin>
And so, even if one interval wanders a little too far from the Harmonics, this success was nonetheless an invitation to proceed further. These, then, were my reasonings. First, these intervals, insofar as they are lengths without motion, are not aptly examined for Harmonics, because <term>Motion</term> is a more familiar subject for Harmonies, by reason of its speed and slowness. Secondly, in these same intervals, insofar as they are the diameters of the Orbs, it is believable that greater account was taken of the <term>five regular solids</term><note>The Platonic solids (tetrahedron, cube, etc.), which Kepler famously used in his earlier work to explain the spacing between planetary orbits.</note>, by analogy: for the same relationship that exists between solid Geometric bodies and the celestial orbs—which are either enclosed on all sides by celestial matter, as antiquity holds, or are to be enclosed by the successive accumulation of many rotations—also exists between Plane figures inscribed in a circle (which are the figures that generate Harmonies) and the celestial circles of motions, and the other spaces in which motions occur. Therefore, if we seek Harmonies, let us seek them not in these intervals as they are the semi-diameters of the Orbs, but in those intervals as they are the measures of motions—that is, in the motions themselves. To be sure, no other intervals can be accepted for the semi-diameters of the Orbs than the Mean <note>Average</note> ones; yet here we are dealing with the Extreme intervals. We are not, therefore, dealing with intervals in respect to their own orbs, but in respect to motions.

For these reasons, when I had moved on to the comparison of the extreme motions, at first the proportions of the motions remained the same in magnitude as those of the intervals had been before, only inverted; for this reason, some proportions were found among the motions that were, as before, unmusical and alien to the Harmonies. But I realized that this happened to me deservedly; for I was comparing arcs of the <term>Eccentric</term><note>An orbital path that is not centered exactly on the Sun.</note> which were neither expressed nor counted by a measure of the same magnitude, but were counted in degrees and minutes, which are of different physical magnitudes in different planets. Nor do they create an appearance anywhere as great as the number of each suggests, except only at the center of each Eccentric—which is supported by no physical body. Furthermore, it is unbelievable that there is any sense or natural instinct in that location of the world capable of perceiving this appearance. Indeed, it is even impossible, since I was comparing the Eccentric arcs of different planets for the sake of their appearance in their own centers, which different planets hold in different places. However, different apparent magnitudes, when compared, ought to appear as such in one single place of the World; so that the faculty which has the power to compare them is present in that common place of appearance. Therefore, I judged that either the appearance of these eccentric arcs must be removed from the mind, or they must be shaped differently. But if I were to remove the appearance and attend with my mind to the actual daily journeys of the Planets, I saw that I must use that rule which I handed down in the previous chapter at Number IX. Therefore, by multiplying the daily arcs of the Eccentrics by the Mean intervals of the Orbs, these journeys were produced.

Regarding, therefore, the daily journeys of the individual planets, the proportions contained within them must be of the same magnitude as those previously found in the intervals, but inverted in type: because the <term>Eccentric arcs</term> <note>The actual paths traveled along the planet's elliptical orbit.</note>, as has been said, have an inverse proportion to their intervals from the Sun.

Indeed, if we consider the extreme journeys of pairs of planets—whether divergent or convergent—far less of anything harmonic appears than before, when we were considering the arcs themselves.

And truly, if we weigh the matter more carefully, it will appear not very likely that the most wise Creator arranged Harmonies primarily among the planetary journeys themselves. For if the proportions of the journeys are Harmonic, then everything else the planets possess would be forced and tied to those journeys, leaving no room to arrange Harmonies elsewhere. But for what good are Harmonies among journeys? Or who will perceive these harmonies? There are two things that reveal harmonies to us in natural things: either light or sound. The former is received through the eyes (or hidden senses analogous to eyes), the latter through the ears. The mind, grasping these <term>species</term> <note>original: "species"; in this context, the mental images or sensory patterns perceived by the soul.</note> either by instinct (of which I spoke abundantly in Book IV) or through Astronomical or Harmonic reasoning, judges the concordant from the discordant. Now, no sounds exist in the heavens, nor is the motion so turbulent that a screech is elicited from the friction of the celestial air. Light remains: if this is to teach us about the journeys of the Planets, it will teach either the Eyes, or a sensory organ analogous to them, located in a certain place; and for light itself to teach immediately by itself, it seems necessary for a sense to be present. There would therefore be a sense in the whole World, so that one and the same sense might be present for the motions of all the Planets at once. For that path—led from observations through the longest detours of Geometry and Arithmetic, through the proportions of the orbits and other things to be learned beforehand, all the way to these very journeys—is too long for any natural instinct, for whose sake it seems reasonable that harmonies were introduced.

<margin>CHAPTER IV</margin>
Therefore, having gathered everything into one view, I have rightly concluded—once the true journeys of the Planets through the ethereal air have been set aside—that it is necessary for us to turn our eyes toward the **Apparent daily arcs**. These are all "apparent" from one certain and distinguished place in the World: namely, from the Solar body itself, the source of Motion for all the Planets. We must see, not how far from the Sun any planet may be, nor through how much space it crosses in a single day (for this is a matter of reasoning and astronomy, not something <term>instinctual</term> <note>Kepler argues that the soul or "instinct" of the universe perceives these proportions directly through light, without needing to perform complex calculations.</note>); rather, we must see what angle the daily motion of each planet subtends at the solar body itself. We look at what arc it is seen to complete each day on one common circle described from the Sun, such as the Ecliptic. In this way, this appearance—brought to the body of the Sun by the benefit of light—can flow with that light directly into creatures who share in this instinct, just as we said in the fourth book that the "scheme of the heaven" <note>An astrological birth chart or configuration.</note> flows into the fetus by the benefit of the rays.

Thus, Tychonic Astronomy <note>The astronomical system and data provided by Tycho Brahe, Kepler's predecessor.</note> teaches us (once the <term>parallaxes</term> <note>The apparent shifts in position caused by Earth's own motion, which create the illusion of planets stopping or moving backward.</note> of the annual orbit, which give them the appearance of stations and retrogradations, are removed from the planets' own motion) that the daily motions of the Planets in their orbits, as they would appear to those watching from the Sun, are as follows.

<margin>CHAPTER IV</margin>
Therefore, I was able to presume in my mind that there would be **Harmonies** and **Tuneful intervals** between these extreme apparent motions of each planet, even from the proportions of the daily eccentric arcs reported above. For I saw that the halves of harmonic proportions reigned everywhere there; and I knew that the proportion of the apparent motions is the square <note>original: "duplam proportionem," meaning a doubled ratio or a ratio squared.</note> of the proportion of the eccentric motions. But it is possible to prove what is asserted by experience itself, even without reasoning, as you see in the following table. The proportions of the individual apparent motions approach harmonies very closely; thus **Saturn** and **Jupiter** encompass little more than **Thirds**, Major and Minor: the excess there is 53 to 54, here 54 to 55, or less, that is, nearly a sesqui-comma <note>A very small musical interval, specifically a ratio of 1/54 or 1/55.</note>; the **Earth** encompasses a little more than a **semitone**, specifically 137 to 138, by scarcely a half-comma; **Mars** somewhat less than a **Fifth** <note>original: "Diapente," the musical interval of a perfect fifth.</note> (specifically 29 to 30, which approaches 34 to 35 or 35 to 36); **Mercury** above an **Octave** <note>original: "Diapason," the interval of an octave.</note>, holds closer to a **Minor Third** than to a **Whole Tone**, having less by about 38 to 39, which is roughly two commas, namely almost 34 to 35 or 35 to 36. **Venus** alone holds something less than all tuneful intervals, even a **Diesis** <note>A small interval, often the difference between a major and minor semitone.</note>: for its proportion is between two and three commas, and it exceeds two-thirds of a Diesis, being about 34 to 35, almost a Diesis diminished by a comma, 35 to 36.

The **Moon** also comes into this consideration: for its hourly motion at **Apogee** <note>The point where the Moon is farthest from Earth.</note> in the **Quadratures** <note>The moon's quarter phases.</note>, which is the slowest of all, is found to be 26 minutes 26 seconds; and at **Perigee** <note>The point where the Moon is closest to Earth.</note> in the **Syzygies** <note>Conjunctions or oppositions, i.e., New and Full Moon.</note>, which is the fastest of all, it is 35 minutes 12 seconds; by which ratio a **Fourth** <note>original: "Diatessaron," the interval of a perfect fourth (ratio 4:3).</note> is formed most exactly. For a third part of 26:26 is 8:49, four times which is 35:15. And note that the Harmony of a Fourth is found nowhere else among the apparent motions; note also the analogy of the **Fourth** in Harmonies with the **Quarter** <note>original: "Quadra," referring to the quarter phase.</note> in the Moon's phases. These things, then, are found in the motions of the individual planets.

<margin>What Harmonies exist between the convergent and divergent motions of two planets.</margin>
But in the extreme motions of two planets compared with each other, the clearest Sun of celestial Harmonies immediately shines out at first glance, whether you compare the **divergent** extreme motions <note>Comparing the slowest speed of one planet to the fastest of the next.</note> or the **convergent** ones <note>Comparing the fastest speed of one planet to the slowest of the next.</note>. For between the convergent motions of **Saturn** and **Jupiter**, the proportion is most exactly double, or an **Octave**; between the divergent ones, a little more than triple, or an **Octave with a Fifth**. For of 5 minutes 30 seconds, a third part is 1 minute 50 seconds, whereas Saturn has 1 minute 46 seconds for that. Therefore, the planetary ratio has one **Diesis** more, or a little less, namely 26 to 27 or 27 to 28: and by subtracting only a single second approaching the Aphelion of Saturn, the excess will be 34 to 35, which is as great as the extreme motions of **Venus**. Between the divergent and convergent motions of **Jupiter** and **Mars**, there reign a **Triple Octave** <note>original: "Trisdiapason."</note> and a **Double Octave plus a Fourth** <note>original: "Disdiapason epidiatrion."</note>, though not perfectly. For an eighth part of 38 minutes 1 second is 4 minutes 45 seconds, while Jupiter has 4 minutes 30 seconds; between these numbers there is still a difference of 18 to 19, which is midway between 15 to 16 and 24 to 25 (a **Semitone** and a **Diesis**), namely, very nearly a perfect **Limma** <margin>See Book III, Chapter IV, page 30</margin> of 128 to 125. Likewise, a fifth part of 26 minutes 14 seconds is 5 minutes 15 seconds, while Jupiter has 5 minutes 30 seconds; here, therefore, it lacks the quintuple proportion by about 21 to 22, just as much as the other previously exceeded it, namely, almost a Diesis of 24 to 25. It comes closer...

Thus the fifth part of 164' is 32' 48", which taken three times makes 98' 24", while Venus has 97½' 37"; the Planetary motion therefore exceeds it by about two-thirds <note>original: "besse," a Roman term for two-thirds.</note> of a comma, that is 126 to 127.

These are, therefore, the Harmonies distributed among the planets; nor is there any of the principal comparisons (namely, of the converging and diverging extreme motions) which does not come so near to some Harmony that if strings were so tuned, the ears would hardly distinguish the imperfection, except for that excess of one between **Jupiter** and **Mars**.

Therefore, perfect Harmonies are found: between the converging motions <note>When the outer planet is at its fastest and the inner planet is at its slowest, bringing their "pitches" closest together.</note> of Saturn and Jupiter, an **Octave** <term>Diapason (2:1 ratio)</term>; between the converging motions of Jupiter and Mars, an **Octave** with nearly a **Minor Third** <term>Tertia mollis (6:5 ratio)</term>; between the converging motions of Mars and the Earth, a **Fifth** <term>Diapente (3:2 ratio)</term>; between their perihelia, a **Minor Sixth** <term>Sexta mollis (8:5 ratio)</term>; between the aphelia of the Earth and Venus, a **Major Sixth** <term>Sexta dura (5:3 ratio)</term>; between their perihelia, a **Minor Sixth**; between the divergent extremes of Venus and Mercury, a **Major Sixth**: between the diverging motions or even between the perihelia, a **Double Octave** <term>Disdiapason (4:1 ratio)</term>. This is so consistent that, without any detriment to Astronomy—which has been constructed with the utmost subtlety from the observations of Tycho Brahe—it seems that the remaining tiny discrepancy could be consumed; especially in the motions of Venus and Mercury.

You will note, however, that where there is no perfect Major Harmony, such as between Jupiter and Mars, it is only there that a nearly perfect placement of a solid figure <note>A reference to Kepler's earlier theory that the distances between planets are determined by the five Platonic solids.</note> is found, since the perihelion distance of Jupiter is nearly triple the aphelion distance of Mars; thus this pair affects a perfect Harmony in their distances which they do not have in their motions. You will further note that the greater planetary ratio of Saturn and Jupiter exceeds the Harmonic—namely the Triple—by nearly the same amount as Venus's own ratio; and nearly the same amount is missing from the common major ratio of Mars and the Earth, and the same from the two common ratios of the extremes of the Earth and Venus, both converging and diverging. You will note thirdly, that in the superior planets <note>Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars.</note> the Harmonies are established between the converging motions; but in the inferior planets, they are between motions of the same region. Note fourthly, that between the aphelia of Saturn and the Earth, there are nearly five **Octaves**; for the thirty-second part of 57 minutes 3 seconds is 1 minute 47 seconds, while the aphelion of Saturn has 1 minute 46 seconds.

Furthermore, a great difference exists between the explained harmonies of individual planets and those of planets joined together. For the former cannot exist at the same moment of time, but the latter certainly can: because the same planet, turning in its Aphelion, cannot be at its opposite Perihelion at the same time. But of two planets, one can be at its Aphelion and the other at its Perihelion at the same moment of time. And so, the proportion is that of a single song or Monody, which we call Choral Music, and which alone was known to the Ancients,

## CHAPTER V.

### That in the Proportions of the apparent planetary motions (as if viewed from the Sun) are expressed the Places of the System, or the Keys of the Musical Scale, and the genera of song, the Hard and the Soft <note>original: "Duri & Mollis"; these terms historically refer to the "Major" and "Minor" modes or scales.</note>.

**T**hat therefore between these twelve terms or Motions of the six Planets running around the sun—upwards, downwards, and in every direction—there stand Harmonic proportions, or those closest to such within an imperceptible part of a very small **concord** <note>original: "Concinni minimi"; a technical term for the smallest interval that the ear can perceive as being "in tune."</note>, has been proven so far through numbers fetched here from Astronomy and there from Harmonics. Just as in the third book we first elicited the individual Harmonic proportions separately in the first chapter; then finally in the second chapter, we joined all of them, however many there were, into one common System or Musical Scale—or rather, we divided one of them, the **Octave** <note>original: "Diapason"</note>, which encompasses the others in power, through those others into its own steps or Places, and by that act brought it about that it was a Scale; so now also, having found the Harmonies which God himself incorporated into the World, it follows that we see whether they each stand separately, so that they have no kinship with the rest, or whether they all agree among themselves? Although it is easy even without further inquiry to conclude: these Harmonies were fitted together by the highest counsel in such a way that within one framework, as it were, they support each other, nor does one cancel the other; since we see that in such a manifold comparison of the same terms, Harmonies occur everywhere. For unless all were fitted to all in one Scale, it could easily have happened (and has happened everywhere, necessity so urging) that many dissonances would exist. As if someone

# HARMONICS BOOK V.

<margin>CHAPTER V.</margin>
Come now, let us see whether what we have already concluded through reasoning is found to be so in actual fact. However, let us first set forth some cautions, lest we stumble as we proceed. First, for the present, we must ignore those excesses or defects smaller than a **semitone** <note>The smallest common interval in a musical scale; Kepler is saying he will overlook tiny mathematical discrepancies for the sake of the larger harmony.</note>; for we shall see later what causes those have. Next, by the continual doubling or contrary halving of the motions, we shall bring everything within the system of a single **Octave** <note>original: "Diapason"</note>, on account of the **identical sound** <note>original: "Identisonantiam"; the musical principle that notes separated by an octave are perceived as the same note at a different pitch.</note> of all octaves.

Therefore, the numbers by which all the Places or **Keys** <note>original: "Claves"; refers to the specific notes on a musical staff.</note> of the octave system are expressed were set out in the table in the eighth chapter of Book Three, on page 47. You should understand those numbers as referring to the length of two strings. Consequently, the speeds of the motions will be in inverse proportions to one another.

Let the motions of the Planets now be compared in parts that are continually halved. Thus it is:

| *Motion* | *Minutes* | *Seconds* |
|---------|:-------:|:------:|
| Mercury’s Perihelion, seventh sub-double, or 1/128th | 3. | 0. |
| Mercury’s Aphelion, sixth sub-double, or 1/64th | 2. | 34. |
| Venus’s Perihelion, fifth sub-double, or 1/32nd | 3. | 3. <insert>+</insert> |
| Venus’s Aphelion, fifth sub-double, or 1/32nd | 2 | 58. |
| Earth’s Perihelion, fifth sub-double, or 1/32nd | 1. | 55. |
| Earth’s Aphelion, fifth sub-double, or 1/32nd | 1. | 47. |
| Mars’s Perihelion, fourth sub-double, or 1/16th | 2. | 23. |
| Mars’s Aphelion, third sub-double, or 1/8th | 3. | 17. |
| Jupiter’s Perihelion, sub-double (halved) | 2. | 45. |
| Jupiter’s Aphelion, sub-double (halved) | 2. | 15. |
| Saturn’s Perihelion | 2. | 15. |
| Saturn’s Aphelion | 1. | 46. |

Now, let the **aphelion** <note>The point in a planet's orbit where it is furthest from the Sun and moving at its slowest speed.</note> of Saturn, which is the slowest motion, designate the deepest place of the System, **G**, with the number 1 minute 46 seconds. Therefore, the aphelion of the Earth will also designate the same place, but five octaves higher, because its number is 1 minute 47 seconds—and who would dare to argue over a single second in Saturn's aphelion motion? Even so, the difference will not be greater than the ratio 106 to 107, which is less than a **comma** <note>original: "commate minus"; a comma is a tiny musical interval, much smaller than a semitone, often considered the limit of human hearing.</note>. If you add a fourth part, 27 seconds, to this 1 minute 47 seconds, the result is 2 minutes 14 seconds, while Saturn’s **perihelion** <note>The point in a planet's orbit where it is closest to the Sun and moving at its fastest speed.</note> has 2 minutes 15 seconds. Jupiter's aphelion is similar, but one octave higher. Therefore, these two motions designate the **Key of B** <note>original: "Clavem ♄"; in early music notation, the symbol for Saturn was often used to represent the pitch B-natural.</note>, or are just slightly higher. Take a third of 1 minute 47 seconds, which is 36 seconds, and add it to the whole; you will produce 2 minutes 23 seconds for the **Key of c**: and behold, the perihelion of Mars is of the same magnitude, but four octaves higher. To the same 1 minute 47 seconds, add also a half, 54 seconds; it will become 2 minutes 41 seconds for the **Key of d**: and behold, here at hand is the perihelion of Jupiter, though one octave higher; for it possesses the nearest number, namely 2 minutes 45 seconds. If you add two-thirds, namely 1 minute 11 seconds, the result is 2 minutes 58 seconds. And behold, the aphelion of Venus is 2 minutes 58 seconds. It therefore designates the place or **Key of e**, but five octaves higher; nor does the perihelion of Mercury, having 3 minutes 0 seconds, exceed it by much, but it is seven octave intervals higher. Finally, divide the double of 1 minute 47 seconds itself, namely 3 minutes 34 seconds, by nine,

Now, therefore, you will no longer wonder that the most excellent order of sounds or steps in the musical system or scale was established by men; for you see that in this matter they are doing nothing other than **acting as the apes of God the Creator**, and playing out, as if in a drama, the ordering of the celestial motions.

But there also remains another way by which we may understand the double musical scale in the heavens: where the system is the same, but the "tension" is conceived as twofold—one for the motion of Venus at aphelion <note>The point where a planet is furthest from the Sun and moving slowest.</note>, the other at perihelion <note>The point where a planet is closest to the Sun and moving fastest.</note>. ...indeed, the <note>Kepler is continuing a list of aphelions from the previous page</note> aphelions of Jupiter, Venus, and nearly that of Saturn; to some extent even that of the Earth; and without a doubt even that of Mercury. For let us suppose that it is no longer the aphelion of Venus, but its perihelion, at 3 minutes 3 seconds <note>Kepler uses arcminutes and arcseconds to measure the angular velocity of planets as seen from the Sun</note>, that occupies the place *e*; the perihelion of Mercury at 3' 0" also approaches this very closely through a <term>Disdiapason</term><note>A double octave, representing a 4:1 ratio</note>, according to the end of Chapter IV. And so in the case of Saturn, the perihelion of Saturn and the aphelion of Jupiter will follow nearly the same tuning. 

But if an eighth part—23 seconds—is taken five times, it gives 1' 55", which is the perihelion of the Earth; although this does not fit into the same scale with the preceding ones (since it does not order the interval 5:8 below *e*, nor 24:25 above G), nevertheless, if the perihelion of Venus, and thus also the aphelion of Mercury, take the place *de* <note>A point between notes d and e</note> outside the normal order for *e*, then this perihelion of the Earth will take the place *G*; and the aphelion of Mercury will also agree; because a third part—1' 1"—taken five times from 3' 3", becomes 5' 5", half of which <note>original: semis</note> is 2' 32", which comes very close to the aphelion of Mercury, which in this extraordinary accommodation will occupy place *c*. All of these, therefore, belong to the same tuning among themselves: yet the perihelion of Venus divides the Scale in one way when grouped with the first three (or five), in the same <term>Harmonic genre</term> as its own aphelion in its tuning—namely, the **Hard genre**; and in another way, the perihelion of the same Venus divides the scale when grouped with the two later ones—namely, not into another Melodious set, but at least into a different order of Melodious notes, which is specifically characteristic of the **Soft genre** <note>Kepler is arguing that the planets' varied speeds require both "major-like" (Hard) and "minor-like" (Soft) musical systems to be fully expressed</note>.

It is sufficient, however, in this chapter, to have placed before your eyes what is involved in the cause; but why each thing was made thus, and what the causes are—not only of the agreements, but even of the disagreements in the smallest details—that will be made clear by the most lucid demonstrations in Chapter IX.

->In the Extremes of the Planetary Motions, the Musical Modes or Tones are Expressed in a Certain Way.<-

**T**his follows from what has been said before, nor is there need for many words; for the individual planets mark individual places of the system, just as if they were notes. With its perihelion motion, so far as it is granted to each, a planet runs through a certain interval in the Musical Scale, encompassed by certain of its keys or locations in the system; and the motion of each begins from that Key or location which, in the preceding chapter, fell to its aphelion motion: for Saturn and the Earth, this is *G*; but for Jupiter, it is *G* (which can be transposed higher); for Mars, *f*; for Venus, *e*; and for Mercury, *A* in a higher system. See each of them in the usual musical notes. They do not, it is true, form the intermediate places (which you see here filled with notes) in an articulate way, as they do the extremes; because from one extreme to the other, they do not move by leaps and intervals, but strive toward the opposite end through a **continuous tension**; all the intermediate...

Venus remains almost at a single tone, not equaling the width of the tension of even the smallest of the concordant intervals. <note>Because Venus has a very circular orbit, its speed—and thus its "pitch"—hardly changes, making it nearly monotone compared to the other planets.</note>

And yet the signature of two keys in a common system, and the formation of the skeleton of the Octave through the inclusion of a certain concordant interval, is a sort of first step in the distinction of the Tones or Modes; therefore, the Musical Modes are distributed among the planets. I know, indeed, that more things are required for the formation and definition of distinct Modes, which are specific to human song (since it consists of discrete intervals); therefore, I have used the term "voice" in a certain sense.

It will be free, however, for the Harmonist to draw forth his own opinion: which Mode each planet expresses more closely, based on the extremes assigned to it here. I would give to Saturn the Seventh or Eighth Mode from those commonly used, because if you set its root key at G, the motion at <term>perihelion</term><note>The point in an orbit closest to the Sun, where the planet moves fastest.</note> ascends to *b*. To Jupiter, I would give the First or Second Mode; because when its motion at <term>aphelion</term><note>The point in an orbit farthest from the Sun, where the planet moves slowest.</note> is accommodated to G, the perihelion reaches to *b*. To Mars, I would give the Fifth or Sixth; not only because it almost achieves a <term>Diapente</term><note>original: "Diapente"; a musical fifth, a ratio of 3:2.</note>, which is an interval common to all modes, but primarily because when reduced with the others to a common system, it reaches *c* at perihelion and alludes to *f* at aphelion; which is the root of the Fifth or Sixth Tone or Mode.

<margin>Earth: MI FA MI. As one might even guess from the syllables: in our home [the Earth], we obtain MI-sery and FA-mine.</margin>
To the Earth, I would give the Third or Fourth Mode; because its motions revolve within a semitone; and indeed the first interval of those Tones is a semitone. To Mercury, truly, because of the great range of its interval, all Modes or Tones will fit it indiscriminately. To Venus, because of the narrowness of its interval, clearly none at all; but because of the common System, also the Third and Fourth; because she herself, in respect to the others, occupies the note *e*.

## ON THE MOTIONS OF THE PLANETS ##

<margin>
CHAPTER VII.

Would it be a crime if I were to demand from each of the composers of this age a skillful Motet <note>A polyphonic choral composition, usually on a sacred text.</note> for this eulogy? The Royal Psalmist <note>King David.</note> and the other Sacred Books can provide a suitable text for this. But listen, you all! In the heavens, no more than six planets harmonize together; for the Moon sings its own melody separately, sitting by the Earth as if at a cradle. Contribute your efforts; I promise to be a diligent curator so that a work in six parts may be published. To the one who more closely expresses the celestial music described in this work, Clio <note>The Muse of History.</note> promises a wreath, and Urania <note>The Muse of Astronomy.</note> promises Venus <note>Here, "Venus" refers to beauty or love as a reward.</note> as his bride.
</margin>

...the genuine Archetype <note>The original divine blueprint or model upon which the world was built.</note> of the fabric of the World is kept hidden and preserved. Follow, you modern Musicians, and judge this matter by your arts, which were unknown to antiquity. In these last centuries, Nature—always prolific—has finally produced you: the first genuine examples of the universe, after a gestation of two thousand years. Through your harmonies of various voices, and through your ears, she has whispered her very self—as she exists in her innermost heart—to the human Mind, the most beloved daughter of God the Creator.

What harmonic proportions the two neighboring planets embrace in the extremities of their motions <note>Their fastest and slowest speeds at perihelion and aphelion.</note> was explained above. But it happens very rarely that two planets, especially the slowest ones, fall into their extreme intervals at the same time. For example, the apsides <note>The points in an orbit closest to or farthest from the Sun.</note> of Saturn and Jupiter are distant from each other by about 81 degrees. Therefore, while this distance between them—through certain leaps in neighboring years—measures out the entire Zodiac, eight hundred years glide by. Yet the leap that closes the eighth century is not brought precisely to the very same apsides; and if it wanders a little further off, another eight hundred years must be waited for, so that a more fortunate leap can be sought with reason. This must be repeated as many times as the measure of the deviation is contained within the length of half a leap. The other pairs also produce such periods, though not so long. 

In the meantime, however, other harmonies between two planets also occur—not between both of their extreme motions, but between an intermediate motion and one or both extremes; and these occur in different "tensions" <note>Kepler uses the word "tension" to describe the range of musical pitches or speeds a planet can move through.</note> as it were. For because Saturn is stretched from G to B-natural and a little beyond, and Jupiter from B-natural to D and further, those harmonies above the <term>Octave</term> <note>original: Diapason</note>—namely both the major and minor Third, and the <term>Fourth</term> <note>original: Diatessaron</note>—can occur between Saturn and Jupiter. One of these occurs through the tension, and the other through the width of the remaining range; this latter one occurs through the width of a major whole tone. For a Fourth will exist not only from Saturn’s G to Jupiter’s C, but also from Saturn’s A to Jupiter’s D, and through all the intermediates between his G and A and the other's C and D. However, the Octave and the <term>Fifth</term> <note>original: Diapente</note> occur only at the exact points of the apsides. 

Mars, having obtained a larger interval of its own, has achieved this: it even makes an Octave with the superior planets <note>The planets further from the Sun: Jupiter and Saturn.</note> through some width of tension. Mercury has obtained such a large interval that it generally forms all harmonies with all the others within its own single period, which is no longer than the space of three months. The Earth, on the contrary, and Venus much more so, restrict their harmonies due to the narrowness of their own intervals—not only with the others, but especially their mutual harmonies with each other—to a remarkable fewness. 

But if three planets are to conspire into one harmony, many turns of the wheels must be waited for. Nevertheless, there are many such harmonies, so that they occur all the more easily while each one follows its neighbor. It seems that among Mars, the Earth, and Mercury, triple harmonies occur quite frequently. However, harmonies of four planets already begin to be scattered across centuries, and those of five planets across tens of thousands of years. But for all six to harmonize, that is an event hindered by the longest spaces of time; and I do not know if it is even possible for it to happen twice in an exact revolution. Rather, it may demonstrate a certain Beginning of Time, from which the entire age of the world has flowed.

# FIFTH BOOK OF HARMONIES

...among many, one is uniquely distinguished; it could undoubtedly be considered the signature <note>original: "charactere"</note> of Creation. We must therefore ask: in how many ways can the motions of all six planets be reduced to a single common harmony? The method of inquiry is this: let us begin with the Earth and Venus, because these two produce no more than two consonances, and—providing the reason for this—they do so through the shortest ranges of motion <term>tensiones</term> <note>Kepler uses the term "tensions" to describe the range of a planet's speed, comparing the stretching of an orbit's velocity to the tightening of a musical string.</note>.

Come then, let us establish two "skeletons," as it were, of the Harmonies, each defined by two sets of numbers (by which the limits of the musical tensions are marked), and let us search for what fits them from the variety of motions granted to each Planet. Astronomical experience therefore testifies <note>original: "Testatur igr."</note> that universal harmonies of all motions can occur, and that they are of two types: the Major and the Minor <note>original: "Duri & Mollis," literally "Hard and Soft."</note>. In each type, there is a double form or (if we may call it so) a double Tone. In any one of these, there are four possible cases, allowing for some latitude in the tuning <term>tensionis</term>, and even some variety in the particular harmonies of Saturn, Mars, and Mercury with the others. Nor is this achieved only by the intermediate motions, but entirely by all the extreme motions <note>The slowest and fastest points of an orbit.</note>, except for the aphelion of Mars and the perihelion of Jupiter. 

Because Mars attains the note *f* and Jupiter attains *d*, while Venus perpetually attains the intermediate *e-flat* or *e*, she does not tolerate those dissonant neighbors in a universal harmony—which she would do if she had been granted the space to exceed *e* or *e-flat*. This is the constraint <note>original: "impedimenti"</note> of this marriage between the Earth and Venus, like that of a husband and wife; these two planets distinguish the types of harmonies: namely, into the major and masculine, and the minor and feminine.

<summary>Kepler calculates the "Minor Genus" (Minor scale) of the universal planetary harmony based on the Earth-Venus relationship and provides a table of these motions. He concludes that these harmonies mirror human gender, labeling the Major scale as masculine and the Minor scale as feminine.</summary>

Therefore, the movements of the heavens are nothing other than a certain perennial harmony (intellectual rather than vocal) through dissonant tensions, like certain **syncopations** or **cadences** (by which men imitate those natural dissonances) tending toward certain and prescribed closures, each of six terms (like voices) and marking and distinguishing the immensity of time with those notes. Thus, it is no longer a wonder that the art of singing in harmony <note>original: "concentum," referring to polyphonic music where multiple voices move independently but harmoniously.</note>, unknown to the ancients, was finally discovered by Man, the **ape of his Creator**; so that he might play out the perpetuity of all cosmic time in some brief portion of an hour through the artistic symphony of many voices, and might taste, to some extent, the satisfaction of God the Craftsman in His own works, through the most sweet sense of pleasure perceived from this music that imitates God.

# CHAPTER VIII.

## Who in the celestial concords
### performs the role of Soprano, who the Alto, who the Tenor,
### and who the Bass?

Although these are terms for human voices, and no literal voices or sounds exist in the heavens because of the supreme tranquility of their motions; and since the very subjects in which we find these Harmonies are not even contained within the category of true motion (as we are only considering the motions as they *appear* from the Sun); and finally, although there is no cause in heaven like that in human song which calls for a specific number of voices to create a Harmony—for first there was the number of six planets circling the Sun, taken from the five intervals of the Regular Solids <note>The five Platonic solids, which Kepler famously used in his earlier work to explain the spacing between the six known planets.</note>; and only afterward (in the order of Nature, not of time) was the agreement of their motions established—nevertheless, I know not how it is, but this wonderful agreement with human song compels me, so that I am forced to pursue this part of the comparison as well, even without a solid natural cause. 

For the properties that practice attributes to the Bass, and which nature claims for it—as I described in Chapter XVI of the third book—those same properties are held in a certain way by **Saturn** and **Jupiter** in the heavens. Those of the Tenor we find in **Mars**; those of the Alto are present in **Earth** and **Venus**; and **Mercury** has those of the Soprano <note>original: "Discanti," the high-pitched part in Renaissance polyphony.</note>, if not in the equality of its intervals, then certainly in their proportion. For however the eccentricities <note>The deviation of a planet's orbit from a perfect circle.</note> of each planet are derived for their own reasons in the following chapter, and through them the specific intervals of each motion, a wonderful result emerges from them—one I suspect was arranged just so, rather than being a purely necessary temperament:

I. Just as the Bass is opposed to the Alto, so there are two planets that have the nature of the Alto, and two that have the nature of the Bass, as if there were one of each on both sides in any genre of song; whereas for the other individual voices, there is only one planet each.

II. Just as the Alto is nearly the highest voice and is constrained in its range—for necessary and natural reasons explained in *Book III*—so the nearly innermost planets, Earth and Venus, have the narrowest intervals of motion; the Earth has not much more than a semitone <note>A small musical interval, roughly the distance between two adjacent keys on a piano.</note>, and Venus has not even a *diesis* <note>An even smaller interval than a semitone, often used to describe the "comma" or tiny discrepancy in tuning.</note>.

III. And just as the Tenor is free, yet proceeds modestly, so Mars—with the single exception of Mercury—can produce the largest interval, namely a Fifth <note>original: "Diapente."</note>.

IV. And just as the Bass makes harmonic leaps, so Saturn and Jupiter possess harmonic intervals, and they themselves move between one another from an Octave <note>original: "Diapason."</note> up to an Octave plus a Fifth <note>original: "Diapente epi Diapason."</note>.

V. And just as the Soprano is the freest of all, more so than all the others, and is also the fastest, so also can Mercury traverse more than an Octave in a very short return. But let this certainly be by chance; let us now hear the causes of the eccentricities.

->( ❦ )<-

## CHAPTER IX.

### The Origin of the Eccentricities in 
### individual Planets from the procurement of Harmonies
->between their motions:<-

**Since** we see, therefore, that the universal Harmonies of all six planets cannot occur by chance—especially through the extremes of their motions, which we have seen all concur toward universal Harmonies (except for two, which concurred with those closest to the universal ones); and since it could even less happen by chance that all the locations of the system of the Octave, established in the third book through Harmonic sections, are marked by the extremes of the planetary motions; and least of all that the most subtle business of the distinction of celestial Harmonies into two types, the major and the minor <note>original: "durum & molle," literally "hard and soft." In the musical terminology of Kepler's time, these referred to the major and minor scales or modes.</note>, should come about by accident without the singular care of the Craftsman: it follows, therefore, that the Creator—the fount of all wisdom, the perpetual approver of Order, the eternal and super-essential source of Geometry and Harmony—that this very Craftsman of the heavens, I say, has joined the Harmonic proportions (arising from the regular plane figures) to the five regular solid figures. From both classes, He has fashioned a single, most perfect <term>Archetype</term> <note>A primal pattern or divine blueprint from which the physical world was constructed.</note> of the heavens. Within this model, just as the Ideas of the spheres in which the six stars are carried might shine forth through the five solid figures, so also through the offspring of the plane figures, the Harmonies (derived from them in the third book) would be contained by the measure of the <term>Eccentricities</term> <note>The degree to which a planet's orbit deviates from a perfect circle. An eccentricity of zero is a perfect circle; higher values are more oval.</note> in each individual sphere, in order to proportion the motions of the bodies. From these two things, a single tempering was made: the larger proportions of the Spheres would yield somewhat to the smaller proportions of the Eccentricities necessary to procure the Harmonies; and conversely, from the Harmonic proportions, those would especially be accommodated to the planets which had a greater kinship with each solid figure, insofar as that could be achieved through the Harmonies. Finally, by this reasoning, both the proportions of the Spheres and the Eccentricities of each would spring forth together from the Archetype; and from the size of the Spheres and the mass of the bodies, the periodic Times of each would result.

While I strive to bring this method into the light of human understanding through the usual <term>elements</term> <note>original: "stoecheiosin," from the Greek word for "elements" or "fundamental arrangement," often used in reference to Euclid's geometry.</note> of the Geometers: may the Author of the Heavens himself favor me, the Father of Intellects, the Giver of mortal senses, himself immortal and most blessed; and may he prevent our mental darkness from bringing forth anything unworthy of His Majesty concerning this work of His; and may He grant that we, as imitators of God, might emulate the perfection of His works through the holiness of life—to which He has chosen His Church on earth and cleansed it from sins by the blood of His Son—by the help of His Holy Spirit. May we keep far away all the dissonances of enmities; all contentions, rivalries, angers, quarrels, dissensions, sects; envy, provocations, and irritations through taunts, and the rest of the works of the flesh. I pray this with all those who [possess] the spirit

Those who have Christ will not only desire but also express it in their deeds; and they will strive to make their calling certain, spurning all the wicked habits of all parties—whether they are masked and disguised by the pretense of Zeal, or a love of truth, or singular erudition, or a feigned modesty toward contentious teachers, or any other such beautiful pretext. ->The Prior Reasons.<-

## I. Axiom

**I**t is fitting that, wherever it was possible at all, harmonies ought to have been established in every variety between the extremes of the motions, both of individual planets and of pairs; so that this variety might adorn the world.

## II. Axiom

The five intervals between the six spheres ought to correspond in size, to some extent, to the proportion of the geometric spheres that are inscribed within and circumscribed around the five <term>regular solid figures</term> <note>These are the "Platonic Solids": the Cube, Tetrahedron, Dodecahedron, Icosahedron, and Octahedron. Kepler believed these shapes dictated the spacing between the planets.</note>: and this should be in the same order that is natural to the figures themselves.

->*Concerning this, see Chapter I, the "Cosmographic Mystery," and the "Epitome of Astronomy," Book IV.*<-

## III. Proposition.

The intervals between Earth and Mars, and between Earth and Venus, ought to have been the smallest in proportion to their spheres, and nearly equal to each other; those between Saturn and Jupiter, and between Venus and Mercury, should be middling and again nearly equal; and the interval between Jupiter and Mars should be the largest.

*For according to Axiom II, those figures which produce the smallest proportion between the geometric spheres must likewise produce the smallest proportion for the planets corresponding to them in position; those which correspond to figures of middling proportion should be middling, and those corresponding to the figure of largest proportion should be the largest. But in the same order as the Dodecahedron and Icosahedron are among the figures, so are the pairs of planets: one of Mars and Earth, the other of Earth and Venus. In the same order as the Cube and Octahedron, so are the pair of Saturn and Jupiter and the pair of Venus and Mercury. Finally, in the same order as the Tetrahedron, so is the pair of Jupiter and Mars; see Chapter III. Therefore, the proportion between the first-mentioned planetary spheres will be the smallest; between those of Saturn and Jupiter, it will be nearly equal to that between Venus and Mercury; and finally, the proportion between the spheres of Jupiter and Mars will be the largest.*

<margin>CH. IX.</margin>

# IV. Axiom

**A**ll planets must have their eccentricities <note>In astronomy, eccentricity is a measure of how much an orbit deviates from a perfect circle.</note>, no less than a motion in latitude, and according to these, they must also have diverse distances from the Sun, the source of motion.

*Just as the essence of motion consists not in BEING, but in BECOMING, so also the species or shape of the region which any planet traverses in its motion is not made solid immediately from the beginning, but in the course of time finally acquires not only its length, but also its width and depth, the perfect triad of dimensions; and thus it is made gradually by the connection and accumulation of many revolutions, so that the appearance of a hollow sphere is represented, having the same center as the Sun; just as the little house of a silkworm <note>original: "Bombyci." Kepler uses the metaphor of a silkworm weaving a cocoon to explain how a planet's single-line orbit, over many years of shifting, "weaves" a three-dimensional shell or "orb" in space.</note> is constructed from very many silk threads connected and tangled among themselves.*

# V. Proposition.

**T**o each pair of neighboring planets, two different Harmonies were to be assigned.

*For by Axiom IV, any planet has a furthest and a shortest distance from the Sun; therefore, by Chapter III of this book, it will also have a slowest and a fastest motion. There are, then, two primary comparisons of the extreme motions: one of the Divergent <note>A comparison between the slowest motion of the inner planet and the fastest of the outer planet.</note> in two planets, the other of the Convergent <note>A comparison between the fastest motion of the inner planet and the slowest of the outer planet.</note>. However, it is necessary that these be different from each other; because the ratio of the divergent will be greater, and the convergent will be smaller. But it was also necessary that there be different Harmonies for different pairs of planets, so that this variety might serve the adornment of the World, according to Axiom I; and also because there are different ratios of the intervals between pairs, according to Proposition III. But to each ratio of the orbs, certain Harmonic ratios respond by a quantitative kinship, as demonstrated in Chapter V of this book.*

# VI. Proposition.

**T**he two smallest Harmonies, 4:5 and 5:6 <note>In music, these correspond to the Major Third and Minor Third.</note>, have no place between pairs of planets.

*For 5 to 4 is as 1000 to 800, and 6 to 5 is as 1000 to 833 <unclear>†</unclear>. But the orbs circumscribed by the Dodecahedron and Icosahedron <note>Two of the five Platonic solids.</note> have a greater ratio to those inscribed within them—specifically, that which is 1000 to 795, etc.—and these two ratios indicate the intervals between the nearest Planetary Orbs, or the smallest spaces; for in the other regular figures, the orbs are distant further from each other. Now indeed, the ratio of motions is even greater than the ratios of the intervals, unless there is a huge ratio of the eccentricities to the Orbs, according to the 13th point of Chapter III. Therefore, the smallest ratio of motions is greater than 4:5 and 5:6 are. Thus, these Harmonies, being hindered indeed by the regular figures, obtain no place among the planets.*
