<margin>CHAPTER IX.</margin>

*But Venus and Mercury, since they do not change their <term>genus of Harmony</term><note>Referring to the Major or Minor scales/modes which Kepler assigns to the planets.</note>, also did not require perfect harmonies between each pair of their aphelion and perihelion motions. Instead, in place of the perfect harmony of the aphelia—which was already "fermented"<note>original: "fermentata"; Kepler uses this term to describe a ratio that has been tempered or adjusted away from a pure mathematical value to fit the physical constraints of the system.</note>—there followed a perfect harmony of the <term>converging motions</term><note>The ratio between the perihelion of the outer planet and the aphelion of the inner planet.</note>. Thus, just as Venus, the higher of the lower planets, has the smallest proper motion-proportion of all (by 28), while Mercury, the lower of the lower planets, has the largest proper proportion of all (by 30), so too the proper ratio of Venus would be the most imperfect of all (or the most distant from the Harmonies), while the proper ratio of Mercury ☿ would be the most perfect of all—that is, an absolute Harmony without "ferment." In this way, finally, the proportions would be opposite in every respect.*

For thus He decorated the great works of His wisdom—He who is before the ages and unto the ages. Nothing is redundant, nothing is lacking, nor is there any room for anyone’s criticism. How desirable are His works, etc. <note>Kepler is paraphrasing Ecclesiasticus (Sirach) 42:24-25.</note> *All things are double, one against another, and He has made nothing incomplete; one thing establishes the good of another* (He established them with the best reasons for ornament and decency); *and who shall be satisfied with beholding His glory?*

# XLVI. Axiom.

**T**he placement of the solid figures between the planetary spheres—if it is free and not hindered by the necessities of preceding causes—ought to follow the perfection of the analogy of geometric inscriptions and circumscriptions, and thus also the conditions of the proportion of the inscribed [solids] to the circumscribed.

*For nothing is more consistent than that a physical inscription should exactly represent a geometric one, as a finished work represents its blueprint.*

# XLVII. Proposition.

**I**f the inscription of the Figures between the planets was free, the **Tetrahedron** ought to touch the <term>perihelion</term><note>The point in an orbit closest to the Sun.</note> sphere of Jupiter exactly with its angles above, and the <term>aphelion</term><note>The point in an orbit furthest from the Sun.</note> of Mars exactly with the centers of its planes below. The **Cube** and the **Octahedron**, however, standing with their angles on the perihelion sphere of their respective outer planet, ought to penetrate the sphere of the inner planet with the centers of their planes, so that those centers are positioned between the aphelion and perihelion spheres. The **Dodecahedron** and **Icosahedron**, on the contrary, touching the perihelion spheres of their planets with their angles on the outside, ought not to fully reach the aphelion spheres of their inner planets with the centers of their planes. Finally, the **Dodecahedral Hedgehog** <note>original: "Echinus Dodecaëdricus"; this refers to a stellated polyhedron, specifically the Great Stellated Dodecahedron.</note>, standing with its angles on the perihelion sphere of Mars, ought to come very close to the aphelion sphere of Venus with the middle points of its inverted sides, where two solid rays meet.

*For the Tetrahedron is the middle figure of the Primary ones <note>The five Platonic solids.</note>, both by origin and by its position in the World; and being equally balanced, if nothing hindered it, it ought to separate both regions of Jupiter ♃ and Mars ♂. Because the Cube was above it and further out, and the Dodecahedron was below it and further in, it was fitting that their inscription should reflect a contrary relationship to that of the Tetrahedron (which held the middle). One of them should create an excess in the inscription, and the other a defect; that is, one should penetrate the inner sphere to some extent, and the other should not reach it. And because the Octahedron...*

# ON THE HARMONIES, BOOK V

<margin>CHAPTER IX.</margin>

*The Octahedron is related to the Cube, having an equal proportion of spheres; the Icosahedron to the Dodecahedron. Therefore, whatever degree of perfection the Cube possesses regarding its <term>inscription</term><note>The way a solid fits inside or around a sphere. Kepler uses these geometric relationships to explain the gaps between planetary orbits.</note>, the same was owed to the Octahedron. Whatever the Dodecahedron has, the same was owed to the Icosahedron. The position of the Octahedron is also similar to the position of the Cube, and the position of the Icosahedron to the position of the Dodecahedron. Just as the Cube holds one extreme toward the exterior, so the Octahedron holds the remaining extreme toward the interior of the World, while the Dodecahedron and Icosahedron are in the middle. Therefore, a similar inscription is appropriate—in the former case, penetrating the interior planetary sphere, and in the latter case, falling short of it. Indeed, the **Echinus**<note>original: "Echinus"; literally 'hedgehog'. Kepler uses this term for a star-polyhedron (specifically the Great Stellate Dodecahedron). He introduces it here as a "subsidiary" shape to bridge the gap between the five standard Platonic solids.</note>, which represents the Icosahedron with the tips of its angles and the Dodecahedron with its bases, was meant to fill, embrace, or arrange both regions: both between Mars and the Earth (assigned to the Dodecahedron) and between the Earth and Venus (assigned to the Icosahedron). The previously stated axiom clarifies which of the opposites fits which association. For the Tetrahedron, having a <term>rational</term><note>original: "effabilem"; in Euclidean geometry, a "rational" or "expressible" line is one whose ratio to another can be expressed through whole numbers or their square roots.</note> inscribed sphere, was allotted the middle place among the primary shapes, flanked on both sides by figures of incommensurable spheres—the Cube on the outside and the Dodecahedron on the inside (according to Chapter 1). This geometric quality, the "expressibility" of the inscribed sphere, represents in Nature the perfect inscription of a planetary sphere. Therefore, the Cube and its companion have inscribed spheres that are at least "half-rational," that is, only in their squares; they should therefore represent a semi-perfect inscription, where it is not the very boundary of the planetary sphere that is touched by the centers of the figure's planes, but at least something interior, namely the midpoint between the <term>Aphelion and Perihelion</term><note>The furthest and closest points to the Sun in a planet's orbit.</note>, if it can be achieved through other reasons. In contrast, the Dodecahedron and its companion have inscribed spheres that are plainly <term>irrational</term><note>original: "ineffabiles"; literally 'unspeakable'. In geometry, these are ratios that cannot be expressed as a simple square root or fraction, reflecting a "less perfect" alignment in Kepler's view.</note>, both in the length of their radius and in their squares. They should therefore represent a plainly imperfect inscription, touching absolutely nothing of the planetary sphere—that is, falling short and not quite reaching the Aphelion of the planet's sphere with the centers of their planes. Although the Echinus is related to the Dodecahedron and its companion, it nevertheless has something similar to the Tetrahedron. For the radius inscribed by its inverted sides is indeed incommensurable with the radius of the circumscribed sphere, but it is meanwhile commensurable in length with the distance between two neighboring angles. Thus, the perfection of the measurement of the radii is almost as great as the Tetrahedron's imperfection on the other side, and as great as that of the Dodecahedron and its companion. It is therefore fitting that a physical inscription also belongs to it—neither purely Tetrahedral nor purely Dodecahedral, but of an intermediate kind. Since the Tetrahedron had to reach the top of the orbit with its planes, and the Dodecahedron had to fail to reach it by a certain space, now this pointed figure with its inverted sides stands between the Icosahedral space and the top of the inscribed orbit, touching this summit very closely—provided, however, that this figure was also to be admitted into the company of the other five, and these laws could be tolerated alongside the laws of those others. Indeed, why do I say they "could be tolerated"? They were things those others could not do without! For if a loose inscription, not touching the orbit, was appropriate for the Dodecahedron, what else could restrain that indefinite looseness within the boundaries of a certain quantity, except this subsidiary figure, related to the Dodecahedron and Icosahedron, which by its own inscription nearly touches it? It falls short (if indeed it does fall short) no more than the Tetrahedron exceeds and penetrates. We shall deal with this quantity in the following section.*

**This cause for the Echinus being associated with the two related figures makes it very likely (namely, to determine the proportion of the spheres of Mars and Venus, which those figures had left indefinite) that the semi-diameter of the Earth's orbit is found to be 1000, almost exactly in the middle of the proportion—**

-> ## Proposition XLVIII. <-

**T**he inscription of the regular solid figures between the *Planetary Spheres* was not a matter of pure freedom; for in its smallest details, it was constrained by the *Harmonies established between the extreme motions.*

*For according to Axioms I and II, the proportion of the spheres for each Figure ought not to have been expressed immediately through itself, but through it, harmonies most closely related to the proportions of the spheres themselves had first to be sought and adapted to the extreme motions.*

*Furthermore, so that (according to Axioms XVIII and XX) the universal harmonies might be of two kinds, it was necessary to add a little <term>leaven</term> <note>original: "fermenti"; Kepler's metaphor for a small mathematical adjustment or "fudge factor" needed to make the physical orbits match the musical scales.</note> to the major harmonies of each pair through subsequent ratios. Therefore, so that these could stand and rely on their own specific ratios, intervals were required that differed slightly from those resulting from the perfect inscription of figures between the spheres, according to the laws of motion explained in Chapter III. To prove this, and to show how much is taken away from each figure by the harmonies established through their own ratios: come, let us construct the intervals of the planets from the Sun from them, using a new form of calculation never before attempted by anyone.*

<margin>
Calculation of the planetary intervals arising from the harmonic policy.
</margin>

*There will be three heads of this inquiry: First, from the two <term>extreme motions</term> <note>The speeds of a planet at its closest (perihelion) and farthest (aphelion) points from the Sun.</note> of each planet, its extreme intervals from the Sun will likewise be sought; from these, the radius of the sphere in that dimension of the extreme intervals specific to each planet. Second, from the same extreme motions, in a dimension common to all, the <term>mean motions</term> <note>The average orbital speed.</note> and their proportion will be sought. Third, from the proportion of the mean motions now revealed, the proportion of the spheres or mean intervals will be investigated, and along with them, the extreme intervals; and that will be compared with the figural proportions.*

*As for the first part: it must be repeated from Chapter III, number VI, that the proportion of the extreme motions is double the inverse proportion of the corresponding intervals from the Sun. Since the proportion of squares is also double the proportion of their sides, the numbers by which the extreme motions of each planet are expressed will be considered as Squares, and their sought-after roots will give the extreme intervals, of which it is easy to take the arithmetic mean for the semi-diameter of the sphere and the <term>eccentricity</term> <note>The measure of how much an orbit deviates from a perfect circle.</note>. <margin>CHAPTER IX.</margin>

For the second of our proposed tasks, we must again use Chapter III, number XII, where it was shown that the number expressing the **mean motion** in the proportion of the extremes is less than their **arithmetic mean**, and also less than their **geometric mean**, by half the difference between those two means. And since we seek to investigate all mean motions in the same dimension, all the proportions established thus far between pairs, and the specific proportions of each planet, should be expressed in a common measure of the least common multiple. Then, the means should be sought: the arithmetic mean by halving the difference of the extreme motions of each; the geometric mean by multiplying one extreme by the other and extracting the square root of the product. Then, by subtracting half the difference between these two means from the geometric mean, the value for the **Mean Motion** will be established in the dimension specific to each planet's extreme motions. This value is easily converted into the common dimension by the rule of proportion.

Therefore, from the prescribed Harmonies, the proportion of the **Mean daily motions** has been found—that is, the ratio between the numbers of degrees, minutes, etc., compared to one another. It is easy to explore how closely this matches astronomical observations.

The third point of our proposal requires Chapter III, number VIII. For once the proportion of the mean daily motions for each planet is found, it is possible to find the proportion of the **Orbs** <note>The "orbs" refer to the planetary orbits or the spheres carrying them.</note>. For the proportion of the mean motions is the **inverse sesquialter** <note>original: "eversa sesquialtera"; this is the mathematical core of Kepler's Third Law. It means the ratio of the periods is the 3/2 power of the ratio of the distances. In terms of speed/motion, the speeds are inversely proportional to the square root of the distances multiplied by the distances, or $v \propto r^{-3/2}$.</note> of the proportion of the Orbs. Furthermore, the proportion of cubic numbers is the **sesquialter** <note>A 3:2 ratio.</note> of the proportion of the squares assigned to the same roots in the **Table of Clavius** <note>Christopher Clavius (1538–1612), a leading mathematician of the era. Kepler is using Clavius's published tables of squares and cubes to perform his calculations.</note>, which he appended to his *Practical Geometry*. 

Therefore, if our mean motion numbers are sought (truncated with an equal number of zeros where necessary) among the cubic numbers of that table, the table will show to the left, under the title of Squares, the numbers for the proportion of the Orbs. Then the **Eccentricities** assigned above to each, in the dimension of their own semidiameters, will be easily transposed into a dimension common to all through the rule of proportion. Thus, by adding and subtracting these from the semidiameters of the orbs, the extreme intervals of each planet from the Sun may be established. We shall give the semidiameter of the Earth's Orb the round dimension of **100,000**, as is the custom in Astronomy. This is done with this intention: because this number, whether multiplied as a square or a cube, always consists of pure zeros. Thus, we shall also express the mean motion of the Earth by the number 1,000,000,000, using the rule of proportion so that as the number of the mean motion of each planet is to the number of the mean motion of the Earth, so...

*The cubic planes descend a little below the mean of Jupiter; the octahedral planes do not quite reach the mean of Mercury itself; the tetrahedral planes a little below the highest point <note>Aphelion</note> of Mars; the sides of the Echinus do not quite reach the highest point of Venus; but the planes of the Dodecahedron fall far short of the aphelion of the Earth; and the planes of the Icosahedron also fall far short, and almost proportionally so, from the aphelion of Venus; finally, the square of the octahedron is clearly unfit—and not without reason, for what are the planes of a [plane] figure doing among the solid ones? You see, therefore, if the intervals of the planets are deduced from the Harmonic proportions of the motions demonstrated thus far, it is necessary that they turn out as large as these permit, but not as large as the laws of free inscription prescribed in Proposition XLV would require: because here the <note>original: "κόσμου γεωμετρικὸς"</note> geometric world-order of perfect inscription was no longer possible according to that other <note>original: "νόμον ἁρμονikὸν ἐνδεχόμενον"</note> "possible harmonic law," to use the words of Galen taken from the frontispiece of this Book V. This much had to be demonstrated by the calculation of the numbers themselves for the elucidation of the prescribed proposition.*

## II. Epiphonema <note>A concluding exclamation or summary reflection</note>.

**I**t was good that the solid figures <note>The five Platonic solids (cube, tetrahedron, etc.) which Kepler previously thought determined the spacing of the planets</note> in the origin of the intervals gave way to Harmonic ratios, and that the Harmonies of pairs gave way to the universal Harmonies of all, as much as was necessary for this purpose.

*By a beautiful chance we have arrived at the second square of seven [49]; so that this may follow as a kind of Sabbath, after the six solid "eight-fold" utterances <note>Likely referring to the preceding sections or sets of axioms</note> about the work of the Heavens. Deservedly also have I made this Epiphonema, which could have been placed among the Axioms: because God also, having now finished the work of Creation, saw all that He had made, and behold, they were very good.*

*There are two parts to this Epiphonema: the first, concerning Harmonies in general, is demonstrated thus. For where a choice is made between diverse things that do not exactly fit one another: there the more excellent things are to be preferred, and the cheaper things must be derogated as much as is necessary; the very word "of the world" <note>original Greek: <gloss>τὅ κόσμϰ</gloss> (tou kosmou), which implies both "the world" and "order/ornament"</note>, which signifies ornament, seems to prove this. And yet, by as much as life excels the body, or form excels matter, by so much does Harmonic ornament excel simple Geometry.*

<margin>See Book IV, page 163.</margin>
*For as life perfects the bodies of living things, because they were born to lead this life—which follows from the World Archetype <note>God's foundational blueprint for the universe</note>, which is the divine essence itself—so life measures the regions attributed to the Planets and the motions of each of its own stars; because so that a star could be moved, its own region was assigned to it. And yet the five solid figures, by the force of the word itself, pertain to the spaces of the regions and to the number of those regions and bodies; <margin>See Book IV.</margin> but Harmony pertains to the motions. Again, as Matter is diffused and undefined of itself, while Form is defined, united, and the very thing that limits matter: so also the Geometric proportions are infinite; the Harmonies are few. For although even among the Geometric proportions there are certain degrees of definitions, formations, and restrictions, and no more than three can exist from the inscription of orbits to the regular figures: nevertheless, these also follow an accident common with all the rest; because the possible infinite division of quantities presupposes them, which those whose terms...*

...be incommensurable among themselves. But *Harmonic* proportions are all expressible <note>meaning they can be stated as a ratio of whole numbers</note>, and the terms of all of them are commensurable <note>measurable by a common unit</note>; and they are derived from a certain and finite species of plane figures. Indeed, infinity represents the material of division; whereas commensurability or expressibility of terms represents the Form. Therefore, just as matter desires Form—like a rough stone of a certain mass desires the Idea of the human body—so too do Geometric Figural proportions desire Harmonies. Not so that they may invent and form them, but because this Matter fits this Form, this quantity of stone fits this image, and even this figural proportion fits this Harmony more aptly: so that they may be further shaped and formed—Matter indeed by its Form, the stone by the Sculptor <note>original: "Colapte"</note> into the likeness of a living creature; and the proportion of the figural spheres by its own Harmony, that is, the near and fitting one.

*What has been said up to now will become clearer from the history of my discoveries. When I fell into this contemplation 24 years ago, I first inquired whether the individual spheres of the planets were distant from each other by equal intervals (for in Copernicus the spheres are distant and do not touch each other): indeed, I recognized nothing more beautiful than the reason of equality. But it lacked a head and tail: for this material equality provided no certain number of moving bodies, and no certain quantity for the intervals. I thought, therefore, about the similarity of the intervals to the spheres—that is, about Proportion. But the same complaint followed; for even if unequal intervals between spheres were indeed produced, they were neither "unequally unequal" as Copernicus wishes, nor was the quantity of the proportion or the number of spheres established. I moved on to regular plane figures; intervals were formed from them by the inscription of circles: but still with no certain number. I came to the five solids <note>The five Platonic solids: cube, tetrahedron, dodecahedron, icosahedron, and octahedron</note>; here both the number of bodies and the size of the intervals appeared nearly true, so much so that I appealed to the perfection of Astronomy regarding the remaining discrepancy. Astronomy has been perfected in these 20 years; and behold, the intervals still disagreed with the solid figures; nor were the causes of the Eccentricities <note>the degree to which a planet's orbit deviates from a perfect circle</note>—distributed most unequally among the Planets—yet clear. Truly, in this house of the World, I was seeking nothing but stones of a more elegant form, but which would suit stones; ignorant that the Architect had fashioned them into the most articulated likeness of a living body. So gradually, especially in these last 3 years, I arrived at the Harmonies, having abandoned the solid Figures regarding the smallest details: both because they stood on the side of the Form which the final hand would impose on the figure from the Matter (which in the World is the number of bodies and the raw extent of spaces), and also because they gave the Eccentricities, which the solids did not even promise. The harmonies, indeed, reconciled the nose, eyes, and other limbs to the statue, for which the solids had prescribed only the external quantity of the raw mass.*

*Therefore, just as the bodies of living creatures are not made, nor is a mass of stone usually made, according to the pure rule of some geometric figure; but the external round figure, however elegant, is diminished (while the proper size of the mass remains) so that the body can obtain the organs necessary for life, and the stone can obtain the image of a living being; so also the proportion which the solid figures were to prescribe for the planetary spheres—as an inferior thing, and only regarding the body and matter—ought to yield to the Harmonies, as much as was necessary for them to stand correctly and to adorn the motions of the globes.*

# THE HARMONIES OF THE WORLD, BOOK V.

<margin>CHAPTER IX.</margin>
...two-fold. For Harmony is a certain ratio of unity: they are therefore more united if all of them together conspire into one harmony, than if each pair separately conspires into two individual harmonies. Therefore, in the conflict between both, one of the two singular harmonies from the pairs of planets had to give way, so that the universal harmonies of all could stand. Moreover, the *Major* harmonies—those of the diverging motions <note>the motions of two planets when they are furthest apart from each other's orbits</note>—had to give way rather than the *Minor* harmonies of the converging motions <note>when the planets are at the points in their orbits closest to one another</note>. For if they diverge, they look not toward the proposed pair, but toward other neighbors; but if they converge, the motions of each planet turn toward the motion of the other, interchangeably. 

For example, in the pair of *Jupiter* and *Mars*, Jupiter's aphelion <term>the point furthest from the sun</term> turns toward *Saturn*, and Mars' perihelion <term>the point closest to the sun</term> turns toward the *Earth*; but Jupiter's perihelion turns toward *Mars*, and Mars' aphelion turns toward *Jupiter*. Therefore, the Harmony of these latter motions is more properly belonging to *Jupiter* and *Mars*; whereas the Harmony of the former, diverging motions, is in some way more foreign to *Jupiter* and *Mars*. The principle of unity, which binds pairs of neighbors together, was less harmed if the harmony that was more "foreign" and remote from them was adjusted <note>Kepler uses the word "fermentaretur," suggesting a tempering or blending</note>, than if the harmony "proper" to them—that is, the one between the motions of neighboring planets when they are closest—was altered. 

Yet this "fermentation" was not very great. For a ratio was found by which both the universal harmonies of all the planets could stand (and those of two distinct types), even with a certain latitude of tension that would at least equal a *Comma* <term>a very small musical interval, the difference between two nearly identical notes</term>; and the two singular harmonies of each neighboring pair were also preserved. Indeed, those of the *Converging* motions in four pairs are perfect; those of the aphelia in one pair and the perihelia in two are likewise perfect. Those of the *diverging* motions in four pairs differ by less than one *Diesis* <term>an extremely small interval, smaller than a semitone</term>—an interval so small that the human voice almost constantly errs by that much in figured song. In the single case of *Jupiter* and *Mars*, the difference is between a *Diesis* and a *Semitone*. It is apparent, therefore, that this mutual yielding is in every respect very good.

Thus far, let us have *concluded our song* <note>original Greek: ἐπιπεφωνήσθω (epipephōnēsthō), a formal concluding shout or musical coda</note> concerning the work of God the Creator. It remains now that, at long last, having lifted my eyes and hands from the table of demonstrations and raised them to heaven, I pray to the Father of Lights with devotion and supplication:

> O You who, through the light of Nature, promote in us a desire for the light of Grace, so that through it You may lead us into the light of Glory; I give thanks to You, Lord Creator, because You have delighted me in Your creation, and I have exulted in the works of Your hands. Behold, I have now finished the work of my profession, using as much strength of intellect as You have given me. I have manifested the glory of Your works to the men who will read these demonstrations, as much as the narrowness of my mind could grasp of Your infinity. My mind was ready for the most accurate philosophizing. If anything unworthy of Your counsels has been brought forth by me—a little worm <note>Kepler uses "vermiculo" to express human insignificance compared to the divine</note> born and nourished in a wallow of sins—which You wish men to know, inspire me also to amend it. If I have been led into rashness by the wonderful beauty of Your works, or if I have loved my own glory among men while proceeding in a work intended for Your glory, be mild and merciful and forgive me. Finally, deign to graciously bring it to pass that these demonstrations may serve Your glory and the salvation of souls, and in no way stand in their way.

# CHAPTER X.

## A conjectural epilogue regarding the Sun.

From the celestial music to the listener; from the Muses to the Master of the Choir, Apollo; from the six orbiting planets making harmonies, to the Sun, immobile in its place at the center of all their circuits, yet revolving upon itself. 

For there exists a most perfect Harmony between the extreme motions of the planets—not in terms of their true speeds through the ethereal air, but in terms of the angles formed by the ends of their daily arcs along their orbits, as seen from the center of the Sun. Since harmony does not decorate the parts by themselves, but only insofar as they are joined and compared to become the object of some Mind; and since no object is arranged in vain without something existing to be moved by it; and since these angles seem to presuppose some action similar to our sight, or certainly to that sensation by which (in Book IV) <note>Kepler refers to his earlier volume where he argued that the "soul" of the Earth senses the aspects or angles of the planets to regulate the weather</note> sublunary Nature <term>the realm of the Earth and its atmosphere</term> perceived the angles of the rays from the planets formed on the Earth: indeed, what kind of sight is in the Sun, what "eyes" there may be, or what other instinct there is for perceiving these angles even without eyes, and for weighing the Harmonies of the motions—which enter the vestibule of the mind through whatever gate—and finally, what that Mind in the Sun might be, is not easy for us inhabitants of Earth to conjecture. 

However these things may be, certainly that arrangement of the six primary orbits around the Sun, honoring him with perpetual revolutions and as if adoring him (just as four moons circle the globe of Jupiter, two circle Saturn, and a single Moon circles, honors, cherishes, and serves our Earth and us its inhabitants); and this special Harmonic business now added to that consideration, provide a most evident trace of the highest providence regarding Solar matters, and wring this confession from me: Not only does Light go out from the Sun into the whole World, as from a hearth or the "Eye of the World"; and life and heat as from a heart; and all motion as from a king and mover; but in turn, there is also gathered into the Sun from every province of the World, by royal right, these "revenues" as it were of most desirable Harmony. Nay, these flowing species of paired motions are bound together into one Harmony by the work of some mind, and are stamped like coins from raw silver and gold. 

Finally, in the Sun is the COURT, the Palace, and the Headquarters or Royal Residence of the whole kingdom of Nature; whatever Chancellors, Palatines, or Prefects the Creator has given it; for whomever He prepared those seats, whether created immediately from the beginning or to be transferred here one day. For even this earthly adornment was for a very long time lacking observers and users for whom it was intended, and the seats were vacant. Thus the thought enters the mind: what did the ancient Pythagoreans <note>Followers of Pythagoras, who believed numbers and ratios were the foundation of the universe</note> mentioned in Aristotle mean, when they used to call the center of the World (where they placed Fire, but understood it as the Sun) the WATCH-TOWER OF ZEUS <note>original Greek: ΔΙΟ'Σ ΦΥΛΑΚΗ'Ν</note>; and what did the ancient interpreter have in mind when he [verse]...

[...] rendering the Psalm thus: **HE HAS SET HIS TABERNACLE IN THE SUN**. <note>Kepler is likely referring to a specific translation of Psalm 19:4, which in the Vulgate reads "In sole posuit tabernaculum suum."</note> But I also recently came across a Hymn by Proclus, the Platonic philosopher, written to the Sun and filled with venerable mysteries—provided you take away that one word <term>κλῦθι</term> <gloss>Hear [me]</gloss>. Although even this was excused to some extent by the ancient interpreter already cited: namely, that he, in invoking the Sun, understood it to be the One who "placed his tabernacle in the Sun." For Proclus lived at a time when it was a crime to profess Jesus of Nazareth, our Savior, as God, and to despise the gods of the pagan poets—a crime punished with every kind of torture by the Monarchs of the world and the common people themselves. Proclus, therefore, who had seen the Son of God from afar, even through his Platonic philosophy and the natural light of his mind—that true light which illuminates every man coming into this world—and who already knew that divinity was by no means to be sought in sensible things alongside the superstitious commoners; yet he preferred to appear to seek God in the Sun rather than in the sensible man Christ. He did this both to deceive the pagans by honoring the Titan <note>A poetic name for the Sun.</note> of the poets in words alone, and at the same time to serve his own philosophy, intending to draw both pagans and Christians away from sensible things: the former from the visible Sun, and the latter from the Son of Mary. Because he rejected the Mystery of the Incarnation, trusting too much in the natural light of the Mind, he finally adopted into his own philosophy what the Christians held to be most divine and most consistent with Platonic Philosophy, having taken it from them.

<margin>
The judgment of the ancients concerning his book **On Motherhood** [*Metroakon*] was this: that in it the entire doctrine concerning God was explained not without divine rapture; and since frequent tears were seen from the author because of it, all suspicion [of insincerity] was removed. Yet the same man wrote 18 Arguments [*Epichiremata*] against the Christians, which John Philoponus <note>A 6th-century Christian philosopher and scientist.</note> opposed, reproaching him for his ignorance of Greek affairs, which he had nevertheless undertaken to defend. Clearly, Proclus had disguised those things which did not suit his philosophy.
</margin>

Therefore, let the Gospel doctrine concerning Christ take legal action for its own property against this Hymn of Proclus: let that Titan keep his own things—his <term>χρυσήνια & ταμιεῖον φάος</term> <gloss>golden reins and storehouse of light</gloss>, his <term>μέσσατινάς θ᾽ αἰθέρος ἕδρας</term> <gloss>and the middle seats of the ether</gloss>, and his <term>κόσμε κραδιαῖον ἐριφεγγέα κύκλον</term> <gloss>the heart-like, very bright circle of the world</gloss>, a beauty which even Copernicus grants to him. Let him also have his <term>παλιννόσεις διφρείας</term> <gloss>returning chariot-drives</gloss>, although he does not possess those through the ancient Pythagoreans, but holds in their place <term>τὸ κέντρον, Διὸς φυλακὴν</term> <gloss>the center, the guard-tower of Zeus</gloss> (a dogma of theirs which Proclus, as a successor, did not recognize, it being deformed by the flood of forgotten centuries). Let him also have the <term>γενέθλην ἐκ σε βλαστήσασαν</term> <gloss>generation that has sprouted from you</gloss>, and whatever else is natural. In turn, let the philosophy of Proclus yield to Christian dogmas; let the sensible Sun yield to the Son of Mary. That Son of God, whom Proclus addresses under the name of Titan, is the one <term>ζωαρκέος, ὦ ἄna, πηγῆς αὐτὸς ἔχων κληῖda</term> <gloss>O King, who yourself holds the key to the life-sustaining spring</gloss>; and it is He who <term>πάντα τεῆς ἔπλησας ἐγερσινόοιο προνοίης</term> <gloss>has filled all things with your mind-awakening providence</gloss>. To Him belongs that immense power <term>μοιρεάων</term> <gloss>over the Fates</gloss>, and those things which were read in no philosophy before the promulgation of the Gospel: the Demons fearing his threatening lash, the demons lying in wait for souls, <term>ὄφρα ὑψιτενές λάθοιντο πατρὸς περιφεγγέος αὐλῆς</term> <gloss>lest they escape the high-reaching, all-shining hall of the Father</gloss>. And who is that, if not the Word of the Father, the <term>εἰκὼν παγγενέταο θεοῦ, οὗ φανέντος ἀπ᾽ ἀῤῥήτου γενετῆρος παύσατο στοιχείων ὀρυμαγδὸς ἐπ᾽ ἀλλήλοισιν ἰόντων</term> <gloss>image of the all-begetting God, at whose appearance from the ineffable Begetter, the tumult of the elements rushing upon one another ceased</gloss>?

"channels from on high the rich stream of harmony," <note>original: "Ὑψοθεν ἁρμονίης ῥύμα πλούσιον ἐξοχετεύει"</note> the same from whose lineage Phoebus <note>A name for Apollo or the Sun.</note> is descended, who "singing divine things with the lyre, stills the great wave of heavy-roaring birth," <note>original: "κιθάρῃ ὑποθέσκελα μέλπων / Εὐνάζει μέγα κῦμα βαρυφλοίσβοιο γενέθλης"</note> and whose choir-mate is Paean, <note>A title for Apollo as healer.</note> "filling the wide world with all-healing harmony." <note>original: "Πλήσας ἁρμονίης παναπήμονος εὐρέα κόσμον"</note> I say he greets this same Sun in the very first verse of the Hymn as King, the bond of intellectual fire. <note>original: "Πυρὸς νοεροῦ δεσμὸν βασιλέα"</note> With this opening, he indicates at the same time what the Pythagoreans understood by the name "Fire" (so that it is a marvel that the disciple [Proclus] should disagree with his masters regarding the Center of the world, which they gave to the Sun itself); at the same time, he transfers the whole Hymn from the body of the Sun and its sensible quality of light to intellectual things. And he assigned a royal seat in the body of the Sun to that "Intellectual Fire" of his (perhaps the "artisan fire" of the Stoics), to that "created God" of his Plato, the "leading Mind" or the Self-governing; <note>original: "Αὐτόνῳ"</note> thus confusing into one the Creature and He through whom all things were created.

But we Christians, taught to distinguish better, know that the eternal and uncreated <term>Lógon</term> <note>The "Word" or "Reason" of God (the Second Person of the Trinity).</note> who was "with God," and who is contained by no dwelling place—although He is within all things and excluded by none, although He is Himself outside all things—we know that He took on flesh from the womb of the most glorious Virgin Mary into the unity of His Person. And when the ministry of the flesh was completed, He occupied the royal seat of the heavens, in which the heavenly Father is also acknowledged to dwell in a manner more excellent than in other parts of the world—namely, through glory and majesty. We also know He promised that in that house of His Father there are many mansions for His faithful. For the rest, we consider it superfluous to inquire too curiously into that seat, or to summon our senses or natural reason to track down that which *eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the heart of man.* We rightly subject the created mind, of whatever excellence it may be, to its Creator. We do not introduce <term>Deos Intelligentias</term> <note>literally "Intelligence-gods"; refers to the Aristotelian idea that each celestial sphere is moved by a conscious spiritual being or "Intelligence."</note> like Aristotle and the pagan philosophers, nor do we introduce the innumerable armies of planetary spirits with the Magi, to be worshiped or...

<summary>Kepler compares the Neoplatonic hymn to the Sun by Proclus with Christian theology, arguing that while the ancients glimpsed the "Intellectual Fire" and "Harmony" of the cosmos, they wrongly confused the physical Sun (a creature) with the eternal Word or Logos (the Creator).</summary>

# BOOK V OF THE HARMONICS #

<margin>CHAPTER X.</margin>
<margin>See Chapter 24 of my book *On the New Star* regarding the World-Soul and some of its functions. <note>original: "de stella nova"; Kepler refers to his 1606 work on the supernova of 1604.</note></margin>
<margin>Sunspots testify to this, as demonstrated in the commentaries *On the Motion of Mars*. <note>original: "comentarijs de motu Martis," referring to his *Astronomia Nova* (1609).</note></margin>
<margin>See folio 117 of Book IV.</margin>
<margin>See Chapter 9 of the *Optical Part of Astronomy*. <note>original: "Opticam Astronomiæ partem," referring to his 1604 work *Ad Vitellionem Paralipomena*.</note></margin>
...or by theurgic superstitions <note>Theurgy: rituals used to communicate with or invoke gods/spirits.</note> to be summoned for mutual commerce; rather, we carefully avoid this, inquiring freely by natural reasons into what kind of Mind each may be—especially if there is one in the heart of the World which, acting as the World-Soul, is more closely bound to the Nature of things (or if indeed any intelligent creatures, of a different Nature than Human, perhaps inhabit or will inhabit a globe thus animated). For if it is permitted to permeate the labyrinths of the mysteries of Nature by leading with the thread of analogy, one might, I think, argue not ineptly as follows: that the same relationship that exists between the six orbits and their common center—and thus the center of the whole world—is the same as the relationship of **discursive thought** to the **intellect** <note>original: "τῆς διανοίας ad τὸν νοῦν" (tēs dianoias ad ton noun); dianoia refers to step-by-step logical reasoning, while nous refers to direct, intuitive understanding.</note>, as these faculties are distinguished by Aristotle, Plato, Proclus, and the rest. And again, the same relationship that exists between the local revolutions of the individual Planets around the Sun and the **unchangeable** <note>original: "ἀμεταθέτον" (ametathetōn)</note> rotation of the Sun in the central space of the entire system is the same as the relationship of the **discursive power** to the **intellectual** <note>original: "διανοητικῆς ad τὸ νοερόν" (dianoētikēs ad to noeron)</note>—the relationship of the multiple journeys of reasoning to the simplest mental understanding. For just as the Sun, rotated within itself, moves all the Planets by means of the *species* <note>term: species — Kepler used this term to describe an immaterial force or power (like light or magnetism) emitted from a celestial body to influence others.</note> emitted from itself, so also the mind—as philosophers teach—understanding itself and all things within itself, stimulates reasonings; and by leading out and unfolding its own simplicity into them, it causes all things to be understood. Indeed, the motions of the Planets around the sun in their center and the journeys of reasonings are so connected and bound together that, unless the Earth, our dwelling place, measured out an annual circle in the middle of the other orbits, changing from place to place and station to station, human reasoning would never have struggled toward the truest intervals of the Planets and the other things depending on them, and would never have established Astronomy. Conversely, the simplicity of understanding follows the rest of the Sun in the center of the world in a beautiful correspondence; for thus far it has always been maintained by us that those solar Harmonies of motions are defined neither by the diversity of regions nor by the magnitude of the spaces of the World. Doubtless, if any mind looks out from the Sun upon these Harmonies, it lacks the aids of motion and of the diverse stations of its seat, from which it might weave the reasonings and journeys necessary for measuring the intervals of the planets. Therefore, it compares the daily motions of each Planet, not as they are in their own orbits, but as they glide by through angles at the center of the Sun. Thus, if it has knowledge of the size of the spheres, it must be present within it *a priori* <note>a priori: knowledge that exists independently of sensory experience or observation.</note>, without the labor of reasonings—which was shown above from Plato and Proclus to be true to some extent both of human minds and of sublunary nature.

<margin>Let me be permitted to imitate Plato’s *Atlantis* through storytelling and Cicero’s *Scipio* through dreaming.</margin>
Since these things are so: it would not be wonderful if someone, having taken a more liberal draft and grown warm from this "mixing bowl of Pythagoras" <note>original: "Pythagoræ cratere"; a reference to the vessel in which the Creator mixed the soul of the world in Platonic tradition.</note> which Proclus offers in the very first verse of his Hymn, and having been lulled to sleep by the sweetest Harmony of the choir of Planets, should begin to dream: that through the remaining globes succeeding from place to place around the Sun, the discursive or Reasoning faculties are scattered—of which that one must be considered the most excellent and complete which is in the middle of those globes, namely the human faculty on Earth—but that in the Sun dwells the simple Intellect, the **intellectual fire** <note>original: "πῦρ νοερόν" (pyr noeron)</note> or **Mind** <note>original: "Νοῦν" (Noun)</note>, the source of all Harmony, whoever he may be.

# ON THE MOTIONS OF THE PLANETS #

<margin>CHAPTER X.</margin>
For if even **Tycho Brahe** <note>Tycho Brahe (1546–1601) was the preeminent observational astronomer whose data Kepler used to derive his laws of planetary motion.</note> believed, regarding the sheer vastness of those celestial globes, that they were not merely empty wastes in the world but were filled with inhabitants, how much more likely is it that we shall form a conjecture about the other globes based on the variety of God’s works and plans which we perceive on this globe of **Earth**? For He who created species to inhabit the waters (even though there is no place for air there for living things to breathe); He who sent birds supported by wings into the vastness of the air; He who gave white bears and white foxes to the snowy regions of the North, providing whales as food for the former and bird eggs for the latter; He who gave lions to the deserts of burning Libya and camels to the wide plains of Syria—granting them endurance against hunger and thirst—would He then have exhausted all His art on the globe of **Earth** so that He could not, or all His goodness so that He would not, adorn the other globes with suitable creatures? Such variety is suggested by the long or short durations of their revolutions, their proximity to or distance from the **Sun**, the variation of their eccentricities, the brightness or darkness of their bodies, or the properties of the geometric figures upon which each region is supported. For behold: just as the generations of living things on this globe of **Earth** carry the image of the male in the Dodecahedron and the female in the Icosahedron <note>In Kepler’s "Mysterium Cosmographicum," he associated the five Platonic solids with the planetary spheres; here he links the 12-sided Dodecahedron and 20-sided Icosahedron to biological principles.</note> (the former of which supports the orbit of **Earth** from the outside, the latter from the inside), and finally possess the image of generation in the divine proportion and ineffability of that union: what shall we suppose the other globes have received from the remaining figures? For what good would four **Moons** <note>The four Galilean moons of Jupiter, discovered in 1610.</note> circle **Jupiter**, and two circle **Saturn**, as our own single **Moon** circles this dwelling of ours? In the very same way, we shall reason about the globe of the **Sun**, and we shall give body, as it were, to our conjectures drawn from the **Harmonies** and other sources—which are weightiest in their own right—by adding other conjectures that lean more toward physical bodies and are better suited to the understanding of the common people. Is that globe empty while the others are full, if all other things correspond so closely? If, just as **Earth** exhales clouds, the **Sun** breathes out black soot? <note>original: "fuligines"; Kepler is referring to sunspots, which he interpreted as smoky emissions from the solar surface.</note> If, just as the Earth is moistened and turns green with rains, the **Sun** shines with those scorched spots of his, while brighter little flames break out upon his body, which is entirely fiery? For what use is this apparatus if the globe is empty? Do not our very senses cry out that fiery bodies dwell here, capable of harboring simple Minds, and that the **Sun** is truly the Palace—if not the King—of <term>intellectual fire</term>? <note>original: "πυρὸς νοεροῦ" (pyros noerou); a Neoplatonic term referring to a divine, thinking fire that governs the cosmos.</note>

I deliberately break off both this dream and this most vast speculation, crying out only this with the **Psalmist King**: <note>Referring to King David, the traditional author of the Psalms.</note>

> Great is our Lord, and great is his power, and of his Wisdom there is no number; praise him, heavens; praise him, Sun, Moon, and Planets, with whatever sense you use to perceive, and whatever tongue to speak of your Creator. Praise him, celestial Harmonies; praise him, you judges of the Harmonies now discovered. And you, my soul, praise the Lord your Creator as long as I shall live: for from him, and through him, and in him are all things, <note>original: "καὶ τὰ αἰσθητὰ , καὶ τὰ νοερά" (kai ta aisthēta, kai ta noera)</note> both those things perceived by the senses and those things understood by the mind; those things of which we are entirely ignorant as well as those things we know, which are the smallest part of them; because there is still more beyond. To him be praise, honor, and glory forever and ever. **AMEN**.

<margin>
And you,
above all,
Maestlin, <note>Michael Maestlin (1550–1631) was Kepler's university professor who introduced him to Copernicanism.</note>
in your happy

# APPENDIX
## TO BOOK V OF THE HARMONICS.

The Appendix which I promised earlier in the Table of Contents for Book V: you should not expect that here, reader. As the saying goes: *The wine jar was begun*—

->I started it, but as the potter’s wheel turns, a mere pitcher comes out.<- <note>original: "Amphora caepit / Institui, currente rotâ verùm urceus exit." A quote from Horace's *Ars Poetica*, used here by Kepler to explain that his grand project had to be scaled back.</note>

I will state the reasons briefly: I was about to navigate a great and overflowing river, when suddenly, as the volume of water subsided into a thin stream, a ford appeared that I could cross on foot, leaving the ship at its mooring for more necessary uses. This is what I mean: the three books of **Ptolemy’s** *Harmonics* <note>Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 AD), a Greco-Roman astronomer and mathematician whose work on music theory Kepler is comparing to his own.</note>—which I possess in Greek manuscripts along with the commentaries of the most profound philosopher **Porphyry** <note>Porphyry (c. 234–305 AD), a Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote an extensive commentary on Ptolemy’s work.</note>, likewise in Greek, from the beginning up to Book II, Chapter VII—always seemed worthy to me to be published in their entirety in a Greek-Latin edition. For that reason, ten years ago, I began to translate them into the Latin language; that translation proceeded as far as the middle of Porphyry's manuscript. What prevented me from going further was a change of location <note>Kepler moved from Prague to Linz in 1612 following the death of Emperor Rudolf II.</note>, joined with many troubles, and after I came to **Linz**, a new beginning of astronomical studies.

But truly, when a year ago I proposed to publish my own five books of the *Harmonics*, I saw that great importance lay in a comparison of my work with that of **Ptolemy**, especially my Book V with the final chapters of **Ptolemy's** Book III—the last three of which contain nothing but "lemmas" or titles provided by **Ptolemy**. Therefore, though my spirit was reluctant, I proposed to pluck out just one part of a work that was itself mutilated, which specifically suited my subject. To this end, I translated **Ptolemy's** Book III from Chapter III to the end; and to the three final empty titles, I supplied their own texts, harmonized with skill as much as possible from the principles of Ptolemaic astronomy and the mind of the author. Finally, I added commentaries or Notes, by which the deficiency of Porphyry’s commentary (which breaks off at Book II, Chapter VII) is supplied in this third book, and **Ptolemy's** discoveries are compared with my own. In these, the distinction is shown between **Ptolemy’s** *symbolisms* and my own *legitimate demonstrations*; from which the weakness and imperfection of those symbolisms, and the primary cause of this—namely, the falsehood of the principles of Ptolemaic astronomy—is made clear.

However, since this appendix alone would have occupied thirty pages of the book, behold: in the meantime, the neighboring **Bohemian War** <note>The Bohemian Revolt (1618), the opening phase of the Thirty Years' War, which caused significant disruption to trade and scholarly work across Europe.</note> broke out, by which roads were blocked and many workers were called to military service. Thus, first the paper, and then the labor of the printing press failed us; finally, time was dragged out by the most tedious delays. Driven by these obstacles, I finally looked back at myself and cut short my plan; I would not publish a mutilated portion of the work of that excellent author **Ptolemy** and his commentator **Porphyry**, lest I almost expose them to ridicule or diminish them. Why not rather spend the remaining half of the labor on finishing the translation of Porphyry’s exposition, write the Notes on the remaining chapters of Books II and III, and join them with those I have already written for almost all of Book III? In this way, the work would be made whole and published as a Greek-Latin edition in the parts where it survives. FOR such an edition, another time, another place, and a suitable printer are required.

Lest the reader should find anything entirely missing from what I promised above, or lest anything be lacking in this final part for the integrity or easier understanding of my work on Harmonics: come now, I shall transcribe the titles of the chapters of **Ptolemy’s** Book III, and I will compare them with their respective places in my own work, and I will write down in a summary fashion what is contained in my Notes.

First, those things which **Ptolemy** handed down in Books I, II, and the beginning of the third regarding the discipline of Harmonics, I have encompassed in my Book III by another method, quite different. While **Ptolemy** seeks the principles of Harmonies from abstract numbers, along with the ancients: I, on the contrary, denying that power resides in numbers as they are used for counting, substitute for those num—

<meta>This page continues Kepler’s comparison between his own work, "The Harmonies of the World," and the ancient "Harmonics" of Claudius Ptolemy. Kepler explains his structural choices and critiques Ptolemy’s more symbolic or "poetic" associations between music and the human soul.</meta>

...counted numbers, <note>original: "numeros numeratos." In Renaissance philosophy, this refers to concrete numbers applied to real objects, as opposed to abstract, mathematical numbers.</note> *that is*, the things themselves subjected to those numbers, namely regular plane figures and the divisions of the circle to be managed by them. Since I was establishing the principles of *Harmonies*, I necessarily placed Books I and II, concerning Harmonic figures, before my third book.

Now, **Ptolemy**, in the third book, chapter 3 of his work, prescribed this title: **Under what class of things the nature or harmonic power, and the knowledge of it, should be categorized**: showing that there is some causal, formal, mental, and therefore divine principle which unites *Harmonies* to things. Chapter 4: **That the power of harmonic tempering is innate in all things whose natures exist at a higher level of perfection; and that this is most apparent in human Souls and in the revolutions of the heavens.** Here you see the division of what remained for **Ptolemy** to discuss: first, *concerning the Harmonies existing in Souls*, and second, *concerning the Harmonies in the movements of the heavens*. Regarding the first part, three chapters follow; regarding the second, the remaining nine chapters. Chapter 5: *He compares individual consonances with the individual faculties of the rational Soul, and does so concisely, through subdivisions of both things being compared.* Chapter 6: *He compares the individual types of Harmonies with the individual types or classes of virtues.* Chapter 7: *He compares the changes of musical Tones with the changes in public interests across different times, and thus also with the sudden changes of emotions in the Soul.*

In this section, I dispute many things against **Ptolemy**; specifically, that those symbolisms are for the most part not necessary, nor causal, nor natural, but rather poetic and oratorical. For those specific faculties and virtues that exist in souls do not receive their "Idea" <note>Kepler uses "Idea" in the Platonic sense: the eternal, perfect pattern after which things are modeled.</note> or the numbers of their constitution from *Harmonies* as if from an Archetype; rather, they have other admitted or evident causes. Indeed, they do not even correspond to the number, but a likeness of equal-multiplied division is forced upon them with far-fetched or poorly-aimed effort. Many excesses, or conversely, many defects, are disguised; certain points that do not work well are "dragged by the hair." <note>A Latin idiom, *crinibus trahi*, meaning something is forced or unnatural.</note> Finally, those things which most aptly and skillfully correspond to each other are nevertheless not taken according to any proportion of quantities of the same kind; yet *Harmonies* cannot exist except in the comparison of quantities.

However, as for the fact that musical Tones are compared to emotions and public morals, I have shown that this is extremely natural and functions as a cause. On the occasion of **Ptolemy's** text, I have brought forward the opinions of various philosophers regarding the kinship between Souls, Numbers, and harmonies, to which I have also joined the Epilogue of my Book V. Regarding specifically the effects of tones in moving the soul in various ways: I have embraced that material in a special chapter (Chapter 15) of my Book III. Similarly, regarding Commutative and Distributive Justice, <note>Commutative justice concerns fair exchange in private dealings; distributive justice concerns the fair allocation of resources by a state.</note> as well as Friendship, Economics, and Politics: regarding this material, and to what extent the proportions of Music are valid within them, I made a Digression at the end of my Book III. Finally, the material of the aforementioned chapters 3 and 4, and what could be said in general about chapters 5, 6, and 7, I have encompassed in the first three chapters and again in the seventh chapter of my Book IV. There, having explained the nature of Souls, I showed that since a circle is geometrically cut by the inscription of plane figures, it defines true and proper Harmonic proportions by the comparison of the parts with the whole. Therefore, a circle exists in souls by some essential reason—formally and abstractly, not only from matter, but also in a way from quantity itself, considered materially. For this reason, since the circle is in the soul, Harmonies are also there, and this is the reason why Souls are moved by Harmonies. But all these things are only in a general sense; no causation follows regarding the distribution of the Soul into specific faculties. This, then, is how the matter stands with human Souls.

As for celestial motions, **Ptolemy**, in chapter 8 of his third book, compares the Zodiac with the system or scale of Music; in chapter 9, he compares the consonances themselves with the Aspects <note><term>Aspects</term>: In astrology and astronomy, the specific angular distances between planets (like 90 or 180 degrees) that were believed to create harmonic or discordant influences.</note>

# APPENDIX

*...of the Planets. Here I have shown in which parts the doctrine concerning Aspects <note>In astrology, "aspects" are the angles between planets, such as a square or a trine, which were thought to have musical qualities.</note> in Ptolemy is lacking, and how, through the integration of numbers—from there of the Aspects, and from here of the Consonances— the natural and causal connection of these things finally appears. This is indeed the genuine material of my Book IV, especially chapters IV, V, and VI.*

*In Chapter X, Ptolemy creates a kind of melody from the movement of a Planet from east to west; in Chapter XI, from the movement of the Planets in height and depth <note>original: "in altum & profundum." This refers to the planet's varying distance from the Earth in the ancient geocentric model.</note>, he creates types of song. In Chapter XII, from the movement across the sides of the equator, he creates a diversity of musical Tones. In Chapter XIII, from the various configurations of the planets with the Sun, he creates the various tetrachords <note>A series of four notes, the building block of ancient Greek musical scales.</note> of the system. In these four chapters, I have shown that Ptolemy indulges in a poetic or oratorical exercise of comparison: since those things which he compares are not real in the heavens, except for a small part of chapter XI, which I wish to be set aside for the last three chapters because of the kinship of the subject matter. I have also shown that here, in part, incomparable things are being compared, against the very nature of the things compared; and in part, those things which correspond in all members do so only accidentally, not truly cohering out of the necessity of any cause. Thus far, therefore, there is nothing or very little that agrees with my celestial Harmonies.*

*But indeed, the following Chapter XIV of Ptolemy proposes to inquire according to which prime numbers <note>original: "numeros primos." In this context, Kepler refers to the fundamental numerical ratios used to divide a string to produce musical intervals.</note> the sounds of the system or musical scale can be compared with the primary spheres in the planetary system. Here I have shown that comparison was impossible for Ptolemy and the Pythagoreans in their usual Astronomy, although I have attempted to devise something consistent with Ptolemaic principles, so that his own context might be supported by a bare title. I have also shown that since the primary spheres consist of their own quantities, no less than strings by their lengths, the comparison ought to have been established according to quantities: since the proportion of the spheres nevertheless shrinks away significantly from the proportion of the consonant strings. Truly, the corrected and causal or Archetypal <note>For Kepler, the "Archetype" was the geometric blueprint used by God to create the universe.</note> connection of the spheres of the World with the regular bodies, I have repeated from the beginning of my Book V, from my Mysterium Cosmographicum <note>Kepler's first book (1596), which proposed that the orbits of the planets are nested within the five Platonic solids.</note>.*

*Chapter XV of Ptolemy asks how the proportions of proper motions can be taken through numbers; but the text is missing. I have therefore shown the same things as in the preceding chapter. For the rest, I have given this for consideration: that here, 1,500 years ago, Ptolemy set out to treat the specific material of my Book V, if he had been able to do so through his astronomy. I therefore, in corrected Astronomy—which retains the true and simple motions of the planets, having eliminated the appearances that consist of ocular deceptions—have shown that in the heavens, according to true and genuine quantitative and measurable reason, and not through a mere superficial symbolism, there exist all the harmonic proportions, the types of harmonies, the musical system or scale and most of its keys, the varieties of tones, the planets as rivals of voices in figured music <note>Polyphonic music, where different voices move independently.</note>, and finally the universal counterpoints of the six primary planets, varied in both types and tones. In Chapter XVI and the last, Ptolemy promises that he wishes to investigate by what reasoning the affinities of the Wanderers <note>original: "Erronum," a common term for planets.</note> can be compared with the affinities of sounds: that is, he busied himself with demonstrating astrological principles—concerning beneficial and harmful planets, or those friendly or hostile to one another—through celestial Harmonies. And because the text for this chapter is also missing, I have arranged it as best I could, especially from Macrobius <note>A 5th-century philosopher whose commentary on "The Dream of Scipio" preserved much ancient Greek musical and cosmological thought.</note>; but at the same time I have shown in the notes what is lacking in this business, so that it might succeed less according to ancient astronomy. In my own work, however, I have no part corresponding to Chapter XVI, except for a few things from the Epilogue of Book V. For astrology deals with the effects of the stars on the earth, but my celestial Harmonies are not formed through rays on the earth, but in the Sun. And this is the end of Ptolemy’s work: with which I would also finish the summary of the Appendix promised in the entrance of Book V, were it not that the affinity of things invited me to satisfy also those who have contended with me, such as Dr. Robert Fludd <note>original: "D. Roberti de Fluctibus." Robert Fludd (1574–1637) was an English occultist and physician who published his own theories on cosmic music, leading to a famous intellectual dispute with Kepler.</note>...*

# APPENDIX.

I should not omit mention in my Harmonic work of the Oxford Physician <note>Robert Fludd (1574–1637), an influential English Rosicrucian, physician, and mystical philosopher.</note>, who filled a book published a year ago concerning the *Microcosm and Macrocosm* <note>original: "Microcosmo & Macrocosmo." This refers to Fludd’s massive work "Utriusque Cosmi Historia" (History of Both Worlds).</note> with harmonic contemplations: but I should show the reader in a few words in which things there is agreement between me and him, and in which, conversely, we disagree.

<margin>
Concerning the World Music of Mr. Robert Fludd, Oxford Physician.
</margin>

*Therefore, that author promised two volumes, of which one entitled* On the Macrocosm <note>The "Macrocosm" refers to the universe at large.</note> *is already published; the other* On the Microcosm <note>The "Microcosm" refers to the human being as a reflection of the universe.</note> *is still awaited. The former volume, comprising two treatises, also came out at different times; for I saw the first treatise* On the Triple World *after the Frankfurt autumn fairs of the year 1617, and the other* On the Arts, *which he calls the* Apes <note>original: "Simias." Fludd viewed human arts and technology as "Nature's Ape," mimicking the natural processes of God.</note> *of worldly nature, at the Easter fairs of the following year, 1618. In the second treatise, therefore, he placed Music among the arts, covering the material of my third book to some extent; but in the first treatise, which is completed in seven books, he dedicated the third book to World Music, using the same title that I fixed to my whole work: he touched upon the material of my books IV and V. Therefore, let us make a beginning from his artificial music.*

*He delivers it in seven books: in the first of which he reviews the authors, the nomenclatures, and the power [of music] over human souls. Concerning authors or the history of discovery, I have said nothing, or certainly little, as my intention is to reveal the causes of natural things. I have included necessary nomenclatures throughout my definitions and omitted the superfluous ones. I deal with the power of music on souls in Book III, Chapter 15, and throughout Book IV. In the second [book], the author approaches the things themselves, which he calls Intervals and Tempos. Again, I have said almost nothing about Tempos or the length or shortness of sounds; for they are arbitrary and do not require an inquiry into causes. Some intervals he calls "simple," which to me are the smallest discordant intervals <note>Kepler calls these "concinnous" intervals—those that fit well in a scale but aren't pure consonances themselves.</note>: the major tone, minor [tone], semitone, and diesis. Others he wants to be composed of these, which I call Consonances. But I expressly refuted this opinion of the ancients—that consonances are composed of smaller intervals as if they were prior in nature—in Chapter 4 of my Book III, having shown that, on the contrary, the smaller ones arise from the larger consonances themselves.*

*In the third book he explains the system or musical scale, which is the principal part of my Book III, from Chapter 4 to 9. The remaining four books of the author contain practice, which I do not even touch upon. For in the fourth, he teaches about the measure of the beat <term>tactus: the steady pulse or downbeat used to keep time in Renaissance music</term> and its various modes, and the value of notes through them, about which I said very little in Book III, Ch. 15 and Book IV, Ch. 3. In the fifth, he has the rules for composing figured song <note>original: "cantus figurati," referring to complex polyphonic or ornamented music as opposed to simple plainchant.</note>, a craft which I do not profess. In the sixth, he even wanders off into various musical instruments, about which I have not even thought. Finally, in the seventh, he reveals a new instrument of his own. In these last four, therefore, he differs from me as a practitioner from a theorist: for instead of describing instruments, I investigate the causes of things or consonances; and instead of teaching how to compose melodies for many voices, I arrange mathematical demonstrations for most of those things that are naturally present in both choral <note>Plainchant or simple unison singing.</note> and figured song. Furthermore, in his work there are very many pictures; in mine, mathematical diagrams labeled with letters. You may see that he delights very much in the dark enigmas of things, while I strive to bring into the light of the intellect things that are wrapped in obscurity. The former is indeed familiar to the Chemists, Hermeticists, and Paracelsians <note>Followers of Paracelsus, who combined medicine with alchemy and occultism.</note>; the latter is characteristic of Mathematicians.*

*And so, even in Books II and III, where he treats the same material as I do, there is this difference between us: that what he borrows from the ancients, I dig out from the things of Nature and establish from their very foundations; he [presents] what he has received [in] a confused [way] (because of...*

<header>APPENDIX</header>
<sig>ÿ 3</sig>

# APPENDIX

*...he adopts the varying opinions of those who have handed down traditions, even using incorrect ones; I proceed in a natural order, so that all things are corrected according to the laws of Nature, and confusion is avoided; thus, I do not even apply my findings to the decrees of the ancients except where no confusion follows. So, where I expressly refute the ancients when they differ on the causes of harmonies, he follows the ancients without a moment’s hesitation; he does not even think of the truer causes. In a single word: in the discipline of Harmony <term>Harmonica: the study of mathematical proportions in music and the cosmos</term>, one acts as a performer of vocal and instrumental music; the other as a philosopher and mathematician.*

*Now let us pass to the author’s second point, where he introduces Music into the World. Here, indeed, there is a vast difference between us. First, those harmonies he intends to teach are mere Symbolisms, about which I say the same as I did regarding the symbolisms of Ptolemy: they are poetic or rhetorical rather than philosophical or mathematical. This is the very soul of that entire work, as is evident from the title,* **Macrocosm** <note>The "Great World," or the universe at large.</note> *and* **Microcosm** <note>The "Little World," or the human being, seen as a reflection of the universe.</note>. *For in the second volume, he undoubtedly intends to demonstrate that noble theme: that the Ideas of the whole great world and all its parts are found in man. This same "soul" is also in the first volume, because he distributes the whole world into three regions; where, according to that most celebrated axiom of Hermes <note>original: "Hermetis." Referring to Hermes Trismegistus and the axiom "As above, so below," common in Renaissance occultism.</note>, he makes the higher things similar or analogous to the lower. But for this analogy to succeed through all things, the comparisons on both sides must often be strained <note>original: "crinibus trahendae," literally "dragged by the hair."</note>. My own opinion on analogies is clear from the digression at the end of my Book III: namely, that although the analogy of proportions in geometric forms is something formal with respect to the quantitative matter itself (which is undefined and indeterminate), it can nevertheless be considered a material attribute with respect to harmonic proportions. Because harmonic proportions define a certain quantity, analogies, by contrast, are apt to run on into infinity, and thus they presuppose the material attribute of infinity.*

*And although I also treat some things similar to those "Macrocosmic" ideas in my work—such as in Book IV, where I make the Earth an animal—it is done for a far different reason. For I do not contend that there is a mere analogy between the Earth and animals, nor do I want the archetype of an animal to be taken from the Earth itself; rather, I simply propose to demonstrate that those works seen on the globe of the Earth cannot arise from the movements of the elements or the solitary attributes of matter, but instead testify to the presence of a Soul <note>Kepler believed in an "Anima Terrae" (Soul of the Earth) that responded to planetary aspects.</note>. Now, so that my arguments might be understood, it was necessary to cite various functions of the soul in the body of an animal. To come closer to the foundations upon which* **Robert Fludd** *builds his Worldly music: first, he occupies the whole world and all three of its parts—the* **Empyrean, Celestial, and Elemental** <note>The three traditional divisions: the fiery heaven of God, the starry heavens, and the realm of the four elements.</note>; *I occupy only the celestial, and not even all of that, but only the motions of the planets as if under the Zodiac. He, trusting in the ancients who believed the power of Harmonies came from abstract numbers, is satisfied if he can demonstrate some concordance between parts, capturing them in numbers however he can, with no care as to what kind of units are accumulated in that number. I, however, nowhere teach the seeking of Harmonies where the things between which the Harmonies exist cannot be measured by the same measure of quantity; so that, by reason of quantity, the same proportion exists between them as exists between two strings of the same tension by reason of their length. For this reason, he divides the whole World into three equal parts by the measure of the radius, knowing well enough that those parts are by no means equal; but he does so only because the first unit is the Elemental world, the second the ethereal World, and the third the Empyrean; and indeed, units cannot be depicted otherwise than by equality of lines. But I, unless astronomy testifies to the same quantitative measure of units, never use them as units for numbering...*

<summary>Kepler critiques Robert Fludd’s mystical "Macrocosm/Microcosm" theory, arguing that Fludd’s cosmic harmonies are merely symbolic and poetic. Kepler insists that true harmonic science must be based on actual astronomical measurements and physical quantities rather than abstract numerology or forced analogies.</summary>
