<meta>Kepler continues his critique of Robert Fludd, moving from general methodology to the specific geometric models Fludd uses to represent the universe. He specifically addresses Fludd's "pyramids" of light and matter.</meta>

<page-num>254</page-num>
<header>APPENDIX.</header>

## APPENDIX.

*...to find Harmonic proportions. He [Fludd], however, insisting on his own principles and raising a pyramid from its base (the great circle of the Earth), places its vertex at the very apex of the Empyrean heaven <note>original: "coeli empyrei"; the highest part of the universe in medieval thought, often associated with pure fire or the residence of the divine.</note>. Having divided its height into three equal parts (as if he truly possessed units that were equal), he counts how many parts go to the Empyrean, how many to the Celestial, and how many to the Elementary regions. By this method, the summit of the Elementary region is twice as far from the top of the Celestial as it is from the top of the Empyrean. In the division of the Pyramid, with respect to the axis, three equal units go to the three regions; but with respect to the triangle through the axis, one unit goes to the Empyrean, three to the Celestial, and five units to the Elementary <note>Kepler is correcting a likely error in Fludd’s geometric progression here: 1, 3, 5.</note>. Finally, with respect to the space or the volume of the figure, one unit goes to the Empyrean, seven to the Celestial, and nineteen units to the Elementary region. What shall I say now of the other, opposite Pyramid of Light, whose base he makes the adorable Trinity itself at the summit of the Empyrean heaven, while he places its vertex on the Earth itself?*

*Since he mixes these two Pyramids together and draws musical proportions from that mixture, he attempts something very different from the purpose of my work. For he compares Light (the giver of form and Soul) and Matter—two things most diverse from one another—in which quantities are by no means present in the same respect. I, however, for the terms of forming Harmonic proportions in the world, admit nothing except those things which receive quantities in the same respect; for example, the daily motion of Mars and the daily motion of Jupiter. Nor is there less diversity between us in this: he ascribes four degrees of obscurity and darkness to the Elementary region because, he says, any thing has four quarters, just as it has three thirds and five fifths. He claims that Earth possesses all four, Water has three (and is therefore now transparent), Air has two, and Fire has one. Elsewhere again, he subdivides every region—whether of an Element or of Heaven—into three spaces: the highest, middle, and lowest, though not always following the probability of the senses. You see, his units are again arbitrary.*

*He nevertheless proceeds because of this to establish a <term>Diatessaron: the musical interval of a perfect fourth</term> between Earth and Water. He applies its three intervals—tone, tone, and semitone—to the three spaces: the highest, middle, and lowest. Yet while those musical intervals have certain quantities for their own reasons, these spaces do not even have boundaries set by nature; their measurements, according to these most general principles, are plainly undetermined. And so it goes for the rest. But for me, natural units—namely, the two extreme motions of the planets (whether daily or hourly, it makes no difference) expressed by nature in their certain quantities—are the subjects in which I seek Harmonies. He seeks harmonic proportions in degrees of darkness and light, without respect to any motion; I seek Harmonies only in motions. He tastes a few small concords and draws them from the mixture of his Pyramids, which he carries around in his mind as a private picture of the World; I have demonstrated that the entire body of harmonic attunement, with all its parts, exists in the extreme proper motions of the planets, according to certain measurements demonstrated by Astronomy. Therefore, his own concept of the World is his subject of Harmony; for me, the subject of Worldly Harmony is the World itself, or the real motions of the planets within it.*

*From these few points, I believe it is clear: although a knowledge of harmonic proportions is entirely necessary to understand the mysteries contained in the profound philosophy Robert [Fludd] teaches, nevertheless, anyone who has learned my entire work will still be quite far from those most perplexed mysteries—just as those mysteries themselves have retreated far from the accurate certainty of mathematical demonstrations. And here now let this* APPENDIX *be at an* **END.**

<summary>Kepler concludes his critique of Robert Fludd, contrasting his own data-driven astronomical harmonies with Fludd's symbolic "pyramids" of light and matter. He argues that while Fludd's work is based on arbitrary mental constructs, his own is based on the real, observable motions of the planets.</summary>

# CORRECTIONS IN THE WORK.

**F**irst, you should know that the first two books, which were printed last, have a unique sequence of page numbers. Therefore, correct these numbers. **Book I: 41. And Book III: 50, 63, 112, 158, 161, 200, 212, 228, 229, 236, 237.** Correct the remaining errors as follows: **Book I, folio 2**, *line before the penultimate:* everywhere <note>original: "undique"</note>. **Page 17, penultimate line:** then those which <note>original: "tunc quæ"</note>.

Between folios 52 and 53, two leaves with copperplate engravings <note>original: "typis æneis"</note> are to be inserted. **Folio 66:** in the margin at corollary 29, let folio 150 be cited, and at corollary 30, folio 82 of Book III.

**Book III, folio 23, 24.** Note that corrections are to be made from folio 103 following. **Folio 25, line 17:** into parts. **Folio 29:** in the first diagram, push the Note at the digit 6 from the space down into the line below; however, fill in the deficiency from folio 86.

**Folio 33, 34, 35** The text was collected from papers written at different times, but it was not assembled quite fitly; although everything in it is true, it has nonetheless acquired some obscurity from the confusion of things that ought to be distinguished, and from the repetition of propositions. These are the distinct questions: 1. Whether <term>Consonances</term><note>Musical intervals that sound harmonious or stable to the ear.</note> have parts which are themselves also consonances, or at least <term>concordant intervals</term>? <note>Intervals that are musically pleasing but not primary harmonies.</note> *The answer is this:* In consonances, these things are distinct: first the <term>proportion</term> (a geometric matter), and then the quality of the proportion (the consonance itself). Insofar, then, as they are proportions, one is exceeded by another, a smaller by a larger, and thus one can be a part of another. But insofar as any of them has received the quality of consonance from its own demonstrable shape, no composition occurs between them. The arguments are these: 1. A species, as a species, is indivisible and one. 2. Its cause constitutes the species: but the causes of individual concords are distinct from one another; therefore, the concords themselves are distinct from one another in species, and one (as the larger) cannot be dissolved into others of its own species (as parts), though it can indeed be dissolved into smaller parts of a different species. 3. If, as a multiplied part increases quantity, so a consonant or concordant part of a consonance were to increase the consonance or concord of the whole, one would not eventually produce <term>dissonance</term> and lack of concord <note>original: "Inconcinna"</note> from the accumulation of parts.

*Question II.* Whether consonances have one common measure, such as a <term>Tone</term>, <term>Diesis</term>, <term>Comma</term>, etc.? *The answer is no:* for they do not have one as they are proportions, because in that way they are <term>incommensurable</term> <note>Lacking a common unit of measurement, like the relationship between a circle's diameter and its circumference.</note> (that is, lacking a commensurable measure); nor as they are species, because they are mutually distinct from one another by the causes from which they arose and by which they were defined. For they have, in a certain way, the nature of shapes: and indeed, a triangle and a pentagon in the same circle have side lengths that are incommensurable. Finally, a measure is indeed prior to the things measured: but concordant things, such as a Tone or Diesis, etc., are posterior to consonances. And note, those parts—the Major Tone, Minor Tone, semitone, etc.—are common to consonances: but not all are common to all, nor is there one of them which alone measures out the consonances.

**Folio 35.** In the first diagram, delete the Note after 8, and the digit 3 next to 9; instead, place another Note above 9 in the space of the 8 itself, followed by the digit 3. In the second diagram, move the digit 4 from the middle line to the penultimate line. **Folio 36, last line:** delete the small word "two" <note>original: "duæ"</note>. **Folio 41.** In the third diagram, for 66 in the middle line, write 96 in the penultimate line. **Folio 45, line 12:** Minor Tone instead of hard <note>original: "duro"</note>. In the same place, in the diagram opposite VI, express the 10 transversely. Regarding **folio 47 and 57**, see **folio 103**. **Folio 49**, write 79562. **Folio 60.** fill the deficiency from **folio 233**, and its Proposition XLIII. In the same place, line 9 from the end, read: For 3. 4. is 60, etc. **Folio 77, line 3:** the square of 3 units. **Folio 82**, in the margin let corollaries 29 and 30 of Book II and proposition 44 of Book I be cited; and immediately below, proposition 47 of the same.

**Folio 111, line 21:** for now by effort <note>original: "enim operâ jam"</note>, **line 22:** of the harmonic faculty, and **penultimate line of the page:** setting those aside. **Folio 113, line 31**, especially. **Folio 118, line 32**, most fortified. **Folio 120, line 11.** divine institutions. **Folio 127, line 33**, indeed species of motions. **Folio 134, last line:** with the diagrams, which from here. **Folio 141, penultimate line:** planets) the side first becomes known: right <note>original: "rect."</note>. **Folio 143, lines 6, 7.** are these: we previously used Prop. **Folio 153, line 24.** add these words: "unless it cannot." From the same foundation we shall also reason thus: An <term>aspect</term> <note>An astrological angle between planets.</note> is an angle measured by an arc smaller than a semicircle: the remainder is larger than a semicircle, and therefore it measures no angle, no aspect: wherefore the Remainder is not considered in the constitution of aspects. But it is considered in the constitution of a <term>harmonic section</term>. Therefore, the section of a harmonic string (which uses the Remainder) and the effective section of the Zodiac (which does not use it) do not agree with each other. And thus defeat it. **Folio 186**, let the engraving <note>original: "schema ex ære"</note> also be inserted. **Folio 193**, in the table, Saturn 10759. **Folio 195.** at the bottom of the table, for Saturn, read Mercury's Aphelion: 470. **Folio 198, in the table,** delete the repeated "daily." ->**Decorative Marbled Endpaper**<-

This page consists of a fine specimen of historical **marbled paper**, typically used as an **endpaper** in high-quality bookbinding. 

<term>marbled paper</term> <note>A decorative paper created by floating oil-based pigments on a tray of thickened water (size). The artisan "combs" the colors into patterns before laying a sheet of paper on top to lift the design. This specific pattern, with its organic, veined appearance, is characteristic of 18th-century European styles.</note>

<term>endpaper</term> <note>The leaves of paper at the very beginning or end of a book. One half is usually pasted to the inside cover (the "pastedown"), and the other half remains loose (the "flyleaf"), protecting the manuscript's text block.</note>

The pattern displayed here features a complex interaction of **teal**, **reddish-brown**, and **ochre** pigments. These colors were chosen not only for their beauty but for their ability to hide the wear and tear that occurs at the hinges of a frequently consulted volume.

<note>The presence of such decorative paper suggests that this manuscript was professionally bound, likely in the 1700s, reflecting the value placed on the scientific or historical documents contained within.</note>

<summary>This page features a well-preserved example of 18th-century hand-marbled endpaper used in the manuscript's binding, showcasing teal, ochre, and brown pigments.</summary>
